BBB permeability, ultrastructural alterations, and tight junction protein expression were evaluated in vivo by Evans Blue extravasation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Western blotting (WB), and immunofluorescence. In parallel, an in vitro BBB model using bEnd.3 cells was employed to examine the direct effects of esketamine on barrier function through measurements of transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and FITC-dextran permeability. Anesthesia and surgery induced significant early postoperative cognitive impairment in aged mice, accompanied by BBB disruption, decreased tight junction protein expression, and elevated C3 levels. Esketamine treatment alleviated cognitive deficits and attenuated BBB injury. Consistently, in vitro studies provided supportive evidence that esketamine enhanced barrier integrity in bEnd.3 cells. These protective effects were accompanied by reduced C3 and C3aR expression. Esketamine attenuated early postoperative cognitive impairment and BBB injury in aged mice, accompanied by reduced C3 expression. These findings suggest a possible contribution of C3-related processes, although the causal involvement of C3a-C3aR signaling remains to be established.

articles.title: Clinical Study of Neuroendoscopic Surgery for Stable Epidural Hematoma Treatment.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Epidural hematoma is a common and life-threatening form of traumatic brain injury, and the role of minimally invasive surgery in epidural hematoma remains controversial. This study aimed to explore the clinical efficacy and advantages of neuroendoscopic surgery in the treatment of stable EDH (sEDH).
METHODS: We retrospectively collected the clinical data of 58 patients with sEDH. According to the surgical procedure, patients were divided into the craniotomy group (n = 35) and the endoscopic group (n = 23). Perioperative indicators, postoperative complications, 3-month functional outcomes, and scar aesthetics assessed using the Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale were compared between the 2 groups.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, admission Glasgow Coma Scale score, hematoma volume, midline shift, and anatomic location, did not differ significantly between the 2 groups (P > .05). Compared with craniotomy, the endoscopic group had significantly shorter incision length, smaller bone window size, and less intraoperative blood loss (P < .001), whereas operative time, hematoma evacuation rate, overall complication rates, and 3-month functional outcomes were comparable (P > .05). At the 3-month follow-up, the endoscopic group reported a significantly higher Patient and Observer Scar Assessment Scale satisfaction score and lower appearance and sensory scores (all P < .001), indicating superior scar aesthetics and greater patient satisfaction.
CONCLUSION: Neuroendoscopic surgery is safe and effective for sEDH, achieving comparable hematoma evacuation rates and functional outcomes while significantly reducing surgical trauma and improving scar aesthetics.

articles.title: Effect of Wrist Extension Angle on Radial and Ulnar Artery Sonoanatomy in Children: A Prospective Ultrasound Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided radial artery cannulation is common in pediatrics but technically challenging. While the ulnar artery is a potential alternative, its sonoanatomy relative to the radial artery is not well defined.
AIMS: This study aimed to compare the sonoanatomic characteristics of the radial and ulnar arteries in children, evaluating how age, weight, and wrist position (0°, 30°, and 45°) influence arterial dimensions and depth to identify the most favorable profile for cannulation.
METHODS: Ultrasound evaluation of the radial and ulnar arteries was performed at 0°, 30°, and 45° wrist extension in 180 anesthetized children aged 0-120 months using custom-made wooden blocks. Arterial dimensions and skin-to-artery distance were evaluated overall and across age (≤ 24 vs. > 24 months) and weight (≤ 12 vs. > 12 kg) subgroups to identify optimal access conditions.
RESULTS: Wrist extension angle did not significantly affect anteroposterior diameter (1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.078), but significantly influenced transverse arterial diameter (1.5-1.6 mm, p = 0.003) and skin-to-artery distance (2.4-2.8 mm at 30°, p < 0.001). The radial artery was widest at 0° (1.6 ± 1.0 mm), while the ulnar artery peaked at 30° (1.6 ± 0.4 mm). Skin-to-artery distance was minimized at 30° for both vessels. In children ≤ 12 kg, radial transverse diameter decreased paradoxically from 0° to 45° (1.6 ± 0.4 to 1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.013), while the ulnar artery was widest at 30° (1.5 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.007). In infants ≤ 24 months, wrist angle did not significantly influence radial artery depth (p = 0.631, mean overall depth between 2.5-2.6 mm).
CONCLUSION: A 30° wrist extension angle provides the most favorable sonoanatomic profile for both arteries. Although a larger vessel caliber may potentially facilitate cannulation, its clinical benefit remains uncertain as cannulation outcomes were not assessed. These findings support individualized ultrasound-guided assessment rather than a fixed positioning strategy.

articles.title: Postoperative Sleep Quality in Children: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of a Questionnaire.
articles.abstract: Sleep in the immediate postoperative period is influenced by multiple perioperative factors. A key limitation in current research and clinical practice is the lack of brief, psychometrically robust instruments specifically designed to assess postoperative sleep. The aim of this study is to evaluate the psychometric properties of a short questionnaire assessing postoperative sleep quality in children and adolescents. The questionnaire was developed based on a literature review and 48 semi-structured interviews. This is a retrospective analysis. Out of 685 postoperative paediatric patients included across three studies (Study 1: n = 120; age: 14.7 ± 1.9 years, female: 43%; Study 2: n = 249; age: median 5.5, IQR: 4.5-6.5, female: 44%; Study 3: n = 312; age: median 12.0, IQR: 9.3-14.0, female: 38%), 88.5% (n = 609) could be included in the final analysis. Item response theory analysis was used to analyse factorial structure, reliability and measurement invariance (differential item functioning-DIF). A two-factor structure was identified: F1: Pain related impaired sleep quality and F2: General sleep quality with three items loading high on each factor could be identified (RMSEA: 0.01, 90% CI: < 0.01 to 0.06; CFI: 0.997, TLI: 0.996). Reliability was good (< 0.8) for relevant sleep quality ranges. No relevant DIF was observed with respect to sex or response mode. The Post-operative Sleep Questionnaire for children (Po-S-C) is a new short questionnaire for assessing postoperative sleep quality in children and adolescents showing good reliability and no measurement invariance. Further studies are needed to replicate these results in other samples.

articles.title: Effect of intelligent robot-assisted care on perioperative anxiety, pain, and postoperative activity compliance in children aged 6-12 years with appendicitis: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of intelligent robot-assisted nursing on perioperative anxiety, postoperative pain, and ambulation adherence in children undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy for acute appendicitis.
DESIGN AND METHODS: This single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial included 100 children aged 6-12 years, allocated equally to routine nursing care or routine care plus robot-assisted education, interactive entertainment, and postoperative ambulation support. Anxiety was assessed using the Chinese version of the modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale, and pain using a visual analog scale. Full ambulation adherence was defined as achieving daily out-of-bed activity duration targets.
RESULTS: All participants completed follow-up. Compared with controls, the intervention group had lower mean anxiety scores in the preoperative waiting area (36.10 versus 43.14) and at 6 h postoperatively (37.96 versus 47.04; both p < .001). Mean pain scores were 0.50-0.60 points lower at 6, 12, 24, and 48 h postoperatively (all p < .05). Full ambulation adherence was higher on postoperative days 1-5 (86%-96% versus 52%-66%; all p < .005).
CONCLUSIONS: Robot-assisted nursing integrating preoperative preparation and postoperative support was associated with lower anxiety and pain scores and higher ambulation adherence in school-aged children undergoing laparoscopic appendectomy.
PRACTICE IMPLICATIONS: Robot-assisted education and activity support may complement routine pediatric perioperative nursing. Further evaluation is needed before broader implementation.

articles.title: Association of growth following laparotomy with white matter and cerebellar injury in preterm infants with surgical NEC.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the impact of perioperative growth measurements following laparotomy on white matter abnormalities (WMA) and cerebellar injury from MRIs performed at term-equivalent in preterm infants with surgical necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).MethodsIn this retrospective cohort, growth parameters were assessed at birth, before NEC diagnosis and exploratory laparotomy, 28 days after bowel resection, before reanastomosis, at 36 weeks corrected gestational age, and at discharge. Term-equivalent MRI was evaluated for WMA, gray matter abnormality (GMA), and cerebellar injury. WMA associations were examined using separate unadjusted logistic models and models adjusted for gestational age. Within-infant and between-group z-score changes across intervals were assessed with Holm adjustment.ResultsAmong 51 infants, 26 (51.0%) had WMA. Any WMA was associated with lower head circumference (HC) at 36 weeks corrected gestational age (p = 0.04), lower discharge length z-score (p = 0.05), and lower HC z-scores at 36 weeks (p = 0.05) and discharge (p = 0.02). Moderate/severe WMA was associated with lower weight (p = 0.04), length (p = 0.03), and HC (p = 0.01) before reanastomosis and lower HC at discharge (p = 0.04). Higher length z-score (p = 0.04) and HC z-score (p = 0.05) at discharge, and greater length (p = 0.04) and HC (p = 0.05) before reanastomosis, were associated with lower odds of moderate/severe WMA after adjustment for gestational age. Cerebellar injury occurred in 8 infants (15.7%) and was associated with lower weight, length, and HC before NEC diagnosis (p = 0.01, p < 0.01, p = 0.01) and 28 days after resection (p = 0.01, p = 0.01, p = 0.01).ConclusionsBetter linear and head growth before reanastomosis and at discharge were associated with lower WMA severity. Our findings are hypothesis-generating and support the possibility that serial linear and head growth measurements may help identify infants at greater neurological risk following the surgical NEC.

articles.title: Image quality and procedural safety in neonatal brain MRI with and without sedation.
articles.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Neontal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is susceptible to motion artefacts, whereas pharmacological sedation or anaesthesia may cause cardiorespiratory adverse events. We compared image quality and adverse events across three MRI strategies in newborns: natural sleep without sedation, pharmacological sedation, and imaging during mechanical ventilation. We retrospectively analysed 151 brain MRI examinations performed in a tertiary neonatal intensive care unit between August 2013 and August 2024. Examinations were classified as non-sedated using a feed-and-swaddle approach (n = 21), pharmacologically sedated without intubation (n = 67), or performed in intubated and mechanically ventilated infants (n = 63). Motion artefacts and documented adverse events were compared between groups. Motion artefacts were more frequent in non-sedated examinations than in sedated or intubated examinations (85.7% vs. 32.8% and 25.4%, respectively; p < 0.001). Moderate/severe artefacts occurred in 14.3%, 7.5%, and 0%, respectively. No adverse events were documented in the non-sedated group, compared with 8/67 (11.9%) in sedated and 7/63 (11.1%) in intubated infants; this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.275). Within the sedated cohort, artefacts were more frequent with chloral hydrate, whereas respiratory complications occurred predominantly with propofol-based sedation.
CONCLUSION: Neonatal MRI strategies involve a clinically relevant trade-off between image quality and procedural safety. Natural-sleep MRI avoids pharmacological exposure and was not associated with documented adverse events but resulted in more motion artefacts. MRI strategies should therefore be individualized according to clinical condition and required diagnostic image quality.
WHAT IS KNOWN: • Motion artefacts may compromise neonatal MRI, and pharmacological sedation or anaesthesia is frequently used to improve image quality. • Feed-and-swaddle MRI can avoid drug exposure, while sedative and anaesthetic agents may cause respiratory and haemodynamic adverse events.
WHAT IS NEW: • Direct comparison of three real-world neonatal MRI strategies demonstrates a trade-off between image quality and procedural safety: sedation and controlled ventilation reduced motion artefacts, whereas no adverse events were documented during natural-sleep MRI. • Exploratory analyses suggest differences between sedation regimens, with more artefacts after chloral hydrate and respiratory events occurring predominantly with propofol-based sedation.

articles.title: Scoping Review of the National Surgical Plans of Small Island Nations.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) report in 2015 established surgical care as an integral part of public health and critical for the achievement of universal health coverage. This review aims to assess the gap that exists by evaluating the presence and or absence of formal surgical plans and the integration of global surgical indicators into national health frameworks of Small Island Development States (SIDS).
METHODS: The review employed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) framework for scoping reviews and was reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) Checklist. A targeted search of both published and gray literature to find national health policy documents from the 39 SIDS was performed. Titles, executive summaries, and full document reviews were searched for any form of surgical component and reporting of the six LCoGS indicators. Twenty-eight documents were found for analysis.
RESULTS: Of the 28 national plans, 11 were from the Caribbean, 13 from the Pacific and 4 from the Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea (AIS). The median publication date was 2019 (2010-2026). Only three countries had National Surgical Obstetric and Anesthesia Plans (NSOAPs), all from the Pacific region. Twenty-three included general National Strategic Plans (NSP), one National Development Plan (NDP) and one other plan. 64% (Caribbean 7/11, Pacific 9/13 and AIS 2/4) reported inclusion of surgical components. At least one LCoGS indicator inclusion was reported by 20 (71%).
CONCLUSION: Planning for safe and affordable surgical, obstetric and anesthesia care remains poorly developed across the SIDS with only 3 countries having developed a standalone NSOAP. Closing this gap requires context specific plans applying WHO's 6 health system building blocks through expanded universal health coverage for surgical and anesthesia services, formalized referral partnerships, and greater recognition of allied health workers.

articles.title: Analgesic efficacy of external oblique intercostal plane block in adult upper abdominal laparoscopic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The External Oblique Intercostal (EOI) plane block is a novel regional anesthesia technique for upper abdominal surgery. Existing meta-analyses have pooled heterogeneous surgical populations or grouped comparators together, leaving its efficacy relative to individual fascial plane blocks unclear.
METHODS: We searched Embase, PubMed, and CENTRAL for RCTs up to December 24, 2025, comparing EOI plane block with control, Local Anesthetic (LA) infiltration, or other fascial plane blocks in adults undergoing upper abdominal laparoscopic surgery. Primary outcomes were pain at rest and on movement at 12- and 24-hours; secondary outcomes were opioid consumption and quality of recovery at 24-hours. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed.
RESULTS: Eleven RCTs (695 participants) were included. EOI plane block significantly reduced pain compared with control at all time points (mean differences -0.88 to -1.14), exceeding the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) only for pain on movement at 24-hours (-1.14; 95% CI -1.43, -0.84). Pain was also reduced versus LA infiltration for most outcomes but remained below the MCID. No significant differences were observed versus Subcostal Transversus Abdominis Plane (STAP) block or Modified Thoracoabdominal nerve block through Perichondrial Approach (MTAPA) for any outcome. Opioid consumption and quality of recovery did not differ in any comparison. Certainty of evidence was low or very low for most comparisons.
CONCLUSION: EOI plane block may reduce postoperative pain compared with control and LA infiltration, although most differences fell below the MCID, with no demonstrated advantage over STAP block or MTAPA for any outcome.

articles.title: Percutaneous-to-paddle conversion versus primary paddle implantation in spinal cord stimulation.
articles.abstract: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established therapy for chronic pain. While percutaneous and paddle leads demonstrate similar efficacy, some patients require percutaneous-to-paddle conversion. Whether prior percutaneous leads contribute to increased operative complexity remains poorly studied. Patients at our institution who underwent paddle SCS implantation between 2017 and 2025 were identified. Patients were grouped into primary paddle implantation (n = 60) and percutaneous-to-paddle conversion (n = 16). Demographics, operative variables, complications, pain scores (Numeric Rating Scale [NRS]), and opioid use (morphine milligram equivalents [MME]) were compared. Percutaneous-to-paddle conversion procedures were significantly longer (131 vs. 90 min, p = 0.002), had higher rates of overnight stay (37.5% vs. 10%, p = 0.015), and more frequent multilevel laminotomy (10/16 [62.5%] vs. 18/60 [30.0%], p = 0.022). Surgical time increased with the number of laminotomy levels (p < 0.001). No statistically significant difference in complication rates was detected between the percutaneous-to-paddle conversion and primary paddle groups (2/16 [12.5%] vs. 4/60 [6.7%], p = 0.600). While preoperative NRS scores were similar (median NRS 7 [IQR 5-8] vs. 7 [IQR 5-8], p = 0.791), 1-month pain scores were significantly higher in the conversion group (median NRS 7 [IQR 4.5-7] vs. 3 [IQR 0-5], p = 0.006). Opioid use at 1 month was higher in the percutaneous-to-paddle conversion group in the unadjusted analysis (median MME 30 [IQR 0-55] vs. 0 [IQR 0-20], p = 0.039), although this difference did not remain statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (adjusted p = 0.062). Percutaneous-to-paddle conversion was associated with increased operative complexity, including longer surgical times and more overnight stays, as well as higher 1-month postoperative pain scores. These findings may assist with operative planning and perioperative patient counseling.

articles.title: From rescue to precision: breaking the salvage-therapy curse in refractory septic shock.
articles.abstract: Refractory septic shock is managed with a small core of evidence-based treatments and a growing number of salvage therapies, including methylene blue, the vitamin C cocktail, and several blood purification devices. Each has a plausible mechanism, may improve physiological or haemodynamic surrogates, and most remain without definitive evidence of survival benefit in unselected patients. Recent biomarker-selected evidence with polymyxin B, however, suggests that patient selection may be critical. This article argues that most remain unproven because of how they are deployed and tested, not because their mechanisms fail. Given late to the sickest patients, they are subject to confounding by indication, a ceiling effect on attribution, and responder-biased reporting, which together generate a misleading reputation independent of any true effect. Drawing on oXiris, vitamin C, and polymyxin B as worked examples, and on methylene blue and therapeutic plasma exchange as unresolved cases now in trials, the article contends that the way to resolve this problem is to identify a measurable treatable trait and randomise the patients who have it. Polymyxin B illustrates this, having been neutral in an unselected trial and beneficial once patients were selected by endotoxin activity.

articles.title: Therapeutic lactate in critically ill patients: Fuel, fluid, or drug?
articles.abstract: Lactate occupies a paradoxical position in critical care. Traditionally regarded as a marker of physiological stress, it is increasingly recognized as an important metabolic substrate with potential therapeutic effects. In their meta-analysis of randomized trials, Labenbacher and colleagues summarize the current clinical evidence for hypertonic sodium lactate treatment (HSL) across heterogeneous critically ill populations. Although no mortality benefit can be established, the available evidence raises several important mechanistic and methodological questions. First, "lactate therapy" is not a single intervention as HSL simultaneously alters lactate availability, sodium load, tonicity, and acid-base balance. Second, currently used regimens differ markedly in dose, duration, and achieved plasma lactate concentrations, precluding a meaningful dose-exposure-response framework. Third, the physiological response may depend strongly on the underlying hemodynamic and metabolic phenotype with signals of improved cardiac output in some cardiovascular settings but inconsistent findings across other disease states. At this stage, the key question is therefore not simply whether lactate "works" nor whether it improves mortality, but which physiological effect is being targeted, in which patient phenotype, at what exposure, and through which mechanism. Future studies should disentangle the metabolic, osmotic, vascular, and acid-base effects of lactate-containing solutions before definitive clinical outcome trials are undertaken.

articles.title: Rehabilitation prescription tools in critical care: why reinvent the wheel?
ICU Mortality Associated With Clinically Important Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Multistate Analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding may increase mortality and time to discharge from the ICU. Conventional analyses ignore timing and treat bleeding as a binary event. We evaluated the association between time-dependent clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding and ICU mortality.
DESIGN AND SETTING: A multicenter cohort study using data from an international stress ulcer prophylaxis trial.
PATIENTS: A total of 4821 invasively ventilated adult participants.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A multistate model was specified with two transient ICU states (bleed-free and post-bleed) and four absorbing states (ICU discharge or death, each with or without bleeding). The Aalen-Johansen method was used to estimate transition and state occupancy probabilities and to describe risks of different clinical courses. Follow-up was censored at 90 days. We fit two Cox models for time to death in the ICU regressing on time-dependent bleeding history while adjusting for age, sex, baseline Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score, admission category (medical/surgical/trauma), vasopressor/inotrope use and renal replacement therapy on study day 1 and randomized allocation of pantoprazole or placebo; a second model also adjusted for time-dependent covariates of advanced life support (invasive mechanical ventilation, vasopressor/inotrope use, and renal replacement therapy). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding developed in 104 patients (2.2%) in the ICU. Median ICU length of stay for those who experienced bleeding was 19 days (interquartile range [IQR], 11-30 d) vs. 9 days (IQR, 5-15 d) for those who did not. Accounting for immortal time bias, the time-dependent indicator of clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding was associated with increased ICU mortality (hazard ratio, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.13-2.15). At any time, patients who experienced bleeding had approximately 1.6 times the hazard of ICU mortality compared with those without a history of bleeding.
CONCLUSIONS: Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding as a time-dependent event is associated with an increased risk of ICU mortality.

articles.title: Age-Related Differences in the Organ Donation Process Among Pediatric Brain-Dead Donors: A Nationwide Study in Japan.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To characterize the pediatric organ donation process and age-related differences among brain-dead donors in Japan and evaluate organ-specific transplantation rates and graft survival across age groups.
DESIGN: Nationwide retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: National donor records maintained by the Japan Organ Transplant Network.
PATIENTS: All pediatric (≤ 17 yr old) brain-dead organ donors in Japan between July 17, 2010, and March 31, 2024.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENT AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 100 pediatric brain-dead organ donors were included. Donors were categorized into three age groups: younger than 6 years (n = 32), 6-14 years (n = 48), and 15-17 years (n = 20). The time intervals from hospital admission to organ procurement showed marked age-dependent prolongation, with median durations of 28, 19.5, and 13.5 days, respectively (p < 0.01). Younger donors were more frequently managed in children's hospitals and pediatric departments, whereas older donors were increasingly managed in emergency and critical care settings. Organ transplantation was achieved in 99% of donors. Organ-specific transplantation rates were consistently high for the heart, liver, and kidneys across all age groups, whereas lung and pancreas transplantation rates increased with donor age. During donor management, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic function were generally maintained or improved until procurement. No significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed for any organ type.
CONCLUSIONS: The pediatric organ donation process in Japan was substantially prolonged in an age-dependent manner, particularly among donors younger than 6 years. Despite prolonged donor management, transplantation rates remained high, and no significant age-related differences in graft survival were observed. These findings highlight the importance of sustained multidisciplinary and family support throughout the donation process and may provide insights for pediatric donation systems in low-volume settings.

articles.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) compared with conventional oxygen therapy (COT) in adults with de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) using a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA).
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception to April 7, 2026.
STUDY SELECTION: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing HFNC with COT in adults with de novo AHRF.
DATA EXTRACTION: Two investigators independently performed study selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and certainty assessment, with discrepancies resolved through discussion.
DATA SYNTHESIS: A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty). TSA indicated that the cumulative evidence was insufficient to establish a conclusive effect for either outcome. Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain. No significant differences were observed in escalation of therapy (RR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.75-1.01; very low certainty), ICU admission (RR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.50-1.39; very low certainty), or ICU length of stay (mean difference, -0.10 d; 95% CI, -0.82 to 0.61; very low certainty).
CONCLUSIONS: In adults with de novo AHRF, HFNC may reduce the need for endotracheal intubation but probably does not improve survival compared with COT.

articles.title: The Radiographic Lung Edema Score in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Failure: Associations With Systemic Inflammatory Biomarkers and Multiple Organ Dysfunction.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Although chest radiographs (CXR) are among the most used imaging modalities in critically ill patients, their interpretation and clinical significance remain incompletely leveraged. The Radiographic Lung Edema (RALE) score is a prognostic bedside tool widely applied in adults to quantify lung edema on CXR. However, this score has been infrequently studied in children, and its potential to reflect broader aspects of critical illness pathophysiology beyond the lungs is unknown. We sought to determine the reproducibility of the RALE score, and whether higher RALE scores were associated with circulating inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers, multi-organ dysfunction, and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric acute respiratory failure (ARF).
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: Multicenter PICUs.
PATIENTS: Critically ill children (2 wk to 17 yr old) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ARF, enrolled in the CAF-PINT (Coagulation and Fibrinolysis in Pediatric Insulin Titration) study (2012-2016).
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A baseline RALE score was calculated for each patient from a single CXR obtained within 72 hours of IMV initiation. Among 212 patients, RALE scores demonstrated good inter-rater reliability (intra-class coefficient 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.87). After adjustment for ARF etiology and illness severity, higher RALE scores were associated with fewer 28-day ventilator-free days (sub-distribution hazard ratio per 1-sd increase, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that this association was mediated through both pulmonary dysfunction, measured by the oxygenation index (β -0.14; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.22 to -0.06), and extrapulmonary organ dysfunction, measured by the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction score (β -0.05; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.10 to -0.002). Similar associations were observed for 28-day PICU-free days. Finally, penalized regression selected soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 as biomarkers associated with higher RALE scores.
CONCLUSIONS: We provide evidence that the RALE score is not solely a lung injury marker but also reflects broader systemic pathophysiology. These findings have important implications for the interpretation and clinical application of this bedside tool in pediatric ARF.

articles.title: Religion and Religiosity in End-of-Life Decisions in Neurocritical Care.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: End-of-life decisions are shaped by diverse biographical, social, and cultural factors. Few studies have systematically examined the impact of religion on end-of-life decisions, and even less data are available on religiosity (i.e., strength of religious faith). The Religion and religiosity in End-of-life deCisiOns in neuroCritIcaL carE (RECONCILE) study aimed to investigate whether religiosity, rather than religion, plays a decisive role in shaping end-of-life decisions.
DESIGN: Prospective observational study.
SETTING: The study was conducted between 2021 and 2024 at two neuro-ICUs at Charité-Universitätsmedizin Berlin.
PATIENTS: We prospectively studied patients with acute brain injury and poor neurologic prognosis defined by the absence of regaining decision-making capacity or sufficient autonomy. A total of 100 patients were included.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS: Relatives were consulted to ascertain the patients' presumed wishes regarding the continuation or withdrawal of life-sustaining intensive care. The 10-item Santa Clara Strength of Religious Faith questionnaire was applied to measure the patient´s religiosity on a scale between 10 and 40 points. We applied the t-test for independent variables to evaluate the influence of religiosity on end-of-life decisions. To adjust for possible confounders like age, sex, nationality, and religion, we calculated a logistic regression as well as an analysis of variance calculation.
MAIN RESULTS: In patients in whom intensive care was continued, the median score was significantly higher compared with patients in whom intensive care was withdrawn (28.1 ± 9.0 vs. 20.5 ± 8.3; p < 0.001; Cohens d = 0.875). This finding was reproduced in each denominational group. Religion, age, and sex showed no significant association with the end-of-life decision behavior. Germans chose withdrawal of therapy significantly more often than non-Germans (p = 0.01) but also showed significantly lower religiosity scores (21.9 vs. 27.9; p = 0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: The RECONCILE study demonstrates that religiosity looks more important in influencing end-of-life decisions than religion. Higher levels of religiosity were associated with a preference for more aggressive treatment, even when neurologic prognosis is poor.

articles.title: The hepatic immune niche in liver diseases and transplantation: from homeostasis to therapeutic targeting.
articles.abstract: The liver combines continuous exposure to gut-derived antigens and metabolites with immune surveillance and tissue repair. Its immune niche is organized by interactions among sinusoidal endothelial cells, Kupffer cells, recruited leukocytes, and parenchymal and stromal cells. At homeostasis, these interactions support antigen clearance and restrained immune activation. Persistent injury changes antigen presentation, metabolite availability, leukocyte recruitment, and extracellular matrix composition, allowing local immune responses to contribute to continued tissue damage. In chronic viral, steatotic, alcohol-associated, cholestatic, and autoimmune liver diseases, distinct patterns of myeloid activation, lymphocyte dysfunction, cytotoxicity, and fibrogenesis emerge at parenchymal, biliary, and vascular interfaces. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) adds tumor-derived signals that suppress antitumor immunity within a heterogeneous hepatic environment. In liver transplantation, perioperative injury intersects with donor-specific cellular and humoral immunity, with outcomes ranging from controlled donor reactivity to distinct, sometimes overlapping forms of rejection and chronic remodeling. Xenotransplantation further exposes the graft to interspecies antibody, complement, endothelial, and coagulation incompatibilities. In inflammatory liver disease and transplantation, blocking local signals that support pathogenic lymphocyte survival or myeloid activation may reduce continued tissue injury. In HCC, limiting tumor-derived metabolic signals that suppress immune-cell function may instead help restore antitumor responses. Continued recruitment from the circulation may replenish pathogenic populations despite suppression of cells already within the liver, making cellular recruitment an additional potential target. Effective treatment must therefore interrupt the processes sustaining injury while preserving antimicrobial defense, antitumor surveillance, graft regulation, and tissue repair.

articles.title: Audit of procedural sedation in a remote Australian hospital 2010 - 2021.
articles.abstract: Procedural sedation is commonly provided in rural hospitals; however, there is little published safety data. The authors conducted a retrospective audit of anaesthetic records from 2010 to 2021 of procedural sedation in a remote hospital in South Australia. The data were collected from 1912 cases, which were provided mainly for gastroenterology procedures in day case theatre and emergency department settings. Sedation was provided by a general practitioner anaesthetist giving boluses of fentanyl, midazolam and propofol. All patients were low risk (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status 1-3). There were few anaesthetic problems and no mortality during sedation or in the recovery area. The most common problem was desaturation requiring airway support and oxygen, and occurred in 2% of cases. Procedural sedation was practiced safely in this remote setting.

articles.title: A Value-Driven Care Approach to Improving Time to Operation for Patients with Low-Impact Geriatric Hip Fractures.
articles.abstract: Timely surgical repair of hip fractures improves outcomes, yet many patients do not receive surgery within 48 hours of ED registration as a result of system-level inefficiencies. This 2-year case study (January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2024) consisted of a bundled, multidisciplinary intervention implemented within a value-based health care framework in a tertiary hospital in Singapore. The intervention included restructuring fragmented workflows by constructing a multidisciplinary task force that cocreated the bundle comprising revised preoperative cardiac guidelines, default surgical listing (formal scheduling of surgery) on admission from the ED, prioritization of operating theater access, real-time communication between departments of orthopedics, geriatrics, and anesthesia, and monthly performance feedback to improve patient-centered outcomes (namely timeliness of surgery, length of stay, and safety outcomes). Among patients 60 years of age and over with fragility hip fractures, the proportion undergoing surgery within 48 hours increased from 38.9% (among 149 patients in a preimplementation period from July to December 2023) to 68.4% (among 117 patients in a postimplementation period from July to December 2024) (P<0.001). In addition, median time to surgery decreased from 58.8 hours to 38.3 hours (P<0.001), and median length of stay improved from 11.0 days to 7.0 days (P<0.001), with more patients discharged within 10 days (from 48.3% to 67.5%; P=0.002). Complication rates, readmissions, and returns to the operating theater were unchanged. Overall, the intervention improved surgical timeliness and hospital efficiency (using bed-day utilization as a pragmatic proxy) without compromising patient safety. Although the Value-Driven Care program of the Singapore Ministry of Health does not include a specific cost component, its principles align clinical outcomes with resource utilization, which are associated with downstream consequences of operational and financial efficiency. Post implementation, for example, reduced length of stay led to 962 fewer bed-days over 1 year (366 days in 2024), with a related cost avoidance of nearly US$900,000. Key enablers of success included the establishment of a multidisciplinary task force that aligned stakeholders around a shared patient-centered goal, which contributed to the development of a shared platform for monitoring and assessing progress, subsequently leading to reduced variability through collaboration in codevelopment of care protocols, and supported implementation through structured workflow redesign, real-time communication, and continuous feedback. These elements most likely contributed to the observed improvements and may provide a practical framework for addressing similar system-level challenges in other health care settings.

articles.title: Percutaneous screw distraction versus open fusion surgery for anatomic restoration after burst fracture.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Open posterior transpedicular screw fixation for thoracolumbar burst fractures involves substantial muscle dissection, resulting in iatrogenic trauma, prolonged hospital stays, and extended recovery times, but minimally invasive techniques like percutaneous pedicle screw fixation cannot be used in all fracture patterns or indications. We compared perioperative and radiographic outcomes of a fixed-angle percutaneous instrumentation technique versus conventional open fixation in patients managed without direct decompression.
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study at our Level I trauma center, patients who underwent either open or percutaneous instrumentation without laminectomy in 2018-2024 were identified. Patients with AO Spine fracture classifications of A2, A3, and A4 were present in the cohort. Student's t-test and Pearson's Chi-square statistical tests were used to compare the perioperative and radiographic outcomes of patients who underwent fixed-angle percutaneous instrumentation with those who underwent conventional open fixation without direct decompression.
RESULTS: Among 63 included patients, 24 underwent percutaneous surgery and 39 had open procedures. Selection varied by on-call surgeon, not fracture characteristics. AO Spine fracture classifications (A2, A3, A4) were similarly distributed between groups (p = 0.25). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups. The percutaneous group experienced significantly less intraoperative blood loss (p < 0.001), showed greater improvement in canal cross-sectional area from preoperative to postoperative (p = 0.01), and had greater improvement in vertebral body index scores from postdistraction to last follow-up (p = 0.02). The groups were statistically similar in all other radiographic outcomes. Elective instrumentation removal was more frequent in patients in the percutaneous cohort (p = 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Percutaneous instrumentation for thoracolumbar burst fractures not involving decompression achieved radiographic outcomes comparable with open techniques in this study. The percutaneous technique demonstrated favorable radiographic outcomes, with greater indirect canal decompression intraoperatively and better vertebral body index scores at last follow-up. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective comparison.

articles.title: Incidence of 1-year Mortality in Elderly Patients Sustaining Proximal Femur Fracture: A Retrospective Observational Study from Rural Western India.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Proximal femur fractures cause substantial morbidity and mortality in older adults. Western cohorts report 1-year mortality rates of 20%-40%, but comparable Indian data remain limited.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate 1-year mortality after surgery for proximal femur fracture in elderly patients and evaluate its association with time to surgery.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent surgery for proximal femur fracture at a rural tertiary teaching hospital in western India between August 2016 and July 2021. Of 265 eligible patients, 228 (86.0%) were contacted and included. Demographic, clinical, fracture, perioperative, and treatment variables were extracted from records. One-year vital status and, where applicable, date and cause of death were obtained by telephone from patients or next of kin. Associations were assessed using Chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and independent-samples t-tests, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
RESULTS: The cohort comprised 130 men and 98 women, with a mean age of 68.5 ± 7.4 years. Mean time from injury to presentation was 3.0 days and from injury to surgery was 5.3 days. Eighteen patients died within 1 year (7.9%). Mortality did not differ significantly between patients operated within 36 h and those operated later (0/4 vs. 18/224; Fisher's exact P = 1.00).
CONCLUSION: One-year mortality in this cohort was lower than commonly reported Western rates. No survival association with surgery within 36 h was demonstrated; however, the early-surgery group was too small for a reliable comparison. Larger multicentric Indian studies are required.

articles.title: Outcomes of Surgical Interventions in the Management of Rectal Prolapse.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rectal prolapse is a debilitating condition associated with significant morbidity and impaired quality of life. Various surgical approaches, including abdominal and perineal procedures, are employed for its management, each with differing outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: The study aimed to assess the etiology and pathophysiology of rectal prolapse and the various investigations and treatment modalities used.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A prospective interventional study was conducted at a tertiary care centre. Thirty patients aged 16-80 years with rectal prolapse undergoing surgical management were included. Surgical procedures included abdominal approaches (open/laparoscopic rectopexy with or without resection) and perineal approaches (Delorme, Thiersch, and stapled transanal rectal resection). Outcomes assessed included operative duration, blood loss, postoperative pain (Visual Analog Scale), hospital stay, complications, and recurrence.
RESULTS: Most patients were over 45 years (66.6%), with male predominance (60%). Mucous discharge (80%) and constipation (50%) were the most common symptoms. Complete prolapse was seen in 83.3% of cases. Laparoscopic suture rectopexy was the most common procedure (26.6%). The mean operative time was 115 ± 25 min, and mean blood loss was 140 ± 35 mL. The mean hospital stay was 6.2 ± 1.5 days, and early recurrence occurred in 6.7% of patients. Abdominal procedures were associated with significantly longer operative time, greater blood loss, higher pain scores, and longer hospital stay compared to perineal procedures (P < 0.05), while recurrence rates were comparable.
CONCLUSION: Rectal prolapse commonly affects middle-aged and elderly individuals. Although abdominal procedures have higher perioperative morbidity, both approaches show similar recurrence rates. Surgical management should be individualized based on patient characteristics.

articles.title: Perioperative methadone: Clinical use and knowledge among Australian anaesthetists.
articles.abstract: Intravenous methadone has re-emerged as a perioperative analgesic, yet uncertainty persists regarding its optimal use. Variation in clinician practice and interpretation of pharmacological principles may influence its safe and effective application. We conducted a mixed-methods survey-based study within a national anaesthesia educational programme (ADVANCE). A voluntary, anonymous pre-presentation clinician survey was distributed to predominantly Australian anaesthetists to characterise methadone use, dosing strategies, adjunct prescribing and patient selection. Real-time audience polling during the educational session assessed clinician responses to pharmacology-based and clinical decision-making scenarios. Survey and polling datasets were analysed independently using descriptive statistics. A total of 726 clinicians completed the survey. Overall, 50.6% (n = 367) of respondents reported using methadone. Among users (n = 367), practice varied widely across surgical contexts and dosing strategies, including weight-based, fixed and procedure-dependent approaches. Concurrent administration of additional opioids and central nervous system depressants was common (86.1%). Clinicians reported avoiding methadone in specific patient groups, most frequently frail patients, those with prolonged QT interval, or obstructive sleep apnoea. Polling responses demonstrated variability in clinician interpretation of pharmacological principles, particularly regarding timing of central effects. Perioperative methadone use is characterised by substantial variation in uptake, dosing and adjunct prescribing. Variability in clinician responses relative to pharmacological reference data, combined with frequent co-administration of additional opioids and sedatives, highlights potential areas for targeted education and institutional safeguards to support safe implementation.

articles.title: Wearable acoustic cardiography for detection of left ventricular and valvular dysfunction: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preoperative cardiac evaluation based on history and physical examination is subjective, risking delayed diagnosis or excessive echocardiography. Acoustic cardiography (ACG) synchronizes ECG and heart sound analysis for rapid point-of-care cardiac screening. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of wearable ACG for left ventricular dysfunction, significant valvular dysfunction, and the consistency of ACG-aided preoperative risk assessment with expert consensus.
METHODS: This prospective single-center study enrolled consecutive patients undergoing major elective non-cardiac surgery. Echocardiography served as the reference standard; the primary endpoint was LVEF <40%.
RESULTS: Among 262 patients, ACG showed excellent performance for LVEF <40% (AUC=0.979, sensitivity 93.3%, specificity 96.4%). It achieved substantial agreement with echocardiography for significant valvular dysfunction (κ=0.69). Adding ACG improved consistency with expert consensus versus physical examination alone (κ=0.71 vs 0.55).
CONCLUSIONS: Wearable ACG provides high accuracy for preoperative screening of systolic and valvular dysfunction. It facilitates targeted echocardiography referral. Further trials are needed to verify its impact on referral decisions and perioperative outcomes.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR2300073695.

articles.title: Supra-Inguinal Fascia Iliaca Block Versus Iliohypogastric-Ilioinguinal Block During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI) Under Conscious Sedation: A Patient- and Outcome Assessor-Blinded Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TF-TAVI) is increasingly performed under conscious sedation (CS), yet optimal analgesia for femoral access remains debated. Regional anesthesia techniques such as the supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block (SIFIB) and iliohypogastric-ilioinguinal block (II-IHB) may offer improved analgesia compared with conventional local infiltration.
AIM: To compare SIFIB and II-IH block in enhancing CS quality during TF-TAVI, focusing on analgesic requirements, patient and surgeon satisfaction, and conversion to GA.
METHODS: This patient- and outcome assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial included 45 patients scheduled for transfemoral TAVI, allocated equally to SIFIB, II-IHB, or control (local infiltration). All procedures were performed under standardized CS with dexmedetomidine. Primary outcomes were rescue analgesia and conversion to general anesthesia. Secondary outcomes included pain and sedation scores, hemodynamic and respiratory variables, pacing, vascular complications, and hospital stay.
RESULTS: Rescue analgesia was required in 33.3%, 46.7%, and 40.0% of patients in the SIFIB, IIIHB, and control groups, respectively (p = 0.927); fentanyl consumption was comparable (p = 0.525). Conversion to general anesthesia occurred in 0%, 13.3%, and 26.7%, respectively (p = 0.141). Both blocks reduced intraoperative pain versus control (SIFIB, p < 0.001; IIIHB, p < 0.001) and were associated with lower intraoperative heart rate (p = 0.005 and p = 0.015, respectively). Postoperative pain, mean arterial pressure, oxygen saturation, pacing, and vascular complications did not differ significantly. Hospital stay was shorter after SIFIB than after IIIHB (p = 0.019) or local infiltration (p = 0.004).
CONCLUSION: No statistically significant between-group differences were found in the primary outcomes of rescue analgesia or conversion to general anesthesia. Both regional blocks reduced intraoperative pain scores compared with local infiltration. SIFIB was associated with a shorter hospital stay; however, this secondary finding is exploratory and requires confirmation in larger studies. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06911463.

articles.title: Pediatric methemoglobinemia in the emergency department: etiology, treatment patterns, and short-term outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aimed to characterize the clinical and etiological features of pediatric methemoglobinemia presenting to a pediatric emergency department, with particular attention to procedure-related local anesthetic exposure, and to explore short-term treatment responses to methylene blue and intravenous ascorbic acid.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included patients presenting between November 1, 2022 1 November 2022 1 November 2022, and November 1, 2025 1 November 2025 1 November 2025, with methemoglobin levels ≥ 5% measured by co-oximetry. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, G6PD, genetic, and disposition data were collected. Baseline characteristics and early treatment responses were compared between patients receiving methylene blue and intravenous ascorbic acid.
RESULTS: Twenty-four patients were included; the median age was 4 months (IQR, 2-5), and 21 (87.5%) were male. Median initial SpO2 was 88% (IQR, 85%-90%), initial methemoglobin was 25.5% (IQR, 21.4%-30.6%), and post-treatment methemoglobin was 5.8% (IQR, 2.6%-8.3%). Drug exposure accounted for 19 cases (79.2%), most commonly lidocaine (n = 10) and prilocaine (n = 7). Among the five patients without documented oxidant exposure, two had pathogenic CYB5R3 variants and two had likely pathogenic CYB5R3 variants. Eleven patients received methylene blue and 13 received intravenous ascorbic acid. Post-treatment methemoglobin was lower with methylene blue (2.6% vs. 7.8%; p = 0.024), whereas relative reduction did not differ significantly (88.8% vs. 72.8%; p = 0.118).
CONCLUSION: Methemoglobinemia predominantly affected young infants and was most often associated with procedure-related local anesthetic exposure, particularly in the context of circumcision. Topical oropharyngeal anesthetic exposure before intubation should also be recognized as a potential source of oxidant exposure. Treatment comparisons were exploratory, and underlying enzymatic or genetic susceptibility should be considered even when an acquired oxidant exposure is identified.

articles.title: Model-informed characterisation of the target therapeutic window for dexamethasone by quantitatively balancing foetal lung maturation and neurotoxicity in pregnant rats.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Dexamethasone, a first-line treatment for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS), promotes foetal lung maturation whilst simultaneously inducing neurotoxicity in offspring. We aimed to define the therapeutic window of dexamethasone for the treatment of NRDS.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Pregnant rats were given dexamethasone at 0.1 or 0.4 mg·kg-1 to simulate clinically equivalent prenatal dexamethasone exposure. Half of the rats were anaesthetised, and surfactant proteins A and B in foetal lungs quantified. A pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) model was developed to determine the minimum effective concentration. The remaining rats, delivered naturally, and their offspring underwent open-field testing. Messenger RNA sequencing of the foetal hippocampus was performed, and concentration-toxicity assays were conducted using H19-7/IGF-IR cells. Data were integrated with a maternal-foetal physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model to determine the maximum tolerated concentration. A clinical PBPK for dexamethasone in pregnant women was used to simulate a potentially optimal dosing regimen.
KEY RESULTS: The PK/PD model adequately characterised dexamethasone-induced foetal lung maturation and indicated a minimal effective concentration of 1.63 ng·ml-1. The offspring of PDE rats exhibited significant behavioural changes. mRNA sequencing analysis suggested that neurotoxicity was mediated via the Wnt pathway and renin-angiotensin system, with BDNF and CMA1 identified as potential biomarkers of neurotoxicity. Cell-based assays suggested a neurotoxic threshold concentration of 17 ng·ml-1. For a therapeutic window of 1.63-17 ng·ml-1, PBPK model simulations indicated that a reduced dose regimen of 2.5 or 3 mg every 8 h for six doses may represent an optimised therapeutic strategy.
CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: This model-informed precision dosing strategy provides a rational approach to optimising clinical dexamethasone dosing regimens.

articles.title: Bleeding Symptoms, Laboratory, and Molecular Genetic Results in Children With Platelet Disorders.
articles.abstract: Diagnosing and classifying platelet disorders (PD) is challenging in children. Therefore, we evaluated clinical, laboratory, and genetic data to improve current algorithms by performing a prospective observational cohort study in children (0-18 years) with a known genetic cause (proven PD), functional abnormalities, or thrombocytopenia without genetic cause (probable PD) or medical suspicion of PD (possible PD). We included 98 children (mean age 11.6 years, 55 females). PD was proven in 44, probable in 43, and possible in 11. Comorbidities were present in 43. Epistaxis, hematomas, menstrual, and perioperative bleeding were reported most frequently. Mean ISTH-BAT bleeding score was 6.1 (SD 4.0, range 0-17), with higher scores in post-pubertal females (mean 7.6) and lower scores in children with moderate thrombocytopenia (mean 4.8). Bleeding as a presenting symptom and older age were associated with higher bleeding scores. Treatment was indicated in 46 children. Most frequently, Light transmission aggregometry was abnormal for ADP, epinephrine, and thrombin. General laboratory parameters can hint to but not identify PD origin. Genetic testing led to novel diagnoses in 10 (23%) children with probable PD. We conclude that bleeding tendency is prominent but variable in children with PD. Routine laboratory tests are useful, but fail to diagnose the origin of PD. Therefore, genetic analysis is essential, especially as PD can be part of a syndrome leading to comorbidities or predispose for malignancies, both impacting counseling and surveillance. We propose a classification based on functional and genetic analysis leading to either an isolated or syndrome-associated inherited PD or a functional PD. Trial Registration: ABR NL55101.078.16.

articles.title: Novel Breath Segmentation and Predictive Quality Classification Model for Pediatric Bag-Mask Ventilation Using Capnography Waveforms.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bag-mask ventilation (BMV) is a critical phase of pediatric airway management, yet objective feedback remains limited.
OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate a two-stage, CO2-only framework for pediatric BMV assessment comprising automated breath segmentation and machine learning classification of breaths according to predefined low-quality criteria for insufficient ventilation. We hypothesized that our model would achieve area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) greater than or equal to 0.75 and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) greater than or equal to 0.75.
DERIVATION COHORT: We retrospectively analyzed capnography waveforms from 85 critically ill children receiving peri-intubation BMV in a quaternary-care PICU. Flow and pressure data established reference-standard low-quality criteria: expiratory tidal volume (VTE) less than 4 mL/kg of ideal body weight, mask leak greater than 40%, or upper airway obstruction (VTE < 4 mL/kg with peak inspiratory pressure > 30 cm H2O and leak > 80%).
VALIDATION COHORT: CO2-based segmentation was validated in 10 randomly selected patients comprising 605 manually adjudicated breaths. Classification performance was internally validated using repeated 10-fold cross-validation within the derivation cohort; no independent validation cohort was used.
PREDICTION MODEL: A rule-based algorithm segmented continuous CO2 waveforms into breaths. Deep learning architectures then used CO2 waveforms alone to classify breaths according to whether they met predefined low-quality criteria.
RESULTS: The CO2-only algorithm identified 6942 breaths (median, 66 per patient [interquartile range, 47-100 per patient]); 49.5% met at least one low-quality criterion. Segmentation achieved positive predictive value 0.95 (95% CI, 0.93-0.96) and sensitivity 0.86 (95% CI, 0.83-0.89). Twenty-seven breaths were adjudicated as false-positive detections (0.05; 95% CI, 0.036-0.074). CO2-only segmentation may miss ventilatory attempts with minimal or absent exhaled CO2. The best-performing classification model achieved AUROC 0.79 (95% CI, 0.66-0.89) and AUPRC 0.75 (95% CI, 0.57-0.88).
CONCLUSIONS: A CO2-only framework showed proof-of-concept feasibility for breath segmentation and quality classification during pediatric BMV, supporting further development of objective bedside feedback systems.

articles.title: Fentanyl co-induction in emergency canine caesarean section: effects on maternal anaesthesia and neonatal outcome.
articles.abstract: The objective of this prospective, randomised, clinical trial was to evaluate the effects of intravenous (IV) fentanyl co-induction before emergency caesarean section (CS) on maternal anaesthetic variables, induction agent requirements, and neonatal viability in dogs. Thirty-six client-owned dams undergoing emergency CS were randomly assigned to receive co-induction with fentanyl (4 μg/kg IV; treatment group [TG], n = 21) or no co-induction (control group [CG], n = 15). Anaesthesia was induced with alfaxalone or propofol to effect. A total of 167 puppies were delivered. Neonatal viability was assessed using Apgar scoring at birth and at 5, 10, 20 min and 1 h after delivery. Maternal anaesthetic variables, induction agent requirements and neonatal viability were compared between groups. Separate general linear mixed models were used with litter affiliation included as a random effect and one covariate per model (delivery time, alfaxalone dose, maternal weight). Fentanyl co-induction reduced the alfaxalone induction dose by 31% compared with controls (p = 0.007). Apgar scores at birth (p < 0.001) and at 5 (p < 0.001) and 10 (p = 0.041) minutes after delivery were significantly higher in TG than in CG. Higher alfaxalone induction doses were associated with lower Apgar scores at birth (p = 0.045). Maternal haemodynamic variables and perinatal mortality did not differ significantly between groups. In conclusion, fentanyl co-induction before emergency canine CS reduced alfaxalone requirements and was associated with higher neonatal Apgar scores during the immediate postnatal period, without significant differences in maternal haemodynamic variables or neonatal mortality between groups.

articles.title: Pediatric T-Cell Lymphoblastic Lymphoma Presenting as Rapidly Progressive Tonsillar Hypertrophy: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: We discuss an 8-year-old male who presented with asymmetric, rapidly progressive tonsillar hypertrophy and cervical lymphadenopathy. He was treated empirically with corticosteroids, antibiotics, and semi-elective tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy. Pathology was consistent with T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. Early recognition of pediatric malignancy and referral to subspecialty care can mitigate perioperative risks and optimize oncologic outcomes.

articles.title: Robotic versus laparoscopic distal gastrectomy post-endoscopic submucosal dissection: A propensity score-matched study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Although endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is commonly used as a less invasive strategy for early gastric cancer (GC), patients undergoing non-curative resections still require additional gastrectomy. ESD-induced fibrosis and adhesions may obscure the anatomical planes and make subsequent surgery more technically demanding. Robotic distal gastrectomy (RDG) may mitigate these challenges; however, comparative evidence for post-ESD cases is lacking. We compared the perioperative and oncological outcomes of RDG and laparoscopic distal gastrectomy (LDG) after ESD.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Of the 312 patients treated with either LDG or RDG for GC, 46 underwent gastrectomy after ESD. Propensity score matching (PSM) using seven clinical variables yielded ten matched pairs. Perioperative outcomes, pathological findings and survival rates were compared between groups. Because the matched cohort was very small ( n = 10 per group), the statistical power of the comparative analyses was limited.
RESULTS: Before matching, the operative time tended to be longer in the RDG group, while other perioperative outcomes were comparable. Post-PSM, the operative time remained slightly longer in the RDG group (293.0 vs. 253.5 min) but was not statistically significant. Blood loss, number of lymph nodes harvested, post-operative complications, inflammatory markers and length of hospital stay showed no significant differences. No post-operative mortality or recurrence was observed. The limited sample size means that modest differences between approaches cannot be excluded.
CONCLUSION: RDG demonstrated perioperative and oncological results similar to those observed with LDG in patients undergoing gastrectomy post-ESD, despite the technical challenges posed by ESD-induced fibrosis. However, because the propensity-matched cohort was very small ( n = 10 per group), these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating equivalence between the two approaches. RDG appears feasible and safe in this technically demanding setting, although cost implications of robotic surgery were not assessed and warrant consideration. Larger multicentre studies with adequate statistical power are needed to validate these preliminary observations and clarify the potential benefits of RDG after ESD.

articles.title: Pancreatic surgery in children: nationwide retrospective observational study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Paediatric patients differ in various ways from adult populations, but comprehensive multicentre or population-based data are missing for paediatric pancreatic surgery. This study evaluated indications, procedures, complications, and mortality in paediatric patients undergoing pancreatic surgery.
METHODS: This retrospective observational population-based cohort study queried the German Diagnosis-Related Group database for all patients aged < 19 years who underwent pancreatic surgical procedures between 2010 and 2023. The primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and complication rates. Sex- and age-based differences in surgical indications and procedures were explored as secondary outcomes. Descriptive statistics and multivariable regression analyses were performed to identify risk factors for mortality and perioperative complications.
RESULTS: Among the 761 patients identified, indications for pancreatic surgery encompassed chronic pancreatitis (284 patients, 37.3%), pancreatic tumours (221, 29.0%), trauma (127, 16.7%), extrapancreatic tumours (70, 9.2%), and other diseases (59, 7.8%), with significant sex- and age-based differences (P < 0.001). Distal pancreatectomies (281, 36.9%) and pancreatoduodenectomies (125, 16.4%) were the most commonly performed operations. The mortality rate in the overall cohort was 2.8% (21), with no deaths recorded in the subgroup of patients with pancreatic tumours. The overall complication rate was 41.9% (319 of 761 patients), and varied depending on the surgical procedure, spanning from 28.6% for pancreatic cyst marsupialization to 92.9% for total pancreatectomy. Severe complications occurred in 244 patients (32.1%), and were again more common after total pancreatectomy (85.7%). In multivariable analyses, a higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (odds ratio (OR) 1.27; 95% confidence interval (c.i.) 1.12 to 1.44) and undergoing surgery for trauma (OR 5.22; 95% c.i. 1.96 to 13.89), other pancreatic diagnoses (OR 3.13; 95% c.i. 1.30 to 7.17), or chronic pancreatitis (OR 2.56; 95% c.i. 1.08 to 6.25) were identified as independent risk factors for the occurrence of complications, as were receiving total pancreatectomy (OR 8.42; 95% c.i. 1.38 to 51.16) and concomitant splenectomy (OR 1.82; 95% c.i. 1.10 to 3.00).
CONCLUSION: Pancreatic surgery in children is most commonly performed for chronic pancreatitis or tumours, with specific sex and age differences in indication. Pancreatic procedures in children are rare, but can be performed with low in-hospital mortality. However, morbidity remains substantial, particularly after extensive procedures.

articles.title: Transfusion-free kidney transplantation in Jehovah's witnesses: a propensity-score matched cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Jehovah's Witnesses (JWs) refuse blood transfusions on religious grounds, creating a major challenge in kidney transplantation (KT), where perioperative bleeding may necessitate transfusion support. Evidence regarding transfusion-free KT in JWs remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility and early clinical outcomes of a transfusion-free KT protocol in JW patients.
METHODS: We performed a single-centre propensity score-matched cohort study including all JW recipients who underwent KT under a transfusion-free protocol between 2016 and 2025. The protocol included pre-transplant haemoglobin optimisation to ≥13 g/dL. JW recipients were matched 1:3 to non-JW controls based on recipient age and sex, donor type, and transplant date. Outcomes included peri-transplant transfusion, anaemia management, bleeding-related complications, and early post-transplant results.
RESULTS: 27 JW recipients and 74 controls were included. Peri-transplant transfusion was completely avoided in JW recipients (0/27), whereas 24/74 controls (32.4%) required transfusion support. Bleeding-related complications occurred in 14.8% of JW recipients and 11.3% of controls (RR 1.65, 95% CI 0.44-6.21). Admission haemoglobin was higher in JW recipients (14.2 vs 11.5 g/dL; MD 2.69, 95% CI 2.15-3.22), as was nadir haemoglobin (10.0 vs 8.5 g/dL; MD 1.50, 95% CI 0.55-2.45). However, the absolute decrease from admission to nadir was greater in JW recipients (4.14 vs 3.01 g/dL; MD 1.13, 95% CI 0.21-2.06). Hospital stay was longer in JW recipients (MD 5.2 days, 95% CI -0.10 to 10.31).
CONCLUSIONS: A transfusion-free KT protocol was feasible in JW recipients managed at an experienced centre and enabled complete avoidance of peri-transplant transfusion. Early outcomes are reported descriptively and should be interpreted with caution because of the small sample size and residual imbalance between groups.

articles.title: Radiological decompression and clinical outcomes following endoscopic unilateral biportal lumbar interbody fusion vs. conventional posterior lumbar interbody fusion.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical, perioperative, and radiological outcomes of endoscopic unilateral biportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (ULIF) and conventional posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF) for single-level degenerative lumbar disease.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 67 patients undergoing lumbar interbody fusion (ULIF, n = 29; PLIF, n = 38). Perioperative outcomes included operative time, blood loss, and hospital stay. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the visual analogue scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Radiological outcomes included changes in spinal canal cross-sectional area (CSA), canal diameter, and fusion status.
RESULTS: Operative time was longer in the ULIF group than in the PLIF group (226.5 ± 50.6 vs. 184.1 ± 57.4 min, p = 0.002). However, ULIF resulted in less blood loss (87.6 ± 56.7 vs. 251.2 ± 198.0 mL, p < 0.001), shorter total hospital stay (11.7 ± 4.0 vs. 14.6 ± 4.6 days, p = 0.008), and shorter postoperative hospital stay (4.1 ± 1.0 vs. 8.5 ± 1.4 days, p < 0.001). VAS improvements were comparable between the two surgical approaches. Although PLIF showed a greater reduction in ODI from baseline, absolute ODI values at 12 months were similar.
CONCLUSIONS: ULIF was associated with less intraoperative blood loss and shorter postoperative hospitalization while achieving similar 12-month pain outcomes and fusion rates to PLIF in this cohort. No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in postoperative complications. The modest radiological differences observed with ULIF should be interpreted cautiously, and the small observational cohort was not powered to establish equivalence or comparable safety between the two procedures. Larger prospective studies with longer follow-up are warranted.

articles.title: Skin barrier impairment and topical local anesthetics: a review of percutaneous absorption and systemic toxicity risks.
articles.abstract: Topical local anesthetics are widely used in dermatologic surgery, laser therapy, and minimally invasive aesthetic procedures. In intact skin, the stratum corneum typically restricts the percutaneous absorption of local anesthetics; however, following skin barrier impairment due to inflammatory dermatoses, ulcers, burns, or post-laser and microneedling treatment, altered local permeation and systemic exposure profiles may affect their safety margin. This narrative review presents a structured synthesis of evidence pertaining to skin barrier dysfunction and the safety of topical local anesthetics. The article outlines the structure and barrier function of the stratum corneum and compares the characteristics of three types of impairment: inflammatory dermatoses, wound-related barrier loss, and iatrogenic barrier disruption. Using Fick's law of diffusion as a conceptual framework, it analyzes the core determinants of percutaneous absorption and compares the pharmacological profiles of commonly used agents, including lidocaine, prilocaine, tetracaine, and benzocaine. Available case evidence is synthesized, and the clinical presentation and differential diagnosis of systemic toxicity are summarized. A clinical risk stratification framework is proposed for patients with compromised skin barriers, and the potential and limitations of emerging strategies, including nanocarrier delivery, microneedle patches, and cryoanalgesia, are discussed. Existing evidence is predominantly derived from case reports, in vitro or animal studies, and small-scale clinical observations; pharmacokinetic data quantitatively relating the severity of barrier impairment to systemic exposure remain limited. Dosing regimens validated in intact skin should not be directly extrapolated to patients with barrier impairment. Future research should focus on developing pharmacokinetic prediction models integrating barrier injury type, administration parameters, and patient characteristics.

articles.title: Biopsychosocial Network Associations in Paediatric Chronic Pain: A Cross-Lagged Panel Network Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Biopsychosocial models of chronic pain emphasize interactions between biological, psychological and social processes, yet little is known about their organization over time in paediatric chronic pain. This study examined cross-sectional and longitudinal network associations among pain intensity, pain interference, pain extent, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, pain catastrophizing, sleep disturbance, fatigue and peer relationships in children and adolescents with chronic pain.
METHODS: The baseline network was estimated using a Gaussian graphical model with regularized partial correlations (N = 744). Cross-lagged panel network models were used to examine autoregressive and cross-lagged associations from baseline to 12 months (n = 357) and 24 months (n = 186) among youth with persistent chronic pain.
RESULTS: Pain interference had the highest cross-sectional strength centrality, followed by depressive and anxiety symptoms. Strongest baseline associations involved fatigue-pain interference, anxiety-depressive symptoms, pain catastrophizing-anxiety symptoms and sleep disturbance-pain interference. In the longitudinal models, pain interference showed the most consistent prospective pattern, with associations to later pain catastrophizing at 12 months and to later sleep disturbance and pain catastrophizing at 24 months. Depressive symptoms and pain catastrophizing were more often associated with prior levels of other domains.
CONCLUSION: Findings extend prior cross-sectional evidence by showing that pain interference was highly connected at baseline and prospectively involved among youth with persistent chronic pain. Pain interference may represent an informative functional domain for understanding how pain-related, psychological and physical difficulties are organized over time, supporting the clinical relevance of assessing interference with daily functioning.
SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: This study extends paediatric chronic pain research by examining cross-sectional and longitudinal associations among pain-related, psychological, physical and social domains. Pain interference showed the highest connectivity at baseline and was consistently involved in prospective associations, particularly with pain catastrophizing and sleep disturbance. These findings highlight multidomain assessment and suggest that interference with daily functioning may help identify broader pain-related difficulties that could otherwise be missed.

articles.title: Discordance Between aPTT and Anti-Xa and Its Association with Hemorrhagic Complications Among ECMO Patients.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine whether discordance between activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and anti-factor Xa (anti-Xa) is associated with hemorrhage or thrombosis among adults supported with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and to identify characteristics associated with discordance.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: High-volume ECMO center.
PARTICIPANTS: One hundred thirteen ECMO patients receiving heparin with time-matched aPTT and anti-Xa measurements.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Activated partial thromboplastin time and anti-Xa pairs were classified as concordant or discordant using a linear mixed-effects model with patient-specific random intercepts. Pairs outside the model-derived 95% prediction interval were classified as either aPTT > anti-Xa or aPTT < anti-Xa discordance. Associations between discordance and composite hemorrhagic or thrombotic complications were evaluated using time-varying Cox proportional hazards models. Among 571 paired assays, 94 (16.5%) were discordant. Seventy-seven patients (68.1%) remained concordant, whereas aPTT > anti-Xa discordance developed in 17 (15.0%) and aPTT < anti-Xa discordance developed in 18 (15.9%). Patients with aPTT > anti-Xa discordance had a significantly greater hemorrhage hazard than concordant patients in unadjusted analysis (hazard ratio, 14.85; 95% confidence interval, 3.10-71.05; p = 0.0007).
