The primary endpoint was DD detected at one or more scheduled ICU assessments, including day 1, defined as quiet-breathing diaphragm excursion ≤ 10 mm on bedside ultrasound. Logistic regression estimated odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with adjustment for age, sex, Charlson comorbidity index, SOFA score, mechanical ventilation, and surgery.
RESULTS: Overall, 126 of 221 patients (57.0%; 95% CI 50.4%-63.4%) had DD detected at least once. The proportions with DD were 0.0% (95% CI 0.0%-43.4%) among 5 underweight patients, 48.0% (95% CI 38.3%-57.7%) among 98 normal-weight patients, 68.1% (95% CI 58.1%-76.6%) among 94 overweight patients, and 62.5% (95% CI 42.7%-78.8%) among 24 patients with obesity. Patients with DD had higher BMI than those without DD [25.40 (23.70-28.30) vs. 24.50 (21.50-26.40) kg/m²; P = 0.0018]. Each 1-kg/m² increase in BMI was associated with higher odds of DD in univariable analysis (OR = 1.116, 95% CI 1.034-1.204) and after prespecified adjustment (adjusted OR = 1.126, 95% CI 1.040-1.218).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher BMI was associated with greater odds of DD being detected during scheduled ICU assessments. Because the endpoint included DD present on day 1 and the study was observational, these findings should not be interpreted as showing that BMI causes incident DD. BMI may nevertheless identify patients in whom closer, context-aware respiratory-muscle assessment is warranted.

articles.title: Evidence-based clinical practice guideline for the prevention and management of phantom limb pain in patients undergoing amputation: a proposal.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is a common and distressing complication that occurs after limb amputation in a large proportion of amputees. Despite advancements in surgical and anesthetic techniques, current medical approaches have not established a universally effective strategy for preventing or controlling PLP. A multidisciplinary approach, together with early identification of risk factors, is essential to reduce both the incidence and severity of PLP.
OBJECTIVE: We aimed to propose an evidence-based clinical practice guideline for the prevention and management of phantom limb pain among patients undergoing amputation surgery.
METHODS: A comprehensive literature review was conducted, including systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and high-quality cohort studies published between 2015 and 2025. Evidence was graded using the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (CEBM) Levels of Evidence, and the Grade of Recommendation (GOR) was assigned accordingly. When high-level evidence was limited, expert consensus was incorporated into the recommendation process.
RESULTS: A total of 24 studies were included in the proposed guideline development. High-level evidence supports non-pharmacologic interventions, particularly the combination of mirror therapy, phantom exercises, and graded motor imagery (LOE 1a, GOR A). Preoperative gabapentin combined with intraoperative regional anesthesia was effective in reducing the occurrence of PLP. Surgical techniques such as targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) and cryoneurolysis demonstrated beneficial effects in prevention and management. Peripheral nerve blocks and epidural analgesia were identified as optimal strategies for perioperative pain control. Neuromodulation, memantine, and calcitonin may be considered for acute or refractory PLP, whereas opioids should be reserved as last-line options due to safety concerns.
CONCLUSION: Effective management of PLP requires proactive prevention strategies integrating preoperative psychological support, pharmacologic prophylaxis, regional anesthesia techniques, and selected surgical interventions. Implementation of these evidence-based recommendations may reduce the burden and improve outcomes for patients undergoing amputation.

articles.title: High-risk ≠ mandatory prophylaxis: a real-world study of 274 PVP patients who omitted antimicrobial prophylaxis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgical site infections (SSIs) following percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) are infrequent but can have serious consequences. Current guidelines suggest that antimicrobial prophylaxis "may be considered" for high-risk patients undergoing PVP due to the implantation of bone cement. However, in practice, this conditional recommendation is often misinterpreted as a requirement, resulting in unnecessary antibiotic use. This study aimed to assess the safety of omitting antimicrobial prophylaxis in high-risk PVP patients.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis of data from patients who underwent PVP at a tertiary hospital between January 2024 and January 2026. These patients did not receive preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis and had at least 90 days of follow-up. The decision to omit prophylaxis was made by a clinical pharmacist during a preoperative multidisciplinary team (MDT) evaluation. This decision was based on the absence of active infection, indicated by no fever, no identifiable infectious focus, and normal procalcitonin levels when measured. The primary outcome was a 90-day SSI, defined by US CDC criteria, which includes a 90-day surveillance window for procedures involving implant placement. Postoperative follow-up was conducted via telephone, and patients were instructed to return immediately if they experienced wound redness, purulent discharge, fever, or any other signs of infection.
RESULTS: The percentage of PVP procedures performed without antimicrobial prophylaxis rose from 52.2% (117/224) in 2024 to 66.3% (136/205) in 2025, and further increased to 87.5% (21/24) by January 2026. Throughout the study period (January 2024-January 2026), 274 PVP patients did not receive preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis. Of these patients, 103 (37.6%) were aged 75 or older, 35 (12.8%) had diabetes mellitus, 21 (7.7%) had malignancy, 79 (28.8%) had chronic pulmonary disease, and 2 (0.7%) had hypoalbuminaemia. Three patients had both diabetes and malignancy. All 274 patients completed a 90-day follow-up, and none developed a surgical site infection. The 90-day SSI rate was 0% (95% CI 0-1.35%).
CONCLUSIONS: Once active infection is definitively ruled out, antimicrobial prophylaxis can be safely omitted, even for patients with conventional risk factors like advanced age, diabetes, and malignancy. A multidisciplinary team (MDT) approach, led by pharmacists and centered on confirming the absence of active infection, offers a safe and practical strategy for managing perioperative antimicrobial use.

articles.title: Assessing electrical bioimpedance across tissue levels in patients undergoing ultrasound-guided axillary brachial plexus block: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bioimpedance measures biological tissues' electrical resistance. Bioimpedance monitoring may improve axillary brachial plexus block by providing real-time feedback alongside ultrasound guidance and nerve stimulation while performing ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia. However, there is a paucity of research examining bioimpedance fluctuations. This study aims to assess bioimpedance changes across various tissue types during an axillary brachial plexus block, characterize these changes, and explore their potential supportive role in tissue identification.
METHODS: This prospective, exploratory observational study included patients undergoing axillary brachial plexus block for upper-limb surgical procedures. Before the procedure, patients received 50 µg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam, with continuous standard monitoring. An anesthesiologist performed a nerve block under ultrasound guidance using nerve stimulation in a sentinel model (0.1 ms, 0.5 mA, 2 Hz) with a nerve stimulator device that continuously displayed bioimpedance. An assistant administered the local anesthetic, while another, blinded to the study, recorded bioimpedance values across subcutaneous tissue, muscle, fascia, and at the proximity of the nerves. A linear mixed model was fitted to assess bioimpedance across tissue types, treating tissue type as a fixed effect and including subject-level random effects to account for within-subject correlation and individual variability. Statistical analysis was conducted using STATA-18.
RESULTS: Among 80 participants (average age: 53.1 ± 18.7 years), bioimpedance measures were statistically significantly different across the pre-specified tissue types. The percentage change in bioimpedance from subcutaneous tissue to muscle was 4.18 ± 14.01, to fascia was 10.47 ± 22.62, to the radial nerve was 15.82 ± 15.14, and to the median nerve was 20.81 ± 13.21. An apparent decrease in bioimpedance was observed from the subcutaneous tissue to the median nerve. Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons showed significant (p < 0.01) differences in this change among various tissue types and nerves. No complications (i.e., intraneural/intravascular injections) were detected.
CONCLUSION: The observed trend demonstrates a consistent reduction in bioimpedance as the needle advances toward nerves. Using bioimpedance monitoring could improve nerve block accuracy by providing an extra parameter for guiding needle placement through tissue layers.

articles.title: Neonatal sevoflurane exposures induced cognitive impairment via Satb2-mediated synaptic deficits.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2 (Satb2) is a DNA binding protein, and involved in transcription regulation and chromatin remodeling. Studies demonstrated that the absence of Satb2 mediated cognitive impairments in humans and rodents. Moreover, animal research reported that neonatal exposure to sevoflurane induced cognitive dysfunction in adolescent period, along with damage of synaptic plasticity, but the mechanisms are still not clear. Herein, we aimed to determine the role of Satb2 in neurotoxicity caused by sevoflurane.
METHODS: A total of 254 neonatal male Sprague-Dawley rats were used in this study. Neonatal rats were exposed to 30% O2 or 3.0% sevoflurane delivered in 30% O2 for 3 h on postnatal day 7 (P7). Cognitive function was evaluated through open field, Y maze, and novel object recognition tests from P28 to P35. The hippocampi were harvested on P14, P21, and P35. Effects of sevoflurane on Satb2, and synapse in the hippocampus were investigated by western blot, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and Golgi staining. To further screen key molecules, another batch of hippocampi were harvested immediately and 24 h after gas exposure, and subjected to RNA sequencing. Finally, Satb2 overexpression was induced by lentivirus injection into the lateral ventricle on P1, followed by gas exposure on P7. Next, some rats underwent behavioral tests on P28-P35. Hippocampi from another group of rats were harvested on P35 for Western blot, qRT-PCR, and Golgi staining.
RESULTS: Y maze test showed that sevoflurane reduced the spontaneous alternation ratio in young rats. Novel object recognition test also revealed that sevoflurane decreased recognition index, the entries, and duration in novel arm, along with prolonged the latency to novel arm. Persistent decrease in Satb2, postsynaptic density protein-95 (PSD95), and spine density were observed. Moreover, RNA sequencing also revealed the decrease in Satb2 mRNA caused by neonatal exposure to sevoflurane. Furthermore, we found that lentivirus (LV)-induced Satb2 overexpression partially restored the decreases in the PSD95, spine density, spontaneous alternation ratio, recognition index, the entries, and duration in novel arm, and the increase in latency to novel arm caused by sevoflurane exposure.
CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that decreased Satb2 may contribute to cognitive disorders by reducing PSD95 levels, resulting in synaptic deficits. Meanwhile, this emphasizes that Satb2 was a potential target to intervening cognitive impairment caused by sevoflurane exposure.

articles.title: Early trabecular bone remodeling and paraspinal muscle preservation after unilateral biportal endoscopic versus minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion for mild degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis: a retrospective comparative study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical and radiological outcomes of unilateral biportal endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (UBE-TLIF) and minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MIS-TLIF) in the treatment of single-level mild degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 80 patients with single-level mild degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis, including 40 patients treated with UBE-TLIF and 40 patients treated with MIS-TLIF. Perioperative parameters, visual analog scale (VAS) scores, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), modified MacNab scores, fusion rates, trabecular bone remodeling (TBR) at 3 months postoperatively, and multifidus atrophy and fat infiltration rates at 12 months postoperatively were compared between the two groups.
RESULTS: The UBE-TLIF group had significantly less intraoperative blood loss and shorter hospital stays, but longer operative times compared with the MIS-TLIF group (all P < 0.001). At 3 days postoperatively, the VAS score for low back pain was significantly lower in the UBE-TLIF group than in the MIS-TLIF group (2.98 ± 1.12 vs. 3.62 ± 1.27, P = 0.018), whereas no significant differences were observed between groups in VAS scores at the remaining time points or in ODI scores (all P > 0.05). The UBE-TLIF group showed significantly higher TBR positivity at 3 months and a higher fusion rate at 6 months postoperatively compared with the MIS-TLIF group (P < 0.05), while no significant difference in fusion rate was observed at 12 months. At 12 months postoperatively, the multifidus atrophy rate (29.50 ± 7.72% vs. 34.04 ± 10.55%, P = 0.031) and fat infiltration rate (34.85 ± 7.69% vs. 38.19 ± 6.02%, P = 0.033) were both significantly lower in the UBE-TLIF group than in the MIS-TLIF group.
CONCLUSION: Both UBE-TLIF and MIS-TLIF achieved comparable clinical outcomes. UBE-TLIF was associated with less blood loss, shorter hospitalization, lower back-pain VAS at postoperative day 3, higher early TBR positivity, and less multifidus degeneration on 12-month MRI, but required a longer operative time. The clinical relevance of the observed radiological and muscle-related differences requires confirmation in prospective studies with longer follow-up.

articles.title: Early acute kidney injury after pulmonary endarterectomy: incidence, associated perioperative factors, and early outcome in a single-centre retrospective cohort.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) is the standard treatment for operable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, but factors associated with acute kidney injury (AKI) remain uncertain. We examined perioperative factors associated with AKI within 48 h and evaluated an exploratory early postoperative risk-identification model.
METHODS: We screened 126 consecutive adults with operable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension who underwent PEA at a tertiary referral centre between January 2018 and December 2020. Eight met predefined exclusion criteria and one of 118 eligible patients had no assessable renal criterion. AKI was defined by the 2012 Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes serum creatinine and urine-output criteria. Eleven patients whose status could not be determined, because one criterion was negative and the other unavailable, were excluded, leaving 106 for analysis. Multiple imputation assessed missing-covariate sensitivity, and the combined model underwent bootstrap validation, calibration and decision-curve analysis.
RESULTS: AKI occurred in 42 of 106 adults (39.6%): 35 stage 1, four stage 2 and three stage 3; alternative handling of the indeterminate cases gave incidences between 35.9% and 45.3%. When extracorporeal circulation (ECC), deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and aortic cross-clamp durations were analysed together, only ECC duration remained independently associated with AKI (adjusted odds ratio 1.032 per minute, 95% confidence interval 1.012-1.052; p = 0.001). Age was the only independently associated preoperative variable (1.034 per year, 1.004-1.065; p = 0.027). An integrated model combining age (1.035 per year, 1.007-1.063; p = 0.014) and ECC duration (1.025 per minute, 1.009-1.041; p = 0.003) gave apparent and optimism-corrected areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.718 and 0.706, with a calibration slope of 0.97. Albumin at intensive care unit admission was inversely associated with AKI in univariable analysis but was not independently associated in the integrated model (p = 0.129) and improved neither fit nor discrimination. Haemodynamic improvement was similar in both groups, but 30-day mortality was higher among patients with AKI (14.3% vs. 0%; p = 0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: Among adults undergoing PEA for operable chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, longer ECC duration and older age were associated with AKI within 48 h. Similar haemodynamic recovery did not exclude renal injury. The model is exploratory and requires external validation.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07132619. Retrospectively registered 13 August 2025.

articles.title: Effect of SEEKflex-guided versus conventional intubation on hemodynamic responses in elderly hypertensive patients: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: In elderly patients with preexisting cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, laryngoscopy and tracheal intubation can provoke substantial hemodynamic disturbances, including hypertension and tachycardia, which may precipitate major cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events and even death. Therefore, the employment of a novel, safe, and straightforward intubation device is therefore of considerable clinical importance.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the effects of tracheal intubation guided by a novel tracheal tube kit (Safe Easy Endotracheal Kit-flexible; SEEKflex) versus a conventional stylet on hemodynamic parameters in elderly hypertensive patients during intubation.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This prospective, randomized study was conducted from August 2024 to November 2024 and included 80 elderly hypertensive patients scheduled for elective surgery requiring oral tracheal intubation at our hospital. All patients had American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status grades of II. Participants were randomly assigned, via a random number table, to one of two groups: the SEEKflex-guided intubation group (SEEKflex group) or the conventional stylet-shaped intubation group (Conventional group). Following intravenous induction of anesthesia, oral tracheal intubation was performed using the assigned device. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at T0 (before induction), T1 (after induction, before intubation), T2 (immediately after intubation), T3 (30 s after intubation), T4 (1 min after intubation), and T5 (3 min after intubation). Intubation time, first-attempt success rate, and incidence of intubation-related respiratory complications were also recorded.
RESULTS: Following intubation, MAP and HR increased from post-induction levels in both groups. At T3 and T4, the SEEKflex group exhibited significantly lower MAP and HR than the Conventional group (P < 0.05). The first-attempt intubation success rate was higher in the SEEKflex group (P < 0.05), although intubation time was shorter in the Conventional group (23.69 ± 4.70 s vs. 33.80 ± 3.32 s, P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed in SpO₂ levels or rates of post-intubation complications between the two groups.
CONCLUSIONS: The use of the SEEKflex for guiding tracheal intubation attenuates the hemodynamic response to intubation and improves hemodynamic stability in elderly hypertensive patients, compared with a conventional stylet. The SEEKflex may be a suitable option for tracheal intubation in this patient population during general anesthesia.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ChiCTR2400087611 (Date: 2024.07.31).

articles.title: Chronic and Acute Low Back Pain After Spinal Anesthesia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
CONTEXT: Spinal anesthesia is commonly used for many surgical procedures because of its rapid onset and reliable anesthetic effects. Nevertheless, postoperative lower back pain (LBP) remains a frequent complication, with reported rates varying substantially across the literature. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize the available evidence and estimate the overall incidence of both short-term acute and long-term persistent LBP following spinal anesthesia.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Major databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science, were systematically searched to identify studies of LBP after spinal anesthesia. Following data extraction, relevant outcomes were pooled for analysis. Given the expected methodological heterogeneity across studies, a random-effects model was used for data synthesis. Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using Cochran's Q test and the I2 statistic. Publication bias was assessed using funnel-plot inspection and established statistical methods.
RESULTS: The review included 15 studies comprising 4,478 patients, of which 11 provided sufficient data for meta-analysis. The pooled overall rate of postprocedural LBP was 25.65% (95% CI: 19.54% - 32.29%), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I2 = 96.84%). Subgroup analyses showed an acute LBP prevalence of 21.96% (95% CI: 16.01% - 28.56%) and a chronic LBP prevalence of 44.98% (95% CI: 26.95% - 63.73%). Marked heterogeneity persisted across these subgroups. Most included studies involved orthopedic, urologic, or obstetric/gynecologic surgery.Discussion: Back pain is frequently reported after spinal blocks during both short- and long-term recovery phases. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity among the primary studies precludes the establishment of a definitive causal relationship. Well-designed prospective studies using standardized assessment tools are needed to clarify the clinical implications of these findings.

articles.title: Occipital Nerve Stimulation in Headache Management: An Umbrella Review of Efficacy and Safety.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: For half the world's population, headaches represent a major health burden that cripples productivity and mental well-being. While newer CGRP-targeted drugs have shown promise for migraines, less is known about how neuromodulation techniques might help with other types of headaches. We designed this umbrella review to investigate how safe and effective occipital nerve stimulation (ONS) is for different headache disorders, and to grade the overall strength of the existing evidence.
METHODS: We looked through PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (from inception to November 12, 2025) for relevant systematic reviews. Two reviewers worked separately to select studies and extract data. We focused on pain intensity as the main outcome, but also looked at safety, patient satisfaction, and quality of life. We used AMSTAR 2 to assess the quality of the included studies.
RESULTS: A total of 207 records were identified, of which nine systematic reviews met the inclusion criteria. ONS was most frequently evaluated in migraine (n = 6), followed by occipital neuralgia (n = 4), cluster headache (n = 3), hemicrania continua (n = 3), SUNCT/SUNA (n = 2), paroxysmal hemicrania (n = 2), cervicogenic headache (n = 1), posttraumatic headache (n = 1), and C2-mediated occipital headache (n = 1).
CONCLUSION: Current evidence is insufficient to determine the overall effectiveness of occipital nerve stimulation (ONS) across different headache disorders. Review quality varied, and results differed by condition, with more favorable outcomes for occipital neuralgia and cluster headache. Findings for migraine remain inconsistent, and data for other disorders are preliminary. Hardware-related complications also remain a notable concern.

articles.title: Can the anesthetic management affect oncological outcome in lung cancer surgery?
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF THE REVIEW: Lung cancer surgery creates a vulnerable perioperative window where anesthetic and physiological interventions may modulate recurrence. This review evaluates the oncological impact of perioperative strategies in non-small-cell lung cancer, proposing a comprehensive 'oncoanesthesia care bundle'.
RECENT FINDINGS: Current clinical data expose a persistent gap between compelling preclinical rationales and observable clinical outcomes. The recent General Anesthetics in CAncer REsection Surgery (2026), a large-scale evaluation of propofol versus volatile anesthesia, enrolled mixed cancer cohorts and demonstrated no oncological advantage of propofol, underscoring that the ongoing Inhalational Gas Anesthesia and Propofol-based Total IntraVenous Anesthesia trial will provide the first adequately powered, lung cancer-specific evaluation. Similarly, prospective randomized data regarding regional anesthesia have failed to show a significant recurrence benefit in lung cancer surgery. For nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, the Adjuvant Low-dose ASpirin in Colorectal CAncer trial's recent biomarker-driven success in colorectal cancer highlights the urgent necessity for analogous molecularly tailored investigations in non-small-cell lung cancer. Beyond pharmacological agents, meticulous physiological optimization remains critical: lung-protective ventilation, restrictive-to-euvolemic fluid management, and maintaining normothermia are biologically coherent strategies that preserve the endothelial glycocalyx, optimize interstitial fluid pressure, and maintain natural killer cell function.
SUMMARY: Current clinical evidence does not justify selecting individual anesthetic agents solely for oncological benefit. Nevertheless, combining tailored pharmacological strategies, specifically opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, with meticulous physiological optimization into a structured 'oncoanesthesia care bundle' provides a biologically coherent, low-risk framework available for immediate implementation. Future oncological trials must shift from pragmatic pan-cancer designs toward large-scale, patient-, cancer-, and gene-expression-specific trial protocols to truly capture personalized oncological outcomes.

articles.title: Postoperative acute kidney injury in thoracic noncardiac surgery: incidence, impact on outcomes, risk and protective factors, and evolving preventive strategies.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) significantly impairs short- and long-term clinical outcomes after thoracic noncardiac surgery, including increased mortality and prolonged hospitalization. This review synthesizes current evidence on the incidence, prognostic impact, risk factors, and evolving preventive strategies for AKI in thoracic surgery.
RECENT FINDINGS: Intraoperative fluid imbalance and hypotension are robust, modifiable risk factors for AKI. While goal-directed fluid therapy and machine learning-based Acumen Hypotension Prediction Index (Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, California, USA) monitoring effectively optimize intraoperative hemodynamics and reduce hypotensive episodes, recent clinical trials and meta-analyses indicate they do not directly reduce postoperative AKI rates after general thoracic surgery. However, optimizing drug administration - such as continuous intravenous tacrolimus and shortened vancomycin duration - has demonstrated clinical benefit. Furthermore, evidence outside thoracic surgery demonstrates that the biomarker-guided Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes care bundle significantly decreases moderate-to-severe AKI in high-risk surgical populations, suggesting potential applicability in thoracic surgical care.
SUMMARY: Given the multifactorial etiology of AKI, single hemodynamic interventions alone are insufficient for prevention. Perioperative care should integrate multimodality strategies, including optimal fluid and pressure management, pharmacological stewardship, and high-risk screening with care bundles. Further studies are needed to establish tailored preventive protocols, particularly for high-risk thoracic procedures such as lung transplantation and pneumonectomy.

articles.title: Risk factors associated with the development of a catheter-related thrombosis in patients with critical illness: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: We sought to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis with the primary objective to identify prognostic factors associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Our secondary objective was to report the incidence of this entity.
SOURCES: We searched, MEDLINE® and Embase® from inception through 4 May 2024 for all studies in patients with critical illness that reported catheter-related thrombosis, with an updated search performed on 23 October 2025. We included English-language studies that described prognostic factors for developing a catheter-related thrombosis or reported the incidence of this complication in the critical care setting. Two authors performed citation screening and data extraction. We pooled adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) separately for prognostic factors using a random-effects model and inverse variance weighting. Risk of bias for individual studies was evaluated using the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool. We assessed certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations approach.
PRINCIPLE FINDINGS: We included 32 studies involving 11,943 patients. Identified prognostic variables with a moderate- or high-certainty association for developing a catheter-related thrombosis include increasing age (aOR per 10-yr increase, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.27; three studies; 1,594 patients; high certainty), trauma-related admission (aOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 0.93 to 2.34; three studies; 3,089 patients; high certainty), surgical-related admission (aOR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.77 to 3.52; three studies; 2,208 patients; aHR, 1.35; 95% CI, 0.60 to 3.02; two studies; 297 patients; high certainty), internal jugular insertion site as compared with other insertion sites (aOR, 3.76; 95% CI, 2.82 to 5.01; four studies; 4,681 patients; high certainty), single/double-lumen as compared with more lumens (aOR, 1.61; 95% CI, 0.82 to 3.13; three studies; 1,594 patients; moderate certainty), and peripheral insertion site (aOR, 2.30; 95% CI, 0.74 to 7.08; two studies; 264 patients; moderate certainty). The median incidence of catheter-related thrombosis was 13.3% [interquartile range, 3.7%-31.3%].
CONCLUSIONS: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we found that increasing age, surgical type admissions, large catheters, and factors potentially related with catheter duration were associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Furthermore, we identified significant variation in the reported rates of catheter-related thrombosis, with an average rate of approximately 1 in every 8 patients. When these identified risk factors are present, clinicians may consider more aggressive thromboprophylaxis regimens to better tailor prevention strategies to individual patient risk profiles.
STUDY REGISTRATION: Open Science Framework ( https://osf.io/5zvg2) ; first submitted 15 June 2024.

articles.title: Effect of sex on the relationship between perioperative risk factors and postoperative pulmonary complications after noncardiothoracic surgery in patients classified American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status III: a secondary analysis of a prospective multicentre cohort study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) importantly contribute to postoperative morbidity and mortality, particularly for patients classified American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status III. Whether PPC risk factors depend on sex remains unclear. We hypothesize that sex modifies the relationship between perioperative risk factors and PPCs in patients assigned an ASA III status undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia.
METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of prospective data from 1,202 patients undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery. We collected data on preoperative patient demographics, comorbidities, intraoperative physiology, medications, and procedure information. The primary outcome was a composite of PPCs by postoperative day 7. Mixed-effects linear models incorporated sex as main and interaction effect.
RESULTS: Age, upper abdominal surgery, and surgical duration significantly increased the odds of ≥ 1 PPC by postoperative day 7. Male patients presented a higher rate of ≥ 3 PPCs, and female patients received higher tidal volumes per predicted body weight and driving pressures. Sex did not significantly modify the relationship between perioperative factors and the primary outcome (no P < 0.05 for the interaction with sex). In the secondary analysis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) affected atelectasis more strongly in male than in female patients (relative odds ratio for female vs male patients, 0.27; 95% confidence interval, 0.13 to 0.57).
CONCLUSIONS: In patients classified ASA III undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia, perioperative factors are predominantly not modified by sex in their relationship to PPCs. The association between GERD and atelectasis in male patients could be explored in future prospective studies as a target for reducing PPCs.

articles.title: Impact of preoperative cardiology consultations on perioperative management in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cardiology consultations may be requested during preoperative anesthetic assessment before non-cardiac surgery. However, data regarding their impact on perioperative management are limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of preoperative cardiology consultations on perioperative patient management.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective, observational, single-center study in the Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care at Angers University Hospital from September 1st, 2024, to August 31st, 2025. All patients referred for cardiology assessment after the anesthetic consultation were included. The primary endpoint was any change in perioperative management, including specific preoperative cardiac treatment, postponement or cancellation of surgery, and modification of anesthetic or surgical protocols. The secondary endpoint was to assess adherence of preoperative cardiac evaluation to current guideline recommendations.
RESULTS: Among 9,621 preoperative anesthetic consultations, 138 (1%) patients were referred for cardiology assessment by the anesthesiologist and included in the study. 59 (43%) patients experienced a change in perioperative management. Of them, surgery was postponed in 52 (38%) patients, with a median delay of 81 [47-145] days, whereas only 6 patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention (angioplasty, valvuloplasty, or electrical cardioversion). A previously unknown cardiac condition was identified in 19 (15%) patients. 111 (80%) cardiology referrals were consistent with current recommendations.
CONCLUSION: In our study, preoperative cardiology consultations requested by an anesthesiologist were rare but frequently responsible for modification of perioperative management. These consultations often resulted in postponement of surgery, while only a small proportion of patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention.

articles.title: Acute postoperative pain in surgical patients with cognitive impairment: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute pain in the postoperative period and pre-existing cognitive impairment (CI) are both independently associated with increased postoperative adverse outcomes. Pre-existing cognitive impairment may interfere with the reporting, recognition, and treatment of pain in this population.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the impact of pre-existing cognitive impairment on pain and analgesic consumption after surgery in adults. MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched for randomized controlled trials and cohort studies for adults undergoing non-cardiac, emergency, or elective surgery until April 9, 2026. Surgical patients with pre-existing cognitive impairment were compared to cognitively intact peers. The primary outcomes assessed were subjective ratings of pain and analgesic consumption postoperatively. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence was rated by GRADE. Meta-analysis used standard mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies (37,918 patients) were included. Approximately one third (33%; 95% CI 0.25-0.41) of adult surgical patients screened positive for preoperative cognitive impairment. Subjective pain scores did not differ significantly between patients with and without cognitive impairment (Hedge's g: 0.11 (SD -0.15-0.36, I2 85.3%, T2 0.073). Patients with cognitive impairment had significantly less analgesic consumption than their cognitively intact counterparts (Cohen's d: 0.53 (0.29-0.76, I2 67.4%, T2 0.028).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite comparable pain scores, those with cognitive impairment received significantly less postoperative analgesia, raising concern for systematic under-recognition and undertreatment of pain. Increased awareness of this discrepancy and the use of standardized analgesia protocols may improve postoperative outcomes.
REGISTRATION: International Registry of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO:1117357).

articles.title: Renal Replacement Therapy in Cardiogenic Shock supported by microAxial Flow Pumps: A European multicentre study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Microaxial flow pumps (mAFP) improve hemodynamics and outcomes in myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (CS) but are associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). We aimed to determine the incidence and factors associated with RRT and evaluate its association with mortality in a real-world cohort of miscellaneous CS patients supported with mAFP.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentre registry including CS patients supported with mAFP across 11 European centres. The association between RRT and the primary outcome of 180-day all-cause mortality (with survival censored at heart transplantation or durable left ventricular assist device implantation) was assessed using a 1:1 propensity score-matched cohort. Factors associated with RRT were identified using multivariable logistic regression.
RESULTS: Among 1043 patients, 972 were included, of whom 340 (35.0%) required RRT. RRT was associated with higher 180-day all-cause mortality both before (Kaplan-Meier estimates, 59.7% vs. 35.2%; HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.67-2.49; p < 0.01) and after propensity score matching (59.0% vs. 41.4%; HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.14-1.92; p < 0.01); restricted mean survival difference -25.5 days, 95% CI - 39.9 to -10.2. Factors associated with RRT included BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² (adjusted OR [aOR] 1.69; 95% CI 1.15-2.46), baseline serum creatinine (per 20 µmol/L increase: aOR 1.18; 95% CI 1.12-1.24), norepinephrine use (aOR 1.72; 95% CI 1.19-2.49), and lactate ≥4 mmol/L at implantation (aOR 1.56; 95% CI 1.11-2.20).
CONCLUSIONS: In this large European registry of mAFP-supported CS, RRT was frequent and associated with increased 180-day mortality and greater shock severity.

articles.title: Perioperative management of patients with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery: A modified Delphi consensus study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Many patients present for surgery soon after concussion, when cerebral physiologic regulation may remain disturbed, and no evidence-based guideline or standardized consensus recommendations exist. We sought expert consensus for adults with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery.
METHODS: We conducted a two-round modified Delphi study (November 2025-March 2026). Round 1 items, drafted from a systematic literature search, included case vignettes. Experts identified by bibliographic screening, directories, and nomination rated items on a five-point Likert scale; "do not know" responses were excluded from the denominator. Consensus was defined a priori as 75% agreement or greater, and strong consensus as 85% or greater.
RESULTS: Thirty-five experts (33 anesthesiologists) from 17 countries completed both rounds; 13 of 16 Round 2 statements reached consensus. Agreement was unanimous for preoperative screening for concussion symptoms and neurologic red flags, and for avoidance of hypoxemia, abnormal carbon dioxide tension, sustained hypotension, and marked hypertension. Strong consensus supported generally deferring elective surgery until concussion symptoms resolve (97%), preoperative counseling (97%), structured follow-up (94%), and extended postoperative monitoring in higher-risk patients (91%). Consensus was not reached for regional anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care over general anesthesia (74%), electroencephalography-based depth of anesthesia monitoring (73%), or cautious long-acting neuraxial opioid use (69%). The panel did not define symptom resolution and established no symptom-independent waiting interval or concussion-specific numeric physiologic threshold.
CONCLUSIONS: This anesthesiology-led consensus supports symptom-guided timing, physiologic stability, counseling, and structured follow-up; anesthetic technique, electroencephalographic monitoring, and neuraxial opioid use remain unresolved. The statements form an expert-informed framework, not an evidence-based practice guideline.

articles.title: Regional Anesthesia Modalities for Spine Surgery: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This narrative review examines the evidence supporting regional and neuraxial analgesic techniques for spine surgery, with particular emphasis on interfascial plane blocks, peripheral regional techniques, and neuraxial analgesia.
RECENT FINDINGS: Randomized trials and meta-analyses suggest that regional analgesic techniques can reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption following spine surgery; however, the strength and consistency of these findings vary considerably. Reduction in postoperative nausea and vomiting is among the most consistent benefits. Neuraxial techniques may provide more profound and prolonged analgesia but are accompanied by the potential for more consequential adverse effects. Current evidence does not clearly establish the superiority of a single regional analgesic technique for spine surgery. Clinicians may benefit from developing technical proficiency in a limited repertoire of regional techniques and applying them at an anatomically appropriate level for the planned surgery.

articles.title: Effect of minimally invasive caries management with silver diammine fluoride on caries progression and subsequent need for dental general anaesthesia in children: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Silver diammine fluoride (SDF) has been reintroduced into paediatric dentistry for managing caries in high-risk patients. This study aimed to describe patient- and tooth-level outcomes following SDF-initiated caries management in children with early childhood caries at a German university dental centre. The primary outcome was subsequent dental general anaesthesia (DGA), and the secondary outcome was tooth-level clinical failure.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Clinical data were retrospectively extracted from the records of children aged 1-8 years who received 38% SDF between 2019 and 2020. Included patients had a high caries burden and/or limited cooperation with invasive chairside treatment. Tooth-level failure was classified as minor (reversible pulpitis or documented caries progression) or major (irreversible pulpitis or abscess). Patient-level outcomes were analysed descriptively. Tooth-level outcomes were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression, accounting for the clustering of multiple teeth within children.
RESULTS: A total of 52 patients (mean age 4.0 ± 1.5 years; mean dmft = 7.8 ± 3.7) with 304 SDF-treated primary teeth (ICDAS 3-5 lesions) were included. After a mean follow-up of 23.4 ± 12.5 months, 46 of 52 children (88.5%) were managed without DGA, while 6 (11.5%) underwent DGA. At the tooth level, 273 teeth (89.8%) remained clinically successful, whereas 31 teeth (10.2%) developed a major failure. No minor failures were documented. Of the teeth without major failure, 165 received no further restorative treatment, while 108 underwent subsequent minimally invasive restorative treatment as part of the staged treatment pathway.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective cohort, an SDF-initiated, minimally invasive treatment pathway was associated with favourable patient- and tooth-level outcomes. Initial caries stabilisation may allow time for cooperation to improve and subsequent restorative treatment to be performed without DGA. Comparative prospective studies are needed to determine the specific contribution of SDF.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: An SDF-initiated treatment pathway may support caries management in young children with a high caries burden or limited cooperation and may help postpone or potentially avoid DGA.

articles.title: Comparison of subarachnoid block using hyperbaric levobupivacaine plus fentanyl versus hyperbaric bupivacaine plus fentanyl in elective lower limb orthopaedic procedures: A randomized controlled study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Racemic bupivacaine is the reference agent for subarachnoid block, but its cardiotoxic potential has prompted interest in its S-enantiomer, levobupivacaine. We compared intrathecal hyperbaric levobupivacaine plus fentanyl with hyperbaric bupivacaine plus fentanyl in lower limb orthopaedic surgery.
METHODS: Eighty patients with American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I or II, aged 18-60 years, undergoing elective lower limb orthopaedic surgery were randomly allocated to 12.5 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric levobupivacaine with 25 µg fentanyl (Group A) or 12.5 mg of 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine with 25 µg fentanyl (Group B). The primary outcome was duration of analgesia; secondary outcomes were block characteristics, haemodynamic variables, and complications.
RESULTS: Seventy-nine patients were analysed (Group A = 40, Group B = 39). Duration of analgesia was comparable (192.3 ± 40.0 vs. 181.6 ± 40.6 min; mean difference 10.7 min, 95% CI-7.4 to 28.7; p = 0.243). Group A had slower onset of complete motor block and longer time to peak sensory level (p < 0.05), but faster motor recovery (76.4 ± 14.1 vs. 119.0 ± 14.8 min; p < 0.001). Postoperative pain scores and rescue analgesic requirements were lower in Group A, and complications occurred only in Group B (p = 0.005). Haemodynamic profiles were comparable.
CONCLUSION: Hyperbaric levobupivacaine with fentanyl has a slower onset, a comparable duration of analgesia, and faster motor recovery than hyperbaric bupivacaine with fentanyl, and is an effective alternative for lower limb orthopaedic surgery.

articles.title: Effectiveness and safety of lumbar erector spinae plane block versus no locoregional block in hip surgery: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided regional anaesthesia in hip surgery has been shown to reduce the need for opioids and conventional analgesics, facilitate ambulation and early recovery, improve respiratory dynamics, and reduce the incidence of venous thrombosis and pneumonia. Lumbar erector spinae plane block (L-ESPB) has been put forward as a novel ultrasound-guided locoregional technique to relieve pain in hip surgery; however, the supporting evidence remains scarce.
OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to provide evidence on the role of L-ESPB in perioperative pain management during hip surgery. We hypothesized that patients receiving L-ESPB compared to no nerve block would require fewer opioids and experience less pain after hip surgery. The primary outcome was the difference in pain intensity between the L-ESPB group and the control group measured at rest at 2 h postoperatively using the visual analogue scale (VAS). We compared postoperative analgesic needs and opioid consumption in both groups, assessed the technical difficulty involved in performing L-ESPB, and recorded any side effects in both treatment arms. Finally, we evaluated the level of patient satisfaction.
DESIGN: This is a pragmatic, single-centre, parallel-group randomized controlled trial in 180 patients.
SETTING: Patients seen at a tertiary care hospital were recruited between June 2024 and May 2025.
PATIENTS: Inclusion criteria were: age >18 years (irrespective of sex), scheduled for hip surgery, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class I to III, willing to sign the study informed consent form, and able to understand and use the VAS for pain assessment. Exclusion criteria were: contraindications for the study technique or drugs used, inability to administer the block due to technical barriers, severe cognitive impairment or documented mental disabilities, and current enrolment in another clinical trial.
INTERVENTION: Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either ultrasound-guided L-ESPB or conventional intravenous analgesia. A total of 180 patients (n = 90, 50% in each group) were enrolled. Data analysis was performed using SPSS.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was resting pain intensity measured using the VAS at 2 h postoperatively.
RESULTS: At 2 h postoperatively, resting VAS pain scores did not differ between groups (L-ESPB [1.81 ± 1.81]; controls: [1.76 ± 1.28]; p = [p = 0.99]).Resting pain scores were slightly lower in the L-ESPB group at 6 and 12 h; however, the magnitude of the difference was small and did not result in reduced postoperative opioid consumption or rescue analgesic requirements. One patient in the L-ESPB group developed a high neuraxial block requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation for approximately 6 h, with full recovery and no sequelae.
CONCLUSIONS: Lumbar ESPB did not reduce resting pain at 2 h after hip surgery and did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption. Small reductions in resting pain scores at 6 and 12 h were observed, but their clinical relevance is uncertain. Our results do not support routine L-ESPB as a standard analgesic technique for unselected hip surgery patients receiving multimodal analgesia. Further research into this topic is warranted.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06567522; https://www.
CLINICALTRIALS: gov/study/NCT06567522.
STUDY PROTOCOL: doi: https://doi.org/10.2196/75854.

articles.title: Erector spinae block and its impact on opioid consumption during the postoperative period following laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is frequently associated with moderate postoperative pain and opioid requirements despite its minimally invasive approach. Evidence regarding erector spinae plane block (ESPB) and postoperative outcomes in Latin American populations remains limited.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between ESPB use and postoperative pain, opioid consumption, and opioid-related adverse events after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with particular emphasis on referred shoulder pain.
METHODS: This prospective analytical cohort study included 176 adults undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy at a tertiary referral center in Colombia (2023-2026). Of these, 84 received ESPB and 92 received standard analgesia. Pain was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale at 5, 60 minutes, and 6, 12, and 24 hours postoperatively. Opioid consumption was converted to morphine milligram equivalents (MME), and multivariable regression analyses were performed.
RESULTS: ESPB use was associated with lower pain scores at all postoperative time points (p<0.001), reduced referred shoulder pain at 12 hours (8.4% vs. 53.3%, p<0.001), lower opioid consumption (β = -3.03 MME; p<0.001), and fewer episodes of postoperative nausea and vomiting.
CONCLUSION: ESPB use was associated with improved postoperative analgesia, reduced opioid consumption, and a lower incidence of referred shoulder pain during the first 24 hours. These observational findings provide prospective evidence from clinical practice in Colombia.

articles.title: Ultrasound-guided intra-articular steroid injection versus combined suprascapular and axillary nerve block in adhesive capsulitis: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection with combined suprascapular and axillary nerve block for pain and functional outcomes in primary adhesive capsulitis.
METHODS: In this single-center, assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial, 80 patients were allocated equally to ultrasound-guided intra-articular methylprednisolone (Group A) or combined ultrasound-guided suprascapular and axillary nerve blocks with methylprednisolone and bupivacaine (Group B). Both groups were prescribed home exercises. The primary outcome was baseline-to-week-12 change in visual analog scale (VAS; 0-10) pain scores. Secondary outcomes included the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI; 0-100), shoulder range of motion, and quality of life.
RESULTS: All 80 patients were included. Mean VAS reductions were 5.27 points in Group A and 5.64 in Group B. The additional Group B reduction was 0.37 points (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.23-0.51; p < 0.001). Mean SPADI reductions were 37.93 and 41.58 points, respectively, with an additional Group B reduction of 3.65 points (95% CI 3.38-3.92; p < 0.001). Both differences were below externally selected, post hoc clinical benchmarks of 1.0 VAS point and 10 SPADI points. Range-of-motion gains varied by movement. Quality-of-life changes could not be established because assessment timing was unverified. No serious adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: Both interventions were associated with improvements over 12 weeks. Combined blocks provided small additional reductions in pain and disability, but a clinically important advantage was not demonstrated.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: IRCT20240901062926N1.

articles.title: Pulsed Radiofrequency in Postherpetic Neuralgia: Predictors of Treatment Response from a Doubly Robust Propensity-Weighted Real-World Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is a debilitating complication of herpes zoster. Evidence supporting pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) in established chronic PHN remains limited, with inadequate adjustment for baseline confounders. We evaluated the association between PRF and treatment success and identified predictors of treatment response.
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 982 patients with PHN (pain persisting ≥ 12 weeks after rash onset) were analyzed. Patients who underwent PRF (n = 504)-targeting the dorsal root ganglion, the Gasserian ganglion, or involved peripheral nerves-were compared with controls who did not undergo PRF at any time during the study period and who received standard pharmacological and non-PRF interventional management (n = 478). Propensity score-based overlap weighting (ATO) balanced 29 baseline covariates. The primary outcome was treatment success at 12 weeks (≥ 2-point reduction on the 11-point numeric rating scale (NRS)). Effects were estimated using doubly robust estimation.
RESULTS: After ATO adjustment, all covariates achieved adequate balance (standardized mean differences < 0.1). Treatment success at 12 weeks was 63.0% (PRF) versus 52.1% (control; doubly robust OR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.12-2.25; P = .009). Greater mean pain reduction was observed at 4 weeks (P = .040) but not sustained thereafter. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested PRF was more effective in patients with dysesthesia, without allodynia, and not receiving pregabalin or tramadol.
CONCLUSIONS: PRF provides clinically meaningful, albeit time-limited, pain reduction in PHN patients. Exploratory findings suggest that treatment response may vary according to sensory phenotype and pharmacological profile, underscoring the importance of profile-guided patient selection.

articles.title: Buttress plate augmentation offers no clear clinical advantage over compression screws alone for Hoffa fractures: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare clinical, functional, and perioperative outcomes after fixation of Hoffa fractures using buttress plate augmentation with compression screws versus compression screws alone.
METHODS: PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through 31 July 2026 for randomized or nonrandomized comparative studies of adults. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using ROBINS-I. Random-effects meta-analysis used restricted maximum likelihood estimation and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO.
RESULTS: Four nonrandomized studies involving 143 patients (BPCS, 63; CS, 80) were included. BPCS was associated with greater knee range of motion at 4 months (mean difference [MD], 10.85°; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.69-20.02; p = 0.04; I² = 0%) and longer operative time (MD, 23.03 min; 95% CI, 7.45-38.62; p = 0.02; I² = 84%). No significant differences were found in range of motion at ≥ 12 months, early or late functional knee scores, blood loss, or time to union. Overall risk of bias was moderate in one study and serious in three.
CONCLUSION: Limited observational evidence suggests that buttress plate augmentation may improve early knee motion but prolongs operative time, without a demonstrated durable functional or union advantage. Because the evidence is sparse and at substantial risk of bias, fixation should be individualized according to fracture characteristics and intraoperative stability.

articles.title: Emergence Delirium and Agitation in Older Adults After General Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Evidence Map of Incidence and Perioperative Risk Factors.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: In recent years, emergence delirium and emergence agitation (ED/EA) have become more clinically significant perioperative brain health phenomena in older adults after a period of early recovery following general anesthesia. Nevertheless, the existing evidence on ED/EA remains fragmented across different definitions, and the role of modifiable perioperative factors remains incompletely defined. We aimed to estimate the incidence of ED/EA in elderly people after general anesthesia, synthesize the adjusted risk-factor evidence, and identify the clinically relevant perioperative domain.
DESIGN: The systematic review and meta-analysis.
METHODS: Searches in PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and Embase were performed from inception to April 30, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled older surgical patients undergoing general anesthesia and reported ED, PACU delirium, or emergence agitation during emergence or PACU stay. Incidence was pooled using logit-transformed random-effects models. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were pooled when at least two clinically comparable estimates were available; heterogeneous or single-study factors were summarized by evidence mapping.
FINDINGS: Twelve reports representing eight independent cohorts or study populations were included. The main incidence analysis included seven independent cohorts with 3601 patients and 1161 ED/EA events, yielding a pooled incidence of 29.7% (95% CI: 23.4%-36.8%). Increasing age (OR = 1.07 per year, 95% CI: 1.04-1.10) and higher early recovery pain score were the most reproducible risk signals. In the NRS-only sensitivity analysis, each one-point increase in pain score was associated with a 29% higher risk of ED/EA (OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.21-1.37), with no observed heterogeneity. Nutritional risk, hypothermia, catheter-related discomfort, urinary catheterization, preoperative anxiety, and selected anesthetic or non-pharmacological interventions emerged as clinically relevant but insufficiently homogeneous candidate factors.
CONCLUSIONS: ED/EA affects approximately one-third of older adults during early recovery after general anesthesia. Current reproducible evidence supports age and early recovery pain as stable risk indicators, while evidence mapping highlights nutrition, temperature management, catheter-related factors and perioperative comfort as promising targets for future prospective prevention studies.

articles.title: Reducing breakthrough pain during labour analgesia: a quality improvement project using PDSA cycles.
articles.abstract: Breakthrough pain during labour analgesia represents a common clinical issue, leading to maternal dissatisfaction and various potential obstetric complications. Despite the high prevalence of epidural labour analgesia, baseline data from our institution indicates a breakthrough pain incidence rate as high as 24%, suggesting significant scope for improvement in analgesic quality. This project aims to substantially reduce the incidence of breakthrough pain during labour analgesia from the baseline level of 24% through a structured Quality Improvement (QI) initiative. Within the anaesthesia department of a large obstetrics and gynaecology hospital, we applied the Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle methodology. Through root cause analysis, we identified three key drivers: inadequate risk identification, suboptimal analgesia initiation protocols and inappropriate maintenance strategies. Based on these findings, we designed a suite of combined interventions and implemented them in phases across three consecutive PDSA cycles. Interventions included establishing a structured risk assessment model, standardising communication protocols, promoting evidence-based advanced techniques and staff training. The baseline incidence of breakthrough pain was 24% (64 out of 264 mothers). Following intervention implementation, the breakthrough pain incidence significantly decreased to 7.1% (29 out of 406 women), meeting the project target (χ²=22.63, p<0.01). Systematic application of the PDSA cycle effectively reduced breakthrough pain during labour analgesia. This project provides a replicable methodological framework and a bundle of effective interventions for other institutions aiming to optimise perinatal analgesia quality.

articles.title: Prospective Bedside Management of Post-Surgical Tracheal Granulation in Older Adults With Cicatricial Tracheal Stenosis.
articles.abstract: Portable otoscope-guided bedside management safely and effectively removes post-surgical tracheal granulation in elderly patients with cicatricial tracheal stenosis, enabling frequent bedside airway maintenance without operating-room bronchoscopy or general anesthesia.

articles.title: Balance between chronological aging and functional reserve: Clinical value of age/mFI-5 ratio in prognostic prediction for elderly brain tumor surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Both advanced age and frailty influence postoperative outcomes in elderly brain tumor patients, but their interaction remains underexplored. We introduced the age/mFI-5 ratio (AMR), a novel composite indicator, and assessed its predictive value for adverse outcomes after brain tumor surgery.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included elderly patients who underwent brain tumor resection at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (January 2023-January 2024). The optimal AMR cutoff was determined by the maximum Youden index, dividing patients into low- and high-AMR groups. Baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes were compared. Univariate and multivariable logistic regressions identified independent predictors of adverse prognosis, and ROC analysis compared AMR with age and mFI-5 alone.
RESULTS: Among 160 patients, the optimal AMR cutoff was 50. The low-AMR group had significantly higher rates of all adverse outcomes (all P < 0.05). Low AMR independently predicted adverse prognosis (OR = 16.17, 95% CI 6.27-41.72, P < 0.001) and was strongly associated with reoperation (adjusted OR = 23.27), complications (8.28), eLOS (10.95), and unfavorable discharge (34.52) (all P < 0.001). AMR showed superior AUC (0.846) versus age (0.561) and mFI-5 (0.795).
CONCLUSIONS: AMR with a cutoff of 50 is a simple, readily available, and independent predictor of adverse postoperative outcomes in elderly brain tumor surgery patients. It outperforms age or frailty alone by capturing their synergistic effect, and routine calculation could potentially aid preoperative risk stratification and guide individualized perioperative care. However, external validation in an independent cohort is required before AMR can be recommended for routine clinical use.

articles.title: Intrathecal Hydromorphone Combined with Transversalis Fascia Plane Block versus Patient-Conmintravenous Analgesia After Caesarean Delivery: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Suboptimal analgesia after caesarean delivery delays recovery. Intrathecal hydromorphone and the transversalis fascia plane (TFP) block have each been proposed within multimodal analgesia, but a composite regimen omitting routine patient-controlled analgesia (PCIA) has not been compared with conventional intravenous PCIA.
METHODS: Eighty women undergoing elective lower uterine segment caesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia (March 2025 to September 2025) were randomly assigned 1:1 to intrathecal ropivacaine 10 mg with hydromorphone 50 µg, bilateral transversalis fascia plane (TFP) block (0.375% ropivacaine 20 mL per side) and no routine PCIA (n=40), or to intrathecal ropivacaine 10 mg alone followed by PCIA with sufentanil 1 µg/mL (n=40). The registered primary outcome analysed here was pain at rest and with activity over 48 h, tested with group × time repeated-measures analysis of variance. Secondary outcomes were protocol-defined rescue analgesia, adverse reactions, time to first ambulation, lactation initiation and satisfaction.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable (all standardised differences ≤0.18). The group × time interaction was significant for pain at rest (P=0.013) and with activity (P=0.019), and pain scores were lower in the hydromorphone-TFP arm at all five time points (mean difference 0.6-0.9 points; all P<0.001). Protocol-defined rescue analgesia was required by 10.0% versus 37.5% (risk ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.10-0.73; P=0.004). Nausea/vomiting (12.5% vs 27.5%; P=0.094) and pruritus (7.5% vs 20.0%; P=0.105) did not differ, and no respiratory depression occurred. Ambulation (-5.3 h, 95% CI -7.0 to -3.6), lactation (-5.7 h, 95% CI -7.8 to -3.6) and satisfaction (+1.7 points, 95% CI 1.3-2.1) also favoured the hydromorphone-TFP arm (P<0.001).
CONCLUSION: A composite regimen of intrathecal hydromorphone and bilateral TFP block without routine PCIA reduced pain scores and rescue analgesia requirements and shortened time to recovery milestones compared with sufentanil PCIA.

articles.title: Impact of Immigration Status on Epidural Analgesia for Management of Labor and Delivery Pain Among Women of Mexican Descent in Colorado.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Epidural analgesia, also named neuraxial analgesia, is the most common strategy to decrease labor and delivery pain. Approximately 70-75% of births in the United States use this method. In the United States, racial/ethnic differences exist for epidural use, with non-Hispanic White women having the highest rates of epidural use and Hispanic-Mexican women having the lowest. Although immigration status has been shown to impact epidural use in Europe, there is limited evidence of the impact of immigration status on epidural use among pregnant women in the United States.
PURPOSE: The objective of this study was to determine whether immigration status influences the likelihood of using epidural analgesia for pain relief among Hispanic-Mexican women in Colorado.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: De-identified data from the Colorado birth certificate database was collected for nulliparous women aged 18-35 years for all singleton births from 2007-2023. Odds of epidural analgesia were calculated for Hispanic-Mexican women compared to non-Hispanic White women and for Hispanic women born in Mexico compared to Hispanic-Mexican women born in the United States using logistic regression models adjusted for maternal age, education, income, payor status, attendant type, access to prenatal care, labor induction, and gestational age at delivery.
RESULTS: 858,716 births were included in the analyses, of which 178,595 (21%) were among Hispanic-Mexican women. Among Hispanic-Mexican women, the odds of having epidural analgesia use were less than non-Hispanic White women (67% vs 76%) (OR: 0.73, 95% CI 0.70, 0.75). In addition, the odds of epidural analgesia for Hispanic women born in Mexico were half those of Hispanic-Mexican women born in the United States (58% vs 75%) (OR: 0.53, 95% CI 0.50, 0.56).
CONCLUSIONS: In Colorado, Hispanic women born in Mexico were half as likely to use epidural analgesia for pain relief during childbirth than Hispanic-Mexican women born in the United States.

articles.title: Comparison of Serratus Posterior Superior Intercostal Plane Block and Pectoral Nerve Block II for Postoperative Analgesia Following Modified Radical Mastectomy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: To compare the postoperative analgesic efficacy of the serratus posterior superior intercostal plane (SPSIP) block and pectoral nerve block II (PECS II) in patients undergoing unilateral modified radical mastectomy (MRM). Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 100 patients who underwent unilateral MRM and received either an SPSIP block (n = 34) or a PECS II block (n = 66). The primary outcome was the time from extubation to the first administration of rescue analgesia. Secondary outcomes included Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) pain scores at 1, 4, 8, and 12 h postoperatively, the maximum NRS pain score, and cumulative opioid consumption within the first 24 postoperative hours. The primary outcome was analyzed using a generalized linear model with a gamma distribution and log-link function adjusted for operative duration. A sensitivity analysis additionally adjusted for age, body mass index, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status, and smoking status. Results: Among 100 patients (SPSIP, n = 34; PECS II, n = 66), operative duration was longer in the PECS II group (p < 0.001). Time to first rescue analgesia was longer with SPSIP (7.5 [5.0-8.8] vs. 5.0 [3.0-8.0] h; p = 0.004), but the difference was not significant after adjustment for operative duration (exp(B) = 1.21, 95% CI 0.98-1.49; p = 0.077) or additional covariates (exp(B) = 1.17, 95% CI 0.94-1.46; p = 0.153). NRS scores were lower with SPSIP at 1 h (p < 0.001) and with PECS II at 8 and 12 h (Holm-adjusted p = 0.013 and p < 0.001). Twenty-four-hour tramadol consumption was similar (p = 0.922). No block-related complications were documented. Conclusions: After adjustment for operative duration, the longer time to first rescue analgesia observed in the SPSIP group did not retain statistical significance, and a similar result was obtained in the sensitivity analysis. The findings should be interpreted cautiously in view of the retrospective design and limited sample size.

articles.title: Ciprofol-Based Total Intravenous Anesthesia During Pediatric Laparoscopic Surgery: A Double-Blind, Randomized Controlled, Non-Inferiority Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, randomized controlled trial evaluated whether ciprofol is non-inferior to propofol as the primary agent for total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) in pediatric laparoscopic surgery, with respect to extubation time and safety profile.
METHODS: Children aged 2-12 years (ASA I-II) undergoing laparoscopic surgery were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ciprofol or propofol for TIVA. The primary outcome was time to extubation, with a predefined non-inferiority margin (Δ) of 4.8 minutes. Secondary outcomes included recovery metrics, emergence delirium, pain scores, hemodynamic profiles, and safety indicators.
RESULTS: A total of 86 children (43 per group) were enrolled. Extubation time was 17.3±4.9 min in the ciprofol group and 20.1±4.9 min in the propofol group (mean difference, -2.79 min; 95% CI, -4.9 to -0.7). The upper bound of the 95% CI (-0.73 min) was well below the non-inferiority margin of 4.8 min, confirming non-inferiority (one-sided P < 0.0001). Anesthesia and surgery times, recovery metrics, and pain scores did not differ significantly between groups. The incidence of emergence delirium was similar (7.0% vs 2.3%, P=0.616). In exploratory analyses, individuals in the ciprofol group seemed to have overall higher systolic, diastolic, and mean blood pressure than those in the propofol group, while heart rate did not differ between the two groups.
CONCLUSION: Ciprofol was non-inferior to propofol for extubation time in pediatric TIVA for laparoscopic surgery. Although exploratory analyses suggested potential favorable hemodynamic trends, larger multicenter studies are needed to evaluate comparative safety and clinical relevance.

articles.title: Bleeding Following Frozen Elephant Trunk Surgery: A Proposed Reporting Dataset and Research Agenda.
articles.abstract: Perioperative bleeding after frozen elephant trunk (FET) surgery is reported using heterogeneous endpoints. This structured narrative review examines bleeding sources, measurement and haemostatic management, prioritising recent literature while retaining established landmark definitions. Twelve primary FET clinical publications are tabulated, with technical reports and wider cardiac-surgery evidence providing context. Re-exploration, postoperative drainage, estimated blood loss, transfusion and fabric oozing describe related but distinct phenomena. Established classifications, particularly the Universal Definition of Perioperative Bleeding (UDPB), provide a severity-reporting reference and should not be displaced by a new FET scale. We propose six parallel reporting domains: procedural context; bleeding measurement; haemostatic status; verified source; treatment exposure; and outcomes.. The study-level mapping shows that published FET reports often permit extraction of drainage, re-exploration or treatment exposure, whereas haemostatic status and a directly verified bleeding source are rarely recoverable from published reports. The dataset therefore makes these information gaps explicit and supports prospective evaluation; it does not infer an anatomical source from laboratory findings, drainage or treatment. The proposed reporting dataset is not a validated severity scale or treatment algorithm.

articles.title: Opioid-Sparing Effect of an Ultrasound-Guided Transversus Abdominis Plane Block Added to a Multimodal Analgesic Protocol in Dogs with Acute Pancreatitis: A Matched-Control Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: Acute pancreatitis in dogs causes severe abdominal pain, typically managed with systemic opioids, which can impair gastrointestinal motility and delay recovery. This prospective clinical communication evaluated the opioid-sparing effect and clinical outcomes of an ultrasound-guided transversus abdominis plane block added to a multimodal analgesic protocol in dogs with acute pancreatitis. Twelve dogs were allocated into a locoregional block group (n = 6) and a control group managed with opioids (n = 6), matched on five severity scores recorded at admission. The primary outcome was opioid consumption during the first 24 h after enrollment; secondary outcomes were pain during the same period, time to first voluntary food intake, hospitalization length, and inflammatory response. The block group received significantly fewer methadone doses (median 0 vs. 4.5; p = 0.015) and five of six dogs required no methadone beyond the enrollment dose. Cumulative pain scores during the first 24 h were also significantly lower in the block group (p = 0.037). The time to first voluntary food intake was shorter in the block group (12 vs. 48 h; p = 0.02). No significant differences were found in hospitalization length or survival. Adding a transversus abdominis plane block to a multimodal protocol was associated with a marked opioid-sparing effect and promoted earlier voluntary food intake, although these preliminary findings require confirmation in larger studies.

articles.title: Metabolic, Gastric, and Psychosocial Correlates of Carbohydrate-Containing Clear-Fluid Intake in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Shortened clear-fluid fasting is increasingly supported in pediatric anesthesia, yet its combined effects on child-centered perioperative outcomes, family satisfaction, metabolic response, and gastric ultrasonography findings remain unclear. This study evaluated the associations of two routine preoperative fasting practices with preoperative anxiety, perioperative blood glucose, hemodynamic parameters, family satisfaction, and gastric ultrasonography findings in children undergoing elective surgery. Methods: This prospective, two-arm, observational cohort study included 66 children aged 3-12 years with American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I-II scheduled for elective adenotonsillectomy under general anesthesia, following either standard overnight fasting or 5 mL/kg carbohydrate-containing clear apple juice approximately 2 h before surgery. Preoperative anxiety was assessed using the Modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale; blood glucose, hemodynamic parameters, gastric antral cross-sectional area, estimated gastric residual volume, Perlas classification, family satisfaction, fasting duration, and nausea and vomiting were also evaluated. Results: Preoperative anxiety scores were significantly lower in the clear-fluid group than in the overnight fasting group (39.95 ± 20.02 vs. 51.88 ± 22.05; p = 0.003). No significant differences were observed between groups in blood glucose, gastric antral cross-sectional area, estimated gastric residual volume, or Perlas scores. Family satisfaction was significantly higher in the clear-fluid group (8.76 ± 1.66 vs. 4.12 ± 2.00; p < 0.001), and fasting duration was markedly shorter. No perioperative pulmonary aspiration occurred. Conclusions: Administration of 5 mL/kg of carbohydrate-containing clear fluid approximately 2 h before surgery was associated with lower preoperative anxiety and higher family satisfaction, with no significant between-group difference in gastric residual volume.

articles.title: Predictors of Blood Transfusion Following Cesarean Delivery in Resource-Constrained Settings: The Impact of Out-of-Hours Surgery.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Perioperative red blood cell (RBC) transfusion after cesarean delivery reflects both obstetric hemorrhagic risk and the capacity of the care environment.
