articles.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) has heterogeneous mechanisms, including structural atrial cardiomyopathy, electrical remodeling and primary ion-channel abnormalities. Aldosterone-mineralcorticoid receptor (MR) signaling may contribute to an arrhythmogenic atrial substrate through redox-sensitive, inflammatory, profibrotic and electrophysiological pathways; however, their direct demonstration in human atria varies. Primary aldosteronism is associated with excess AF risk, but circulating aldosterone, renin-independent secretion, tissue MR activation and MR-antagonist exposure are not interchangeable biological measures. This narrative review critically distinguishes evidence from human atrial tissue, atrial experimental systems and extrapolation from other cardiovascular models, with particular emphasis on the cardiac surgical setting. Preoperative aldosterone has been associated with postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF), whereas perioperative MR-antagonist studies have reported discordant findings and observational analyses remain susceptible to confounding. We propose a testable, rather than established, two-hit framework in which a pre-existing endocrine-associated atrial substrate may interact with perioperative inflammation and hemodynamic stress. The review identifies gaps in endocrine phenotyping and the need for adequately powered prospective and interventional studies before aldosterone-directed POAF prevention can be recommended.

articles.title: Safety and Analgesic Consumption Impact of Continuous Peripheral Regional Analgesia in Earthquake-Related Crush Injury: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background: The 6 February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake caused an unprecedented burden of crush-related extremity trauma. Continuous peripheral regional analgesia is frequently used in these patients, but its safety regarding renal outcomes and its effect on systemic opioid consumption have not been quantified in comparative cohort data. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, exploratory cohort study of 181 hospitalizations (141 patients) following the earthquake, comparing patients who received a continuous peripheral nerve catheter with those managed without one. No prospective sample-size calculation was performed. The primary outcome was acute kidney injury (AKI), defined per adapted KDIGO criteria; the secondary outcome was systemic opioid exposure, assessed both as opioid-days and, in a dose-based sensitivity analysis, as morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Because patients contributed multiple admissions, regression models used cluster-robust standard errors. A propensity-score-matched sensitivity analysis (age, sex) addressed confounding by indication, and intensive care unit (ICU) days were added as a further covariate in sensitivity models. Results: Catheter and non-catheter groups had similar age (p = 0.369) but differed in length of stay (median 42 vs. 16 days) and surgical procedures (10 vs. 2), reflecting catheter-selection criteria; detailed injury-severity and comorbidity data were not available for either group. Catheter use was not significantly associated with AKI (adjusted OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.16-1.47, p = 0.203) or with systemic opioid-day rate (adjusted RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.88-1.51, p = 0.294). Results were materially unchanged after adding ICU days as a covariate (AKI OR 0.42, p = 0.148, n = 123; opioid-days RR 1.23, p = 0.223, n = 160) and when opioid exposure was expressed as MME per day (adjusted ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.73-2.38, p = 0.361, n = 165). A propensity-matched analysis (26 pairs) was concordant for all outcomes. Conclusions: In this exploratory, hypothesis-generating cohort, we did not detect a significant association between continuous regional analgesia and either AKI risk or opioid consumption across six complementary analyses. These non-significant findings do not establish equivalence or safety, particularly given wide confidence intervals, a modest number of events, incomplete clinical characterization, and residual confounding that could not be fully resolved with the available data; they should be regarded as hypothesis-generating pending confirmation in better-characterized, adequately powered, multicenter cohorts.

articles.title: Comparison of Perioperative Risk Assessment Tools for Major Postoperative Complications After Radical Cystectomy.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: To compare the discriminatory performance of commonly used perioperative risk assessment tools, including the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification, Estimation of Physiologic Ability and Surgical Stress (E-PASS), Surgical Outcome Risk Tool (SORT), and modified 5-item Frailty Index (mFI-5), for major postoperative complications after radical cystectomy. Methods: This retrospective observational study included 193 patients who underwent open radical cystectomy for bladder cancer between January 2017 and January 2025. Major postoperative complications were defined as Clavien-Dindo grade III or higher. The discriminatory performance of ASA, E-PASS Comprehensive Risk Score (CRS), SORT, and mFI-5 was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Pairwise comparisons of the areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) were performed using the DeLong test. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations with major complications, and exploratory analyses examined secondary postoperative outcomes. Results: Major postoperative complications occurred in 58 (30.1%) patients. The numerical AUC was highest for E-PASS CRS (0.618, 95% CI 0.536-0.701), followed by SORT (AUC 0.610, 95% CI 0.525-0.694), ASA (AUC 0.595, 95% CI 0.509-0.680) and mFI-5 (AUC 0.578, 95% CI 0.489-0.668). However, pairwise DeLong tests showed no statistically significant difference in discrimination between E-PASS CRS and SORT, or any of the other scores tested. In univariable analysis, high E-PASS CRS, high SORT score and mFI-5 ≥ 2 were significantly associated with major complications, while ASA classification was not. When all scores were entered into the multivariable model at the same time, none of the scores remained statistically significant. Conclusions: All of the risk assessment tools evaluated in this study demonstrated poor discriminatory ability for major postoperative complications following radical cystectomy. Although E-PASS CRS had the highest numeric AUC, its discrimination was not statistically better than the other scores analyzed. Existing risk tools may help with perioperative risk stratification but should not be used as stand-alone prediction models for major postoperative morbidity after radical cystectomy.

articles.title: The perioperative sensory-cognitive interface: multimodal neuroimaging of hierarchical network reconfiguration in perioperative neurocognitive disorders.
articles.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) are commonly attributed to neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular stress, anesthetic neurophysiology, and pre-existing brain vulnerability. These mechanisms identify important insults but do not fully explain how they become disturbances of attention, perception, memory, executive control, and fluctuating awareness. We examine whether changes at the sensory-cognitive interface help explain these symptoms, focusing on postoperative delirium (POD) and early recovery within the broader PND classification. The interface comprises distributed, bidirectional operations that transform sensory evidence into context-sensitive representations through thalamocortical routing, integration, attention, and association systems. The framework makes three testable predictions: sensory function should add explanatory value beyond frailty and brain burden; perioperative effects should vary across hierarchical levels and time rather than reflect uniform suppression; and within-person recovery trajectories should explain outcome better than isolated scans. Anesthetic state-transition studies show that primary sensory responses can persist while feedback, thalamic broadcasting, and distributed integration are disrupted, but whether these changes cause PND remains unproven. Direct perioperative MRI and EEG studies identify pre-existing dysconnectivity, altered sensory and association-network organization, abnormal slow-wave and auditory-feedback dynamics, and incomplete postoperative recovery; nevertheless, findings are heterogeneous and sensory-specific tasks remain uncommon. These observations are compatible with established vulnerability-perturbation models and suggest that symptoms may depend on which networks recover and when. Structural-functional connectivity (SC-FC) coupling is one candidate measurement, not an established biomarker or a requirement of the framework. Longitudinal studies integrating sensory phenotyping, domain-specific cognition, delirium surveillance, MRI, EEG, physiology, and molecular markers should test whether this framework adds reproducible value beyond vascular injury, diffuse arousal failure, and latent neurodegeneration.

articles.title: High-Dose Nitroglycerin for Prevention of Coronary Artery Spasm During Arrhythmia Ablation.
Perioperative Risk Assessment and Management in Patients With CKD, Dialysis Dependence, and Kidney Transplantation.
articles.abstract: As the prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD), end-stage kidney disease, and kidney transplantation continues to rise, these patients are increasingly undergoing elective surgical procedures. This unique population presents significant clinical challenges due to extensive comorbidities, heightened cardiovascular risk, and high susceptibility to acute kidney injury (AKI). In patients with advanced CKD, an episode of perioperative AKI can exhaust renal reserve, often precipitating a transition to acute or chronic dialysis. This review provides a comprehensive framework for perioperative risk assessment from a nephrology perspective. Beyond standard cardiovascular evaluation, we examine kidney-specific nuances, including AKI prediction models for cardiac and non-cardiac surgery and the perioperative management of hypertension and anemia. Furthermore, we detail specialized care for hemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), and transplant recipients, including the optimal timing of dialysis and the management of perioperative medications. Distinct considerations for PD patients, such as the risk of peritonitis, dialysate leakage, and wound dehiscence following abdominal surgery, are addressed. By integrating these strategies, providers can mitigate complications and improve outcomes in this high-risk surgical cohort.

articles.title: Staying Alive; Addressing the Educational Gaps Between the See One, Do One Bag Mask Ventilation Teaching with Simulation.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Medical students receive limited exposure to pediatric airway management during clinical clerkships, creating a critical gap in a life-saving skill. Bag-mask ventilation (BMV) is fundamental to neonatal resuscitation, yet no standardized just-in-time simulation curriculum exists for teaching this skill to medical students using low-fidelity task trainers.
METHODS: We developed and implemented a just-in-time, simulation-based curriculum for third-year medical students during their Surgery, Anesthesia, Obstetrics, and Gynecology clerkship block. During one-hour sessions, through the lens of Kirkpatrick's evaluation model we evaluated level 2 (learning) by individually assessing students on BMV technique using the Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) Checklist, 2nd Edition, before and after rapid cycle deliberate practice coaching on a low-fidelity pediatric airway task trainer. We compared pre- and post-intervention scores using a paired two-tailed t-test.
RESULTS: Over one academic year, 120 medical students completed the curriculum across two sites with a 100% participation rate. Mean HBB Checklist score improved significantly from 8.3 ± 2.17 to 12.9 ± 1.22 (mean difference 4.52, 95% CI 4.09-4.95, p < 0.0001). Step-level analysis revealed the greatest deficits in corrective resuscitation measures at baseline, with the greatest gains observed in these steps following training. An incidental finding identified that 44% of students demonstrated incorrect hand placement over the submental space, a technique associated with airway occlusion in neonates.
DISCUSSION: This low-fidelity, just-in-time simulation curriculum significantly improved medical student BMV skills and is feasible to implement at a low cost outside of a formal simulation center.

articles.title: Predicting Gastrointestinal Complications After Cardiac Surgery From Mean Arterial Blood Pressure Under a Data-Driven Threshold for Hypotension: Protocol for an Advanced Database Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypotension during cardiopulmonary bypass may increase the risk of gastrointestinal complications due to insufficient splanchnic autoregulatory capacity. We hypothesize that both duration and level of blood pressure below a data-driven threshold during cardiopulmonary bypass are associated with the risk of gastrointestinal complications.
METHODS: Patients who underwent cardiac surgery at Copenhagen University Hospital, Rigshospitalet, during 2018-2022 will be included if they underwent on-pump valve surgery, coronary artery bypass grafting, and/or surgery on the ascending aorta. The primary outcome is major gastrointestinal complications within 30 days, defined as acute intestinal ischemia, abdominal surgery, bowel perforation, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Secondary endpoints are serious gastrointestinal complications, delayed recovery of bowel function, cholinesterase inhibitor administration, and 30-day mortality. The exposure is the exposure to lower blood pressure, calculated as the product of the duration and level of blood pressure below a data-driven threshold. To identify the optimal threshold, we split the population in a training (75%) and validation cohort (25%). In the training cohort we will identify the threshold with the highest area under the receiver operating curve for the primary outcome. The selected threshold will then be applied to quantify the exposure to lower blood pressure for each patient. Patients will be grouped using a modified Youden's index (weighing sensitivity 80%) as a cutoff for high versus low exposure to lower blood pressure, and association with the study endpoints will be determined in the validation cohort.
CONCLUSION: Under the assumption of pressure-dependent perfusion outside of an autoregulatory plateau, the exposure to blood pressure below a threshold might reflect the risk of gastrointestinal complications more accurately than point measures or averages. The results from this study may lead to relevant hypotheses for prospective testing.

articles.title: Digital Versus in-Person Pre-Anaesthetic Assessment and Postoperative Outcomes in Low-Risk Patients: An Observational Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pre-anaesthetic assessment is essential for identifying perioperative risk and optimising patient safety. Digital alternatives, including video consultation and structured electronic health record (EHR) review, may improve efficiency, but comparative evidence regarding postoperative safety remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate postoperative outcomes across pre-anaesthetic assessment through EHR review, video consultation, and in-person assessment. We hypothesised that patients selected for digital pre-anaesthetic assessment within a structured triage system would have similar low 30-day rates of major postoperative complications compared with in-person assessment.
METHODS: We conducted a single-centre cohort study at Copenhagen University Hospital-Rigshospitalet, Denmark, including adult patients undergoing elective otorhinolaryngologic, oral, or maxillofacial surgery. Patients underwent pre-anaesthetic assessment by one of three modalities: in-person consultation, EHR review, or video consultation. The primary outcome was a composite of major postoperative complications within 30 days, including all-cause mortality, intensive care unit admission, bleeding requiring transfusion, infection requiring antibiotics, or hospital readmission. A multivariable generalised linear model with a log-link function was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: A total of 862 patients were included (in-person n = 300; EHR review n = 300; video consultation n = 262). Patients in the in-person group were older and had a higher comorbidity burden. Using in-person as reference, neither video consultation nor EHR review showed a significantly different risk of major postoperative complications. Hospital readmission was lower in both digital groups in pairwise comparisons with the in-person group. Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses, including inverse probability weighting and win ratio analysis.
CONCLUSION: Patients selected for digital pre-anaesthetic assessment had low rates of major postoperative complications. However, substantial baseline differences between groups indicate that assessment modality was strongly linked to clinical triage and baseline patient risk, thereby limiting direct comparison between pathways. Thus, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence or non-inferiority between pathways.
EDITORIAL COMMENT: Preoperative anesthesia assessment is managed in different ways, based on local preferences logistics and resource availability, and perceived perioperative risk for complications. This study assessed this process for planned surgery in section at a university hospital. Those during a number of recent years chosen for in-person preoperative assessment (for any reason) were compared to those who had some form of digital assessment chosen by the anesthesia personnel. The selection process for in-person preoperative assessment seemed to identify those who had a higher chance of a major postoperative complication.

articles.title: Avoidance Versus Use of Neuromuscular Blocking Agents for Optimising Video Laryngoscopy-Assisted Tracheal Intubation-A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tracheal intubation during anaesthesia carries risks, and difficult intubation can lead to severe complications. Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are widely recommended to improve intubation conditions, but they have potential adverse effects. Video laryngoscopy is widely used, yet evidence on the role of NMBAs in this setting is sparse. We aimed to assess whether avoidance versus use of NMBAs affects first-pass success and intubation conditions during video laryngoscopy in adults.
METHOD: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs for tracheal intubation in adults during video laryngoscopy were included. The primary outcome was failed first-pass intubation, as defined by the individual trials. Secondary outcomes were failed intubation, adverse effects (AEs) and serious adverse effects (SAEs), and acceptable intubation conditions. Furthermore, trial sequential analysis (TSA) was undertaken.
RESULTS: 9483 records were screened. Eight RCTs (744 participants) met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcome was extractable from seven trials (690 participants). Individual trial estimates showed either no clear effect or an increased risk of failed first-pass intubation when NMBAs were avoided. We found a statistically non-significant RR: 1.81 (95% CI: 0.93-3.55, p = 0.08, Cochran's Q = 12.0, p = 0.04, I2 = 58%, D2 = 74%, TSA adjusted RR: 1.77, TSA adjusted 95% CI: 0.48-6.50, GRADE = very low certainty of evidence) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs. TSA showed that the trial sequential monitoring boundaries were not crossed, and the required information size of 2334 was not achieved.
CONCLUSION: The effect of avoidance of NMBAs for facilitating video laryngoscopy-assisted tracheal intubation in adult patients is uncertain (very low certainty), and the required information size was not reached.
EDITORIAL COMMENT: This systematic review assessed trial evidence concerning whether or not muscle relaxant use is related to first pass failure in intubation attempts using video laryngoscopy. Evidence to date does not support a clear conclusion on whether avoidance of muscle relaxants in this context is beneficial or not, at least for first pass intubation success, though the evidence has very low certainty for this question.

articles.title: Does inferior alveolar nerve block influence immediate postoperative outcomes in orthognathic surgery? A scoping review.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This scoping review aimed to systematically map and synthesize the available evidence regarding the impact of inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) block on the immediate postoperative outcomes of orthognathic surgery.
METHODS: The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) guideline. A comprehensive and systematic search strategy was implemented across MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, The Cochrane Library, Livivo, LILACS, Web of Science, Scopus, Epistemonikos, and Google Scholar for grey literature. The search employed the descriptors descriptors "Nerve Block," "Postoperative Pain," and "Mandibular Osteotomy," combined with the Boolean operators AND and OR and their respective synonyms. The findings were synthesized narratively.
RESULTS: The search yielded 2,235 records, of which 11 studies fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Substantial heterogeneity was identified regarding the type, dosage, formulation of the anesthetic agents, and timing of IAN block administration. Despite such variations, beneficial effects were consistent across the included studies: 63.6% reported a statistically significant reduction in postoperative pain, 62.5% demonstrated reduced opioid consumption, and 66.7% showed a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). The visual analogue scale (VAS) was the most frequently used instrument for postoperative pain assessment.
CONCLUSION: The available evidence suggests that the IAN block is associated with reduced postoperative pain, decreased opioid requirements, and a lower incidence of PONV in patients undergoing orthognathic surgery. The heterogeneity observed across anesthetic protocols underscores the need for standardization in future primary studies.

articles.title: Risks and medico-legal aspects of pediatric tonsillectomy: a comprehensive and systematic review.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aims to provide a comprehensive systematic review of risk management strategies and medico-legal aspects associated with pediatric tonsillectomy.
METHODS: We performed a review with particular emphasis on identifying clinical factors and outcomes linked to malpractice claims.
RESULTS: Pediatric tonsillectomy, although generally safe, remains associated with potentially severe complications, particularly post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage and anesthesia-related adverse events. These complications represent the primary drivers of medico-legal litigation involving both otolaryngologists and anesthesiologists. ​A structured analysis of perioperative risk factors-including those capable of influencing surgical decision-making and clinical judgment-is essential for effective risk management.
CONCLUSION: The implementation of standardized preventive strategies and procedural safeguards may significantly reduce postoperative complications and limit medico-legal exposure. This review highlights the importance of integrating clinical risk assessment with medico-legal awareness and system-level safeguards-including standardized pathways, appropriate staffing and workload management-to improve patient safety and optimize surgical outcomes.

articles.title: Genetics-first versus muscle biopsy-first approach to investigating malignant hyperthermia susceptibility: a retrospective cost-consequence analysis.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare pharmacogenetic condition with substantial morbidity and mortality. The current gold standard for diagnosis, caffeine-halothane contracture testing (CHCT), is invasive, costly, and available only at a single centre in Canada. Genetic testing offers a less invasive alternative, but access remains inconsistent across Canadian provinces. We sought to evaluate the cost-consequences and diagnostic wait times of a genetics-first vs biopsy-first strategy for MH susceptibility.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cost-consequence analysis of 1,208 patients referred to the Canadian Malignant Hyperthermia Investigation Unit (2015-2024) with a personal or family history suggestive of MH, and their first-degree relatives. We compared the direct, indirect, and societal costs of the Ontario genetics-first approach with those of a hypothetical biopsy-first approach used in other provinces. We analyzed diagnostic timelines using Kaplan-Meier survival analyses.
RESULTS: In the genetics-first strategy, 7.2% of probands (88/1,208) had a diagnostic variant and did not require biopsy for contracture testing, resulting in modest societal cost reduction for probands compared with the biopsy-first strategy (CAD 23.5M vs CAD 24.3M, respectively; CAD 700 saved per proband tested). The costs of cascade testing of their first-degree relatives were three-fold lower for the genetics-first strategy (CAD 3.6M vs CAD 11.3M). The median [interquartile range] time to diagnosis was 2 [1-5] months for patients with diagnostic variants, compared with 39 [22-51] months for those requiring biopsy (log-rank P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with a hypothetical biopsy-first approach, offering genetics testing as initial step to all individuals with clinical suspicion of MH susceptibility did not increase societal costs, and resulted in substantial cost savings for cascade testing of their relatives, markedly shortening time to diagnosis for individuals who harbour a diagnostic variant.

articles.title: Effectiveness of ultrasound-guided versus surgeon-delivered superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIP) block in adult cardiac surgery: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIP) block is increasingly used to improve analgesia after cardiac surgery. This study compared the analgesic efficacy and clinical outcomes of ultrasound-guided versus surgeon-delivered SPIP block in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery via median sternotomy.
METHODS: This prospective, randomised controlled trial included 88 adult patients undergoing elective valve replacement surgery. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either ultrasound-guided SPIP performed by an anaesthesiologist (Group P, n = 44) or surgeon-delivered parasternal block under direct vision (Group S, n = 44). Both groups received 40 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine. The primary outcome was postoperative pain intensity assessed using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) during the first 24 h after extubation. Repeated pain measurements were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model. Secondary outcomes included time to first rescue analgesia, 24-h fentanyl consumption, extubation time, ICU length of stay, chronic pain assessed using the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (LANSS) questionnaire at 3 and 6 months, and patient satisfaction.
RESULTS: Exploratory pairwise analyses suggested lower postoperative NRS scores in Group P at 6, 12, 16, 20, and 24 h after extubation. However, the primary linear mixed-effects analysis demonstrated a significant effect of time (p < 0.001) but no significant overall treatment effect (p = 0.198) or group × time interaction (p = 0.408). Compared with Group S, Group P had a longer median time to first rescue analgesia (20 [16-24] vs 12 [9.5-12] h; p < 0.001), lower 24-h fentanyl consumption (100 [0-125] vs 300 [200-300] µg; p < 0.001), and a shorter ICU stay (2 [2-3] vs 3 [3-4] days; p < 0.001). Group P also demonstrated lower LANSS scores at 3 months (2 [2-3] vs 4 [3-5]; p = 0.001) and 6 months (0.5 [0-1] vs 2 [2-3]; p = 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Although the predefined longitudinal mixed-effects analysis did not demonstrate a significant overall treatment effect on postoperative pain intensity, ultrasound-guided SPIP was associated with lower opioid requirements, prolonged time to first rescue analgesia, shorter ICU stay, and reduced long-term neuropathic pain compared with surgeon-delivered parasternal block. Although exploratory analyses showed lower pain scores at selected postoperative time points, the primary longitudinal mixed-effects model did not demonstrate a significant overall treatment effect. Ultrasound-guided SPIP may therefore be considered a valuable component of multimodal analgesia for adult cardiac surgery, particularly where ultrasound expertise and equipment are available.

articles.title: Impact of Right Ventricular Dysfunction on Acute Kidney Injury and Major Adverse Cardiac and Cerebrovascular Events in Isolated Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) may influence perioperative hemodynamics after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). This study evaluated the association between preoperative RVD, defined by tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), and postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) after isolated CABG.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort included 392 adults undergoing isolated CABG between 2020 and 2023. RVD was defined as TAPSE < 17 mm. AKI was assessed at 24 and 48 hours according to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. MACCE was evaluated as a predefined composite outcome. Logistic regression was used to explore factors associated with AKI and MACCE.
RESULTS: Preoperative RVD was present in 2.3% of patients and was associated with a higher rate of KDIGO stage 1 AKI at 24 hours (P < 0.001). RVD was not independently associated with MACCE. Higher preoperative white blood cell count (odds ratio [OR] 1.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03 - 1.24; P = 0.013) and KDIGO stage at 48 hours (OR 7.44, 95% CI 3.32 - 18.77; P < 0.001) were associated with MACCE.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative RVD was associated with early renal vulnerability after CABG but not with MACCE. Postoperative AKI severity and preoperative inflammatory status were independently associated with MACCE. These exploratory findings require validation in larger cohorts and suggest that right ventricular assessment may improve perioperative risk stratification.

articles.title: Selective lung isolation in thoracic spine tumour resection: an integrated anaesthetic approach.
Suprascapular nerve block with versus without ultrasound-guided T2 erector spinae plane block for chronic shoulder pain: A retrospective comparative study.
articles.abstract: Suprascapular nerve block (SSNB) is widely used for chronic shoulder pain but may provide suboptimal analgesia because of incomplete coverage of the shoulder's sensory innervation. High thoracic (T2) erector spinae plane block (ESPB) provides broad craniocaudal spread and may complement SSNB. This study evaluated whether SSNB with T2 ESPB was associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with SSNB without T2 ESPB in patients with chronic, conservative-refractory shoulder pain. This retrospective comparative study included 84 adult patients with chronic shoulder pain lasting at least 3 months despite conservative treatment at a tertiary academic hospital. Patients underwent ultrasound-guided SSNB without T2 ESPB (n = 57) or SSNB with T2 ESPB (n = 27). The primary outcome was the proportion of responders, defined as achieving a ≥30% reduction in numeric rating scale (NRS) pain score at 4 weeks. Secondary outcomes included NRS pain score at 4 weeks, patient global impression of change (PGIC), and procedure-related adverse events. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to adjust for potential confounders. At 4 weeks, the responder rate was higher in the SSNB with T2 ESPB group than in the SSNB without T2 ESPB group (59.3% vs 17.5%, P < .001). The combined group also had a lower mean NRS pain score (3.9 ± 2.8 vs 5.2 ± 2.6, P = .049) and higher PGIC scores (median [IQR], 4 [4-5] vs 4 [3-4]; P = .010). In multivariable analysis, SSNB with T2 ESPB remained associated with a positive response (OR 5.931, 95% confidence interval: 2.01-17.50, P = .001). No procedure-related adverse events were identified. SSNB with T2 ESPB was associated with better short-term clinical outcomes than SSNB alone in patients with chronic shoulder pain. Prospective randomized, dose-matched studies are needed to confirm these findings and clarify the specific contribution of T2 ESPB.

articles.title: Pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block with lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) block versus fascia iliaca compartment block (FICB) for hip surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective analgesia that preserves motor function is essential for early mobilization after hip surgery. Although fascia iliaca compartment block (FICB) is recommended for total hip arthroplasty, the comparative efficacy of combined pericapsular nerve group and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve blocks (PENG + LFCN) remains uncertain.
METHODS: Databases including Embase, Web of Science, PubMed, Cochrane Central, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure were searched up to December 8, 2024. Statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan) (computer program, version 5.4, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020).
RESULTS: Seven randomized controlled trials involving 572 participants were included. Compared with FICB, PENG + LFCN significantly reduced static pain at 12 hours (mean difference [MD] = -0.19; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.28 to -0.11; P < .0001) and dynamic pain at 6 hours (MD = -0.87; 95% CI, -1.64 to -0.10; P = .03) and 48 hours (MD = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.49 to -0.02; P = .03). It also lowered quadriceps weakness (odds ratio = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.04-0.21; P < .00001), improved limb strength (MD = 1.03; 95% CI, 0.05-2.01; P = .04), reduced patient-controlled intravenous analgesia frequency (MD = -1.64; 95% CI, -3.13 to -0.15; P = .03), and shortened mobilization time (MD = -9.04; 95% CI, -14.28 to -3.80; P = .0007).
CONCLUSION: PENG + LFCN may provide superior early analgesia and better preserve lower-limb motor function than FICB after hip surgery. However, the evidence is limited by few trials, small sample sizes, and substantial heterogeneity. Larger, adequately powered trials are warranted.

articles.title: Postoperative quality of recovery after erector spinae plane block versus intraperitoneal local anesthetic instillation in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: A prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Erector spinae plane block (ESPB) and intraperitoneal local anesthetic (IPLA) instillation are used for analgesia after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, but comparative data on multidimensional postoperative recovery are limited. We compared 24-hour quality of recovery between these techniques. This prospective, non-randomized observational study included 82 analyzed adults (41 ESPB and 41 IPLA), allocated by operating room. The primary outcome was 24-hour global quality of recovery-40 (QoR-40) score. Multivariable regression adjusted for baseline QoR-40, age, sex, body mass index, and American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status; an additional sensitivity model included surgical duration. Repeated pain scores were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. Postoperative QoR-40 scores were 193.05 ± 8.26 with ESPB and 182.85 ± 10.93 with IPLA (adjusted mean difference 9.45, 95% confidence interval 5.63-13.28; P < .001). This estimate was similar after additional adjustment for surgical duration (9.47, 95% confidence interval 5.62-13.32). Overall resting and movement pain score differences were modest (-0.90 and -0.92; P = .02 and P = .02, respectively); after Holm adjustment, only the 1-hour time-specific contrasts were significant. Median 24-hour morphine consumption was lower in the ESPB group than in the IPLA group (1.0 [0.0-3.0] vs 4.0 [2.0-6.0] mg; P = .004), although the clinical importance of this difference is uncertain. Postoperative nausea and vomiting did not differ significantly. Bilateral ESPB was associated with higher 24-hour QoR-40 scores compared with IPLA. Non-randomized allocation and residual confounding preclude conclusions regarding causal superiority. Randomized studies are warranted.

articles.title: Prevalence and Association of Undiagnosed Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Perioperative Neurocognitive Disorders, and Quality of Life After Brain Surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is increasingly seen in neurosurgical patients and can impact patient outcomes. There is a paucity of literature regarding the OSA burden in the neurosurgical population and its link with perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) and quality of life (QoL).
OBJECTIVES: Our primary objective was to evaluate the OSA prevalence in patients undergoing brain surgery and, secondarily, to assess its association with postoperative complications of emergence delirium (ED), postoperative delirium (POD), and delayed neurocognitive recovery, sleep, respiratory events, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, hospital stay, 28-day QoL, and functional recovery.
METHODS: This secondary analysis of a primary study was conducted among adults undergoing elective brain surgery over a 14-month period. Patients were screened preoperatively for undiagnosed OSA using the STOP-BANG questionnaire. ED was evaluated using the Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale, POD using the Confusion Assessment Method and PND using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Sleep, Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOSE) scores and QoL were also assessed.
RESULTS: The prevalence of OSA was 31.5% (117/371). OSA was not associated with PND, except at baseline (P = 0.039). Similarly, OSA was not associated with sleep disturbances, respiratory complications, or ICU admission. Higher STOP-BANG scores correlated with longer hospital stays (P = 0.042), lower GOSE scores (P = 0.006), and worse cumulative QoL scores (P = 0.018).
CONCLUSIONS: Approximately one-third of patients undergoing brain surgery had undiagnosed OSA. Higher STOP-BANG scores were associated with preoperative cognitive impairment. Although OSA was not associated with sleep disturbances or PND, higher STOP-BANG scores were associated with unfavorable functional recovery and poorer QoL 28 days after surgery.

articles.title: Comparing surgical shunting with transcatheter stenting for initial palliation of cyanotic tetralogy of fallot: An inverse probability treatment weighting study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND/PURPOSE: To compare surgical shunting with transcatheter stenting for initial palliation of cyanotic tetralogy of Fallot, including high-risk infants.
METHODS: This retrospective two-center study included 101 infants who underwent palliation before 1 year of age, including 76 who underwent surgical shunting and 25 who underwent transcatheter stenting. Outcomes were evaluated using stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting with doubly robust adjustment. The primary composite outcome was death, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Secondary outcomes included recovery, reintervention, medical expenses, and pulmonary artery (PA) development.
RESULTS: After adjustment, the primary composite outcome and overall perioperative complication rate did not differ significantly between groups. Surgical shunting was associated with longer log-transformed intubation duration (β = 0.948, 95% CI 0.203-1.693; P = 0.013), intensive care unit stay (β = 0.584, 95% CI 0.050-1.118; P = 0.032), and hospital stay (β = 0.558, 95% CI 0.071-1.046; P = 0.025), but lower odds of reintervention (OR = 0.112, 95% CI 0.033-0.379; P < 0.001). In high-risk patients, surgical shunting was associated with more perioperative complications (OR = 7.712, 95% CI 1.569-37.913; P = 0.013), higher medical expenses, and lower McGoon and PA symmetry indices at total correction.
CONCLUSION: No significant between-group differences were observed in the primary composite outcome or overall perioperative complication rate. Transcatheter stenting was associated with faster recovery but more frequent reintervention. Among high-risk infants, it was associated with fewer perioperative complications, lower index hospitalization expenses, and more favorable PA development.
CLINICAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: The Research Ethics Committee of National Taiwan University Hospital (No. 202602073RIND), waived informed consent.

articles.title: Adenotonsillectomy in Children With Cerebral Palsy: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Outcomes.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of adenotonsillectomy in children with cerebral palsy (CP) and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted of children with CP and OSA who underwent adenotonsillectomy between 2011 and 2022 at a tertiary pediatric medical center. Inclusion criteria required pre- and postoperative polysomnography within 24 months. Data collected included demographics, comorbidities, perioperative complications, and polysomnography parameters. The primary outcome was the change in obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (OAHI). Secondary outcomes included changes in central apnea index, oxygen nadir, transcutaneous carbon dioxide (TcCO2), and need for noninvasive positive pressure ventilation. Logistic regression identified predictors of postoperative OAHI < 5 events/h.
RESULTS: Sixty-five children (median age: 5.0 years) met inclusion criteria. Mean preoperative OAHI was 19.6, which improved to 7.7 postoperatively (p < 0.001). OAHI was reduced by >50% in 63%; 62% achieved OAHI < 5, and 12% achieved OAHI < 1. Oxygen nadir improved from 84% to 88% (p < 0.001), TcCO2 improved from 49.2 mmHg to 45.2 mmHg. No significant change in central apnea index was noted. Postoperatively, 40% required noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, and 55% were electively admitted to the intensive care unit. Complication rate was 12%. Preoperative OAHI was the strongest and most consistently selected predictor of achieving postoperative OAHI < 5 (p = 0.002).
CONCLUSION: Adenotonsillectomy significantly improves OSA severity and oxygenation in children with CP; however, complete resolution is uncommon. Preoperative OAHI severity predicts surgical success. Postoperative polysomnography and multidisciplinary follow-up are essential due to the high rate of residual disease.

articles.title: Results of Pulmonary Valve Replacement with The INSPIRIS RESILIA Prosthesis: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary valve replacement is increasingly common in patients with congenital heart disease. The limited durability of conventional bioprostheses has led to the introduction of the INSPIRIS RESILIA valve, initially designed for the aortic position. However, evidence on its performance in the pulmonary position is limited and heterogeneous.
METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement in PubMed®, Excerpta Medica dataBASE, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials. Observational studies with patients undergoing pulmonary valve replacement with the INSPIRIS RESILIA bioprosthesis were included. Data on baseline characteristics, transvalvular gradients, mortality, complications, prosthetic insuficiency, and need for reintervention were extracted. This study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251117859).
RESULTS: Three retrospective cohort studies and two retrospective case series were identified that included pediatric and adult populations, mainly with a diagnosis of tetralogy of Fallot. The findings were consistent in showing adequate perioperative safety. Smaller studies showed favorable results. In contrast, larger studies with longer follow-up reported more rapid progression to moderate/severe pulmonary insuficiency and shorter durability of the bioprosthesis.
CONCLUSION: INSPIRIS RESILIA may be associated with acceptable short-term outcomes in pulmonary valve replacement, but its medium- and long-term durability may be inferior to that of reference bioprostheses. Medium- and long-term safety remains inconclusive due to limited follow-up, modest sample sizes, heterogeneity in definitions, possible confounding by anatomical substrate, and study limitations.

articles.title: Does Perineural Dexamethasone Prolong the Time to First Rescue Opioid Analgesia Compared With Intravenous Dexamethasone in Pediatric Hip Surgery? A Randomized Blinded Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The pericapsular nerve group (PENG) block is an increasingly utilized regional anesthesia technique for pediatric hip surgery. Dexamethasone prolongs the duration of peripheral nerve blocks and can be administered either intravenously or perineurally; however, the comparative pediatric evidence on postoperative analgesia and metabolic effects with these two routes is limited.
QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does perineural dexamethasone prolong the time to first rescue opioid analgesia compared with intravenous dexamethasone when used as an adjunct to PENG block in pediatric hip surgery? (2) Does perineural dexamethasone reduce postoperative opioid consumption and pain intensity? (3) Does the route of dexamethasone administration influence postoperative inflammatory markers and blood glucose levels? (4) Is perineural dexamethasone associated with an increased risk of neurologic complications?
METHODS: This randomized, blinded trial was conducted at a single urban tertiary university referral center in Poznań, Poland, providing subspecialty pediatric orthopaedic care. Parents and caregivers, treating anesthesiologists, surgeons, and outcome assessors were unaware of group allocation. Between February 2025 and March 2026, we assessed 72 children scheduled for elective reconstructive hip surgery. Children age 3 months to 6 years with developmental dysplasia of the hip or neurogenic hip displacement associated with cerebral palsy were considered potentially eligible. Of the 72 children assessed, 92% (66) met the eligibility criteria. Nine percent (6 of 66) of these children were not enrolled because four families declined participation and two declined regional anesthesia. The remaining 83% (60 of 72) were randomized. No participants were lost during the 48-hour in-hospital follow-up or had incomplete outcome data, and all 60 were included in the analysis. The perineural and intravenous groups had mean ± SD ages of 4.8 ± 1.2 and 5.2 ± 1.1 years, respectively; 47% (14 of 30) and 50% (15 of 30) were boys, and 70% (21 of 30) and 73% (22 of 30) had developmental dysplasia of the hip. The remaining children had neurogenic hip displacement associated with cerebral palsy. There were no clinically important between-group differences in these baseline characteristics. All patients received standardized spinal anesthesia and multimodal postoperative analgesia consisting of paracetamol 15 mg/kg and metamizole 15 mg/kg every 6 hours, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, and rescue nalbuphine 0.1 mg/kg for Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) scores of ≥ 4. The primary endpoint was time to first rescue opioid analgesia within 48 hours. Secondary endpoints included total opioid consumption, postoperative pain scores, inflammatory markers (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio [NLR] and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio [PLR]), blood glucose levels, and peripheral nerve injury assessed at 12, 24, and 48 hours.
RESULTS: We found no difference between the perineural and intravenous dexamethasone groups in time to first rescue opioid analgesia after adjustment for age, body weight, and duration of surgery (HR 0.56 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.28 to 1.08]; p = 0.08). Perineural dexamethasone reduced total opioid consumption during the first 48 postoperative hours (mean ± SD 0.131 ± 0.048 versus 0.225 ± 0.053 mg/kg morphine milligram equivalents (MMEs), mean difference -0.095 mg/kg [95% CI -0.121 to -0.068]; p < 0.001), corresponding to approximately 42% lower mean opioid consumption and an absolute difference of approximately 1.9 mg MME for a child weighing 20 kg. No differences were observed in NLR or PLR between groups, whereas mean ± SD blood glucose levels were lower in the perineural dexamethasone group at 12 hours (112 ± 17 versus 139 ± 20 mg/dL; p < 0.001) and 24 hours (112 ± 14 versus 134 ± 25 mg/dL; p < 0.001). No neurologic complications occurred in either group during the 48-hour follow-up period.
CONCLUSION: After adjustment for age, body weight, and duration of surgery, we found no difference between perineural and intravenous dexamethasone in time to first rescue opioid analgesia. Perineural dexamethasone was associated with lower opioid consumption and lower early postoperative blood glucose levels. Larger multicenter studies are needed to evaluate these findings in pediatric regional anesthesia.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.

articles.title: The Use of Regional Anesthesia in Pediatric Orthopaedic Surgery-Review of the Literature, Controversies, and Current Status.
articles.abstract: Regional anesthesia (RA) has become an increasingly important component of perioperative care in pediatric orthopaedic surgery. RA utilization in pediatric patients is well documented as part of the management of upper and lower extremity trauma, both at the time of fracture reduction as well as during definitive surgical stabilization. Elective management of both upper and lower extremity deformities and reconstruction of chronic injuries with RA support are common practices in many centers. Use of RA to mitigate postoperative pain and improve patient mobilization after elective spinal deformity procedures in pediatric patients is also well established. Despite extensive studies reporting successful and safe use of RA in his patient cohort, questions remain regarding potential risks and complications, particularly potential issues with postprocedure neurologic evaluation. Continued modifications in anesthetic techniques, in combination with an increased use of peripheral nerve blocks in place of neuroaxial blockades, may further limit the risk of potential postoperative issues.

articles.title: Association between cerebrospinal fluid confirmation during attempted combined spinal-epidural placement and documented early neuraxial analgesic failure: a retrospective cohort study.
Understanding general anesthesia and related characteristics in the context of obstetric acuity.
Physician Job Choice and Support for Abortion Access in the Post Dobbs Landscape: a Survey Study of High-Risk Specialty Trainees.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physicians have always had to balance personal ethics, professional obligations, and legal constraints when providing abortion care; however, since the United States Supreme Court ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, the legal framework governing this care has shifted substantially, raising concerns about physician workforce stability. The primary aim in our pilot study was to assess how likely states' abortion laws will influence where physicians accept their first job after residency or fellowship. Our other objectives were to assess physician support for abortion access and well-being post Dobbs. We hypothesized that the majority of physicians would be likely to consider states' abortion laws when looking for first post training jobs, would support abortion access, and would have had their well-being affected.
METHODS: We surveyed anesthesiology, emergency medicine, and obstetrics-gynecology (OB-GYN) residents and fellows.
RESULTS: We achieved only a 1.2% response rate. In this small data set, a majority (65.6%) of residents and fellows said that they are likely to consider state abortion laws when deciding where to accept their first post-training job, with OB-GYNs (90.7%) having the greatest majority. Eight out of ten physicians were supportive of medical and surgical abortion access (87.2%; 86.1%). A majority of physicians were supportive of abortion across all demographics, even Catholics, deviating only when assessed by political party affiliation. A majority of physicians (56.5%) were negatively affected by the Dobbs decision, regardless of the abortion law where they practice. Cisgender women and OB-GYN trainees were most impacted.
CONCLUSIONS: The response rate limits any generalizability of our findings, and future research is needed. In this pilot study, the majority of physicians indicated that they will consider states' abortion laws when accepting their first job, and a minority of physicians may be willing to work in states with abortion bans. To promote physician retention and recruitment, future research should investigate how access to reproductive care impacts physicians' professional and personal well-being.

articles.title: Clinical indications for stellate ganglion block: beyond anaesthesiology.
articles.abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) is an interventional procedure traditionally performed by anaesthesiologists with expertise in regional anaesthesia. Its therapeutic effects are based on the temporary interruption of sympathetic autonomic innervation to the head, neck, and upper extremity. The main indication for SGB is the management of acute and chronic pain syndromes in which the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is believed to play a role in the development and maintenance of symptoms. However, abnormal SNS activation is also involved in the pathophysiology of several other diseases and clinical conditions. Therefore, temporary interruption of sympathetic tone may provide symptomatic relief when conventional therapies are insufficient. This review summarizes the main clinical indications for SGB and the available scientific evidence, aiming to define its current role within the therapeutic algorithm across different clinical settings.

articles.title: Beyond the blind epidural: sensing, robotics, and artificial intelligence for safer neuraxial anesthesia.
Factors associated with postanesthesia care unit length of stay in adult patients undergoing elective surgery: A prospective observational cohort study.
articles.abstract: Postanesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay (LOS) is a key determinant of perioperative patient flow and resource utilization, yet the factors that prolong it remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify perioperative factors associated with PACU LOS in adult patients undergoing elective surgery. This prospective observational cohort study was conducted in a tertiary care hospital over a 6-month period. A total of 409 adult patients who underwent elective surgery under general anesthesia, spinal anesthesia, or peripheral nerve block were included. Demographic characteristics, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status, anesthetic technique and agents, surgical category and grade, anesthesia duration, PACU vital signs, body temperature, pain scores, postoperative nausea and vomiting, shivering and rescue analgesia were recorded. PACU LOS was defined as the time from PACU admission until a modified Aldrete score of 9 or higher was achieved. Univariate associations were assessed with nonparametric tests, and independent predictors were identified using a gamma generalized linear model with a log link. The median PACU LOS was 45 minutes (interquartile range, 45-50). In univariate analyses, PACU LOS was associated with anesthesia duration (ρ = 0.158, P = .001), surgical grade (P = .002), anesthetic technique (P = .021; shorter stay after peripheral nerve block), pain score at PACU admission (ρ = 0.110, P = .026), rescue analgesia (P = .027), and postoperative shivering (P < .001), but not with demographic characteristics, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status, anesthetic agents, surgical category, body temperature, or postoperative nausea and vomiting. In the multivariable model, major surgery (vs minor surgery; ratio of means 1.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03-1.23), anesthesia duration (1.06 per hour, 95% CI 1.04-1.08), and postoperative shivering (1.07, 95% CI 1.03-1.12) were independently associated with longer PACU LOS, whereas the associations of peripheral nerve block and admission pain score did not persist after adjustment. Surgical grade, anesthesia duration, and postoperative shivering were independent predictors of PACU LOS, whereas patient characteristics and the choice of anesthetic agent were not. Although their absolute effects were modest, prevention of postoperative shivering may represent a practical, modifiable target for improving PACU efficiency.

articles.title: Enhanced multi-object detection in brachial plexus ultrasound images using transformer-based semantic and spatial feature fusion.
articles.abstract: Advances in medical imaging have led to the widespread use of ultrasound for diagnosing and treating peripheral nerve blocks. However, challenges such as speckle noise and low spatial resolution hinder the accurate identification of neural structures. To address these issues, a model named transformer-based detection with semantic and spatial feature fusion (TDSS) was introduced, integrating spatial edge adaptive enhancement, multi-scale semantic fusion, and spatial distillation-assisted detection modules. These components improve edge perception, multi-scale semantic reasoning, and localization accuracy. Experiments on the Ultrasound Brachial Plexus Dataset demonstrated the superior performance of the model: TDSS achieved an AP of 0.407 for nerve detection and an overall mAP of 0.583, providing robust support for clinical medical image detection. The source code for the proposed TDSS framework is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18824199 .

articles.title: A Surface Landmark-Based Scanning Algorithm for Selected Ultrasound-Guided Nerve Blocks of the Upper and Lower Limb in Orthopedic Surgery: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Performing an ultrasound-guided nerve block requires two cognitively distinct phases: image acquisition, in which the operator positions the transducer and identifies the target anatomy, and image maintenance, in which that image is preserved during needle advancement. Without a pre-formed expectation, scanning can become an open-ended search. This review proposes structuring image acquisition as a confirmatory task by linking a defined surface landmark to an expected sonographic target through a defined scanning path. The present article consolidates the correspondence between surface landmarks and sonographic targets, for a selected set of upper and lower limb nerve blocks used in orthopedic surgery, into a single landmark-based scanning algorithm. Four steps (anchor, place, trace, and confirm) structure each block: a surface anchor defines the starting reference; an initial transducer position is derived from it; a directional search vector defines the trajectory of probe displacement; and a sonographic endpoint confirms correct placement and marks the transition to the needling phase. Anchors are described for the cervical plexus and brachial plexus blocks of the upper limb, and for the femoral nerve, fascia iliaca, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, iliopsoas plane, pericapsular nerve group, obturator nerve, femoral triangle/adductor canal, popliteal sciatic nerve, and saphenous nerve blocks of the lower limb. A common graphic notation renders every block as a single instance of this sequence, making the set directly comparable. Whether this structure reduces cognitive demand, or renders the spatial reasoning of experienced operators transferable, is a hypothesis that requires prospective validation.

articles.title: The Migraine Treatment Journey in US Veterans: A National Cohort Study of Prescribing Patterns.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Migraine in veterans is poorly understood due to limited real-world treatment data. This study aimed to characterize pharmacotherapeutic pathways for US veterans with migraine and evaluate the impact of care setting on therapy progression.
METHODS: This was a national, population-based, retrospective cohort study utilizing deidentified electronic health record data between January 2019 and June 2024 extracted from the Veterans Affairs Corporate Data Warehouse. Eligible patients were aged > 18 years with at least one diagnosis of migraine (ICD-10: G43.x) or one migraine-specific medication. The primary objective was to describe treatment patterns for veterans. Differences between primary care (PC) and specialty care (SC) were assessed using subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR).
RESULTS: Of 285,509 patients with newly diagnosed migraine, 252,661 (88.5%) received pharmacologic treatment and 150,684 (59.6%) received ≥ 1 preventive medication. The median (25th-75th percentile) number of treatment sequence steps was two (1-2), with a median time of 3 (0-40) days between diagnosis and initial treatment steps and 72 (5-295) days between subsequent treatment steps. For patients who received preventive medication, the median number of treatment sequence steps was one (1-2), with a median time from diagnosis to initial treatment steps of 46 (5-225) days and 128 (28-418) days between subsequent treatment steps. Of patients who received preventive medications, 91,793 (60.9%) received care from a PC provider only, and 21,268 (14.1%) from a SC provider only. Veterans receiving care within SC settings were > 50% more likely to transition to a second sequential step of preventive treatment (sHR 1.54 [95% CI 1.51-1.58]) and > six times more likely to initiate preventive calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antagonists (sHR 6.43 [95% CI 5.94-6.97]).
CONCLUSIONS: Most veterans with migraine received pharmacologic treatment. Intervals for initiating and transitioning preventive therapies were longer than recommended by guidelines. Veterans under SC were more likely to progress through preventive therapies, including CGRP antagonists, than those in PC.

articles.title: Perioperative Pregabalin for Persistent Postsurgical Pain After Lumbar Spine Surgery In Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether perioperative pregabalin, compared with placebo, reduces persistent postsurgical pain and improves functional disability and health-related quality of life 3 months or more after lumbar spine surgery in adults.
METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL were searched for placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials of perioperative gabapentinoids in adults undergoing elective lumbar spine surgery with a minimum follow-up of three months (PROSPERO CRD420261401910). The primary outcome was pain intensity at 3 months. Sufficiently homogeneous outcomes were pooled with random-effects meta-analyses (restricted maximum likelihood), and robustness was assessed with leave-one-out analyses; health-related quality of life was synthesized narratively. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty of evidence with GRADE.
RESULTS: Five randomized controlled trials (335 participants) were included, all evaluating pregabalin. Pregabalin did not reduce pain intensity at 3 months (4 trials, 275 participants; standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.41 to 0.47; I² = 69%; low certainty) or at the latest follow-up (SMD -0.13, 95% CI - 0.59 to 0.32; I² = 73%). Functional disability was lower with pregabalin (2 trials, 143 participants; SMD -0.51, 95% CI - 0.86 to - 0.16), but the differences were below minimal important change thresholds (very low certainty). Health-related quality of life (two trials, non-equivalent instruments) was synthesized narratively; early differences favoring pregabalin were not sustained at 1 year. In an exploratory analysis of four trials, a favorable functional outcome was more frequent with pregabalin (risk ratio 1.44, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.86; very low certainty). Adverse events were inconsistently reported.
CONCLUSIONS: In adults undergoing lumbar spine surgery, low-certainty evidence suggests that perioperative pregabalin results in little to no difference in pain intensity 3 months after surgery. Evidence on functional disability and quality of life is limited to few small trials and is very uncertain. Adequately powered trials enrolling patients at high risk of persistent postsurgical pain, with standardized outcomes and systematic reporting of harms, are needed.

articles.title: Antimicrobial stewardship in critical care: Applying PK/PD and optimised antimicrobial dosing to improve care.
articles.abstract: Life-threatening infections are common in critically ill patients and remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU). Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) aims to optimise antimicrobial use by balancing effective treatment with minimising toxicity, resistance and unnecessary exposure. This review examines AMS in critical care with a focus on antimicrobial dose optimisation. Core AMS principles in the ICU include diagnostic stewardship, appropriate antimicrobial initiation, de-escalation and treatment duration. Dose optimisation is fundamental but challenging because critical illness causes profound and dynamic changes in pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD). These alterations result in marked interpatient variability and increase the risk of subtherapeutic or toxic drug exposure. Understanding key PK parameters, including volume of distribution, clearance and half-life, together with PD targets such as Cmax/MIC, fT > MIC and AUC0-24/MIC is essential for individualising therapy. Factors including sepsis, organ dysfunction, augmented renal clearance and extracorporeal support can substantially alter antimicrobial exposure and dosing requirements. Strategies to improve target attainment include loading doses, prolonged infusions, therapeutic drug monitoring and model-informed precision dosing, although implementation may be limited by local resources. Integrating PK/PD-informed dosing into routine ICU practice can improve clinical outcomes, reduce toxicity and strengthen AMS in critically ill populations.

articles.title: The association between normal capillary refill time and 28-day mortality in septic shock patients subjected to early hemodynamic resuscitation.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Capillary refill time (CRT)-guided resuscitation improves outcomes in septic shock by targeting abnormal CRT. However, whether a normal baseline CRT, resulting in no additional attempts to optimize hemodynamics, is associated with mortality remains unclear. We evaluated the association between normal baseline CRT and 28-day mortality in patients with septic shock undergoing protocolized resuscitation.
METHODS: This post-hoc analysis included all randomized patients from the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 1 and 2 trials. CRT was classified as normal (≤3 s) or abnormal (>3 s). The primary outcome was 28-day mortality, analyzed using Cox proportional hazards regression and reported as hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Secondary outcomes included ICU and hospital length of stay and 90-day mortality.
RESULTS: Among 1885 patients, 691 (36.7%) had normal baseline CRT. Despite normal CRT, many had abnormal hemodynamic features: 335 (48.5%) had heart rate > 100/min, 258 (37.3%) systolic arterial pressure < 100 mmHg, 152 (22.0%) mean arterial pressure < 65 mmHg, 157 (22.7%) diastolic arterial pressure < 50 mmHg, and 683 (98.8%) lactate >2 mmol/L. Patients with normal baseline CRT had significantly lower 28-day mortality than those with abnormal CRT (21.1% vs. 34.3%; HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.50-0.74; p < 0.001) similarly for 90-day mortality (25.9% versus 40.6%; HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.52-0.73; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: In the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trials, normal baseline CRT was associated with significantly lower 28- and 90-day mortality, although mortality remained still quite high. Further research should investigate how treatment of septic shock patients with normal CRT can be improved.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 1 trial: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03078712 (study start at: 2017-03-01). The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK 2 trial: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05057611 (study start at: 2022-03-18).

articles.title: Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets in septic shock: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Resuscitation strategies incorporating peripheral perfusion targets (RSIPPT) have emerged as promising tools in septic shock. However, whether they improve clinically relevant outcomes remains uncertain. We aimed to evaluate whether these strategies reduce 28/30-day mortality and improve other clinical outcomes compared with usual care.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using a random-effects model was conducted. Electronic searches of PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL were performed through May 27, 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420261400115). The RoB 2 and GRADE tools were used for assessment of risk of bias and certainty of evidence (CoE), respectively.
RESULTS: Five RCTs involving 2180 patients with septic shock were included. Compared with conventional strategies, RSIPPT were not associated with significant differences in 28/30-day mortality (four RCTs; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.09; I2 = 10%; moderate CoE) or 90-day mortality (three RCTs; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.83-1.05; I2 = 0%; low CoE). However, RSIPPT were associated with fluid reduction during the first 6-8 h of resuscitation (three RCTs; MD -264.53 mL, 95% CI -425.28 to -103.77; I2 = 1%; low CoE). No significant differences were observed in intensive care unit or hospital length of stay, organ dysfunction, vasopressor-free days, ventilator-free days, or renal replacement therapy-free days.
CONCLUSION: In early septic shock, RSIPPT were associated with a modest reduction in resuscitation fluid during the first 6-8 h. A mortality reduction was not demonstrated, although clinically important benefit or harm cannot be excluded. Differences in intervention algorithms and comparators limit attribution of these findings to peripheral perfusion monitoring itself.

articles.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for ICU pharmacotherapy training: Supporting learning while preserving clinical judgment.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in critical care practice at a time when pharmacotherapeutic decisions are becoming more complex, data-intensive, and time-sensitive. For medical residents and fellows, this creates both educational opportunities and challenges, as AI may support learning but must not replace the development of independent clinical judgment. This perspective examines potential applications of AI in ICU pharmacotherapy training, including support for just-in-time learning, case-based practice, and bedside decision support. Key limitations and risks, such as misinformation, cognitive offloading, deskilling, privacy and data security, and bias in model outputs, are discussed along with possible mitigation strategies. Future training should prioritize building competencies related to AI-assisted clinical decision-making, including critical appraisal of AI-generated outputs and communication of AI-informed decisions within interprofessional teams. AI-supported pharmacotherapy training should be guided by clear boundaries around use and continued emphasis on building foundational pharmacotherapy knowledge, patient-specific reasoning, and clinical judgment.

articles.title: Distinct associations of age, frailty, and comorbidity with AKI occurrence, mortality, and kidney function recovery in older ICU patients: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common in critically ill older adults, but the associations of chronological age and baseline vulnerability to kidney outcomes remain uncertain. We examined associations of age, frailty, and comorbidity with AKI occurrence, in-hospital mortality, and kidney function recovery. This retrospective cohort included adults aged ≥60 years admitted to six intensive care units at a Brazilian university hospital from 2023 to 2025. AKI followed KDIGO creatinine criteria; frailty was measured by the modified frailty index (MFI) and comorbidity by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI). Modified Poisson (AKI occurrence), time-dependent Cox (mortality), and Fine-Gray (kidney function recovery, with death as a competing event) models were used. Among 2387 patients, illness severity and chronic kidney disease prevalence increased with age. AKI developed in 1396 patients (58.5%), rising from 56.2% (60-69 years) to 63.3% (≥80 years); age, MFI (adjusted risk ratio 1.030 per point), and CCI (1.028 per point) were each associated with AKI occurrence. AKI (hazard ratio 3.135, 95% CI 2.585-3.801) and age (1.039 per year) were associated with in-hospital death, whereas MFI and CCI were not after adjustment for acute illness. Of 927 survivors with AKI, 50.2% recovered by discharge. Age was not independently associated with recovery, whereas greater MFI and CCI were associated with lower recovery. Age, frailty, and comorbidity captured distinct dimensions of risk: AKI and age were associated with in-hospital mortality, whereas baseline vulnerability, more than age, was associated with kidney function recovery, supporting frailty and comorbidity assessment in ICU risk stratification.

articles.title: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature.
DESIGN: Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study.
SETTING: Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations.
PATIENTS: Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR).
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80-1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79-1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, -1.03; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.80; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

articles.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016-March 2024).
PATIENTS: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92-1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92-1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75-0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71-0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918-49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018-58,624) met the U.S. threshold.
CONCLUSIONS: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

articles.title: The Impact of Early Changes in Albumin Levels on Long-Term Kidney and Mortality Outcomes in Patients With Acute Kidney Injury Undergoing Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the association between early changes in the levels of serum albumin during continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) and long-term dialysis dependence and mortality in patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 days or more days after CKRT initiation.
DESIGN: A multicenter retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: Eight university-affiliated tertiary hospitals in South Korea participating in the LINking health medical records, biospecimens, and biosignals in Korean patients with Acute kidney injury consortium cohort.
PATIENTS: The study involved 1087 adult patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 or more days after CKRT initiation between January 2017 and June 2022.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
