CONCLUSIONS: The Green-Lyte project was associated with decreased utilization of electrolytes and reduced environmental burden, as demonstrated by decreases in generated waste and estimated material-associated carbon footprint.

articles.title: Ventilator Modes Used to Facilitate Liberation From Mechanical Ventilation: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Liberation from invasive ventilation involves gradual decrements in respiratory support, spontaneous breathing trials, or both. Although various ventilator modes have been studied to facilitate weaning, the approaches used across trials for the highest risk patients are not well summarized. We sought to summarize the different ventilator modes and liberation strategies that have been investigated in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of critically ill adults at risk for difficult or prolonged weaning from invasive ventilation.
DATA SOURCES: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 2026.
STUDY SELECTION: We conducted a scoping review of RCTs that enrolled critically ill adults (≥ 18 yr) who received invasive ventilation for greater than or equal to 24 hours and were considered to have either difficult or prolonged weaning (Weaning according to a New Definition [WIND] group "no wean," "difficult weaning," or "prolonged weaning") and compared two or more assisted ventilatory modes. We excluded trials that compared ventilatory modes for spontaneous breathing test (SBT) conduct, invasive vs. noninvasive ventilation, or tracheostomized patients at the time of randomization.
DATA EXTRACTION: We extracted data related to eligibility criteria, outcomes, and weaning protocols and assessed risk of bias using a modified Cochrane risk of bias tool in duplicate.
DATA SYNTHESIS: Among 38 eligible trials, the most studied ventilatory modes were pressure support ventilation (71.1%, 27 trials) and synchronized intermittent or intermittent mandatory ventilation (31.6%, 12 trials). The most frequently studied automated modes were SmartCare/pressure support (15.8%, six trials) and proportional assist ventilation (15.8%, six trials). Weaning typically used a gradual reduction in support without a mode change (52.6%, 20 trials), or with intermittent SBTs (31.6%, 12 trials). Overall risk of bias was commonly high due to a probably high risk of selective reporting.
CONCLUSIONS: Diverse modes and strategies have been evaluated to achieve liberation. Future research should focus on adequately powered, high-quality trials of the effect of commonly used and widely available modes and strategies on clinically important outcomes for liberation from mechanical ventilation of high-risk patients.

articles.title: Optimizing Sepsis Time Zero Definitions Through Associations between Antibiotic Timing and Mortality.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Sepsis performance measures require operational definitions of "time zero", but SEP-1's heterogeneous organ dysfunction criteria may not all identify patients vulnerable to harm from antibiotic delays.
OBJECTIVES: To determine which SEP-1 organ dysfunctions identify patients in whom antibiotic delays are associated with increased mortality.
METHODS: We analyzed adults with suspected infection using electronic health record data from 145 U.S. hospitals (2018-2023). We estimated associations between antibiotic timing (1-3 vs. 0-1h and 3-6 vs. 0-3h) and in-hospital mortality for each SEP-1 organ dysfunction criterion, alone and in combination: hypotension, elevated lactate, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy. We used inverse probability weighting to adjust for baseline and time-varying confounders.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Among 1,849,729 encounters with suspected infection, 624,416 had ≥1 organ dysfunction and received antibiotics within 6h of time zero. Antibiotics at 1-3 vs. 0-1h were associated with higher mortality when time zero was defined by hypotension (aRR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.10) or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L (aRR 1.10; 1.05-1.15), but not for other dysfunctions alone or in combination. Among patients without hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, antibiotics at 3-6 vs. 0-3h were only associated with higher mortality in patients with acute respiratory failure (aRR 1.11; 1.05-1.18).
CONCLUSIONS: Mortality associations with antibiotics beyond 1 hour were most evident when sepsis time zero was defined by hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, and with antibiotics beyond 3 hours when defined by acute respiratory failure. These findings could inform refinements to sepsis time zero definitions to better guide antibiotic urgency and performance measurement.

articles.title: Single-Stage Full-Endoscopic Pars Crisscross Decompression and Discectomy for Combined Foraminal Stenosis and Lateral Disc Herniation: A Report of 2 Cases.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Full-endoscopic pars crisscross decompression has recently been introduced as a local-anesthesia procedure for foraminal stenosis associated with stable L5 isthmic spondylolisthesis. Although transforaminal endoscopic foraminoplasty combined with discectomy has been described in patients with spondylolisthesis, the pars crisscross technique may provide a distinct working corridor for simultaneous treatment of bony foraminal stenosis and concomitant lateral disc pathology. We present 2 cases treated with single-stage pars crisscross decompression and discectomy under local anesthesia.
CASE PRESENTATION: Two patients, a 51-year-old woman and a 60-year-old man, presented with unilateral L5 radiculopathy refractory to conservative treatment. Imaging demonstrated L5 isthmic spondylolisthesis, ipsilateral L5/S1 foraminal stenosis, and concomitant lateral disc herniation without significant segmental instability.
CASE MANAGEMENT: Both patients underwent single-stage full-endoscopic pars crisscross decompression and endoscopic discectomy under local anesthesia. Adequate decompression of the exiting L5 nerve root was achieved by sequential resection of the bony components of the pars defect, followed by removal of the herniated disc. Leg pain improved immediately after surgery in both patients. Postoperative imaging confirmed adequate foraminal decompression. No perioperative complications occurred. At 18 months in case 1 and 12 months in case 2, neither patient demonstrated recurrence of radicular symptoms, progression of low back pain, or radiographic evidence of segmental instability.
CONCLUSION: Transforaminal full-endoscopic spine surgery using the pars crisscross technique provided effective decompression of both bony and discal pathology in carefully selected patients with stable L5 isthmic spondylolisthesis and concomitant lateral disc herniation. Larger studies with longer follow-up are required before its role relative to fusion surgery can be established.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The pars crisscross technique may offer a minimally invasive, motion-preserving surgical option for selected patients with stable isthmic spondylolisthesis and concomitant foraminal stenosis and lateral disc herniation, potentially avoiding fusion surgery while allowing treatment under local anesthesia.

articles.title: The Long Way to the Operating Room: In-Hospital Operative Delay and Outcomes in Colorectal Surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In-hospital operative delay may reflect patient complexity and perioperative care processes, but its association with outcomes after colorectal surgery remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated whether surgery after the day of admission identified a clinically distinct subgroup with worse inpatient outcomes and greater resource utilization.
METHODS: Using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample, adults undergoing colorectal surgery following elective hospital admission between 2016 and 2022 were identified. Patients were categorized as same-day surgery (hospital day 0) or operative delay (surgery after admission). Delay duration was categorized as day 1, days 2-5, and days 6-10. Outcomes included postoperative complications, non-home discharge, length of stay, in-hospital mortality, and total hospital charges. Survey-weighted multivariable models adjusted for patient demographics, socioeconomic factors, transfer status, procedure type, All Patient Refined Diagnosis Related Group severity of illness and risk of mortality, and hospital characteristics. Sensitivity analyses excluded transferred patients, evaluated postoperative length of stay, replaced APR-DRG measures with individual Elixhauser comorbidities, and assessed robustness to unmeasured confounding using E-values.
RESULTS: Among 175,515 patients, 14,336 (8.2%) underwent surgery after admission. Patients with operative delay were older and more frequently had major or extreme illness severity, major or extreme risk of mortality, and interhospital transfer. After adjustment, operative delay was associated with higher probabilities of postoperative complications (14.91% vs. 12.95%; adjusted difference, 1.96 percentage points), non-home discharge (27.45% vs. 22.25%; adjusted difference, 5.20 percentage points), and in-hospital mortality (0.78% vs. 0.58%; adjusted difference, 0.19 percentage points), as well as longer length of stay (6.82 vs. 5.01 days; adjusted difference, 1.81 days) and higher total hospital charges ($96,656 vs. $87,823; adjusted difference, $8833). Complications, length of stay, and charges increased across longer delay intervals, with the largest differences after delays of 6-10 days.
CONCLUSIONS: In-hospital operative delay among adults undergoing colorectal surgery was associated with worse inpatient outcomes and increased resource utilization. Longer total length of stay appeared to reflect hospital days accrued before surgery rather than prolonged postoperative recovery. Operative delay may reflect patient complexity and perioperative care processes although the clinical necessity or modifiability of longer preoperative intervals could not be determined.

articles.title: Hybrid resection in upper tracheal stenosis: balancing unequal diameters through sliding technique: A five-year single-center experience.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Segmental tracheal resection with primary end-to-end anastomosis is the standard treatment for benign upper tracheal stenosis; however, proximal-distal luminal diameter mismatch may increase anastomotic tension and predispose to restenosis. We evaluated the feasibility, safety, and clinical outcomes of a hybrid tracheal resection with sliding technique designed to improve airway caliber while maintaining low anastomotic tension.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted including consecutive patients who underwent hybrid tracheal resection with sliding technique for upper tracheal stenosis between January 2019 and December 2023. The technique was selectively used in cases with anticipated diameter mismatch based on clinical and intraoperative assessment. The primary outcome was primary surgical success, defined as decannulation without the need for additional airway intervention. Secondary success was defined as achievement of a stable airway following adjunctive endoscopic treatment Secondary outcomes included perioperative morbidity, restenosis, and hospital stay.
RESULTS: Fifteen patients were included (mean age 25.3 ± 6.1 years; 60% male). The most common etiology was post-intubation stenosis (60%). Mean stenosis length was 2.3 ± 0.6 cm and mean resection length was 2.6 ± 0.5 cm. Mean operative time was 152 ± 17 min and mean hospital stay was 9.1 ± 2.3 days. Complications occurred in 6 patients (40.0%; 95% CI, 16.3-67.7%), predominantly minor. Restenosis requiring endoscopic balloon dilatation developed in 2 patients (13.3%; 95% CI, 1.7-40.5%). Primary surgical success was achieved in 86.7% of patients. Two patients required adjuvant endoscopic intervention and ultimately achieved secondary success with a stable airway at final follow-up. No anastomotic dehiscence or mortality occurred.
CONCLUSION: Hybrid tracheal resection with sliding technique appears to be a feasible and safe reconstructive option for selected patients with short-segment upper tracheal stenosis and diameter mismatch. This approach may facilitate tension-free anastomosis and satisfactory airway outcomes. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the retrospective design, small sample size, and absence of a comparator group.

articles.title: Association of Cutaneous Keloids and Hypertrophic Scarring with Risk of Postoperative Arthrofibrosis After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Arthrofibrosis is a debilitating postoperative complication and a leading cause of readmission, failure, and revision surgery. The purpose of this study was to assess the association between cutaneous keloids, hypertrophic scarring, and risk of arthrofibrosis after primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
METHODS: Patients undergoing TKA (n = 248,094) were identified using a large national database. Exclusions included a TKA for fracture, post-traumatic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or congenital deformity, or a second TKA within two years. Remaining patients were assigned to a keloid cohort (prior diagnoses of hypertrophic scarring, acne keloids, or scar fibrosis; n = 6,307) and matched 1:1 to controls by demographics and comorbidities. After propensity score matching, 6,305 patients remained per cohort with no significant baseline differences. Outcomes were compared using Chi-square tests at 30 days, 60 days, one year, and two years postoperatively, with significance set at P < 0.0083 (0.05 of 6).
RESULTS: The Keloid cohort demonstrated significantly higher rates of arthrofibrosis at 60 days (odds ratio (OR) = 2.06, P < 0.001), one year (OR = 1.54, P < 0.001), and two years (OR = 1.55, P < 0.001); revision TKA at one year (OR = 1.74, P = 0.002), and two years (OR = 1.50, P = 0.006); manipulation under anesthesia at 60 days, one year, and two years (P < 0.001); and periprosthetic joint infection within 30 days (OR = 2.05, P < 0.001). There were no significant associations found for lysis of adhesions or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
CONCLUSION: Patients who had preoperative cutaneous keloids or hypertrophic scarring demonstrate significantly higher rates of arthrofibrosis, revision TKA, manipulation under anesthesia, and periprosthetic joint infection following primary TKA. A dermatologic history of keloids and hypertrophic scarring may serve as a risk factor for identifying high-risk TKA patients.

articles.title: Pregnancy-Related Hand and Wrist Conditions.
articles.abstract: Pregnancy is associated with significant physiologic and biochemical changes that affect the musculoskeletal and peripheral nervous systems. Hormonal fluctuations, fluid retention, immune modulation, and connective tissue remodeling all contribute to pregnancy-related hand and wrist conditions. Hand and wrist complaints are common in pregnancy, particularly during the third trimester, and may significantly affect daily function and quality of life, yet they are frequently underdiagnosed and misattributed to normal pregnancy discomfort. This review summarizes the current literature on pregnancy-related hand and wrist conditions, including carpal tunnel syndrome and de Quervain tenosynovitis, as well as lesser reported conditions such as ligamentous laxity with transient joint instability, neuralgic amyotrophy, pyogenic granuloma, and small joint arthralgia. Our aim is to improve awareness of these conditions and to provide evidence-based guidelines for patient care and insight into the complexities of the physiologic changes of pregnancy. Although these conditions may mimic traumatic, inflammatory, or degenerative disease, most follow a benign and self-limited course. Conservative management is effective in most cases and surgical intervention is less commonly required. When surgery is warranted, certain perioperative measures need to be considered. Improved recognition of pregnancy-specific conditions is essential to guide appropriate management and patient counseling.

articles.title: Early Balloon Kyphoplasty Across Different Age Groups in Elderly Patients With Vertebral Compression Fractures: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Center.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vertebral compression fractures (VCFs) are common, particularly in elderly patients. VCFs are often associated with significant pain, functional impairment, and spinal deformity. The aim of this study was to compare the outcomes of early balloon kyphoplasty across age groups.
METHODS: This retrospective study analyzed patients treated with early balloon kyphoplasty for VCFs at a tertiary hospital from 2015 to 2024. Early balloon kyphoplasty was defined as surgical treatment performed within 7 days of radiological diagnosis of an acute osteoporotic VCF. Patients were divided into 2 age groups: those younger than 80 years (group A) and those 80 years or older (group B). Data collected included time to diagnosis, time to surgery, total hospital stay, American Society of Anesthesiologists score, complication rates, and visual analog scale score. Radiological outcomes were assessed using the Beck Index. Rates of cement leakage, re-fracture, and adjacent fracture were also evaluated.
RESULTS: Ninety-eight patients were included (53 in group A; 45 in group B). Both groups showed significant improvement in visual analog scale scores and Beck Index following kyphoplasty (P < 0.0001). Cement leakage, re-fracture, and adjacent fracture rates were comparable between the 2 groups. Minor complications differed between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, early balloon kyphoplasty was associated with significant improvements in pain and vertebral body restoration in elderly patients with osteoporotic VCFs, with similar short-term trajectories in patients aged <80 and ≥80 years.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Comparable short-term clinical and radiographic outcomes were observed between patients <80 and ≥80 years, suggesting that advanced age alone may not preclude consideration of early balloon kyphoplasty in appropriately selected patients.

articles.title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery in Gastrointestinal Cancer: A Narrative Review of Perioperative Evidence, Compliance-Associated Outcomes, and Geriatric Considerations.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) has become an important component of perioperative care in gastrointestinal oncology, although its implementation remains challenging because of heterogeneous patient profiles. This review critically examines current perioperative evidence, integrates the 2025 ERAS Society guidelines, and discusses three key areas for future development in ERAS: frailty-stratified care, compliance-associated clinical outcomes, and the potential effects of ERAS on perioperative inflammation and oncologic recovery.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent evidence highlights three key areas. First, frailty is an important determinant of perioperative vulnerability in older patients, and Geriatric 8 (G8) screening combined with geriatric co-management can help identify vulnerable individuals and guide individualized perioperative care. Second, ERAS compliance shows a graded association with postoperative morbidity, while machine learning-based analyses suggest that patient characteristics are associated with differences in adherence and recovery trajectories, supporting the implementation of risk-stratified pathways. Third, clinical studies have reported reductions in postoperative inflammatory markers following ERAS implementation, providing a biological rationale for further investigating its effects on perioperative immune function. ERAS implementation is also associated with earlier return to intended oncologic therapy (RIOT), although its impact on long-term oncologic outcomes requires further evaluation. The future development of ERAS lies in dynamic, risk-adapted decision-making rather than rigid protocol enforcement. Integrating continuous quality audits, frailty assessment, geriatric co-management, and individualized perioperative interventions provides an important framework for optimizing recovery across diverse patient populations. Further research should clarify the immunological effects of ERAS, determine whether improvements in short-term recovery translate into long-term oncologic benefits, and extend coordinated perioperative care beyond hospital discharge, as explored in the ERAS 3.0 paradigm.

articles.title: Quality-of-life following emergency laparotomy: is frailty a factor?
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: More than half of patients undergoing emergency laparotomy (EL) are over 65 years of age, and frailty doubles the inpatient mortality for these patients. This study aims to measure quality-of-life (QoL) following EL, and determine whether outcomes are impacted by preoperative frailty.
METHODS: We present four years of follow-up data (7 February 2020 to 5 February 2024) for patients who underwent EL at our single centre. Patients completed the 5-Level EQ-5D and 12-Item Short Form questionnaires at follow-up, the outcomes of which are presented. The responses of patients in low-risk (Clinical Frailty Score [CFS] 1-3, American Society of Anesthesiologists [ASA] grade 1-2) and high-risk (CFS 4-8, ASA 3-5) groups were compared.
RESULTS: Some 988 patients were prospectively entered into the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit database during the study period. Of these, 590 patients (60%) were followed up, 40% were frail (CFS 4-8) and 57% had a high ASA grade (3-5). Overall, our cohort of patients had QoL outcomes that were between 4.6% (mental component) and 17.4% (physical component) lower than would be expected for the baseline population. Frail (CFS 4-8) and physiologically less fit (ASA 3-5) patients had significantly worse QoL outcomes (p < 0.001). Interestingly, stoma formation and presence of malignancy were not associated with significantly different QoL outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Our cohort of patients had a lower QoL following EL than the baseline population. High preoperative CFS or ASA grade was associated with lower QoL. Where appropriate during the consent process, surgeons should consider counselling frail and unfit patients regarding the potential for low QoL postoperatively.

articles.title: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery in children-experience of two pediatric hospitals.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To describe the indications, complications, and outcomes of minimally invasive video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) in children by reviewing our institutional experience with VATS and comparing it with the existing literature.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational study of 75 patients in the 1-month to 18-year age bracket undergoing VATS between February of 2020 and July of 2024 at either of two pediatric hospitals. Data were collected from medical records and analyzed for demographic and clinical variables, including sex, age, symptoms, underlying diseases, procedural indications, prior chest drainage, duration of hospitalization before VATS, culture results, postoperative chest tube duration, length of hospital stay, complications, and perioperative mortality.
RESULTS: Pleuropulmonary infections, predominantly empyema, accounted for most of the cases (89.3%). Primary VATS (without prior chest tube drainage) was performed in 26% of the patients with empyema. In cases of empyema, performing VATS within seven days of admission was not associated with a shorter postoperative chest tube duration when compared with a delayed intervention (10.8 days vs. 12.8 days; p = 0.511). However, the mean total hospital stay was significantly shorter in the early VATS group (25.5 days vs. 36.6 days; p < 0.001). The overall complication rate was 21.3%, with bleeding and subcutaneous emphysema being the most common. There were no conversions to thoracotomy and no perioperative mortality.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study confirms that VATS is a safe and effective approach for managing thoracic conditions in children, particularly when performed by an experienced team. Further research is warranted to refine the timing and indications for VATS in the pediatric population.

articles.title: Ropivacaine in oblique subcostal transversus abdominis plane block for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy: a randomized, double-blind clinical trial.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the analgesic efficacy, opioid consumption, and inflammatory response of oblique subcostal transversus abdominis plane (OSTAP) block with 0.2% ropivacaine versus control in patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG).
METHODS: This is a prospective, randomized, double-blind, clinical trial. After standardized anesthetic induction, patients received a bilateral OSTAP block with 0.2% ropivacaine or 0.9% saline. Pain, rescue morphine, postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15), enhanced recovery after bariatric surgery (ERABS) discharge criteria, and inflammatory markers were assessed.
RESULTS: Rest pain was similar between groups at all time points. During movement, a lower score was observed at 24 h in the ropivacaine group (RG), median 1 (0-6) versus 2 (0-6), but the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment (p = 0.024; Benjamini-Hochberg [BH] adjusted p = 0.096). Total morphine consumption was similar, 10 (2-50) versus 11 mg (1-30), p = 0.926, as were PONV, QoR-15 118 points, p = 0.717, diet resumption 98, ambulation 76, and ERABS discharge criteria. Interleukin-8 at T3 was numerically lower in the RG, 7.2 (0.6-27.1) versus 9.8 (1.3-18.6) pg/mL, without statistical significance after adjustment (p = 0.073; BH adjusted p = 0.142).
CONCLUSION: OSTAP block with 0.2% ropivacaine was not associated with consistent differences in analgesic, recovery, or inflammatory outcomes.

articles.title: Budget Impact of Adopting Office-Based Ultrasound-Guided Carpal Tunnel Release: A Commercial Claims Cost-Comparison Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Ultrasound-guided carpal tunnel release (UGCTR) is an office-based alternative to open (OCTR) and endoscopic carpal tunnel release (ECTR), which are typically performed in ambulatory surgical centers or hospital outpatient departments. The economic implications of transitioning surgical volume to an office-based UGCTR pathway from a commercial payer perspective have not been evaluated. This study estimated the per-episode cost differences and annual budget impact of adopting office-based UGCTR compared with conventional OCTR and ECTR from a US commercial payer perspective.
METHODS: A decision-analytic cost comparison model was developed using the 2020 IBM MarketScan Commercial Claims and Encounters database. Episode costs included preoperative evaluation (physician visit, diagnostic ultrasound, electrodiagnostic testing), procedural costs (physician fees, facility fees, anesthesia), and postoperative rehabilitation. UGCTR costs were modeled at 150% of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rate for the anticipated CPT code. One-way deterministic sensitivity analyses were performed for all varying parameters. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis using Monte Carlo simulations assessed model robustness.
RESULTS: Total per-episode costs were $3646 for the blended standard of care (75% OCTR / 25% ECTR) and $2598 for UGCTR. UGCTR was associated with per-episode savings of $1048 (28.7%), primarily driven by elimination of facility fees and anesthesia charges, which accounted for 86.8% of total savings. For a hypothetical 2-million-member commercial health plan, annual savings were $2,096,000 at 50% conversion to office-based UGCTR (per-member-per-month savings: $0.09). The UGCTR physician fee and standard of care facility fees were the dominant drivers of model uncertainty. Office-based UGCTR was cost-saving in 100% of the simulations (mean savings: $1123; 95% credible interval: $620-$1664).
CONCLUSION: Office-based UGCTR was associated with lower per-episode costs compared with facility-based OCTR and ECTR, driven primarily by elimination of facility fees and anesthesia charges. These findings support the economic rationale for commercial payer coverage of office-based UGCTR.

articles.title: "It wasn't up to me; I trusted the doctors": Understanding the perioperative experiences of patients with limited English proficiency undergoing emergency general surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Emergency general surgery (EGS) requires rapid decision-making, which may limit patient-reported outcome measure (PROM) development for limited English proficiency (LEP) patients.
STUDY DESIGN: We performed a convergent mixed-methods study of adults (≥18 years) undergoing EGS who required interpreter services; patients not meeting these criteria were excluded. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed using grounded theory and thematic analysis, with Fisher's exact and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests examining associations between themes and clinical characteristics.
RESULTS: Among 20 patients, 50% felt they had no choice but surgery, and 80% reported limited choice or pain-constrained decision-making. Unclear communication or confusion was reported by 30%. Dissatisfaction with translator services occurred in 30%; 67% used alternative communication methods. Dissatisfied patients were older (median age, 77 vs 49 years; p = 0.015).
CONCLUSIONS: LEP patients undergoing EGS reported limited autonomy, unclear communication, and interpreter dissatisfaction, supporting PROM development focused on communication, autonomy, and language services, specifically for older patients.

articles.title: Perioperative factors related to postoperative mechanical ventilation duration after thoracic surgery requiring one-lung ventilation: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: One-lung ventilation (OLV) is essential for thoracic surgery but may contribute to perioperative gas-exchange impairment and delayed respiratory recovery. Postoperative mechanical ventilation may serve as a pragmatic marker of early respiratory recovery and ICU resource use after thoracic procedures.
AIM: To explore the relationship between a simple set of clinically available perioperative variables and postoperative mechanical ventilation duration after elective thoracic surgery requiring OLV.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective observational cohort study included adult patients undergoing elective thoracic surgery requiring OLV. The primary outcome was the time from ICU admission to successful extubation, defined as the absence of reintubation within 48 hours. The multivariable linear regression model of log-transformed ventilation duration included ARISCAT score, OLV duration, intraoperative P/F ratio, and surgical approach.
RESULTS: Ninety-seven patients had complete data for the main multivariable analysis, and no patient required reintubation within 48 hours after extubation. The overall model was statistically significant (F (4,92) = 3.85, R2 = 0.1435, adjusted R2 = 0.1063, p = 0.0061). OLV duration showed the strongest hypothesis-generating trend: each additional 30 minutes of OLV corresponded to an estimated 8.4% longer postoperative ventilation duration (95% CI, -1.1% to +18.9%, p = 0.082). ARISCAT score, P/F ratio, and thoracotomy versus VATS showed no statistically significant relationship with ventilation duration.
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, commonly available perioperative variables explained only a small proportion of the variability in postoperative ventilation duration, and no individual variable demonstrated an independent statistically significant relationship with the outcome. The non-significant trend observed for OLV duration should be considered hypothesis-generating and evaluated in larger cohorts.

articles.title: Current strategies of cerebral oxygenation monitoring in general intensive care units: a narrative review.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cerebral hypoxia represents the final metabolic consequence of sustained intracranial pressure and impaired autoregulation. Continuous cerebral oxygen monitoring is essential to prevent secondary ischemic injury in neurocritical care particularly in severe traumatic brain injury, malignant infarction, and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage. It also guides management of systemic disturbances such as shock, sepsis, and respiratory failure and is increasingly used perioperatively in high-risk cardiac, carotid, and neurosurgical procedures.
AIM OF THE STUDY: To synthesize physiological principles, monitoring modalities, and clinical applications of cerebral oxygenation across neurocritical care and perioperative settings, emphasizing bedside interpretation and integration within multimodal neuromonitoring.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed and Scopus were searched (January 2010-January 2025) using MeSH terms and keywords including "cerebral oxygenation," "brain tissue oxygen tension," "jugular bulb saturation," and "near-infrared spectroscopy." Fifty-eight English-language studies (randomized controlled trials, observational studies, reviews, and editorials) were included. Non-English publications, animal studies, conference abstracts, unavailable full texts, and non-peer-reviewed articles were excluded.
RESULTS: Brain tissue oxygen tension, jugular bulb oximetry, and near-infrared spectroscopy provide complementary insights. Brain tissue oxygen tension is invasive and region-specific (<25 mmHg indicates high risk), jugular bulb oximetry reflects global cerebral oxygen extraction, and near-infrared spectroscopy enables noninvasive regional trend monitoring. Multimodal neuromonitoring integrating these with intracranial pressure, transcranial Doppler, and electroencephalography improves detection and management of secondary ischemia. In neurocritical care, invasive monitoring supports targeted interventions, whereas in ICU and perioperative settings, multimodal strategies balance diagnostic yield and feasibility.
CONCLUSIONS: Cerebral oxygen monitoring should be routinely implemented in high-risk patients. Multimodal neuromonitoring should be prioritized to detect hypoxia early and guide individualized cerebral perfusion strategies. Near-infrared spectroscopy should be used for continuous monitoring, while invasive modalities should be reserved for high-risk neurocritical patients. Standardized thresholds and protocolized approaches should be established through prospective, outcome-driven research.

articles.title: Pediatric stone disease: a urologist's perspective.
articles.abstract: Pediatric urolithiasis is increasing in prevalence worldwide and differs from adult stone disease because of its strong associations with metabolic abnormalities, genetic disorders, congenital urinary tract anomalies, and a lifelong risk of recurrence. Urologic management extends beyond stone removal to achieve durable stone-free status while preserving the developing urinary tract and minimizing cumulative treatment burden, including radiation exposure, repeated general anesthesia, reintervention, and stent-related morbidity. Ultrasonography is the first-line imaging modality, whereas low-dose noncontrast computed tomography should be reserved for cases with equivocal ultrasonographic findings or complex stones requiring operative planning. Small, uncomplicated stones may initially be managed expectantly, with selective use of medical expulsive therapy. Shock wave lithotripsy remains a useful option for selected small renal and proximal ureteral stones. Ureteroscopy is effective for midto- distal ureteral stones, while retrograde intrarenal surgery has expanded the treatment options for renal stones, particularly in older children. Miniaturized percutaneous nephrolithotomy offers high single-session stone clearance rates for large, lower- pole, and complex stones. Routine prestenting is not supported by current evidence and should be reserved for cases in which ureteral access or drainage is problematic. Stone analysis, metabolic evaluation, and long-term ultrasound-based surveillance are essential components of postoperative care. This review summarizes surgical decision-making, procedure-specific considerations, and emerging technologies in pediatric urolithiasis from a urologist's perspective.

articles.title: Does Aquablation wash away holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP)?: a comparison of the techniques and outcomes.
articles.abstract: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the most prevalent urological condition in aging men and often requires surgical treatment. While traditional procedures such as open simple prostatectomy (OSP) and transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) have been widely used, newer modalities, including holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP)/anatomic endoscopic enucleation of the prostate (AEEP), initially described in 1997, and Aquablation robotic waterjet therapy (RWT) with FDA approval in 2018, have emerged as modern contenders as a new gold standard. This review study aimed to compare HoLEP and Aquablation RWT across various clinical domains, including symptom relief, quality of life (QoL), sexual function, perioperative outcomes, durability, and learning curves, to guide evidence-based surgical decision-making for BPH treatment. A comprehensive analysis of published randomized trials, registry data, and institutional experience was conducted and outcomes were compared. Both techniques result in significant improvements in LUTS and QoL. HoLEP remains a durable treatment, especially for large prostates, with <2% retreatment rates; however, it is associated with a steep learning curve, temporary or permanent stress urinary incontinence (SUI), and high rates of ejaculatory dysfunction. In comparison, Aquablation RWT is associated with a shorter learning curve, comparable improvements in LUTS, minimal SUI, and superior preservation of antegrade ejaculatory function. Same-day discharge is feasible for both techniques. Both HoLEP and Aquablation offer superior urinary outcomes compared to TURP for prostates of all volumes. However, given the low learning curve, minimal risk of stress incontinence and ejacultory function preservation, Aquablation is an increasingly attractive option for both physicians and patients.

articles.title: Severity, duration, and pattern of intraoperative hypotension and early postoperative cognitive decline in adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery: a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is known to pose risks for myocardial and renal injury, but its links to early postoperative cognitive decline (ePOCD) are ambiguous due to varying definitions of IOH across studies.
METHOD: This prospective observational cohort study at a tertiary teaching hospital in Ajman, United Arab Emirates, involved 261 adults undergoing elective non-cardiac surgeries under general anaesthesia. The study defined IOH as a decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) exceeding 20% from the pre-induction baseline and categorised it by severity (mild, moderate, severe) and duration/pattern (controlled episodes, prolonged episodes, frequent short episodes). Cognitive assessment was conducted using the Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment pre-surgery, immediately after, and on postoperative day 1.
RESULTS: The results indicated that 93.1% of patients experienced IOH as defined, primarily mild and moderate cases, with no severe instances recorded. ePOCD was identified in 3.1% of patients. Scores on both cognitive assessments dropped significantly right after surgery but showed partial recovery by day 1. Notably, the presence of IOH did not correlate with ePOCD, whereas the severity and pattern of hypotension were associated with it, with higher ePOCD rates in patients with moderate hypotension and in those with a single prolonged episode or frequent short episodes than in those with a single short (controlled) episode. In addition, patients experiencing ePOCD were significantly older and had longer durations of hypotension. The findings suggest that a simple threshold of >20% relative change in MAP fails to predict ePOCD risk, whereas cumulative exposure, severity, and pattern of hypotension were associated with ePOCD in this exploratory analysis. Because all ePOCD events occurred in the oldest patients, these associations could not be separated from the effect of age and should not be interpreted as evidence that these measures predict ePOCD independently.
DISCUSSION: These results argue against relying on binary definitions of IOH in neurocognitive studies and highlight the importance of exposure metrics. Confounding, particularly by age, prevented causal inference because of the small number of ePOCD events and collinearity between age and hypotensive exposure.

articles.title: Clinical safety assessment of implanted brain-computer interfaces: current evidence and a pathway to standardization.
articles.abstract: Implanted brain-computer interfaces are beginning to move beyond short laboratory sessions into long-term and home use. The evidence used to judge clinical safety remains fragmented. This review examines penetrating intracortical, cortical-surface (including subpial) and cerebral-venous systems, with stimulation considered as an additional exposure. Published studies report perioperative neurological and wound complications, vascular patency, stimulation-related effects, changes in devices and materials, and loss of functions on which participants may depend. Comparison across architectures remains difficult because cohorts are small and sometimes overlap, exposure denominators vary, long-term surveillance is incomplete, and retrieval data are limited. Chronic safety cannot be inferred from one test. Clinical review, problem-directed imaging, device interrogation and participant-level outcomes capture different parts of the safety record and need to be read together over time. We use this evidence to set out a lifecycle framework spanning the preimplant baseline, implantation, recovery, chronic use, new findings and end-of-use. It combines a small common dataset with architecture-specific modules and an event-triggered route for confirmation, attribution, escalation and outcome recording. Before this approach can inform formal guidance, it requires prospective multicentre testing, independent adjudication, input from participants and caregivers, registry follow-up and periodic revision. The near-term task is to make safety evidence comparable and clinically useful without treating any implanted BCI architecture as generally safe.

articles.title: Impact of administration timing of subanesthetic doses of esketamine on emergence agitation in patients undergoing nasal endoscopic surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emergence agitation (EA) is a common complication following general anesthesia, particularly after nasal endoscopic surgery with nasal packing. This study investigated whether the administration timing of subanesthetic esketamine influences its efficacy in preventing EA.
METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial registered at the China Clinical Trial Registry (No. ChiCTR2500115004), 108 adult patients undergoing elective nasal endoscopic surgery were randomized (1:1:1) to receive intravenous normal saline (Group C), esketamine 0.25 mg.kg⁻1 during anesthesia induction (Group E1), or esketamine 0.25 mg.kg⁻1 20 min before surgical completion (Group E2). The primary outcome was the incidence of EA in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU), defined as a Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale (SAS) score ≥ 5. Secondary outcomes included SAS scores, postoperative NRS pain scores, hemodynamics, and adverse events.
RESULTS: Ninety-five patients completed the study (Group C: n = 32; Group E1: n = 32; Group E2: n = 31). Baseline characteristics were comparable across groups. The overall EA incidence differed significantly among groups (13/32 [40.6%] in C, 8/32 [25.0%] in E1, 3/31 [9.7%] in E2; P = 0.018). Group E2 had a significantly lower EA incidence (absolute risk reduction [ARR], 30.9%, [95% CI, 11.0%-50.9%]; number needed to treat [NNT], 3.2 [95% CI, 2.0-9.1]; P = 0.011) and lower SAS scores (adjusted P = 0.016) than Group C, whereas Group E1 showed no significant difference compared with Group C (P = 0.287). Postoperative pain scores, rescue analgesia, extubation time, PACU stay, hemodynamic stability, and adverse event rates were comparable across all groups.
CONCLUSIONS: The preventive effect of subanesthetic esketamine on EA is timing-dependent. Administration 20 min before the end of surgery (0.25 mg.kg⁻1 IV) significantly reduces EA incidence in nasal endoscopic surgery patients. However, this single-center finding requires multicenter validation, and NRS scales remain limited in capturing packing-related suffocation discomfort.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: identifier ChiCTR2500115004.

articles.title: Postoperative hypoalbuminemia, albumin supplementation, and short-term complications after radical gastrectomy in elderly gastric cancer patients.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between early postoperative hypoalbuminemia and complications within 30 days after radical gastrectomy in older patients with gastric cancer, and to further explore the association between postoperative albumin supplementation and short-term outcomes among patients who developed hypoalbuminemia.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 378 elderly patients who underwent radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer at the First Hospital of Jilin University from January to December 2023. Patients were classified into a hypoalbuminemia group (<30 g/L) and a normal albumin group (>=30 g/L) according to the lowest serum albumin level within the first 7 postoperative days. The primary outcome was Clavien-Dindo grade >=3 complications within 30 days after surgery, and the secondary outcome was Clavien-Dindo grade >=2 complications and postoperative length of stay. Covariates in the main adjusted models were prespecified on the basis of clinical relevance. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for the primary outcome because of the limited number of events, whereas conventional logistic regression was used for Clavien-Dindo grade ≥2 complications. Postoperative nadir albumin was also examined as a continuous variable. Among patients with hypoalbuminemia, propensity score matching was used to explore the association between postoperative albumin supplementation and short-term outcomes. A POD1 landmark sensitivity analysis was additionally performed to reduce temporal overlap between postoperative albumin assessment and complication occurrence.
RESULTS: Among the 378 patients, 246 were classified into the hypoalbuminemia group and 132 into the normal albumin group. The incidence of Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications was higher in the hypoalbuminemia group than in the normal albumin group (15.9% vs. 2.3%, P < 0.001). After adjustment for age, body mass index, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status, preoperative serum albumin, surgical approach, surgical method, intraoperative blood transfusion, and pathological TNM stage, postoperative hypoalbuminemia remained associated with Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications (adjusted OR, 4.51; 95%CI, 1.55-17.54; P = 0.004). When postoperative nadir albumin was modeled continuously, each 5-g/L decrease was associated with an adjusted OR of 4.71 (95%CI, 2.43-9.51; P < 0.001). The incidence of Clavien-Dindo grade ≥2 complications was also higher in the hypoalbuminemia group (61.8% vs. 24.2%, P < 0.001). The corresponding adjusted ORs were 3.75 (95%CI, 2.16-6.62; P < 0.001) for the categorical model and 4.21 (95%CI, 2.54-7.21; P < 0.001) per 5-g/L decrease in postoperative nadir albumin. Postoperative length of stay was longer in the hypoalbuminemia group [6.0 (5.0-9.0) d vs. 5.0 (4.0-6.0) d, P < 0.001]. In the POD1 landmark sensitivity analysis, the associations were attenuated. Lower POD1 serum albumin remained associated with Clavien-Dindo grade ≥2 complications in both the categorical model (adjusted OR, 1.90; 95%CI, 1.09-3.34; P = 0.024) and the continuous model (adjusted OR per 5-g/L decrease, 2.08; 95%CI, 1.36-3.22; P < 0.001), whereas the associations with grade ≥3 complications were no longer statistically significant. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 154 patients with hypoalbuminemia were included, with 77 patients in each supplementation group. Conditional logistic regression accounting for the matched-pair structure showed an association between recorded postoperative albumin supplementation and Clavien-Dindo grade ≥2 complications (OR, 2.00; 95%CI, 1.12-3.58; P = 0.020).
CONCLUSIONS: Lower serum albumin levels during postoperative days 1-7 were associated with Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 and grade ≥2 complications within 30 days after radical gastrectomy in older patients with gastric cancer. However, these associations were attenuated in the POD1 landmark sensitivity analysis, particularly for grade ≥3 complications, highlighting the potential influence of temporal overlap and reverse causation. Because the albumin assessment window overlapped with the complication surveillance period, the main findings should be interpreted as associations rather than evidence of temporal sequence or causality. Among patients with hypoalbuminemia, recorded postoperative albumin supplementation was not associated with a lower incidence of complications; this finding may have been influenced by confounding by indication, residual confounding, and reverse causation. Postoperative assessment should therefore consider surgical trauma, inflammatory response, volume status, and overall recovery rather than relying on a single serum albumin value.

articles.title: Association of the admission albumin-hemoglobin index with postoperative outcomes in older adults with hip fracture: a post-hoc analysis of a prospective study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older adults with hip fracture are at high risk of postoperative mortality and impaired health-related quality of life. The albumin-hemoglobin index (AHI) combines nutritional and anemia-related information, but its prognostic value remains unclear. We evaluated the associations of admission AHI with 3-year all-cause mortality and postoperative health-related quality of life.
METHODS: Patients aged ≥65 years who underwent hip fracture surgery between November 2018 and November 2019 were prospectively enrolled. AHI was calculated from admission serum albumin and hemoglobin levels and analyzed continuously, by quartiles, and using an exploratory cutoff. The primary outcome was 3-year all-cause mortality; the secondary outcome was longitudinal change in EQ-5D utility. Kaplan-Meier analysis, Cox models, restricted cubic splines, linear mixed-effects models, and LASSO Cox regression were used.
RESULTS: Among 1,092 patients screened, 947 were included. Lower AHI was associated with older age, lower body mass index, poorer prefracture mobility, and worse overall health status. Three-year survival differed significantly across quartiles, with the lowest survival in Q1 and the highest in Q4. Each 1,000-unit increase in AHI was associated with a 43% lower mortality risk (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.57; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47-0.70; P < 0.001). Compared with Q1, the adjusted HRs for Q2, Q3, and Q4 were 0.69 (95% CI, 0.48-0.98), 0.45 (95% CI, 0.28-0.70), and 0.28 (95% CI, 0.16-0.49), respectively. Patients with AHI >4673 had lower mortality than those with AHI ≤ 4673 (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.32-0.66; P < 0.001). In the multivariable-adjusted restricted cubic spline analysis, the overall association was significant (P for overall <0.001), with no evidence of nonlinearity (P for nonlinearity = 0.855). Higher AHI was also associated with more favorable EQ-5D recovery, and LASSO sensitivity analysis supported the primary findings.
CONCLUSIONS: Lower admission AHI was independently associated with higher 3-year mortality and poorer recovery in health-related quality of life after hip fracture surgery. AHI may provide a simple tool for perioperative risk stratification and individualized management.

articles.title: Latent profiles of day-7 cognitive performance and associated ecological factors in older adults after elective surgery: an observational study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To identify latent profiles of postoperative day-7 cognitive performance among older adults after elective surgery and to explore demographic, behavioral, clinical, and social factors associated with profile membership.
METHODS: This prospective observational study included 308 consecutively recruited patients aged ≥65 years who underwent elective surgery under general anesthesia. Cognition was assessed with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), and latent profile analysis used five study-defined postoperative domain scores. Candidate correlates were organized with the health ecological model and examined using univariate tests and posterior-probability-weighted exploratory multinomial regression.
RESULTS: Three severity-ordered profiles were identified: low (n=83, 26.9%), intermediate (n=72, 23.4%), and high postoperative cognitive performance (n=153, 49.7%). Older age and lower education were associated with both lower-performance profiles. Greater activities-of-daily-living dependence, lower income, and living alone were associated with the low-performance profile, whereas poorer sleep was associated with the intermediate-performance profile.
CONCLUSIONS: Day-7 MMSE performance formed a severity gradient across three data-driven profiles. These cross-sectional profiles do not demonstrate postoperative decline, a clinical diagnosis, or an effect attributable specifically to general anesthesia. Longitudinal studies with retained baseline scores, appropriate comparison groups, and broader neuropsychological assessment are required before profile-specific interventions can be recommended.

articles.title: Real-world use of pembrolizumab in early-stage triple-negative breast cancer: Data from the French Early Access Program.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab improves outcomes in high-risk early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in KEYNOTE-522. In France, an Early Access Program (EAP) enabled its use prior to reimbursement, providing real-world evidence on its implementation.
METHODS: FR-POP was a prospective, multicenter observational cohort including adults with stage II-III TNBC treated with pembrolizumab within the French EAP (April 2022-November 2024). A limited dataset, defined by the French Health Technology Assessment authority, was collected at predefined time points. Analyses were descriptive and assessed patient characteristics, treatment patterns, pathological complete response (pCR), safety, treatment modifications, and quality of life.
RESULTS: Overall, treatment requests were received for 7687 patients across 427 centers. The cohort included populations underrepresented in trials, including older patients (32.3% ≥ 60 years) and those with comorbidities. Chemotherapy regimens were consistent with KEYNOTE-522 in 96.1% of patients. The pCR rate was 70.8% [69.1 - 72.6] among evaluable patients. Temporary pembrolizumab interruptions occurred in 1105 patients and permanent discontinuations in 1,240, mainly due to suspected adverse events. Immune-related adverse events were reported in 841 patients (10.9% [10.2 - 11.6]), including 417 patients (5.4% [4.9 - 5.9]) with 654 serious events, of which eight were fatal. Quality-of-life scores remained stable over time. Follow-up completion exceeded 50%.
CONCLUSION: This nationwide cohort shows that perioperative pembrolizumab can be implemented at scale in routine practice, with outcomes consistent with clinical trial data. Despite limitations related to observational design and incomplete data, these findings provide complementary evidence on feasibility and safety in a broader, unselected patient population.

articles.title: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in elderly patients undergoing high-complexity colorectal surgery: a retrospective cohort study from a Latin American tertiary center.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols have been shown to improve perioperative outcomes in colorectal surgery; however, evidence focusing specifically on elderly patients undergoing high-complexity resections remains limited. This study assessed the association of ERAS implementation among patients aged 65 years and older undergoing elective major colorectal surgery.
METHODS: A single-center cohort study using a historical control design was conducted between January 2018 and January 2026. Elderly patients (defined as ≥65 years) undergoing elective high-complexity colorectal surgery were included. Exclusion criteria included synchronous liver metastasis resection, urgent/emergency surgery, or a World Health Organization performance status of 4. The primary outcome was overall postoperative complications within 30 days after surgery. The risk analysis of the outcomes was performed using crude and adjusted risk ratios (aRR) with robust Poisson regression, adjusted for demographic and clinical confounders.
RESULTS: A total of 192 patients were included (non-ERAS: 83; ERAS: 109). The median age was 74 years [interquartile ranges (IQR): 70-79], and 52.6% were women. The most common procedures were anterior rectal resection (39.6%) and right hemicolectomy (29.7%). ERAS patients had a significantly shorter hospital stay [3 days (IQR: 2-5) vs. 4 days (IQR: 3-9); P = 0.002]. An adjusted relative risk reduction for overall postoperative complications of 59% [aRR = 0.41, 95% confidence intervals (CI) = 0.27-0.63, P < 0.001] was found. Adjusted relative risk reductions were also found for unplanned intensive care admission, readmissions, and reinterventions.
CONCLUSION: ERAS implementation in elderly patients undergoing high-complexity colorectal surgery was associated with lower postoperative morbidity, intensive care unit admission rates, and hospital length of stay, without any documented adverse outcomes.

articles.title: Outcomes of living-donor liver transplantation for Budd-Chiari syndrome: a retrospective comparative cohort study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) for Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) poses unique technical and management challenges. The outcomes of LDLT for BCS, compared with other indications, are unclear and warrant further elucidation.
METHODS: Data from 26 BCS recipients (20 adults and 6 children) who underwent LDLT between January 2019 and June 2023 were retrospectively analyzed to evaluate outcomes. In addition, adult BCS recipients (n = 20) were compared with a matched control group of recipients (n = 50) transplanted for other indications for perioperative parameters and outcomes.
RESULTS: The median age of adult BCS recipients was 25 years, while that of pediatric patients were 11 years. The majority (84.62%) of BCS recipients were male, and all (100%) had a primary form of the disease. The most common symptom was ascites (73.07%). Only five patients (19.23%) underwent radiological intervention before transplantation. Retrohepatic caval replacement was performed in five patients (19.23%). Clavien-Dindo major morbidity (grade 3b/4) was documented in eight patients (30.76%). Hepatic arterial thrombosis and venous outflow obstruction were documented in three patients (11.53%) each. Compared with the control group, BCS recipients experienced prolonged cold ischemia and operative time, heightened blood loss, a greater need for transfusions, a longer hospital stay, and a higher incidence of outflow obstruction (P < 0.05). The BCS cohort had 1-year and 3-year survival rates of 84.6 and 73.1%, respectively, compared with 90 and 82% in the non-BCS group (log-rank, P = 1.08).
CONCLUSION: Although patients with BCS present technical challenges, they can achieve outcomes comparable to those of non-BCS recipients with a good operative strategy, optimal postoperative anticoagulation, and regular surveillance for outflow complications.

articles.title: Percutaneous cryoablation for local control of breast cancer in patients unsuitable for conventional surgery: a prospective study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Management in elderly or medically frail patients is often limited by comorbidities and surgical risk. Cryoablation provides a minimally invasive option for local disease control under local anaesthesia; however, evidence supporting its use in palliative settings remains limited. This study aimed to assess the safety, feasibility, and radiological response of percutaneous cryoablation in patients unsuitable for conventional surgery or general anaesthesia.
METHODS: In this prospective study, consecutive patients with histologically confirmed invasive carcinoma or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) ≤ 3 cm were included if they had radiologically stable metastatic disease or were medically unfit for surgery. All underwent ultrasound-guided cryoablation using the IceCure ProSense™ system under local anaesthesia or monitored anaesthetic care. The primary endpoint was complete radiological response at one year; secondary outcomes included procedural success, same-day discharge, pain scores, and complications.
RESULTS: Between January 2023 and December 2024, twenty patients were treated (median age 87 years, range 53-93); 95% were ASA III. Most tumours were T1-T2 hormone receptor-positive carcinomas (median size 1.7 cm). Procedures were successfully completed under local or monitored anaesthesia in 95%, with 45% discharged the same day. Median ice-ball diameter was 5.3 cm, achieving 100% complete ablation. Complications were minor (10% superficial frost injury). At one year, most patients showed no recurrence except one developed multifocal disease outside the ablation zone.
CONCLUSION: Cryoablation is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective palliative option for local control of breast cancer in elderly or frail patients unfit for surgery.

articles.title: Clinical Outcomes and Patient Satisfaction Following WALANT Hand and Wrist Surgery in a Regional Island Hospital: A Retrospective Observational Study From the Maldives.
articles.abstract: Background Wide Awake Local Anaesthesia No Tourniquet (WALANT) is increasingly used for hand and wrist surgery because it permits procedures to be performed without sedation, general anaesthesia, or pneumatic tourniquet application. These characteristics may be particularly advantageous in regional healthcare systems with limited anaesthesia and operating theatre resources. However, evidence regarding WALANT outcomes in regional island healthcare settings such as the Maldives remains limited. Objective To evaluate clinical outcomes, postoperative functional status, patient satisfaction, recovery characteristics, and complications following hand and wrist procedures performed using the WALANT technique at a regional hospital in the Maldives. Methods We retrospectively analysed routinely collected operative records, completed questionnaires, and follow-up data of 62 adults who underwent WALANT hand or wrist surgery at Kulhudhuffushi Regional Hospital between June 2024 and May 2025. A commercially premixed solution of 2% lignocaine with adrenaline 1:80,000 was used without sodium bicarbonate. Outcomes included perioperative visual analogue scale pain scores, postoperative QuickDASH scores, patient experience, recovery, and complications. Complete data for the reported outcomes were available for all 62 included patients. Results The mean age was 44.5 ± 12.8 years, and 38 patients (61.3%) were female. Carpal tunnel syndrome was the most common diagnosis (24/62, 38.7%). Mean VAS pain scores were 3.10 ± 1.30 during local anaesthetic injection and 1.40 ± 0.79 intraoperatively. Fifty-five patients (88.7%) described the intraoperative experience as comfortable or very comfortable. Same-day discharge was achieved in 56 patients (90.3%), 50 (80.6%) returned to daily activities within one week, and 54 (87.1%) returned to work within four weeks. The mean postoperative QuickDASH score was 28.50 ± 12.93. Fifty-four patients (87.1%) were satisfied or very satisfied with their WALANT experience, and 57 (91.9%) indicated that they would undergo WALANT again if required. Five patients (8.1%) had recorded postoperative complications, comprising two wound infections (3.2%), two cases of transient numbness (3.2%), and one haematoma (1.6%). One patient undergoing a trauma-related fracture procedure required reoperation because of poor fracture alignment. No major anaesthetic complication or digital ischaemia was recorded. No conversion to general anaesthesia was required. Conclusions In this single-centre series, WALANT was feasible for selected hand and wrist procedures in a regional island hospital and was associated with low perioperative pain, high patient satisfaction, and frequent same-day discharge. Postoperative complications were recorded in five patients (8.1%), with no major anaesthetic complications or digital ischaemia observed. These findings support further evaluation of WALANT as an ambulatory surgical approach in comparable regional and resource-constrained healthcare settings. Prospective multicentre comparative studies incorporating baseline and longitudinal functional assessment are warranted.

articles.title: Navigating ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia: narrative review on techniques, evidence, and evolving clinical practice.
articles.abstract: Ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia (UGRA) has emerged as a new technical approach to provide real-time visualization of the needle pathway to minimize the risk of trauma to surrounding structures, notably vessels and nerves. This review will examine the basic concepts of UGRA and describe how regional anesthetic methods are categorized by region. Additionally, it explores technological approaches, offers block-specific insights, and discusses their clinical practice indications, such as postoperative pain management, as well as emergency physicians' use of these techniques to treat severe conditions like fractures, trauma, and muscular injuries, or even as an adequate substitute for procedural sedation. UGRA is also being used more frequently in obstetrics to relieve pain during labor and delivery because of its broad safety and effectiveness. Although UGRA increases block accuracy and safety, there are risks such as hematoma, nerve damage, and local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Careful dosing, monitoring, sterile technique, and preparedness to handle emergencies - including lipid rescue therapy for LAST - are all necessary components of safe practice. On the other hand, artificial intelligence (AI), simulation, portable ultrasonography, augmented reality, and robotics are improving UGRA by enhancing accuracy, safety, training, and access, and making operations more effective and accessible. The implementation of UGRA is constrained by institutional hurdles, costs, and skill requirements; consistent training and credentialing are essential to increase proficiency and safety. UGRA promotes healing, reduces opioid use, and improves pain management. Although there are risks, safety and accessibility are enhanced by careful technique, monitoring, and advances such as portable ultrasonography and AI. Standardized training is necessary for optimal use.

articles.title: A temporary suture-loop occlusion technique for myomectomy during cesarean section: initial experience with 50 consecutive cases.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To describe a novel temporary suture-loop occlusion technique and report its perioperative outcomes when applied to patient-requested myomectomy for asymptomatic FIGO type 6 fibroids during cesarean section.
METHODS: In this single-center retrospective case series, 50 patients underwent cesarean section with concurrent resection of FIGO type 6 fibroids using this technique. The key steps included: placing a circumferential 0-gauge absorbable suture around the fibroid base and securing it with a single throw; an assistant then maintained continuous traction on the suture ends to occlude the blood supply, followed by blunt enucleation under traction.
RESULTS: The median intraoperative blood loss was 400 mL (IQR, 400-500), with a median hemoglobin decrease of 6.0 g/L. No patient required transfusion. The median operative time was 72.5 min.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective series of asymptomatic patients who chose to undergo myomectomy during cesarean section, the application of a temporary suture-loop occlusion technique was associated with a perioperative blood loss profile that did not necessitate transfusion. These findings describe the feasibility of the technique in this specific context but do not establish its efficacy compared to other methods or support routine myomectomy for asymptomatic fibroids. Prospective studies with separate outcome measures are needed. Importantly, this technique was applied only in highly selected asymptomatic patients who, after extensive counseling, explicitly requested concurrent myomectomy. These findings are descriptive and do not support routine myomectomy for asymptomatic fibroids during cesarean section.

articles.title: Routine without understanding: patients' experiences of preoperative preparation in surgical care at St. Martin de Porres Hospital, Eikwe.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Preoperative preparation is essential for safe surgical care, yet in many low-resource settings it often prioritises biomedical readiness over holistic, patient-centred support, contributing to patient anxiety, confusion, and unmet information needs. This study explored patients' experiences of preoperative preparation at St. Martin de Porres Hospital, Eikwe, Ghana.
METHODS: An exploratory descriptive qualitative design was employed. Fifteen adult patients who had undergone elective or emergency surgery within four weeks prior to data collection were purposively sampled. Data were collected through face-to-face semi-structured interviews conducted in either English or Akan, based on participant preference. All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework, supported by NVivo version 12.
RESULTS: Two themes emerged: physical/physiological preparation and psychological preparation. Routine procedures such as fasting, shaving, vital signs monitoring, and laboratory tests were commonly reported, but were often undertaken without adequate explanation, causing confusion and anxiety. Painful procedures, particularly catheterisation, heightened distress. Psychological preparation was inconsistent and mostly limited to reassurance without clear procedural information.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative preparation in this setting remains predominantly routine-driven and focused on biomedical readiness, with inadequate psychological and informational support.
IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE: Integrating structured patient education, effective communication, and strengthened nursing roles is essential to improve perioperative experiences, reduce anxiety, and enhance patient-centred surgical care in similar resource-constrained settings.

articles.title: More vasopressors were required during anesthesia maintenance with sevoflurane than remimazolam in a high-risk patient: a case report.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Remimazolam besilate is known to cause less hypotension than other anesthetics. We experienced an anesthetic switch from remimazolam to sevoflurane in a high-risk patient, allowing us to compare the intra-individual hemodynamic effects of the two anesthetics.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 57-year-old woman with multiple cardiovascular complications underwent a lower-limb amputation. We selected remimazolam anesthesia with peripheral nerve blocks to minimize the risk of intraoperative hypotension. During the closure of the surgical site after deflating the tourniquet, we switched anesthetics from remimazolam to sevoflurane because the attending anesthesiologist had to leave for other duties. Then, repeated doses of phenylephrine were required throughout the remainder of the surgery, despite comparable surgical and other anesthetic conditions before and after the switch. After discontinuation of sevoflurane and remifentanil, noradrenaline was no longer required.
CONCLUSIONS: This case report has shown that additional vasopressors were required during anesthesia maintenance with sevoflurane after switching from remimazolam.

articles.title: Feasibility and perceived educational value of extended reality trauma simulation for emergency medical teams in a multinational training context.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Large-scale civil military medical live simulation exercises such as NATO Centre of Excellence for Military Medicine's (NATO MILMED COE) Vigorous Warrior (VW) series provide authentic environments to test interoperability and clinical performance of Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs). However, such exercises are resource intensive, logistically demanding, and infrequent, raising challenges for sustained workforce readiness. Extended Reality (XR) has emerged as a complementary modality with potential to extend access to trauma training, reduce costs, and support distributed learning. This study aimed to examine the educational feasibility of XR trauma simulation when embedded in multinational large scale live simulation.
METHODS: We conducted an educational feasibility study during Vigorous Warrior 2024 in Hungary, embedded within NATO MILMED COE's multinational large scale medical live simulation. Twenty-five EMT members from three countries (physicians, anaesthesiologists, nurses, and radiographers) participated in an XR-based penetrating chest trauma scenario using the MilExTS XR platform (Meta Quest 3 headset). Feasibility outcomes were evaluated across recruitment, implementation, usability, acceptability and perceived educational value using session logs, post-simulation surveys (Likert scales 1-5), and open-ended qualitative feedback. Data were analysed descriptively and thematically, in line with published feasibility frameworks for medical education.
RESULTS: Recruitment and completion thresholds were fully achieved (100% participation, 100% survey completion). Acceptability was high, with 88% of participants rating XR as good or excellent for trauma training and indicating willingness to use it in future education. Two-thirds (66%) endorsed XR for enhancing teamwork, while 68% valued opportunities for individual decision-making practice in a safe environment. Usability findings were mixed: 56% of participants rated scenario realism as average or below, cited limited physiological fidelity, lack of tactile feedback, headset navigation challenges, and insufficient role differentiation. Qualitative data supported XR's perceived educational value while identifying areas requiring further technological and pedagogical development.
CONCLUSION: XR trauma simulation demonstrated educational feasibility, high acceptability, and perceived learning value when embedded within a complex multinational large scale live simulation exercise. While limitations in realism and interface design remain, XR shows promise as a complementary modality for interprofessional trauma training. Further research should progress to efficacy testing, cost-effective analysis and curricular integration before wider adoption.

articles.title: Latency to and duration of desensitization following cornual nerve blocks of 3 local anesthetics in goat kids.
articles.abstract: Local anesthetic nerve blocks are widely used to reduce pain during the disbudding procedure. In dairy calves, lidocaine is the standard choice because it is fast-acting and inexpensive. However, in goat kids, lidocaine's efficacy is constrained by its short-acting duration, narrow safety margin, and challenges in administration. Longer-acting anesthetics have been shown to improve pain control in other species. Our objective was to describe the latency to and duration of desensitization for buffered lidocaine (BL), bupivacaine (BUP), and bupivacaine liposome injectable suspension (BLIS) for a cornual nerve block in goat kids. Twenty-four kids (5 ± 2 d old) met study inclusion and retention criteria and were randomly assigned to one of 3 treatments (n = 8/group). A single horn bud was anesthetized with 1 mL of anesthetic divided equally between the cornual branches of the infratrochlear and lacrimal nerves. A nerve stimulator was used to assess baseline sensitivity before and at predefined intervals after treatment to assess latency to (2.5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.5, 15 min) and duration of (BL and BUP every 0.25 h; BLIS at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24, 48, 72 h) desensitization. All treatments achieved a complete cornual nerve block within 8 min after injection (BL: 5-6 min, BUP: 5-7 min, BLIS: 5-8 min), demonstrating a similar latency. The duration of desensitization varied among treatments. The BLIS lasted the longest (8-72 h), although the number of desensitized kids decreased over time (n = 8 at 6 h; n = 5 at 8 h; n = 1 between 24 and 72 h). In contrast, desensitization with BUP lasted 1.75 to 3.5 h (n = 8 at 1 h; n = 6 at 1.75 h; n = 4 at 2.25 h; n = 2 at 3.25 h), whereas BL offered the shortest period of desensitization, lasting 1 to 2.25 h (n = 6 at 1 h; n = 1 at 1.75 h). Our findings suggest that BLIS offers the greatest potential for extended pain relief without compromising the latency to desensitization.

articles.title: Association of Opioid Dependence with the Clinical Performance of Intrathecal Ropivacaine During Spinal Anesthesia: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Opioid dependence may be associated with altered pain processing and may influence the efficacy of local anesthetics during spinal anesthesia.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the association of opioid dependence with sensory and motor block characteristics and early postoperative analgesic outcomes following intrathecal ropivacaine anesthesia.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 60 patients undergoing surgery under spinal anesthesia were enrolled, including 30 opioid-dependent patients and 30 non-dependent controls. Opioid dependence was characterized by a history of regular use of heroin-containing opioid preparations, with recent exposure confirmed by blood-based screening. All participants received intrathecal 0.5% ropivacaine (8 - 10 mg) with fentanyl 25 μg. Sensory block onset and duration, time to maximum sensory block, motor block characteristics, recovery-room pain scores, rescue analgesia, hemodynamic parameters, adverse events, and patient satisfaction were assessed.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 28 patients in each group were analyzed. No statistically significant differences in baseline demographic characteristics were observed between the groups. Opioid-dependent patients had shorter sensory and motor block durations (P = 0.003 and P = 0.001, respectively), longer sensory block onset time (P = 0.001), and longer time to maximum sensory block (P = 0.002).
