articles.title: SINGLE-SHOT FEMORAL NERVE BLOCK VERSUS LOCAL INFILTRATION ANALGESIA FOR PATIENTS UNDERGOING TOTAL KNEE ARTHROPLASTY: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Early postoperative rehabilitation is essential for optimal outcomes after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Femoral nerve block and local infiltration analgesia (LIA) are commonly used for postoperative pain control. However, the relative efficacy of single-shot femoral nerve block (sFNB) versus LIA remains uncertain. This meta-analysis compared both strategies in patients undergoing TKA.
METHODS: Medline, Cochrane Library, and Embase databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing sFNB and LIA in TKA patients. Outcomes included postoperative pain scores, opioid consumption, range of motion (ROM), and length of hospital stay.
RESULTS: Of 922 studies identified, 11 RCTs comprising 1,109 patients were included. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding early postoperative pain scores (mean difference [MD] = 0.25 points; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.19 to 0.69) or opioid consumption (MD = 0.55 mg; 95% CI: -3.28 to 4.38). However, the LIA group demonstrated improved ROM on postoperative day 2 (MD = -6.15 degrees; 95% CI: -9.16 to -3.14) and shorter hospital stay (MD = 0.23 days; 95% CI: 0.06 to 0.41).
CONCLUSIONS: LIA was associated with improved ROM on the second postoperative day and shorter hospital stay compared with sFNB, without significant differences in pain scores or opioid consumption. Level of Evidence II; Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.

articles.title: A Low-Cost Serratus Anterior Plane Block Phantom With a Thoracodorsal Artery Analogue and Pleural-Breach Feedback.
articles.abstract: Ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) is an evidence-supported component of multimodal analgesia for rib fractures, but training requires learners to integrate chest-wall sonoanatomy with safe needle control near vascular and pleural structures. We describe a low-cost part-task trainer, meaning a simulator designed to rehearse selected components of a procedure rather than the entire clinical encounter, and propose a staged pathway from simulation to supervised patient practice. Four wooden stacking blocks support a tongue-depressor scaffold. Transverse tongue depressors represent ribs, and a water-filled examination glove sits immediately beneath them as a simulated pleural safety boundary. Two chicken fillets represent serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi, with a single layer of cling film creating the superficial fascial plane. A fluid-filled thermometer probe cover placed in this plane represents the thoracodorsal artery. The primary task is superficial SAPB, with in-plane needle visualisation, vessel avoidance and hydrodissection. An optional deep-plane station is designed to provide immediate visible feedback if an unsafe trajectory breaches the water-filled glove; it does not simulate pneumothorax physiology. One final prototype was evaluated in a proof-of-concept bench session. Post hoc estimates from archived ultrasound images placed the superficial target plane at approximately 8-10 mm, and the rib surrogates at approximately 18-22 mm depth. No validity, reliability, durability or learner-outcome testing was performed. The model and proposed seven-step pathway are therefore offered as a starting point for structured preclinical preparation, not as a stand-alone competency or entrustment tool.

articles.title: Esketamine-Based Versus Sevoflurane-Based Anesthesia with Dexmedetomidine for Emergence Agitation in Pediatric Corneal Suture Removal: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Corneal suture removal, particularly microsurgery requiring complete immobility, demands adequate anesthetic depth while ensuring rapid recovery. Emergence agitation (EA) is a common postoperative complication in children and may compromise recovery quality. This study aimed to compare the incidence of emergence agitation between esketamine-based and sevoflurane-based anesthesia in children undergoing corneal suture removal.
METHODS: In this prospective randomized controlled trial, 116 children scheduled for elective ophthalmologic suture removal were enrolled. Patients were subsequently randomly assigned to receive either esketamine (group E, n = 58) or sevoflurane (group S, n = 58). In both groups, propofol 1.5 mg/kg was administered as pre-anesthetic sedation to facilitate parental separation. Atropine 0.01 mg/kg was administered to prevent excessive salivation, followed by intravenous dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg as baseline sedation. In group E, anesthesia was induced with esketamine 0.25 mg/kg at induction, with an additional 0.25 mg/kg before eye speculum placement, and maintained with 10 mg propofol every 5 min when surgery exceeded 5 min after intubation. In group S, anesthesia was induced with 4% sevoflurane and maintained with 2-4% sevoflurane. The primary outcome was the rate of EA. Secondary outcomes included hypertension, tachycardia, bradycardia, desaturation, respiratory depression, intraocular pressure, extubation time, and post-anesthesia care unit discharge time.
RESULTS: The incidence of EA was significantly lower in group E than in group S (6.9% vs 27.6%, RR: 0.25; 95% CI, (0.09 to 0.70); P = 0.003). Group E also showed a lower incidence of respiratory depression (3.4% vs 43.1%, P = 0.001) and a shorter time to discharge from the post-anesthesia care unit (19.50 [8] vs17.00 [5] min, P = 0.02). However, group E was associated with a markedly higher incidence of hypertension (22.4% vs 0.0%, P = 0.001) and a higher intraocular pressure compared with group S (16.00 [6] vs 13.00 [5] mmHg, P = 0.003).
CONCLUSION: Compared with sevoflurane-based anesthesia, esketamine-based anesthesia reduced the incidence of emergence agitation in pediatric patients receiving dexmedetomidine, but hypertension and elevated intraocular pressure were more frequently observed.

articles.title: Maternal and fetal anesthetic management during in utero embolization for fetal vein of Galen malformation: a case series.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: In utero embolization for fetal vein of Galen malformation is a novel ultrasound-guided transuterine, transcranial fetal neurointervention. We describe the anesthetic management for this procedure.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective case series of the anesthetic management of patients undergoing in utero vein of Galen malformation embolization at a fetal surgery program. Maternal and fetal anesthetic techniques and perioperative complications were assessed using descriptive statistics.
RESULTS: Nine patients underwent attempted embolization. Combined spinal-epidural anesthesia was employed in all cases, with conversion to general anesthesia in one. Fetal anesthesia consisted of intramuscular fentanyl, rocuronium, and atropine. Complications included fetal bradycardia and emergent delivery.
CONCLUSIONS: Fetal vein of Galen malformation embolization can be performed under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia with general anesthesia in reserve. Direct fetal anesthesia provides analgesia and immobility. Multidisciplinary maternal-fetal anesthetic coordination and preparedness for emergent delivery are essential. These findings provide guidance for anesthetic management of this novel procedure.

articles.title: Chronic pain-like responses revealed by allodynia and hyperalgesia in the ant Lasius niger.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Allodynia (pain in response to normally non-noxious stimuli) and hyperalgesia (increased sensitivity to painful stimuli) are well-established indicators of pain sensitization after tissue damage in vertebrates. These phenomena may also offer valuable insights into nociceptive processing in invertebrates. We assessed behavioural evidence for allodynia and hyperalgesia following two types of peripheral injury (tarsus amputation or burning) and sham treatment in black garden ants (Lasius niger, Hymenoptera: Formicidae). At 20 min, 24 h, and 96 h post-anaesthesia, a ramping hot plate assay with sublethal, but increasingly noxious, temperatures was used to assess allodynia and hyperalgesia. Locomotor speed and proportion of time spent moving were quantified to detect increased responsiveness at normally non-noxious temperatures (allodynia) or exaggerated responses at higher temperatures (hyperalgesia).
RESULTS: We observed an earlier onset of responsiveness in ants with tarsus amputations and burns compared to controls, consistent with allodynia, which was stronger and more consistent in tarsus-amputated ants and at later time points. Evidence for hyperalgesia was limited and time-dependent: amputated ants showed a steeper response increase at higher temperatures at earlier time points, but not at 96 h. Burn-treated ants showed less consistent evidence of allodynia and no evidence of hyperalgesia.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that sensitization extends beyond the acute injury phase and align with broader evidence for chronic, pain-like processing in insects. As a new injury model in insects, the burn treatment needs to be refined, or the underlying mechanisms may be different to those involved in classic, amputation-induced sensitization.

articles.title: Comparative Clinical Outcomes of Bilateral Decompression via Two Endoscopic Approaches for L4/5 Central Lumbar Disc Herniation with Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study compared the decompression extent and clinical efficacy of transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (TELD) and endoscopic unilateral laminotomy for bilateral decompression with discectomy (Endo-ULBDD) in the treatment of L4/5 central lumbar disc herniation (CLDH) combined with lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS).
METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted on patients with L4/5 CLDH combined with LSS who underwent surgery between 2021 and 2024, with a minimum follow-up of 1 year. A total of 72 patients were included, of whom 38 underwent endoscopic TELD and 34 underwent Endo-ULBDD. Perioperative outcomes, radiological parameters, and complications were compared to evaluate the relative advantages and limitations of the two approaches.
RESULTS: The Endo-ULBDD group had fewer fluoroscopic exposures and a shorter operation time than the TELD group. Endo-ULBDD achieved a greater DSCA expansion rate and showed a more bilateral distribution of facet-related bony decompression, whereas TELD demonstrated a more ipsilateral-dominant resection pattern. Although the ipsilateral and contralateral facet-related resection patterns differed significantly between the two procedures, postoperative TCSA-FJ and the TCSA-FJ resection rate were not significantly different between groups. No significant preoperative-to-postoperative changes or between-group differences were observed in DH, LL, SS, IVA, or Cobb angle. Clinical scores improved significantly in both groups, with no significant between-group differences during follow-up.
CONCLUSION: Endo-ULBDD and TELD both achieved favorable 1-year clinical outcomes in patients with L4/5 CLDH combined with LSS. Endo-ULBDD required fewer fluoroscopic exposures, had a shorter operation time, and achieved greater DSCA expansion. The two procedures differed mainly in the spatial distribution of facet-related bony decompression, while the overall extent of facet-related resection, as reflected by TCSA-FJ, was comparable. Short-term lumbar alignment parameters remained stable in both groups.

articles.title: Cadaveric Model of Pneumothorax (the GASP model): A Realistic, Reusable and Cost-Effective Simulator for Chest Drainage Training.
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: The gastrostomy-assisted simulated pneumothorax (GASP) model is designed to train residents in emergency medicine, anesthesiology, pulmonology, cardiothoracic surgery, and paediatric surgery in the various techniques used to perform chest drainage (CD).
INTRODUCTION: Pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency, particularly in the case of a tension pneumothorax. Failure to perform timely CD can rapidly result in cardiorespiratory arrest.1 Needle decompression, chest tube insertion, and finger thoracostomy are the three main CD procedures that healthcare professionals must master. However, these are technically challenging procedures with potentially severe and sometimes fatal complications. The literature reports significant complication rates (19%) and failure rates (18-21%).2,3Synthetic simulators for CD are commonly used in simulation centres due to their availability. While they are useful in the early stages of training to teach the fundamental steps of the procedure, they lack realism, are expensive, and do not provide the tactile feedback essential for safe and effective performance. The GASP model was developed to provide a realistic, easily reproducible, and accessible pneumothorax simulation tool aimed at improving CD training for medical trainees.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: By the end of this educational session using the GASP model, learners should be able to: 1) identify the two main thoracic anatomical landmarks commonly used in clinical practice for CD: the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and the fifth intercostal space at the midaxillary line, 2) become familiar with the tactile sensation of palpating the superior border of the rib, a key landmark for directing the chest tube safely and with the correct angulation, 3) mastering the three main techniques of CD: needle decompression, chest tube insertion, and finger thoracostomy, and 4) demonstrate proficiency while performing the procedure within a complex simulation scenario.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: The GASP model utilises fresh cadavers prepared with an insufflation device and a gastrostomy button to simulate pneumothorax or haemopneumothorax. Manual or automated ventilation may be added to enhance realism. This model can be used to teach residents how to perform the three main CD procedures effectively and safely. Each learner can perform multiple repetitions on each cadaver.
RESEARCH METHODS: At the Institute of Anatomy and Surgical Simulation (IASC) in Toulouse, France, 10 fresh cadavers preserved by refrigeration were used for this study. Each donor had provided informed and written consent during their lifetime for the use of their body in experimental research. Demographic data related to the cadavers, such as age, sex, and body mass index, were collected.The GASP model was tested on 20 hemithoraces from the 10 cadavers. The presence and quality of the pneumothorax were assessed via ultrasound by an experienced radiologist. The two main CD approaches commonly used in clinical practice (axillary and anterior) were tested, along with several CD techniques: needle decompression, direct insertion using a Pleurocath® drain and Monod trocar, the Seldinger technique with a Fuhrman-Cook drain, and finger thoracostomy.The GASP model was subsequently introduced to first-year residents in anesthesiology, emergency medicine, and pulmonology. Participants used Likert scales to evaluate the model's realism, its transferability to clinical practice, and its overall educational value. Additionally, the study assessed learners' perceived self-efficacy and the level of discomfort associated with performing simulations on cadaveric specimens.
RESULTS: In all 20 hemithoraces (10 right and 10 left), a large pneumothorax was confirmed by ultrasound. All major CD techniques were successfully performed, using a variety of drainage devices appropriate to different clinical scenarios. The model provided a realistic simulation of the procedure, offering the same tactile sensation as on a live patient. It enabled repeated CD in each hemithorax (exceeding 40 procedures per side) without compromising the structural integrity of the model.Eight first-year residents (from anesthesiology, emergency medicine, and pulmonology) were enrolled in the first CD course on cadaver-based training at our faculty, using the GASP model. Pre- and post-training assessments based on 10-point questionnaires demonstrated significant improvements in baseline confidence in technical skills, stress management, and overall performance. The GASP model was also evaluated by participants using a 5-point Likert scale, revealing high levels of realism, strong transferability to patient care, and increased perceived self-efficacy among learners. Finally, the cadaveric model was associated with minimal discomfort for participants.
DISCUSSION: The GASP model is realistic, easy to implement, reproducible, low-cost, and reusable multiple times. It serves as a valuable tool for enhancing skill acquisition among a wide range of healthcare professionals who need to master this procedure, providing a level of tactile realism that is often lacking in synthetic models. Its successful integration within our medical simulation centre supports the development of additional cadaveric simulation models for other emergency procedures.
TOPICS: Pneumothorax, chest drainage, emergency medicine, simulation, anatomy.

articles.title: Priapism Got You Down? A Novel Method to Build Your Own Moderate Fidelity Task Trainer.
articles.abstract:
AUDIENCE: This task trainer was designed to instruct emergency medicine (EM) residents and faculty at all levels of training.
INTRODUCTION: Priapism management is time-sensitive, and the clinical opportunities to perform dorsal penile nerve block and corporal aspiration are seldom practiced. Despite knowledge of the importance of prompt recognition and management of priapism, many emergency physicians may not actually perform the recommended procedures to manage it for a variety of reasons.1 Due to the sensitive nature of the condition, physicians are eager to learn about and practice these intimate maneuvers in the safe setting of simulation; however, there is not a commercial task trainer available.2 Some low-fidelity creations have been published as solutions, but they are less realistic and time consuming to make, limiting feasibility and usability.3-7 One published creation inspired this task trainer, but the main structure is no longer available to be purchased, underscoring the need for a model that can be reproduced and recreated by the educator with flexible starting materials.3 Others are more time-consuming to make and require specific simulation equipment4 or may not be easily reused.5, 6 Other published low-fidelity creations are less anatomically accurate, limiting the fidelity of practice regarding the most intimate aspects of the procedure.7, 8.
EDUCATIONAL OBJECTIVES: By the end of this educational session, participants should be able to: 1) identify indications, contraindications, and potential complications of priapism management, 2) gather appropriate supplies and describe relevant landmarks, anatomy, and patient positioning for management of priapism, 3) demonstrate a dorsal penile nerve block, aspiration of corpus cavernosum, and intracavernosal phenylephrine administration to treat priapism, and 4) develop an approach to manage common pitfalls of priapism care.
EDUCATIONAL METHODS: We developed a more realistic and replicable priapism task trainer using materials readily accessible in a simulation lab. Emergency medicine faculty and simulation center staff collaborated to create a task trainer constructed from silicone and internal tubing, using the mold of a phallic-shaped candle (see attachment). This model was then used in a 30-minute training session, which included ten minutes of interactive discussion reviewing the steps of dorsal penile block and priapism management with PowerPoint images as a visual aid. Next, learners performed the procedure from start to finish with faculty guidance, followed by an opportunity to ask questions. The training session was open to EM residents, pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) fellows, EM community physicians, and EM academic faculty.
RESEARCH METHODS: This study was approved as exempt status by the Indiana University Institutional Review Board. Following the educational session, participants completed a voluntary survey evaluating the task trainer's realism, its usefulness as a teaching tool, and their change in confidence in performing priapism management.
RESULTS: The mixed group included 14 EM residents, five PEM fellows, four EM community physicians, and four EM academic physicians. Of 27 participants who used the task trainer, the majority (92.6%) of survey respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the task trainer was realistic. Learners reported increased confidence in knowledge of the procedural steps and increased confidence in potentially performing the procedure in the clinical setting (Table 1). Most participants would recommend the training to a provider of a similar level of training.
DISCUSSION: Overall, the educational content was effective since learners reported an increase in knowledge of the steps of the procedure in addition to improved confidence to perform the procedure safely and successfully in the clinical environment. While many learners had never performed this procedure before in the clinical setting, the majority would recommend this training to a colleague of the same level of training. While the need for training in this procedure is clear,1-2 the options for available task trainers have remained limited. There is no commercial priapism task trainer, and published creations have varied strengths and weaknesses in balancing fidelity, cost-effectiveness, reproducibility, and reusability.3-7 The main takeaway from this training is that a realistic, durable, and low-cost task trainer can be developed to effectively teach how to treat a rare and sensitive procedure.
TOPICS: Priapism, penile nerve block, dorsal nerve block, urology, aspiration, decompression.

articles.title: Clinical features of external auditory canal foreign bodies in children: A retrospective analysis of 678 cases.
articles.abstract: This study sought to characterize the clinical features of external auditory canal (EAC) foreign bodies (FBs) in pediatric patients and identify safe and effective removal strategies. A retrospective cohort study was performed on 678 children with EAC FBs who presented to the Department of Otorhinolaryngology at Shenzhen Children's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2025. Demographic data, FB types, affected ear laterality, clinical symptoms, duration of impaction, removal modalities, complications, and clinical outcomes were extracted and analyzed from medical records. The cohort comprised 437 males (64.45%) and 241 females (35.55%), with children under 8 years old accounting for 73.45% of cases. The right ear was most commonly affected (57.82%), followed by the left ear (36.73%) and bilateral ears (5.46%). Stones/sand (25.22%) and beads (23.30%) were the most prevalent FB types. Most patients (83.78%) sought medical attention within 1 day of impaction. In 635 cases (93.66%), FBs were removed by the self-made irrigator in the otolaryngology department; in 19 cases (2.80%), they were removed by McClintock forceps or gun-shaped tweezers under otoscope; while in 24 cases (3.54%), removal was performed under general anesthesia (GA). Complications included EAC abrasion (44, 6.49%), tympanic membrane injury (15, 2.21%), and tympanic membrane perforation (10, 1.47%). The self-made irrigator achieved high removal success within our selected cooperative pediatric cohort and represents a safe, efficient tool associated with lower observed charges in this cohort, with clinical practical value under appropriate patient selection. Otoscopic removal under GA is a necessary alternative for uncooperative pediatric patients with EAC FBs.

articles.title: Research trends and hotspots in publications jointly addressing remimazolam and midazolam: A bibliometric analysis, 2016-2025.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This bibliometric study characterized the research landscape of literature jointly addressing remimazolam and midazolam from January 2016 through September 2025, with emphasis on publication trends, collaboration patterns, intellectual structure, and emerging research topics.
METHODS: Records published from January 1, 2016 through September 30, 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on October 30, 2025 using a predefined topic search designed to identify publications in which remimazolam and midazolam were jointly represented. After eligibility screening, 349 publications were analyzed using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix to evaluate publication trends, collaboration networks, co-citation patterns, and keyword evolution.
RESULTS: Publication output increased markedly over the study period. China contributed the largest number of publications, followed by Japan, South Korea, and the United States. Major research themes included pharmacokinetics, safety, efficacy, and procedural sedation. Recent keyword signals included flumazenil, risk, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Research productivity was concentrated within a limited number of journals and institutions, whereas international co-authorship was limited in this dataset.
CONCLUSION: Research jointly addressing remimazolam and midazolam expanded markedly during the study period and was geographically concentrated, with prominent attention to pharmacokinetics, safety, efficacy, and procedural sedation. These findings provide a structured overview of how the field has evolved and highlight priorities for multinational collaboration, direct comparative studies, and patient-specific dosing research.

articles.title: The influence of robotic assistance on hidden blood loss in the treatment of posterior pelvic ring injuries with sacroiliac screw fixation: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Pelvic posterior-ring injury is a severe traumatic condition accompanied by substantial perioperative hidden blood loss (HBL). Minimally-invasive sacroiliac screw fixation is widely applied for this injury, yet postoperative anemia remains common and is predominantly caused by HBL. Whether robotic-assisted screw placement can reduce HBL in patients with posterior pelvic-ring injuries remains unclear. We retrospectively analyzed the data of 64 patients with posterior pelvic ring injury treated with sacroiliac screw fixation in our hospital from January 2020 to June 2023. Based on the use of intraoperative robot assistance during surgery, the 64 patients were divided into 2 groups. The total blood loss (TBL) and HBL were compared to analyze the difference between the 2 groups. In the robotic surgery group, TBL was 335.51 ± 31.46 mL, and the HBL was 300.96 ± 37.01 mL. In the freehand group, the TBL was 410.57 ± 54.55 mL, and the HBL was 370.34 ± 54.51 mL. The difference between the 2 groups was statistically significant (P < .001). However, there was no statistically significant difference in visible blood loss (VBL) and surgical duration between the 2 groups (P > .05). The robotic group presented a significantly smaller postoperative maximum hemoglobin drop (P < .001), whereas transfusion-related indicators were comparable between the 2 groups (P > .05). In the treatment of posterior pelvic ring injuries with sacroiliac screws, the assistance of surgical robots plays a significant role in reducing intraoperative blood loss, particularly hidden blood loss. Compared to traditional freehand screw placement, we recommend considering the incorporation of robotic assistance during surgery.

articles.title: Risk factors for perioperative venous thromboembolism in patients undergoing colorectal cancer surgery: A single-center retrospective study.
articles.abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, is a serious perioperative complication after colorectal cancer surgery. Although guidelines recommend prophylaxis, bleeding risks complicate decision-making, and evidence regarding Japanese patients remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to identify perioperative risk factors associated with VTE in colorectal cancer surgery to inform effective risk stratification and targeted prevention strategies. A retrospective analysis of 397 patients who underwent elective colorectal cancer resection at a single institution between June 2014 and May 2024 was conducted. Preoperative and postoperative D-dimer levels were measured, and lower extremity venous ultrasonography was performed when indicated. When deep vein thrombosis was detected by venous ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography was subsequently performed to evaluate the presence of pulmonary embolism. Univariate analyses were used to determine factors significantly associated with VTE, and a P-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. Preoperative VTE was observed in nine of 397 patients (2.3%), and postoperative VTE was observed in nine of 388 patients (2.3%). The univariate analysis suggested that age ≥75 years, female gender, albumin levels < 3.5 g/dL, and hemoglobin levels < 10 g/dL were significantly associated with preoperative VTE, while operative time ≥ 240 minutes and intraoperative blood loss ≥ 50 mL were significantly associated with postoperative VTE. Advanced age, female gender, hypoalbuminemia, anemia, prolonged operative time, and increased intraoperative blood loss were significantly associated with perioperative VTE in univariate analysis. Effective perioperative risk stratification and targeted surveillance may contribute to the early detection and prevention of VTE in Japanese patients undergoing colorectal cancer surgery.

articles.title: Reassessing pharmacologic amnesia: benzodiazepines and intraoperative awareness in adults: a perspective on the limits of the evidence and the primacy of anesthetic depth.
articles.abstract: Perioperative benzodiazepines (BZDs) have long been given to adults in part for their anterograde amnestic effect: a pharmacologic safety net intended to prevent explicit memories of intraoperative awareness, should it occur. Recent evidence calls for a reassessment of that rationale, though not for its abandonment. In the 2025 B-Free trial (n = 19,768), a cluster-randomized crossover trial in adult cardiac surgery, no patient in either the BZD-free or the BZD-liberal group spontaneously reported awareness. Awareness is rare, however, and the trial ascertained it by spontaneous report rather than structured interview, so this observation says little about small or infrequent effects. The trial was powered for postoperative delirium. Its primary intention-to-treat analysis was neutral (14.0% vs 14.9%; adjusted odds ratio 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.01; P = 0.07). A per-protocol analysis suggested lower odds of delirium (odds ratio 0.90, 95% confidence interval 0.82 to 0.99; P = 0.02), an exploratory result open to selection and adherence bias. Systematic reviews and randomized trials do not establish a reliable awareness-preventive benefit of routine BZD administration, and several suggest possible harm. We argue that prevention of intraoperative awareness should rest on the assurance of adequate anesthetic depth, supported by preoperative risk stratification, monitoring beyond vital signs, and protocolized depth management. We also set out the principal limitations of the evidence base.

articles.title: A retrospective case series and technological review of post-surgical analgesia for orthopedic surgery using a smart connected infusion pump: an opioid-sparing protocol.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Opioid-sparing analgesia (OSA) strategies aim to reduce perioperative opioid exposure while maintaining effective pain control. Continuous peripheral nerve blocks (cPNBs) supported by ambulatory infusion pumps have demonstrated efficacy in reducing opioid consumption, yet data on electronic infusion systems in the home environment remain limited.
METHODS: A retrospective, single-center, uncontrolled feasibility series evaluated the performance of a smart connected electronic infusion pump within a multimodal opioid-sparing postoperative analgesia protocol in routine clinical practice. Twenty orthopedic surgery patients with continuous peripheral nerve catheters and patient-controlled boluses received an initial 20 mL nerve block (adductor canal, with or without supplemental iPACK, or interscalene/infraclavicular brachial plexus) followed by 0.2% ropivacaine via a standardized infusion regimen (8 mL/h basal rate with 3 mL patient-controlled bolus, 30-min lockout).
RESULTS: Postoperative opioid consumption over 3 days varied by procedure type and regional anesthesia technique. Overall, a median of 15 MME (IQR: 0-39.4 MME, range: 0-90 MME). Shoulder surgery patients (n = 12, 60% of cohort) receiving interscalene brachial plexus catheters had a median consumption of 15 MME (IQR: 0-45 MME, range: 0-90 MME), with 42% (5/12) using no opioids. ACL reconstruction patients (n = 3, 15% of cohort) receiving adductor canal blocks had even lower consumption, with a median of 0 MME (range: 0-22.5 MME) and 67% (2/3) reporting no opioid use. Patients undergoing other procedures (TKA, PFL and humerus fracture; n = 4, 20% of cohort) had a median consumption of 41.25 MME (range: 7.5-52.5 MME), and the thumb surgery patient (5%) reported no opioid use. Seventeen patients (85%) completed the full programmed infusion; the remaining three (15%) discontinued early due to catheter dislodgement, not pump malfunction. All alarms were resolved at home without interrupting therapy, and no pump-related discontinuations occurred.
CONCLUSION: In this small, real-world retrospective, single-center, uncontrolled feasibility series, a smart electronic infusion pump reliably delivered opioid-sparing perineural analgesia within a multimodal OSA protocol following orthopedic surgery in ambulatory and home settings, with no pump-related discontinuations and successful patient management of alarms. These observations support feasibility; analgesic adequacy was assessed only as a binary outcome (pain controlled or uncontrolled). Future comparative studies evaluating different ambulatory infusion platforms would help identify optimal device characteristics for home-based perineural analgesia.

articles.title: Comparison of internal fixation outcomes in young femoral neck fractures: three cannulated compression screws versus the femoral neck system.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Femoral neck fractures in young patients typically result from traumatic injury, present significant treatment challenges, and are associated with a high risk of complications. The cannulated compression screw (CCS) is a common fixation device, whereas the femoral neck system (FNS) is a newer fixation device.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical efficacy of the FNS and CCS in the treatment of femoral neck fractures in young patients.
METHODS: Between September 2021 and September 2023, 82 patients with femoral neck fracture aged 18-60 years were admitted to our hospital. According to the different fixation methods, the patients were divided into the FNS (38 cases) and CCS (44 cases) groups. The perioperative indicators, complications and follow-up function scores were compared between the two groups, and the follow-up time was ≥ 12 months.
RESULTS: The FNS group had shorter operation time (53.71 ± 11.20 vs. 64.61 ± 11.27 min, p < 0.001) and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times (14.05 ± 3.13 vs. 21.55 ± 5.06, p < 0.001). However, the incision length (38.05 ± 8.85 mm vs. 20.32 ± 6.34 mm, p < 0.001) and intraoperative blood loss (85.82 ± 23.62 mL vs. 65.89 ± 20.98 mL, p < 0.001) were greater. The FNS group demonstrated a lower rate of fixation failure (5.26% vs. 22.73%, p = 0.026) and a lower incidence of lateral thigh irritation (7.89% vs. 29.55%, p = 0.014), along with less severe femoral neck shortening (4.68 ± 2.04 vs. 7.14 ± 2.27 mm, p < 0.001). Patients in the FNS group achieved partial weight-bearing (3.08 ± 1.16 vs. 5.30 ± 1.50 weeks, p < 0.001) and full weight-bearing (11.71 ± 1.84 vs. 14.39 ± 2.07 weeks, p < 0.001) significantly earlier. The VAS scores at 3 and 7 days after surgery were significantly lower (p < 0.001), and the Harris scores at 3, 6, and 12 months after surgery were significantly higher (p < 0.05); however, the magnitude of Harris score differences fell below the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), and both groups achieved excellent final outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Compared to CCS, FNS has better intraoperative efficiency, a lower internal fixation failure rate, and less severe femoral neck shortening in the treatment of femoral neck fractures in young adults. However, given the retrospective design, relatively small sample size, limited follow-up time, and differential follow-up duration between the groups, these conclusions should be interpreted with caution.

articles.title: External validation and cross-center transportability of phenotypic age acceleration and laboratory frailty for postoperative mortality prediction: a dual-center cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Phenotypic Age Acceleration (PAA) and the Laboratory Frailty Index (FI-Lab) can be derived from routine biomarkers to describe biologic aging and accumulated laboratory deficits. Their prognostic behavior across different clinical settings, however, remains uncertain. We examined whether associations with postoperative mortality were consistent between two hospitals and whether either measure added predictive information beyond standard clinical variables.
METHODS: We analyzed 1,223 adults (671 from Shandong and 552 from Jiangsu) with linked health-examination/questionnaire information, perioperative characteristics, and follow-up through 540 days. Phenotypic Age was calculated from chronological age and nine biomarkers. Primary PAA used the Shandong age-Phenotypic Age relation as a fixed reference, and FI-Lab was the proportion of 17 prespecified laboratory deficits. Center-specific and center-stratified Cox models assessed 540-day mortality. Ridge logistic models were trained in Shandong and externally validated in Jiangsu for 365-day mortality; the reverse direction was treated as a secondary reciprocal transportability sensitivity analysis. As the fixed Shandong reference induced age dependence in Jiangsu, sensitivity analyses recalculated PAA as center-specific age-Phenotypic Age residuals with center-specific standardization. Secondary analyses covered the 12-month composite of death or incident diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease. Longitudinal analyses of within-person PAA and FI-Lab changes were exploratory; exact person-specific reassessment intervals were unavailable, and follow-up chronological age for PAA was approximated as baseline age + 1 year. All laboratory measurements used to calculate PAA and FI-Lab were obtained from the preoperative panel within 24 h before the index operation, and completeness of this panel was required for inclusion.
RESULTS: During 1,694.66 person-years, 74 participants died, including 57 within 365 days. In the fully adjusted center-stratified model, each 1-SD increase in PAA was associated with mortality [hazard ratio (HR), 1.34; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.03-1.75], whereas the FI-Lab estimate was borderline (HR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.00-1.65). Cross-center interaction estimates were imprecise (PAA interaction ratio, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.68-1.65; FI-Lab interaction ratio, 1.48; 95% CI, 0.94-2.32). Fixed-reference PAA was strongly inversely correlated with chronological age in Jiangsu (r = - 0.74); when PAA was recalculated using center-specific age-Phenotypic Age residuals and standardized within center, the fully adjusted pooled association remained (HR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.09-1.77). In the primary Shandong-to-Jiangsu external validation, the study clinical model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.60 (95% CI, 0.45-0.73); adding PAA, FI-Lab, or both yielded AUCs of 0.60, 0.63, and 0.63, respectively, without a consistent decision-curve net-benefit gain. FI-Lab, but not PAA, was associated with the 12-month death-or-incident-disease composite (RR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.08-1.71). Among 820 participants with repeated measurements, exploratory mean changes were + 2.90 years for PAA and + 0.02 for FI-Lab. Calibration estimates in the primary external-validation cohort were imprecise because only 23 deaths occurred by 365 days; nonsignificant calibration tests were not interpreted as evidence of good calibration.
CONCLUSIONS: Laboratory-derived aging and frailty measures were related to postoperative mortality across the two cohorts, and the PAA association was robust to center-specific residualization. However, absolute fixed-reference PAA values were not directly transportable across centers because the age-Phenotypic Age relations differed. Neither marker consistently improved prediction beyond the study clinical model, whose external discrimination was modest; calibration remained imprecise. Larger multicenter studies with rigorous cross-center laboratory harmonization are needed before routine perioperative use.

articles.title: Continuous ultrasound-guided rhomboid intercostal-subserratus plane block versus thoracic paravertebral block for analgesia and respiratory recovery in patients with multiple rib fractures: a single-center randomized trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Effective analgesia is essential in multiple rib fractures to preserve respiratory function. Thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB) is effective but may be limited by technical difficulty and complications. Rhomboid intercostal-subserratus (RISS) plane block is a newer ultrasound-guided alternative.
AIM: To compare the analgesic efficacy and pulmonary function recovery associated with ultrasound-guided RISS block and TPVB in patients with traumatic multiple rib fractures.
METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, blinded trial conducted in an emergency ICU, 50 adults aged 18-60 years with unilateral traumatic fractures of three or more ribs were randomized 1:1 to receive continuous ultrasound-guided TPVB or RISS block with catheter infusion in addition to standardized systemic analgesia. The primary endpoint was pulmonary function at 24 h, assessed using forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Secondary outcomes included pain scores at rest and during coughing, pulmonary function, diaphragmatic excursion, rescue opioid consumption, adverse events, and ICU and post-ICU ward stay.
RESULTS: Fifty patients were randomized, with 25 patients in each group. At 24 h, FEV1 increased from 56.2 ± 3.2% to 72.8 ± 5.4% in the TPVB group and from 57.7 ± 3.0% to 73.8 ± 5.6% in the RISS group. The baseline-adjusted between-group difference was not statistically significant (adjusted RS-TP difference, 0.47 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.63 to 3.57; p = 0.768). At 24 h, median VAS pain scores at rest were 1 (0-2) and 0 (0-2), while scores during coughing were 3 (2-4) and 2 (2-4), in the TPVB and RISS groups, respectively. Total rescue morphine consumption over 72 h was comparable between groups (13.3 ± 3.2 mg vs 11.7 ± 4.6 mg; p = 0.205). Needle visibility was significantly better with RISS. Vascular puncture and block-related pneumothorax each occurred in two TPVB patients and no RISS patients, although the between-group differences were not statistically significant.
CONCLUSIONS: Continuous ultrasound-guided RISS block provided analgesia and 24 h pulmonary-function recovery similar to TPVB in stable, spontaneously breathing patients with unilateral multiple rib fractures. RISS also provided better needle visibility. Although procedure-related complications were observed only in the TPVB group, this trial was not powered to establish comparative safety.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05898958. Registered on June 12, 2023. Retrospectively registered.

articles.title: Beware of Tall Stature: Growth Hormone Excess Associated with a Rare Parasellar Extra-Axial Tumour-Diagnostic and Management Challenges in a Resource-Limited Setting.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tall stature can be the sole indicator of growth hormone (GH) excess, which causes pituitary gigantism before epiphyseal fusion. In developing regions like Indonesia, a lack of systematic screening often delays diagnosis. While classic presentations involve accelerated linear growth, atypical cases may be dominated by neurological signs, such as seizures secondary to tumour mass effect.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 14-year-old boy presented with a 2-year history of rapidly accelerating growth velocity, increasing shoe size, and a 6-month history of severe morning headaches accompanied by drug-resistant focal seizures. Endocrine evaluations revealed significantly elevated basal GH (4.27 ng/ml) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels (536 ng/ml). Brain magnetic resonance imaging identified a large parasellar extra-axial tumour with suprasellar extension. The patient underwent a craniotomy and tumour excision; histopathology subsequently confirmed a rare, aggressive malignant mesenchymal tumour. Postoperatively, the patient achieved seizure resolution and normalization of GH and IGF-1 levels. However, he developed evolving pituitary dysfunction consistent with multiple pituitary hormone deficiency (MPHD), specifically central hypothyroidism, necessitating targeted hormonal replacement therapy and continuous clinical follow-up.
CONCLUSION: GH excess and gigantism can arise secondary to parasellar pathology rather than intrinsic pituitary disease, with neurological features like refractory epilepsy occasionally preceding classic endocrine manifestations. Rapid adolescent growth paired with neurological signs warrants urgent structural neuroimaging. Meticulous perioperative pituitary monitoring and early multidisciplinary involvement are essential to optimize long-term patient outcomes.
LEARNING POINTS: Pituitary gigantism can be driven by extra-axial parasellar masses rather than intrinsic pituitary adenomas, operating via mass-effect compression that disrupts hypothalamic somatostatin inhibition.Drug-resistant epilepsy and severe headaches caused by local tumour infiltration can dominate the clinical picture, meaning rapid adolescent growth paired with neurological symptoms mandates urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.Postoperative multiple pituitary hormone deficiency often evolves silently over weeks or months, requiring lifelong, multidisciplinary surveillance to detect late-stage deficiencies like secondary adrenal insufficiency.
articles.journal: Eur J Case Rep Intern Med

articles.title: Dysphagia After Cardiac Surgery: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Dysphagia is a significant clinical concern associated with increased risk of aspiration, prolonged hospital stay, and higher health care costs. In cardiac surgery, the reported incidence of postoperative dysphagia varies widely, ranging from approximately 3% to 60%, and contributing factors have not been definitively clarified. This scoping review aims to survey the current evidence associated with dysphagia following cardiac surgery involving cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). A systematic search of PubMed and Embase was conducted for original studies involving adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB. Relevant variables were extracted, including study design, patient characteristics, surgery type, assessment methodology, evaluation timing, outcomes, and risk factors. Risk factors were categorized as patient related, procedure related, or postoperative and were identified as independent or non-independent predictors. Systematic database searches yielded 85 results from PubMed and 73 results from Embase. Following manual review and citation tracking, 21 studies were selected for inclusion. Significant heterogeneity in assessment methods, study design, and definitions of swallowing impairment complicate the interpretation of findings across studies. Variables consistently associated with the development of swallowing dysfunction included intubation duration, transesophageal echocardiography use, reoperation, and multi-valve procedures. There were differences in types of predictors identified based on methodology used. Instrumental assessment methodologies (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing, videofluoroscopic swallowing study) identified specific, granular independent predictors, while studies that used universal bedside screening identified independent predictors related to functional status and perioperative management. Procedure-related predictors may offer opportunity for modification and perioperative interventions.

articles.title: Endoscopic Drainage of An Intra-Abdominal Chylous Collection.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chylous leak is an increasingly recognised complication following pancreatic surgery. It results from the disruption of the lymphatic system and may lead to persistent chylous ascites or collection. Ongoing chyle loss is associated with significant morbidity including malnutrition, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, hypoalbuminaemia, immunosuppression and impaired wound healing. Clinicians managing patients in the perioperative setting should remain vigilant for the development of chylous leak, particularly following high-risk surgery. While most cases respond to conservative management with dietary modification and use of somatostatin analogues, refractory cases remain challenging and may require technically demanding or morbid interventions. We report a novel minimally invasive approach using endoscopic ultrasound-guided cyst gastrostomy for a post-operative chylous collection.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 53-year-old woman underwent distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy and lymph node clearance for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with associated extensive lymphadenopathy. On post-operative day seven, she developed abdominal pain and elevated inflammatory markers. Computed tomography demonstrated a 14 × 5 cm thin-walled collection within the lesser sac. Percutaneous drainage yielded turbid milky fluid consistent with chyle. Despite initial conservative management, a persistent high output chyle leak developed. EUS-guided cyst gastrostomy was performed, allowing internal drainage of chyle into the stomach. The patient recovered without complications, resumed oral intake and was discharged two days following the procedure.
CONCLUSION: EUS-guided cyst gastrostomy may represent a safe, minimally invasive therapeutic option for selected patients with persistent chylous collections. This approach may mitigate risks associated with prolonged or repeated external drainage and facilitate earlier discharge, allowing ongoing outpatient conservative management.
LEARNING POINTS: Post-operative chylous leak and chylous collections are associated with significant morbidity, particularly when diagnosis is delayed. Perioperative medical teams should maintain a high index of suspicion and actively monitor for this complication following high-risk surgery.Persistent chyle loss can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, immunosuppression, hypoalbuminaemia and impaired wound healing, highlighting the importance of early nutritional, fluid and electrolyte support.Endoscopic ultrasound-guided cyst gastrostomy may represent a safe, minimally invasive alternative which allows internal drainage of a chylous collection, ameliorating risks associated with repeated or prolonged external drainage.

articles.title: Deep Parasternal Intercostal Plane Block for Cardiac Surgery via Median Sternotomy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether bilateral deep parasternal intercostal plane (DPIP) block improves quality of recovery in patients undergoing cardiac surgery via median sternotomy.
DESIGN: Randomized, controlled, single-blind, single-center superiority trial.
SETTING: French cardiac surgery center, September 2022 to May 2025.
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 128 adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.
INTERVENTIONS: Bilateral ultrasound-guided DPIP blocks with ropivacaine (40 mL total) versus standard care.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Primary outcome was the Quality of Recovery-15 score at 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included pain scores, opioid consumption, and pulmonary function. Among 126 analyzed patients, Quality of Recovery-15 scores at 24 hours did not differ significantly between groups (101.2 ± 19.9 in the DPIP group v 97.3 ± 19.8 in the control group), with a mean difference of 3.9 points (95% confidence interval [CI], -3.3 to 11.2; p = 0.230). The DPIP block group had significantly lower resting pain scores at hours 2, 6, and 48. In a subgroup analysis of patients undergoing internal mammary artery harvesting (n = 71), Quality of Recovery-15 scores were significantly higher with the block at 24 hours (103.8 ± 17.1 v 93.3 ± 19.6; mean difference 10.4 points; 95% confidence interval, 1.1-19.5; p = 0.027).
CONCLUSIONS: DPIP block did not improve 24-hour quality of recovery in mixed cardiac surgery patients, despite reducing early postoperative pain. An exploratory, non-prespecified subgroup analysis suggested a potential benefit in patients undergoing internal mammary artery harvesting, warranting confirmatory trials.

articles.title: Elevated pulse perfusion index values and interleukin-6 levels as associated factors for epidural-related maternal fever: a nested case‒control study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To date, the mechanism of epidural-related maternal fever (ERMF) remains unclear. Studies have pointed to various noninfectious factors linked to ERMF, yet relevant conclusions remain inconsistent. This study aimed to investigate whether the elevated pulse perfusion index (PI) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were associated with ERMF and further evaluated their interactive biological effects.
METHODS: A total of 100 parturients receiving epidural analgesia were analyzed in this unmatched nested case‒control study on the basis of a cohort study conducted within ten months. Baseline characteristics and intrapartum data were collected. Maternal blood samples were taken at admission (T1), before epidural analgesia (T2), and at the end of the second stage of labor (T3). Plasma was isolated to detect IL-6 concentrations. PI on the second toe of the right foot was monitored continuously. The PI 30 min after labor analgesia (PI30) was determined. Binary logistic regression and Andersson's interaction model were adopted to identify independent factors associated with ERMF.
RESULTS: Analysis revealed that elevated PI30 (≥ 9.30) and high levels of IL-6 at T3 (≥ 50.07 pg/mL) were significantly associated with an increased risk of developing ERMF, with corresponding odds ratios (ORs) of 3.697 and 5.031, respectively. No statistically significant biological interaction was detected between PI30 and T3 IL-6 on the incidence rate of ERMF.
CONCLUSION: Elevated PI30 (≥ 9.30) and T3 IL-6 (≥ 50.07 pg/ml) were each independently associated with ERMF, with no significant interaction detected between the two factors. .Targeted modulation of the two factors is hypothesized as a possible approach to lower ERMF incidence.

articles.title: Sigh ventilation versus conventional protective ventilation in cardiac surgery: a proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung protective ventilation is crucial for preventing ventilator-induced lung injury in cardiac surgery. The protective role of a low tidal volume (VT) has been established, whereas the added protection afforded by lung recruitment remains uncertain. We investigated whether sigh breaths could provide additional lung protection, when added to protective ventilation with low VT.
METHODS: This randomized, assessor-blinded, phase 2 proof-of-concept trial enrolled 192 patients undergoing elective on-pump cardiac surgery from February to August 2024. Patients were randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive sigh ventilation (sigh breaths plus protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients) or conventional ventilation (protective ventilation with low VT; 96 patients). Sigh breaths targeting a plateau pressure of 35 cmH2O (or 40 cmH2O for BMI >35 kg/m2) were delivered once every 6 min. Perioperative respiratory mechanics and gas exchange were monitored. The primary outcome was postoperative oxygenation, a marker of lung injury, as measured by the time-weighted average SpO2/FiO2 ratio during the first postextubation hour. There were 9 predefined secondary outcomes, including the severity of respiratory failure within postextubation day 7.
RESULTS: All 192 patients completed the trial (53% male; median age, 64 [55-72] years). Perioperatively, sigh ventilation produced sustained improvements in oxygenation and respiratory system compliance, together with reductions in driving pressure and mechanical power (All P interaction<0.001). After extubation, the mean time-weighted SpO2/FiO2 ratio was higher in the sigh ventilation group (380 ± 86 vs 338 ± 93; mean difference 42.1, 95% CI [16.7 to 67.5]; P=0.001). The severity and occurrence of respiratory failure was reduced in the sigh ventilation group compared with conventional ventilation group (common odds ratio for lower severity 2.2; 95% CI [1.2 to 3.8]; P=0.007). There was no difference in adverse events of interest between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, adding sigh breaths was safe and resulted in a statistically significant improvement in postoperative oxygenation. Nevertheless, the clinical importance of this finding is uncertain because oxygenation was adequately maintained in both groups. Reduction in driving pressure and mechanical power, together with findings in secondary outcomes, suggest additional lung protection and justify future trials.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06248320); registered on January 30, 2024.

articles.title: Early albumin use and mortality in critically III children with severe hypoalbuminemia: a target trial emulation study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypoalbuminemia is highly prevalent in critically ill children and is an established independent risk factor for mortality. Whether albumin supplementation is associated with improved survival remains unclear, particularly in pediatric populations where causal evidence is sparse.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used data from the Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database, a single-center pediatric-specific critical care database in China, and adopted a target trial emulation (TTE) framework. Children whose first albumin measurement within 24 h of ICU admission was below 30 g/L were included (N = 1,649). Time zero was defined as the first detection of albumin below 30 g/L. The exposure was receipt of at least one dose of human albumin within 24 h after time zero. Primary outcomes were 7-day and 28-day all-cause mortality, estimated using IPTW-weighted Cox proportional hazards models with doubly robust adjustment. Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding was assessed by E-value.
RESULTS: Among 1,649 children, 374 (22.7%) received early albumin therapy. After doubly robust adjustment, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.24-0.74; P = 0.003; E-value = 4.21). The association with 28-day mortality was not significant (HR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.45-1.36; P = 0.393). Relaxing the hypoalbuminemia threshold to below 35 g/L attenuated the 7-day association (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.39-1.05). Extending the treatment window to 48 h further attenuated the association (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.40-1.91). A significant interaction was observed between vasoactive agent use and albumin therapy (P for interaction = 0.045), with the strongest association among children not receiving vasoactive agents (HR, 0.17; 95% CI, 0.04-0.70).
CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill children with severe hypoalbuminemia, early albumin therapy was associated with reduced 7-day mortality. This association showed clear threshold- and time-dependence, suggesting that any potential benefit may concentrate within a narrow clinical window early in the disease course. Prospective confirmation is needed.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable. This is a retrospective observational study using de-identified data; the study protocol was not prospectively registered in a clinical trials registry.

articles.title: Dynamic reprogramming of alveolar epithelial-immune cell interactions in ARDS: from mechanisms to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by disruption of the alveolar-capillary barrier and refractory hypoxemia. Despite advances in supportive care, effective targeted therapies remain lacking. A major challenge to therapeutic success is the marked heterogeneity of ARDS, in which distinct biological mechanisms may drive different etiologies, inflammatory subphenotypes, and disease stages. Increasing evidence suggests that alveolar epithelial cells (AECs) are not merely passive targets of injury but active regulators of immune responses. Dynamic interactions between AECs and macrophages, neutrophils, and lymphocytes occur throughout the course of ARDS and contribute to inflammatory amplification, tissue repair, and aberrant remodeling. In this review, we summarize epithelial-immune interaction patterns across the inflammatory exudative, proliferative repair, and fibrotic phases of ARDS. We further discuss how disease stage transitions, immunometabolic regulation, and ARDS heterogeneity shape these interaction networks. Based on these findings, we present an AEC-centered dynamic reprogramming framework that organizes current evidence on how epithelial-immune interactions change during ARDS progression. We also discuss candidate biomarkers, approaches for clinical stage and phenotype identification, therapeutic opportunities, and current evidence limitations, aiming to provide a conceptual framework for stage-specific and precision interventions in ARDS. We further contextualize existing and controversial immunomodulatory strategies, including corticosteroids and IL-6/IL-1 blockade, within this dynamic framework to illustrate how disease stage and patient phenotype may influence therapeutic responses. Throughout the review, we distinguish evidence derived from experimental models from observational data in human ARDS and separately identify human interventional evidence and therapies supported by current clinical guidelines.

articles.title: Sequential method for determining the effective dose of remimazolam combined with sufentanil for cervical dilation in hysteroscopic surgery.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study investigated the 50% and 95% effective doses (ED50 and ED95) of remimazolam combined with sufentanil for cervical dilation during hysteroscopic surgery.
DESIGN: Prospective single-center dose-finding study using a modified Dixon up-and-down sequential method.
METHOD: Twenty-five patients who underwent hysteroscopic surgery were enrolled in 2024. All patients received an intravenous injection of sufentanil at 0.15 μg/kg for intraoperative analgesia. We used a modified Dixon sequential method. The initial dose of remimazolam was 0.15 mg/kg. The dose of remimazolam administered to each patient was determined by whether hysteroscope placement had failed. Failure was defined as inadequate cervical dilation and difficulty in hysteroscope placement, accompanied by patient manifestations such as limb movements, frowning, or a Modified Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation (MOAA/S) score ≥1. If cervical dilation failed (i.e., a positive response), the dose of remimazolam was increased by 0.02 mg/kg for subsequent subjects. Conversely, in the case of a negative response, the dose was decreased by the same gradient. Formal testing started from the first crossover point and continued until the eighth crossover point appeared.
STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: The probit method was used to calculate the 50% and 95% effective doses (ED50 and ED95) of remimazolam combined with sufentanil for cervical dilation during intravenous anesthesia, along with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs).
RESULTS: The ED50 and ED95 of remimazolam combined with 0.15 μg/kg sufentanil for cervical dilation were 0.18 mg/kg (95% CI: 0.17-0.20) and 0.22 mg/kg (95% CI: 0.19-0.25), respectively.
CONCLUSION: Administering 0.22 mg/kg remimazolam combined with 0.15 μg/kg sufentanil is safe and effective for intravenous anesthesia during cervical dilation in hysteroscopic surgery.

articles.title: Conflict in intensive care units: a conceptual framework for patient, family, team, and inter-service disagreement.
articles.abstract: For clinicians, conflict in the intensive care unit (ICU) is both common and expected owing to the nature of critical illness and its treatment. Examination of conflict in this context has been conceptually diffuse. Studies of moral distress, psychological safety, ethical climate, and other fields offer valuable insights that can be challenging to synthesize cohesively, due to differences in concepts, methods, and disciplinary perspectives. This narrative review integrates this literature using a task-process-relationship framework from organizational psychology. Conflict in the ICU arises in two principal arenas: between clinical teams and patients, families, or surrogates, and within and across clinical teams. Patients who retain decision-making capacity are a distinct and often overlooked party to conflict, as the focus has primarily been on the families and surrogates who speak for those who cannot. The task-process-relationship framework suggests a recurring escalation pattern for both arenas. Genuine task disagreements about treatment, prognosis, or goals of care can become destructive in the presence of process gaps or failures. These include role ambiguity, inconsistent messaging, and perceived unfairness. From there, conflict can enter the relationship domain wherein mistrust or identity threat makes resolution far harder, and two implications follow. First, much of what clinicians may describe as a "difficult family" can often be a response to antecedent process failures rather than a purely interpersonal problem, emphasizing the importance of engineering robust processes and systems in the ICU to avoid conflict reaching the relationship domain. Second, family and team conflict are linked in that unresolved team disagreement can reach families as contradictory recommendations and mixed messaging. Challenging family situations can expose team misalignment and damage collegial relationships. Evidence-based interventions, organized by conflict type and escalation stage, suggest that the most promising investments are structural, namely those built into rounds, improving role clarity, ensuring pre-conference team alignment, and fostering ethical climate. When conflict becomes entrenched, formal supports such as mediation and ethics consultation are matched to the nature of the dispute. While disagreement in intensive care is inevitable, destructive conflict is not.

articles.title: The evolution of biocontainment unit care for high-consequence infectious diseases: progress, lessons learned, and future directions.
articles.abstract: Biocontainment units (BCUs) are specialized facilities designed to treat patients with high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) which are pathogens with high mortality rates, limited treatment options, and significant potential for healthcare-associated transmission. Since the opening of the first modern BCU in 1971, these units have evolved from simple isolation environments into advanced centers capable of delivering comprehensive critical care while maintaining rigorous infection control. This evolution has been driven from the lessons learned from past outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), among other emerging infectious threats. Four key domains contribute to the care of patients with HCIDs - laboratory capabilities, critical care delivery, healthcare workforce readiness, and safe patient transport. Improvements in diagnostic capabilities have allowed for earlier disease recognition while greater access to routine laboratory tests better inform clinical decision making. Clinical care capabilities now match those seen in intensive care units while maintaining infection control standards. Training of specialized workforce and multidisciplinary staffing models have improved bedside care and operational readiness. Meanwhile, innovations in ground and air transport have enhanced the ability to safely transfer HCID patients to facilities best suited to provide care. This review synthesizes the evolution of BCU capabilities globally, examining advances in critical care, diagnostics, investigational therapeutics, workforce models, and patient transport.

articles.title: Using capnography to differentiate airway from gastrointestinal placement of nasogastric tubes: a prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient safety incident reports and case reports have repeatedly highlighted factors contributing to inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes, including misleading pH readings, insufficiently documented placement checks, and misinterpretation of radiographs. The study aimed to: (i) evaluate the diagnostic performance of capnography compared with radiography for detecting inadvertent airway placement of nasogastric tubes; and (ii) estimate the average cost incurred when radiography is used alone versus when capnography is used in conjunction with radiography.
METHODS: A multicentre, prospective, observational diagnostic study was conducted. The diagnostic accuracy of capnography was examined using three end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds (> 5 mmHg, > 10 mmHg, > 15 mmHg), with radiographic confirmation as the reference standard. For each threshold, true positives, false negatives, true negatives, and false positives were determined. Cost savings per patient were estimated using a bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrapping method with 20,000 replications.
RESULTS: A total of 508 participants were recruited from 39 study sites across 21 hospitals, including medical or geriatric wards, intensive care units, and emergency departments. Most participants (n = 485; 95.5%) had end-tidal carbon dioxide readings ≤ 5 mmHg. Radiography confirmed correct gastric placement in 452 cases (89.0%), with one case (0.2%) of inadvertent airway placement. Estimated cost savings per patient, were HK$210.3, HK$214.5, and HK$217.5 for the three respective end-tidal carbon dioxide thresholds, based on a hypothetical strategy in which radiographic confirmation was performed only when the end-tidal carbon dioxide value exceeded a predefined threshold, compared with a radiography-only strategy in which all patients underwent radiographic confirmation of nasogastric tube placement.
CONCLUSIONS: Given the favourable outcomes and the simplicity of capnography measurement, capnography can be considered a first-line tool for excluding airway placement of nasogastric tubes, used alongside pH testing of aspirates.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, Number NCT05817864 (Registration date: 18 April 2023).

articles.title: Endoscopic-Assisted Transcervical Transparotid Approach to the Jugular Foramen Region.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The transcervical transparotid approach was developed for the management of lesions in the parapharyngeal space, while its application for addressing lesions at the jugular foramen region (JFR) has not been sufficiently assessed. This study retrospectively reviewed the clinical outcomes of eight patients who underwent an endoscopic-assisted transcervical transparotid approach (EATTA) for management of lesions at the JFR.
METHODS: The study comprised a retrospective analysis of patients who underwent an EATTA for the management of lesions at the JFR. The demographics and perioperative-related indices were analyzed.
RESULTS: Benign tumors at the JFR in eight patients were completely removed via EATTA, including two primary and six recurrences. An expanded jugular foramen was detected in three patients. The endoscopic assistance could help enhance exposure of the residual lesions at the JFR and those that extended to the posterior cranial fossa via the expanded foramen. Worsening of preexisting hoarseness ( n = 5) and new emergence of Horner syndrome ( n = 1) were observed. No intraoperative inadvertent carotid artery injury or CSF leak occurred. Temporary facial nerve palsy was observed in six patients and resolved uneventfully. No recurrence occurred with an average follow-up of 23 months.
CONCLUSION: An EATTA serves as an alternative for the management of benign tumors at the JFR. For select lesions, this approach can also address lesions extending to the posterior cranial fossa via an expanded jugular foramen.
