Total and partial hospitalization costs were also compared. A generalized linear model (GLM) was employed to identify independent predictors of total hospitalization cost.
RESULTS: With regard to perioperative parameters, intraoperative blood loss was significantly greater in UBED group than in PELD group, whereas fluoroscopy times were significantly lower in UBED group (p < 0.05). No significant intergroup differences were detected in operative time, time to postoperative ambulation, or length of hospital stay (p > 0.05). Both groups showed significant improvements in ODI, VAS, and JOA score from baseline at all follow-up points (p < 0.05). In GEE analysis, UBED group showed lower VAS score for leg pain at 1 month, lower ODI at 1 and 6 months, and higher JOA score at 1 month (p < 0.001). Excellent-good rate was 97.6% in UBED group, significantly higher than that in PELD group (p = 0.039). Complication rate was significantly lower in UBED group (4.76%) than in PELD group (19.23%; p = 0.037). Total hospitalization cost was higher in UBED group than that in PELD group (17.46 vs. 15.82 × 103RMB, p = 0.012). Multivariate regression analysis by GLM confirmed surgical approach, length of hospitalization, and intraoperative bleeding were independent predictors of total hospitalization cost.
CONCLUSION: Both UBED and PELD are safe and effective minimally invasive approaches for single-segment DLSS. UBED was associated with slightly better early functional outcomes at 1 month and a numerically lower complication rate, but at a higher hospitalization cost. However, PELD was associated with lower hospitalization cost. In clinical practice, the selection of operative strategy should be individualized, with consideration given to both the patient's clinical characteristics and socioeconomic circumstances, to optimize the balance between therapeutic benefit and healthcare resource utilization.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency trauma perioperative management: applications, performance benchmarks, and translation barriers.
articles.abstract: This review examines the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in the perioperative management of emergency trauma. Published studies suggest performance advantages of AI over traditional methods in prehospital triage, radiographic injury detection, massive transfusion prediction, and early warning of postoperative complications, although findings vary across study designs and validation settings. However, actual adoption in trauma care remains limited due to data heterogeneity, performance degradation in external validation, workflow integration challenges, lack of interpretability, and a scarcity of prospective interventional evidence. This review further argues that methodologically inflated benchmark performance constitutes an underrecognized barrier to adoption in its own right, and that bridging the implementation gap will likely require a shift from area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)-centered reporting toward reporting sensitivity at prespecified clinical thresholds and evaluating patient outcomes in prospective interventional trials.

articles.title: Preoperative frailty risk in older patients with colorectal cancer admitted to the ICU after surgery: prevalence, associated factors, and association with in-hospital outcomes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Frailty is recognized as an important predictor of adverse outcomes in older surgical patients. However, evidence regarding preoperative frailty among older patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) admitted to the ICU after surgery remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence, associated factors, and impact of preoperative frailty risk on in-hospital outcomes in this high-risk population.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 308 older CRC patients who underwent radical surgery and were admitted to the ICU postoperatively between June 2023 and March 2026. Preoperative frailty risk was assessed using the five-item modified Frailty Index (mFI-5). Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with frailty risk and evaluate the association between preoperative frailty risk and postoperative complications. Generalized linear models were applied to assess the associations of frailty risk with total hospital stay, ICU stay, and hospitalization costs.
RESULTS: The prevalence of preoperative frailty risk was 55.52% in this study. Higher albumin levels were a protective factor, whereas higher blood glucose levels, elevated NLR, BMI ≥ 26.9 kg/m², polypharmacy, pain, and high fall risk were significantly associated with increased frailty risk. After adjustment for confounders, frailty risk remained an independent predictor of overall complications and severe complications and was significantly associated with prolonged total hospital stay, longer ICU stay, and increased hospitalization costs.
DISCUSSION: Preoperative frailty risk is highly prevalent among older CRC patients admitted to the ICU after surgery and is independently associated with adverse in-hospital outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating frailty assessment into perioperative management. The mFI-5 is a simple and feasible tool for preoperative risk stratification in this high-risk population and may help guide prehabilitation strategies to ultimately optimize postoperative recovery.

articles.title: Templated lymph node sampling during surgery for pediatric renal tumors increases lymph node yield and does not increase long-term postoperative complication rates.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: We previously demonstrated that higher yield during lymph node sampling for suspected renal malignancy did not increase clinically significant complications. We evaluated the incidence of complications over a longer follow-up period as well as when random sampling versus formal "templated" lymph node dissection was performed. We also compared overall lymph node yields between techniques.
METHODS: A single-institution, retrospective review of patients aged 0-18 years old undergoing extirpative renal surgery with lymph node sampling for a suspected malignancy between 2005 and 2019 was performed. Intraoperative and postoperative complications within 4 years of surgery were recorded and categorized based on the Clavien-Dindo scale. The number of lymph nodes sampled and its influence on the odds of experiencing a clinically significant complication was examined. The Wilcoxon rank sum test was used for continuous variables and Chi-Square analysis was used for categorical variables. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression was used to build a complete case multivariable model. Sex, race, age at surgery, tumor laterality, tumor thrombus, overall disease stage, preoperative chemotherapy, nephrectomy type, tumor size, estimated blood loss (EBL), and intraoperative fluid volume were included. P-values were calculated at a significance threshold of 0.05.
RESULTS: One hundred forty-one patients met study criteria. Templated lymph node dissection was associated with higher median lymph node yield [12 (8-20) vs. 6 (3-10), p < 0.001]. There were 22 (15.6%) clinically significant complications. There were no observed statistically significant differences in sex (p = 0.060), patient age (p = 0.5), overall disease stage (p = 0.2), presence of tumor thrombus (p > 0.9), tumor size (p = 0.7), or exposure to perioperative chemotherapy (p = 0.088). Tumor laterality (p = 0.003), EBL (p = 0.001), and intraoperative fluid volume resuscitation (p = 0.007) demonstrated unadjusted statistically significant associations with postoperative clinically significant complications. There was no observed statistically significant association between sampling approach and surgical complications (OR, 1.32; 95% CI, 0.47-3.60; p = 0.59).
CONCLUSIONS: Templated lymph node sampling in children with suspected renal malignancy is not associated with clinically significant complications after extended follow-up and demonstrated increased lymph node yield. We hope that this data will further inform future studies into whether templated sampling can increase surgical protocol adherence and improve staging accuracy.

articles.title: Early Deep Sedation and Short-term Outcomes After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: A Retrospective Multicenter Cohort Study Using the MIMIC-IV and eICU Databases.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the association between early sedation depth and short-term outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), and to characterize the dose-response relationship between sedation depth and mortality.
DESIGN: Retrospective multicenter observational cohort study using the MIMIC-IV (v3.1) and eICU (v2.0) databases.
SETTING: Multi-institutional; intensive care units contributing to the MIMIC-IV (v3.1) and eICU (v2.0) databases.
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 2,556 adults (≥18 years) undergoing isolated CABG with invasive mechanical ventilation ≥24 hours. This cohort represents a higher-acuity subset of CABG patients requiring prolonged postoperative mechanical ventilation (≥24 hours).
INTERVENTIONS: None. Participants were stratified by mean Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) score during the first 24 hours after intensive care unit admission: deep sedation (RASS ≤-3), light sedation (-3 < RASS < 1, reference), and agitation (RASS ≥1).
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes were ventilation duration and intensive care unit length of stay. Deep sedation was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (41.0% v14.1%, p < 0.001), which persisted after adjustment (pooled generalized linear mixed-model odds ratio 3.17, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.52-4.00; propensity-matched odds ratio 3.08, 95% CI 2.33-4.10). Deep sedation was associated with increased mortality hazard (hazard ratio 2.05, 95% CI 1.71-2.44) and reduced successful extubation in Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.57-0.74). Restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a J-shaped relationship between RASS and mortality, with the lowest risk between RASS -1 and 0. Exploratory XGBoost/Shapley Additive Explanations analysis showed consistent patterns.
CONCLUSIONS: Early deep sedation was independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality and reduced extubation success in mechanically ventilated CABG patients requiring prolonged postoperative mechanical ventilation. The RASS range of -1 to 0 was associated with the lowest mortality and may inform prospective studies of sedation optimization in this high-acuity population. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective validation before clinical implementation and should not be extrapolated to routine low-risk CABG patients with an uncomplicated postoperative course and early extubation.

articles.title: Supradiaphragmatic Epicardial Pacemaker Implantation for Pseudoatrioventricular Block in Neonatal Long QT Syndrome: Genotype-agnostic Anesthetic Strategy Pending Genetic Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: A late-preterm female neonate (35+3 weeks gestation) was delivered via emergency cesarean section due to fetal bradycardia. Electrocardiography revealed a 2:1 pseudoatrioventricular block, a wide QRS complex, and a corrected QT interval of 495 ms, a pattern typically associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (KCNH2) or type 3 (SCN5A). Additional findings included a large patent ductus arteriosus, moderate apical muscular ventricular septal defect, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, neonatal hypoglycemia, and hyperbilirubinemia. Following preoperative QT stabilization with intravenous magnesium sulfate, the infant underwent epicardial single-chamber permanent pacemaker implantation (VVI 120 bpm) via lower partial sternotomy, with a supradiaphragmatic pericardial generator pocket, on day of life (DOL) 4, at an operative weight of 2.37 kg. Anesthesia was administered using a genotype-agnostic total intravenous anesthesia strategy, comprising propofol and remifentanil with cisatracurium neuromuscular blockade, while avoiding volatile and QT-prolonging agents, optimizing electrolytes, and maintaining external defibrillator readiness. This approach was designed to be safe irrespective of the underlying channelopathy. No intraoperative arrhythmia was observed. Postoperative genetic testing unexpectedly identified a heterozygous KCNQ1 variant c.1273C>A p.(Leu425Met), confirming LQT1 (a potassium channelopathy), contradicting the preoperative electrocardiography-based assumption of sodium channelopathy. Device interrogation on DOL 14 confirmed satisfactory parameters, and the infant was discharged on propranolol on DOL 15 without further arrhythmic events. This case demonstrates that 2:1 pseudoatrioventricular block, typically associated with LQT2/LQT3, can manifest in LQT1, and that a genotype-agnostic total intravenous anesthesia strategy is an appropriate anesthetic approach when the genetic subtype is unknown prior to urgent neonatal long QT syndrome surgery.

articles.title: Regional Anaesthesia Training in a United Kingdom Postgraduate Anaesthesia Programme: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Training Opportunities, Supervision and Competency Development.
articles.abstract: Background Regional anaesthesia is an integral component of contemporary anaesthetic practice and a core competency within the 2021 Royal College of Anaesthetists curriculum. Despite increasing emphasis on regional anaesthesia training, concerns remain regarding trainees' access to sufficient clinical exposure and supportive clinical supervision. Objective This study described regional anaesthesia training experiences reported by anaesthesia trainees within a United Kingdom (UK) postgraduate training programme, including training opportunities, procedural exposure, self-reported curriculum attainment and barriers to competency development. Methods A cross-sectional electronic survey (questionnaire) was distributed to all anaesthesia trainees within the Yorkshire and Humber School of Anaesthesia between January and February 2024. The questionnaire explored access to educational resources, procedural exposure, self-reported attainment of curriculum competencies, perceived training adequacy, and perceived barriers to training. Descriptive analyses were performed, with secondary exploratory analyses examining differences in perceived training adequacy according to respondent characteristics and reported training experiences. Results Sixty-four trainees completed the survey (estimated response rate: 25.6%). Twenty respondents (31.2%) reported sufficient opportunities to achieve curriculum-mandated regional anaesthesia competencies, while 25 (39.1%) reported insufficient opportunities. The most frequently reported barriers were lack of supportive supervising anaesthetists (60.9%) and limited access to suitable operating lists (59.4%). In exploratory comparisons, respondents reporting adequate access to clinical regional anaesthesia practice had higher perceived training adequacy scores, while respondents reporting limited access to suitable operating lists or lack of supportive supervision had lower scores. Reported access to educational resources and perceived training adequacy also varied among respondents from different training hubs. Stage 3 respondents reported variable procedural exposure across individual regional anaesthesia techniques and variable self-reported ability across anatomical regions. Conclusions This regional survey identified variation in reported regional anaesthesia training experiences among respondents from a single UK postgraduate training programme. Exploratory comparisons identified differences in perceived training adequacy according to reported clinical opportunities, suitable operating lists, and supportive clinical supervision; these findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective evaluation. Stage 3 respondents reported variable procedural exposure and self-reported ability, neither of which should be regarded as a surrogate marker of objectively assessed competence. The findings support continued emphasis on competency-based assessment and further evaluation of supervised clinical training and consistency of curriculum delivery.

articles.title: Containing Chronic Disease Costs With the Ambulatory Specialty Model.
articles.abstract: On July 14, 2025, CMS proposed and requested comment on establishing the Ambulatory Specialty Model, a mandatory payment model for specialists treating heart failure (eg, cardiologists) and low back pain (eg, anesthesiologists, neurosurgeons, physical medicine and rehabilitation). Comments were due on September 12, 2025, with notable responses from various stakeholders (eg, surgery centers, cardiologists, consulting firms). The model is notable for several reasons, including strict implementation of a 2-sided risk model, inclusion of specialists typically insulated from involvement in alternative payment models, and a new approach to performance measurement. In this article, we aim to inform clinicians-specialists in particular-about key aspects of the model, as they are likely to be unaware of its impending mandatory nature, and to provide recommendations for how the model can be improved to achieve its intended goal while mitigating unintended clinical and economic consequences.

articles.title: Enhanced recovery after cardiac surgery: evidence-based pathways for contemporary perioperative care.
articles.abstract: Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) programmes have transformed perioperative care across multiple surgical specialties. In cardiac surgery, ERAS Cardiac pathways integrate multimodal, evidence-based interventions to attenuate surgical stress, expedite recovery, and optimise resource use. This systematic review summarises contemporary evidence for ERAS protocols in adult cardiac surgery and evaluates their impact on clinical and health-system outcomes. This review was conducted in line with PRISMA 2020 recommendations. Electronic databases (Medline, Embase, and the Cochrane Library) were searched for studies from 2010 to October 2025 evaluating ERAS or fast-track pathways in adult cardiac surgery. Eligible studies compared a multicomponent ERAS/fast-track protocol with usual care and reported at least one of the following: length of stay (LOS), complications, mortality, costs, or patient-reported outcomes. Narrative synthesis was undertaken due to heterogeneity in interventions and outcome reporting. A PRISMA 2020 flow diagram is shown in Figure 1. Recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses, together with large observational cohorts, demonstrate that ERAS Cardiac programmes are generally safe and are associated with reduced ICU and hospital LOS, lower rates of selected complications (especially pulmonary complications and delirium), decreased opioid exposure, and improved mobilisation without evidence of an increase in reintubation, readmission, or mortality. Key protocol elements include preoperative optimisation (education, prehabilitation, and anaemia management), minimally invasive surgical approaches when appropriate, goal-directed anaesthesia with structured early extubation pathways, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, and standardised early mobilisation and nutrition. Emerging economic evaluations suggest that ERAS Cardiac is cost-saving or at least cost-neutral despite upfront implementation costs, while limited data on patient-reported outcomes indicate high satisfaction and perceived control over recovery. The available evidence supports ERAS Cardiac as a comprehensive framework that may improve recovery after cardiac surgery, primarily by shortening LOS and reducing complications and opioid use, without clear evidence of compromised safety. Wider implementation requires multidisciplinary engagement, local adaptation of turnkey order sets, robust audit, and inclusion of patient-centred outcomes in future trials. High-quality randomised and pragmatic studies focusing on long-term functional recovery, health-related quality of life, and cost-effectiveness remain priorities.

articles.title: Complications of Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumors: A Contemporary Review.
articles.abstract: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor remains the cornerstone of diagnosis and management for non-muscle invasive bladder cancer, yet it carries meaningful perioperative and cumulative risks. Beyond bleeding, perforation, and infection, contemporary morbidity increasingly reflects frailty, postoperative delirium, cognitive decline, readmissions, and financial toxicity associated with repeated procedures. This article synthesizes recent evidence on intraoperative, early postoperative, and delayed complications, emphasizing modifiable risk factors and prevention strategies. Enhanced visualization, en-bloc resection, immediate intravesical chemotherapy, enhanced recovery after surgery principles, and frailty-informed care pathways may reduce repeat anesthetic exposure and procedural burden while preserving oncologic outcomes.

articles.title: Perioperative esketamine and postoperative sleep quality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is common among surgical patients and adversely affects recovery. The benefits of perioperative esketamine on sleep remain incompletely defined.
METHODS: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ketamine or esketamine with saline or other drugs for postoperative sleep quality were identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library until 6 September 2025. The primary outcome was postoperative sleep quality scores, and effect sizes were calculated using the ratio of means (ROM). Secondary outcomes included incidence of PSD, postoperative pain and depression scores, and adverse events.
RESULTS: Twenty-three trials including 2868 participants met inclusion criteria. Esketamine improved sleep quality on postoperative day (POD) 1 (ROM, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.80 to 0.90; P < 0.001; I2 = 84%; 21 studies), POD 2 (ROM, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.57 to 0.93; P = 0.01; I2 = 92%; 8 studies), POD 3 (ROM, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.90 to 0.99; P = 0.02; I2 = 25%; 12 studies), and POD 7 (ROM, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.82 to 0.95; P = 0.001; I2 = 36%; 8 studies); no benefit was observed at 1 month. The incidence of PSD was reduced on PODs 1 through 3 (RRs, 0.71, 0.70, and 0.61, respectively; all P ≤ 0.01), with no effect on POD 7. Esketamine also lowered postoperative pain and depression scores. However, it increased drowsiness (RR, 12.64; 95% CI, 6.04 to 26.46; P < 0.001; I2 = 21%).
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative esketamine is associated with short-term improvements in postoperative sleep quality and a lower incidence of PSD, alongside reductions in pain and depressive symptoms. However, these benefits are accompanied by an increased risk of drowsiness, and the current evidence does not yet support routine clinical use. Larger multinational trials are warranted.

articles.title: Bridging the experience gap: reasoning-oriented LLMs as cognitive scaffolds for junior anesthesiologists-a multi-arm controlled study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The gap between junior and senior physicians in anesthesia is exacerbated by the reliance on experience. Large language models like DeepSeek-R1 offer a potential solution as "cognitive scaffolding."
METHODS: A simulation-based, multi-arm controlled study with randomized junior groups and a non-randomized senior expert comparator was conducted. Forty-eight (48) anesthesiologists, including 16 senior experts and 32 junior residents, were recruited and randomly assigned (using a computer-generated randomization sequence) to two groups: Junior-alone and Junior + AI. Participants evaluated 20 standard clinical scenarios across four clinical domains: airway management, hemodynamic regulation, anesthetic pharmacology, and crisis management. The AI-assisted group followed a triple-step method: independent initial decision, subsequent AI consultation, and decision revision. Their final performance was compared against sixteen (16) senior expert anesthesiologists who served as the gold standard.
RESULTS: DeepSeek-R1 successfully improved performance in all four domains for junior doctors. Compared to the Junior-alone group, the Junior + AI group achieved significantly higher scores in accuracy (86.00 ± 16.61 vs 61.67 ± 19.45, P < 0.0001) and comprehensiveness (84.33 ± 17.18 vs 53.67 ± 23.27, P < 0.0001). However, further analysis revealed that while significantly improved, both accuracy and comprehensiveness remained lower than the senior expert scores (differences not statistically significant in mixed-effects analysis: P = 0.349 for Accuracy; P = 0.335 for Comprehensiveness). Performance in safety showed no significant difference to expert standards (P = 0.644). The AI-assisted group required slightly less total time (33.3 vs 33.8 min), showing no significant delay. 65% of AI suggestions were adopted overall.
CONCLUSION: DeepSeek-R1 shows promise as "cognitive scaffolding", supporting knowledge externalization for junior anesthesiologists. It substantially improves decision-making, though a numerical gap with experts persists in certain dimensions. The high risk of automation bias in critical scenarios requires targeted training on critical evaluation of AI outputs.

articles.title: Comparison of modified thoracoabdominal nerve block via perichondrial approach with serratus intercostal plane block and rectus sheath block combination in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) may experience severe postoperative pain. Peripheral nerve blocks, as a component of multimodal analgesia, are now widely employed in postoperative pain management. This study investigated the effects of modified thoracoabdominal nerve block (M-TAPA) compared with the combination of rectus sheath block (RSB) and serratus intercostal plane block (SIPB) on postoperative NRS scores, tramadol consumption, and dermatomal spread.
METHODS: This randomized, assessor-blinded trial enrolled 72 patients scheduled for LC. One group received bilateral M-TAPA (Group 1, n = 35), while the other received a combination of bilateral RSB and right-sided SIPB (Group 2, n = 37). All peripheral nerve blocks were performed following surgery and prior to emergence from general anesthesia, using 0.25% bupivacaine; RSB was administered as 10 mL per side, M-TAPA as 20 mL per side, and SIPB as 20 mL on the right side. The primary outcome was postoperative tramadol consumption within the first 24 h; NRS scores, rescue analgesia requirement, and dermatomal spread were secondary outcomes.
RESULTS: Static NRS (Numeric Rating Scale) scores measured at 0, 1, and 6 h differed significantly between groups (mean difference [Group 2 - Group 1] 1.27 [95% CI 0.54-2.00], 0.69 [0.14-1.24], and 0.56 [0.12-1.00], respectively). Dynamic NRS scores assessed at 0, 12, and 18 h were also found to be statistically significant between groups (mean difference 1.06 [95% CI 0.25-1.87], 0.45 [0.05-0.85], and 0.52 [0.05-0.99], respectively). Total tramadol consumption over the first 24 h, the primary outcome, did not differ significantly between groups (92.6 ± 26.3 mg vs. 103.9 ± 39.3 mg; mean difference 11.3 mg, 95% CI - 4.4 to 26.9; p = 0.108); however, tramadol consumption between 12 and 24 h was significantly higher in Group 2 compared to Group 1 (24.0 ± 11.7 mg vs. 31.7 ± 17.3 mg; mean difference 7.6 mg, 95% CI 0.7 to 14.6; p = 0.030). The number of patients requiring rescue analgesia was also significantly greater in Group 2 than in Group 1 (absolute risk reduction 24.4%, 95% CI 2.5% to 46.3%; p = 0.034).
CONCLUSIONS: Both M-TAPA and the combination of RSB with SIPB provided effective postoperative analgesia following LC. Under the conditions of this trial, M-TAPA was associated with lower NRS scores and lower opioid requirements than the combination of bilateral RSB and unilateral SIPB.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06241794, registered on January 28, 2024.

articles.title: Long-term respiratory outcomes following successful decannulation after tracheostomy: association of patient-reported dyspnea with spirometric findings and CT-defined tracheal stenosis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Persistent respiratory symptoms following successful decannulation after tracheostomy remain insufficiently characterized, and the relationship between patient-reported dyspnea, pulmonary function, and structural airway abnormalities has not been well defined. This study investigated the association between dyspnea severity, spirometric findings, and computed tomography (CT)-defined tracheal stenosis during long-term follow-up after tracheostomy and compared respiratory outcomes between open surgical tracheostomy (OST) and percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT).
METHODS: This prospective, single-center observational cohort study included 156 adult patients evaluated 12-84 months after successful decannulation. Dyspnea severity was assessed using the modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) scale. All participants underwent spirometry and neck and chest CT. Patients were classified according to previous tracheostomy technique (OST, n = 76; PDT, n = 80). Associations between mMRC scores, spirometric findings, and CT-defined tracheal stenosis were evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation and ordinal logistic regression.
RESULTS: Most patients reported minimal dyspnea (mMRC grade 0), observed in 56.6% of the OST group and 43.7% of the PDT group. Spirometric abnormalities were identified in both groups without significant differences in overall spirometric distribution. CT-defined tracheal stenosis was present in 27.6% of OST patients and 25.0% of PDT patients with mild stenosis, whereas moderate and severe stenosis occurred exclusively in the PDT group (5.0% each; p = 0.014). Higher mMRC scores correlated significantly with worsening spirometric category (Spearman's ρ = 0.343, p < 0.001) and increasing CT-defined tracheal stenosis grade (ρ = 0.461, p < 0.001), whereas no significant correlation was observed with the FEV₁/FVC ratio. In multivariable ordinal logistic regression, both spirometric category (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.17-1.89; p = 0.001) and CT-defined tracheal stenosis (OR 4.26, 95% CI 2.53-7.18; p < 0.001) remained independently associated with greater dyspnea severity.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients evaluated after successful decannulation, patient-reported dyspnea was significantly associated with both spirometric abnormalities and CT-defined tracheal stenosis during long-term follow-up. Moderate and severe tracheal stenosis occurred only after percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy. These findings support the use of symptom assessment as part of a comprehensive evaluation of post-tracheostomy respiratory outcomes while emphasizing that the observed associations are exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of diagnostic or screening utility. Larger prospective multicenter studies are required to confirm these findings.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN24668317 (registered April 23, 2019; IRB No. YSMU 7/18-19).

articles.title: Transthoracic echocardiography as a predictor of spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension in cesarean section: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension (SAIH) is a common complication during cesarean delivery and is closely associated with maternal intravascular volume status. However, reliable real-time assessment of volume changes remains challenging. This study aimed to evaluate whether transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)-derived ventricular volume parameters could dynamically reflect peri-anesthetic volume changes and predict SAIH.
METHODS: A total of 100 healthy singleton parturients scheduled for elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia were prospectively enrolled. Left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV) and left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV) were measured by transthoracic echocardiography using the biplane Simpson method at three predefined time points: after admission (T1), after crystalloid fluid preloading (T2), and after stabilization of the sensory block (T3). Systolic blood pressure (SBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and heart rate (HR) were recorded simultaneously. SAIH was defined as an SBP < 90 mmHg or a decrease of > 30% from baseline. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to identify independent predictors of SAIH.
RESULTS: Eighty-four parturients completed the study, and 26 (30.95%) developed SAIH. Following crystalloid fluid preloading at T2, both LVEDV and LVESV increased significantly compared with baseline. At T3, parturients who subsequently developed SAIH exhibited significant reductions in LVEDV and LVESV compared with T2. Multivariable logistic regression identified baseline LVEDV (T1) and LVESV (T1) as independent predictors of SAIH (P = 0.023 and P = 0.010, respectively). The predictive model demonstrated moderate discrimination, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.725 (95% confidence interval, 0.600-0.850).
CONCLUSION: TTE-derived LVEDV and LVESV were associated with peri-anesthetic volume changes and demonstrated moderate ability to identify parturients at risk of SAIH. These findings suggest that bedside TTE may provide complementary information for peri-anesthetic volume assessment rather than serving as a standalone predictor.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2100042973). February 2, 2021 (Retrospectively registered).

articles.title: Clinical efficacy of unilateral biportal endoscopic spinal decompression for lumbar intraspinal pneumatosis.
articles.abstract:
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective observational study.
OBJECTIVE: To analyze the short-term clinical efficacy of unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) spinal decompression in the treatment of lumbar intraspinal pneumatosis.
BACKGROUND: Lumbar intraspinal pneumatosis is extremely rare with an incidence of 0.15%, mainly caused by intervertebral disc degeneration. It compresses nerve roots, causing low back and radicular pain, and often requires surgery when conservative treatment fails. Unilateral biportal endoscopic technology offers advantages like clear visualization and flexible manipulation, but its application in this condition remains underreported.
METHODS: Five patients with a mean age of 69.0 ± 3.8 years and symptomatic lumbar intraspinal pneumatosis who underwent unilateral biportal endoscopic surgery between May 2022 and June 2024 were analyzed. Perioperative parameters including operation time, hospital stay and complications were recorded. The Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) was used to assess low back pain and lower extremity pain, the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) to evaluate lumbar spine function, and the MacNab criteria to assess clinical efficacy.
RESULTS: All surgeries succeeded with a mean operation time of 57.0 ± 9.3 min and a mean hospital stay of 4.2 days, and no complications occurred. At 1 day, 3 months, and 6 months postoperatively, Visual Analogue Scale scores for low back pain (F = 119.95, P < 0.001) and lower extremity pain (F = 197.25, P < 0.001), as well as Oswestry Disability Index scores (F = 229.97, P < 0.001) were significantly lower than preoperative values. At 6 months postoperatively, MacNab excellent and good rate was 100%.
CONCLUSION: UBE for the treatment of lumbar intraspinal pneumatosis has the advantages of minimal trauma, clear field of vision, flexible operation, and rapid postoperative recovery, representing a potentially safe and effective option. Large-scale multicenter prospective trials are still needed to further verify its long-term clinical efficacy and safety.

articles.title: Development of a comprehensive peri-anaesthetic bundle of postoperative delirium interventions for thoracic surgery patients: a Delphi method consensus study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a preventable complication that can prolong hospitalisation and increase healthcare costs.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to establish a streamlined and comprehensive peri-anaesthetic bundle of interventions to prevent postoperative delirium in patients undergoing thoracic surgery.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary team of experts was convened, and the Delphi method was used to develop bundle strategies. An initial intervention questionnaire was formulated based on a literature review. Two to three rounds of expert consultations were performed to finalise the prevention strategy.
RESULTS: A panel of 12 experts was convened. After two rounds of consultation, an initial version of the peri-anaesthetic bundle was developed. The main content comprised four programmes: perioperative neurocognitive function assessment and cognitive function exercises, perioperative pain management with multimodal analgesia, intraoperative anaesthesia management, and post-anaesthesia recovery management.
CONCLUSION: A peri-anaesthetic bundle for patients undergoing thoracic surgery was developed using the Delphi method. Clinical trials should be conducted to confirm its effectiveness and to offer a new approach for preventing POD.

articles.title: Feasibility analysis of negative pressure wound therapy for odontogenic ascending necrotizing fasciitis: a single-center single-arm retrospective case series.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Odontogenic ascending necrotizing fasciitis (ANF) is an extremely rare, rapidly progressive, and destructive craniomaxillofacial necrotizing soft tissue infection. Advanced surgical drainage is essential to improve cure rates, shorten the disease course, and alleviate patient suffering.
METHODS: This study was designed as a single-center, single-arm, retrospective feasibility case series. A total of 15 consecutive patients diagnosed with odontogenic ANF and treated with standardized NPWT from March 2016 to March 2024 were enrolled. Uniform standardized perioperative treatment, surgical debridement, and NPWT placement protocols were implemented for all enrolled patients. Clinical data including baseline demographic characteristics, systemic comorbidities, infection distribution, surgical incision selection, NPWT application frequency, intraoperative and postoperative complications, drainage duration, and hospitalization outcomes were systematically collected and descriptively analyzed.
RESULTS: The enrolled cohort consisted of 10 males and 5 females, with a mean age of 62.5 ± 16.9 years. Most patients presented with underlying systemic comorbidities, including hypertension (8/15) and diabetes mellitus (7/15), which were the most common concurrent diseases. The vast majority of cases (14/15) originated from mandibular dental lesions. Preoperative CT examination detected characteristic soft tissue gas accumulation in 7 patients (46.67%). All patients exhibited multi-space infection involvement, with the infratemporal space being the most commonly involved anatomical site, followed by the superficial temporal space and masseteric space. Individualized surgical incisions were formulated according to the infection scope, including single temporal incision (3 cases), single submandibular incision (1 case), and combined temporal and submandibular incision (11 cases). In terms of NPWT application, 8 patients received one-stage debridement and NPWT treatment, 6 patients underwent secondary debridement and NPWT replacement due to residual necrotic fascia, and 1 patient received three rounds of surgical debridement. The mean NPWT drainage duration was 12.47 ± 5.79 days, the mean dressing change frequency was 3.53 ± 0.64 times, and the average total hospitalization length was 23.40 ± 10.90 days. No severe intraoperative or postoperative complications, in-hospital mortality, or recurrent infection occurred in all patients.
CONCLUSION: NPWT appears to possess favorable clinical operability and acceptable perioperative safety in the management of rare odontogenic ANF. Individualized incision planning tailored to the anatomical extent of infection may reduce surgical trauma and yield improved postoperative cosmetic results. Regular NPWT dressing changes combined with staged repeated debridement represent essential procedural measures suitable for the dense anatomical properties of craniomaxillofacial fascia. This single-arm case series only preliminarily demonstrates the potential clinical feasibility of NPWT for odontogenic ANF, with satisfactory short-term wound healing and infection control observed in the cohort. Owing to the limitations inherent to a non-controlled retrospective design, large-scale multicenter prospective controlled trials are still needed to verify its long-term efficacy and establish standardized application protocols.

articles.title: Valvular Shock in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Perioperative Care for Transcatheter Valve Interventions.
articles.abstract: Valvular heart disease is an uncommon but high-risk cause of cardiogenic shock requiring rapid, multidisciplinary management aimed at bridging patients to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve intervention. Early comprehensive Doppler echocardiography is essential, as clinical signs may be subtle. Distinguishing decompensated chronic valvular disease from acute unstable lesions guides urgency and treatment strategy. Medical stabilization and mechanical circulatory support vary markedly between stenotic and regurgitant lesions, and standard shock therapies may be harmful in specific contexts. Transcatheter approaches are preferred when feasible, though their expanding use introduces added complexity in cardiac intensive care.

articles.title: Contemporary concepts in intraoperative ventilation during thoracic surgery.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Thoracic surgery requiring one-lung ventilation (OLV) remains one of the most challenging settings in perioperative respiratory care. During OLV, anesthesiologists must continuously balance two frequently competing goals: maintaining adequate gas exchange despite a markedly reduced ventilated lung volume while simultaneously minimizing ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) through lung-protective ventilation. Despite widespread adoption of lower tidal volume ventilation, postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remain frequent. This review summarizes contemporary concepts in mechanical ventilation during noncardiac thoracic surgery, focusing on ventilatory modes, individualized ventilator settings, mechanical and chemical power, and perioperative respiratory support strategies.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent randomized trials and meta-analyses suggest that individualized approaches to positive end-expiratory pressure and driving pressure may improve intraoperative respiratory mechanics and oxygenation during OLV, although consistent reductions in PPCs remain unproven. Mechanical power has emerged as a potentially important determinant of VILI, whereas chemical power represents a novel framework integrating hyperoxia, oxidative stress, and carbon dioxide management. Emerging ventilatory approaches, such as flow-controlled ventilation, have shown promising physiological effects during OLV, but their impact on patient-centered outcomes remains to be established. In addition, perioperative respiratory support bundles incorporating postoperative high-flow nasal oxygen may further contribute to perioperative lung protection.
SUMMARY: Contemporary thoracic ventilation is evolving from isolated ventilatory variables toward individualized perioperative respiratory management concepts. Although physiological benefits are increasingly demonstrated, robust evidence linking these approaches to improved patient-centered outcomes remains limited. Future studies should clarify the roles of individualized ventilation, mechanical and chemical power, and postoperative respiratory support within integrated perioperative respiratory care pathways.

articles.title: Evaluation of deep learning for the modified Cormack-Lehane classification in videolaryngoscopic images: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery.
METHODS: In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set.
RESULTS: Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3.
CONCLUSIONS: The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

articles.title: Paratracheal air cysts and their associations with postoperative pulmonary complications in patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia: a retrospective propensity-score-matched study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs.
METHODS: In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association.
RESULTS: Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS: The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

articles.title: Videolaryngoscopy vs. direct laryngoscopy for tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors (VILARE): a pragmatic multicentre randomised trial.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Videolaryngoscopy has been associated with improved glottic visualisation and higher first-attempt tracheal intubation success compared with direct laryngoscopy. However, multicentre evidence evaluating its effectiveness when tracheal intubation is performed by anaesthesia resident doctors in routine practice is limited.
METHODS: Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring tracheal intubation were assigned to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the initial attempt. All tracheal intubations were performed by anaesthesia residents under consultant supervision. The primary outcome was successful tracheal intubation on the first attempt. Secondary outcomes included glottic visualisation; number of tracheal intubation attempts; need for adjunct airway devices; procedural difficulty; and procedural complications.
RESULTS: We enrolled 1001 patients and assigned 501 to videolaryngoscopy and 500 patients to direct laryngoscopy. Successful first-attempt tracheal intubation was achieved in 397 (79.2%) patients allocated to the videolaryngoscopy group and 351 (70.2%) patients allocated to the direct laryngoscopy group (absolute risk difference 9.0%, 95%CI 3.7-14.4%, p < 0.001). Videolaryngoscopy improved glottic visualisation, with more patients having a modified Cormack-Lehane grade 2 or 2a view (467/501 (93.3%) vs. 404/500 (80.8%); p < 0.001); decreased operator-reported tracheal intubation difficulty (168/501 (33.5%) vs. 236/500 (47.2%); p < 0.001) and reduced procedural complications (39/501 (7.7%) vs. 91/500 (18.2%); p < 0.001), without a clinically meaningful difference in tracheal intubation time or the need for adjunct airway devices.
DISCUSSION: In adult patients undergoing tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors, videolaryngoscopy increased first-attempt success and improved overall procedural performance compared with direct laryngoscopy.

articles.title: Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes: a scoping review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Expert clinical guidelines discourage routine benzodiazepine premedication in older adults because of associations with adverse postoperative outcomes, including delirium and prolonged length of stay. However, these recommendations primarily address acute administration, whereas chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use for non-surgical indications remains incompletely understood, and the relevant evidence has not been comprehensively synthesised. This scoping review characterised the literature on chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes by mapping study characteristics, definitions of chronic use, and associated outcome domains and trends.
METHODS: Published and grey literature were searched across MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, and thesis databases. Screening and full-text review were performed independently in duplicate. Eligible studies included adults undergoing surgery with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and excluded studies in which benzodiazepines were administered exclusively within 24 h of surgery. This scoping review was preregistered with the Open Science Framework (10.17605/OSF.IO/573JG).
RESULTS: A total of 130 studies were included. Most were observational cohorts (n=109, 83.8%) and examined benzodiazepines as a secondary variable (n=100, 77.0%). Definitions of chronic use were heterogeneous, ranging from 1 month to >1 yr before surgery; duration was not systematically defined in 62 studies (47.7%). Postoperative opioid use (n=53, 40.8%) and delirium or cognitive impairment (n=19, 14.6%) were the most frequently examined outcome domains, with most studies reporting adverse associations with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use.
CONCLUSIONS: Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use is an inconsistently defined but clinically relevant perioperative exposure. As this scoping review did not include a risk-of-bias assessment, its findings map the evidence but cannot support causal inference. Standardised definitions and prospective studies are needed to inform perioperative medication optimisation.

articles.title: Reference values and web-based tool for intraoperative heart rate and blood pressure in paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac procedures.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Heart rate (HR) and arterial blood pressure (BP) monitoring is standard of care during paediatric anaesthesia, yet evidence-based reference values for anaesthetised children remain limited. Existing BP reference values do not account for the combined effects of age, sex, weight, and height, and HR reference values in this population are lacking.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentre study using data from the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group anaesthesia registry (2016-22). Included patients were aged <18 yr, ASA physical status 1 or 2, and undergoing noncardiac procedures under general anaesthesia. We used quantile regression to model the 2.3rd, 16th, 50th, 84th, and 97.7th centiles for HR, mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic BP, and diastolic BP at two time points: the preparation phase (end of induction) and surgical phase (15-35 min after procedure start). Model covariates included age, sex, weight, and height. We selected the best model for each outcome using cross-validation with pinball loss.
RESULTS: A total of 284 385 patients from 57 institutions were analysed. Optimal model complexity varied by outcome: a two-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for preparation phase HR and surgical phase MAP. A three-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for the remaining outcomes. Comprehensive prediction tables and an interactive web-based tool were developed for all outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: This study provides integrated HR and BP reference values for healthy paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia, incorporating age, sex, weight, and height simultaneously. These reference values with an interactive website can support clinical decision-making and haemodynamic monitoring.
authors: Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group Perioperative Clinical Research Committee

articles.title: Preincision Soft-point Pinprick Testing during Awake Shoulder Arthroscopy after Interscalene and Superficial Cervical Plexus Blocks.
Development and implementation of an objective framework for measuring clinician faculty research contributions in a Canadian anesthesiology department.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department.
METHODS: A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis.
RESULTS: Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance.
CONCLUSIONS: The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

articles.title: Comparative analgesic efficacy of superficial parasternal intercostal plane block versus erector spinae plane block after cardiac surgery in Türkiye: protocol for a multicentre randomised non-inferiority trial.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Median sternotomy is associated with substantial acute postoperative pain, which may impair respiratory function, delay mobilisation and increase opioid exposure. The superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIP) block directly targets the anterior cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves supplying the sternotomy region, whereas the erector spinae plane (ESP) block is performed posteriorly and relies on extensive interfascial spread. Direct, adequately powered comparisons of these approaches after cardiac surgery remain limited. This trial will test whether bilateral SPIP block is non-inferior to bilateral ESP block with respect to cumulative intravenous morphine milligram equivalent (IV-MME) consumption during the first 24 hours after extubation.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This multicentre, assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomised non-inferiority trial will enrol 308 adults aged 18–80 years undergoing first-time on-pump cardiac surgery through median sternotomy. Participants will be allocated 1:1, stratified by centre, to a bilateral single-shot SPIP block or a bilateral single-shot ESP block before induction of general anaesthesia. Both groups will receive a standardised perioperative anaesthetic and postoperative multimodal analgesic regimen, including intravenous patient-controlled morphine analgesia after extubation. The primary outcome is cumulative opioid consumption from extubation to 24 hours after extubation, expressed as IV-MME. The three prespecified secondary outcomes are time-weighted average pain intensity during coughing over 0–24 hours after extubation, cumulative 0–12-hour postextubation IV-MME consumption and Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) scores at 24 hours after extubation. Other exploratory outcomes include resting pain, QoR-15 at hospital discharge and chronic postsurgical pain at 3 months. The primary non-inferiority analysis will be performed in both the intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations using the between-group difference in mean cumulative 24-hour IV-MME consumption, expressed as SPIP minus ESP, with a two-sided 95% CI. The primary opioid-consumption comparison will be conditional on survival through the complete assessment window. Assuming a true between-group difference of zero, a non-inferiority margin of 3 mg IV-MME, a common SD of 6.48 mg, 95% power and a one-sided α of 0.025, 123 evaluable participants per group will be required. Allowing for 20% attrition, 308 participants (154 per group) will be enrolled.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Central ethics approval was obtained from the Ondokuz Mayıs University Clinical Research Ethics Committee (2026/392; 18 March 2026). Approval will also be obtained at each participating centre before recruitment. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. Results will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal and presented at national and international scientific meetings regardless of the direction or magnitude of the findings.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT07780773.

articles.title: Safety and Feasibility of Single-Port Robotic Lung Cancer Resection: Initial United States Experience of 145 Consecutive Cases.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The da Vinci single-port (SP) robotic system was approved for thoracic surgery in the United States in July 2024. Reports of its application in lung cancer remain limited. We present the initial experience with 145 consecutive SP resections for primary lung cancer at a single institution, with an emphasis on safety and oncologic quality.
DESCRIPTION: The SP robotic platform enables lung resection through a single subcostal incision, avoiding intercostal nerve injury.
EVALUATION: Three surgeons performed 34 SP lobectomies, 23 segmentectomies, and 88 wedge resections (95% stage I, 5% post-induction) between 6/2025-7/2026. Perioperative outcomes, oncologic quality, and learning curve were analyzed. Median operative time was 113 minutes, estimated blood loss 10mL, and length of stay 2 days. There were 3 conversions. R0 resection occurred in 99.3% of cases. Median lymph node yield was 5 nodes. There were zero mortalities and 4.8% major complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥III). Cumulative-sum analysis identified a learning curve plateau after 23 cases.
CONCLUSIONS: Subcostal SP robotic lung resection is feasible and safe with acceptable perioperative and oncologic outcomes. Comparative studies are warranted.

articles.title: Single-port robotic thoracic surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative outcomes versus multiport robotic surgery and uniportal VATS.
articles.abstract: Single-port robotic-assisted thoracic surgery (SP-RATS) has expanded rapidly, but its comparative effectiveness remains uncertain across platforms and access strategies. We systematically evaluated SP-RATS against multiport robotic-assisted thoracic surgery (MP-RATS) and uniportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (uVATS). PubMed/MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and supplementary sources were searched through October 5, 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses with modified Knapp-Hartung inference were used for continuous and common binary outcomes, whereas rare events were analyzed using fixed-effect Peto odds ratios. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, and certainty using GRADE. Sixty reports were included; 23 provided Group A or B comparative data, with one study at critical risk of bias excluded from the primary quantitative synthesis. Compared with MP-RATS, SP-RATS demonstrated broadly similar perioperative outcomes without a consistent disadvantage. Lymph-node yield was nominally lower (MD, - 1.18 nodes; 95% CI, - 2.31 to - 0.05; P = 0.043), but this finding did not persist across sensitivity analyses. Compared with uVATS, SP-RATS was associated with shorter chest-tube duration (MD, - 0.49 days; 95% CI, - 0.85 to - 0.13; P = 0.013), with additional favorable signals in lymph-node yield, chest drainage, and conversion, although these were less consistent across sensitivity analyses. Complications, R0 resection, and mortality did not differ significantly between approaches. Certainty of evidence was low or very low across all pooled outcomes. SP-RATS appears to be a viable minimally invasive alternative, achieving reduced robotic access without an evident trade-off in perioperative safety or immediate oncologic outcomes. Prospective comparative studies are needed to determine whether reduced robotic access provides reproducible clinical benefit.

articles.title: Beyond the cortex, early deficits, late recovery: a systematic review of language outcomes and subcortical mapping after awake craniotomy for diffuse gliomas.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To evaluate immediate and long-term postoperative language outcomes in patients undergoing awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation (DES) for diffuse gliomas in eloquent regions.
METHODS: PRISMA-compliant systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261342690) of adults (≥ 18 years) with supratentorial diffuse glioma in the language-dominant hemisphere enrolled in both randomised and non-randomised studies of awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation and language mapping. Databases searched included PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL (from 2010 to March 2026). Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by multiple reviewers using standardised tools (JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists). Due to methodological heterogeneity, narrative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten studies (532 patients enrolled; 55.3% male) published 2011-2025 were included; tumour grade was reported inconsistently, with higher-grade tumours predominating in the larger cohorts and at least 114 patients having WHO grade 4 disease. Early postoperative deficits ranged from 2.2 to 100% depending on assessment timing and measure (immediate post-op: up to 100%; day 7 to week 1: 2.2-22%). Persistent deficits at ≥ 3 months ranged from 0 to 47%. In three studies reporting whole-cohort outcomes with standardised assessment, rates were 0-5.6%. Papagno et al., using 3-month cut-offs, found that 47% of patients with uncinate fasciculus resection had impairment in famous face naming versus 10% with the tract preserved. The general trend was early decline followed by improvement, with most reported deficits resolving by around 3 months. Heterogeneous deficit definitions and inconsistent baseline assessment preclude treating this as a prognostic pattern, and resections involving the uncinate fasciculus were a notable outlier, underscoring the need for systematic subcortical tract mapping.
CONCLUSION: Awake craniotomy with DES remains the gold standard for preserving language. Early deficits are common but predominantly transient, and reported deficit rates appear closely associated with the timing of assessment. Persistent deficits assessed at ≥ 3 months were low in most studies, although rates varied considerably with the outcome measure used and with subcortical tract involvement. Subcortical tract involvement warrants systematic mapping. We advocate for the global adoption of standardised perioperative linguistic protocols to improve data comparability.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261342690.

articles.title: Association of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery Protocol Utilization with Postoperative Delirium in Inpatient Total Joint Arthroplasty: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Postoperative delirium following total hip and knee arthroplasty (THA and TKA) is associated with worse outcomes. Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols may mitigate delirium risk, but this association has not been explored in THA and TKA. We evaluated the associations between ERAS utilization and postoperative delirium in inpatient TKA and THA.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used a national database to identify adult patients undergoing elective inpatient primary THA and TKA, respectively. Perioperative ERAS utilization was defined by eight components: multimodal analgesia, tranexamic acid, antiemetics, corticosteroids, physical therapy, avoidance of urinary catheters, avoidance of patient-controlled analgesia, and avoidance of wound drains. The ERAS implementation was operationalized as both a binary and a three-level categorical variable. The primary outcome was any delirium during the index hospitalization or within 30 days after index hospitalization. Mixed-effects models estimated adjusted odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI).
RESULTS: Among 463,877 THAs and 706,140 TKAs, delirium incidence increased from 2016 to 2023 (THA; 2.0 to 5.1%, TKA: 2.2 to 3.9%, P < 0.001). In binary models, utilization of greater than six ERAS components was associated with reduced delirium risk in THA (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88 to 0.96, P < 0.001), but not TKA (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.02, P = 0.28). In categorical models for THA, high ERAS utilization was also associated with lower odds of delirium compared to low ERAS utilization (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.98, P = 0.01). Medium ERAS utilization was not associated with delirium odds compared to low.
CONCLUSIONS: In this national cohort study, higher ERAS utilization was associated with lower odds of postoperative delirium following THA, but not TKA. While the effect size was modest, these findings provide large-scale observational evidence of an association between ERAS utilization and postoperative delirium in THA.

articles.title: Neurocognitive Outcomes After Cranial and Craniofacial Surgery: Global Research Trends and Emerging Themes.
articles.abstract: Neurocognitive outcomes are increasingly recognized as important after cranial and craniofacial procedures, but the structure and evolution of this literature have not been characterized comprehensively. The Web of Science Core Collection was used to identify 657 publications from 1991 through June 2026. Publication output, citations, contributing countries and institutions, international collaboration, and keyword co-occurrence were examined using Web of Science, VOSviewer, and Microsoft Excel. Annual publication output increased substantially over the study period. The United States produced the most publications (n=241), followed by China (n=81), Italy and Japan (n=49 each), and England (n=34). The University of California system and Harvard University were the leading institutional contributors. Keyword mapping demonstrated an interdisciplinary literature spanning craniotomy, craniosynostosis, traumatic brain injury, anesthesia, neuro-oncology, neurodevelopment, cognition, and quality of life. Research on neurocognitive outcomes after cranial and craniofacial surgery has expanded and become increasingly patient-centered. Recent themes emphasize neurodevelopment, long-term cognitive function, quality of life, and multidisciplinary perioperative management.

articles.title: Surgical outcomes and functional morbidity after retrosigmoid/retrocondylar and midline suboccipital approaches for foramen magnum meningiomas: a single-arm meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Foramen magnum meningiomas (FMMs) are surgically challenging due to their proximity to the cervicomedullary junction, lower cranial nerves, and vertebrobasilar circulation. Although far-lateral transcondylar approaches are commonly used for ventral lesions, less extensive posterior/posterolateral corridors are increasingly employed. We performed a single-arm meta-analysis to quantify oncologic control and functional morbidity following retrosigmoid/retrocondylar and midline suboccipital approaches for FMMs. A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception through July 2025 (last search 31 July 2025). Eligible studies were original clinical case series with ≥ 5 patients (all eligible series proved retrospective) reporting FMM resection via posterior midline suboccipital or lateral/posterolateral suboccipital corridors, including retrosigmoid/retrocondylar approaches with limited condyle drilling ≤ 1/3 when performed. Studies with nonseparable outcomes from more extensive transcondylar/far-lateral approaches were excluded. Pooled proportions were calculated using a random-effects model with Freeman-Tukey transformation and reported with 95% confidence intervals. Seven retrospective case series from 1997 to 2019 contributing 133 eligible patients were included; one series was restricted to its 34 intradural cases operated through eligible corridors. Weighted mean age was 54.4 years, 75.2% (100/133) were female, and sample-size-weighted mean follow-up was 58 months. Retrosigmoid/retrocondylar corridors were used in 74/133 patients (55.6%) and midline suboccipital craniectomy in 59/133 (44.4%), often with C1 laminectomy. Dedicated retrosigmoid/retrocondylar series included predominantly anterior/anterolateral tumors, whereas midline series included mixed attachments. Formal approach-specific comparisons were limited by heterogeneous reporting. When performed, condyle drilling was generally limited to the posterior one-third; no postoperative craniocervical instability or fusion was reported. Pooled gross total resection was 91% (95% CI: 84-96%; 119/133 patients, 7 studies), recurrence was rare (3/133, 2.3%; pooled 1%, 95% CI: 0-4%), and long-term functional independence was 83% (95% CI: 71-93%; 60/74 patients, 5 studies). New cranial nerve deficits, transient or permanent, occurred in 21% (95% CI: 13-30%; 22/99 patients, 6 studies), cerebrospinal fluid leak in 12% (95% CI: 6-20%; 13/99, 6 studies), and perioperative mortality in 3% (95% CI: 0-9%; 7/133, 7 studies), with two additional late deaths from aspiration pneumonia during follow-up. Taken together, retrosigmoid/retrocondylar and midline suboccipital approaches for FMMs achieve high resection rates, low recurrence, and favorable long-term function, often without extensive condylectomy. These pooled estimates represent a combined figure across two anatomically distinct corridors applied to topographically different tumors (retrosigmoid/retrocondylar routes predominantly for anterior/anterolateral lesions and midline suboccipital exposure predominantly for posterior/posterolateral lesions), and do not imply that the approaches are interchangeable. Cranial nerve morbidity, cerebrospinal fluid leak, and perioperative mortality remain important considerations.

articles.title: Incidence rate and factors associated with periprocedural hypoxia during bedside intravitreal ranibizumab injection for retinopathy of prematurity: a multicenter retrospective study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy has become an established treatment for type 1 retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). However, evidence regarding intraprocedural hypoxia during bedside intravitreal injection remains limited. This study evaluated the incidence, severity, and predictors of hypoxia during intravitreal ranibizumab injection for treatment-requiring ROP.
METHODS: This retrospective multicenter observational study included premature infants with treatment-requiring ROP who underwent bedside intravitreal ranibizumab injection under topical anesthesia between July 2020 and June 2026 in neonatal intensive care units across the Al Qassim region, Saudi Arabia. Continuous pulse oximetry was used during the procedure and for 30 min afterward. Hypoxia was classified as mild (oxygen saturation 85-89%), moderate (80-84%), or severe (< 80%). Demographic, perinatal, maternal, and ophthalmic variables were analyzed. Logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with hypoxia.
RESULTS: Seventy-four premature infants out of 1430 were included. The mean gestational age was 27.5 ± 2.2 weeks, the mean birth weight was 986.8 ± 265.8 g, and the mean postmenstrual age at treatment was 36.6 ± 2.2 weeks. Hypoxia occurred in 12 infants (16.2%; 95% CI, 8.7-26.6%), including 10 (13.5%) with mild hypoxia and 2 (2.7%) with moderate hypoxia; no episodes of severe hypoxia were observed. Lower gestational age (OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.35-0.76; P = 0.001), lower birth weight (OR 0.991 per gram increase, 95% CI 0.984-0.997; P = 0.004), and longer duration of oxygen therapy (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.03-1.77; P = 0.028) were associated with hypoxia in univariate analysis. After adjustment, birth weight remained the principal predictor of increasing hypoxia severity. At follow-up, regression of ROP was achieved in 60 infants (81.1%), while 4 (5.4%) required repeat ranibizumab injection and 10 (13.5%) underwent adjunctive laser photocoagulation.
CONCLUSIONS: Bedside intravitreal ranibizumab injection under topical anesthesia was associated with a low incidence of transient hypoxia, and no severe oxygen desaturation events occurred. Lower birth weight and lower gestational age were associated with an increased risk of hypoxia. These findings support the short-term cardiorespiratory safety of bedside ranibizumab injection in premature infants while emphasizing the importance of continuous physiological monitoring, particularly in extremely low-birth-weight infants.
CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: NCT07701759 obtained on July 8, 2026.

articles.title: Outcomes of Proton Beam Therapy in Infants and Very Young Children.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Radiation has historically been deferred or avoided in infants and very young children because of concern about late toxicity. Although proton beam therapy (PBT) is increasingly used in this age group, outcome data remain limited. We evaluated disease control, patterns of failure, and late toxicity in children aged ≤3 years treated through the UK national proton pathway.
METHODS AND MATERIALS: We retrospectively reviewed 76 consecutive children aged ≤3 years at PBT initiation who were treated at XXXX (anonymized) between December 2018 and January 2025. Diagnoses included central nervous system (CNS) tumors (n=33; ependymoma, 20; embryonal tumors, 12; other, 1) and non-CNS tumors (n=43; sarcoma, 20; neuroblastoma, 12; renal tumors, 11). All patients received daily image-guided, optimized pencil-beam-scanning PBT under general anesthesia. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), local control (LC), and Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade ≥3 late toxicity-free survival were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method.
RESULTS: Median age at PBT start was 28.1 months (range, 9.4-36.0 months). Treatment was completed as planned in 72 of 76 patients (94.7%); 23.7% were hospitalized and 38.2% required enteral feeding support during PBT. With a median follow-up of 2.9 years, 1-, 2-, and 3-year OS were 87.9%, 85.1%, and 81.1%, respectively; 2-year PFS and LC were 65.5% and 85.2%. All 9 local failures (12.0%) occurred within the high-dose target volume. High-grade late toxicity occurred in 11 patients (14.9%); 2-year high-grade toxicity-free survival was 90.4%. One treatment-related death occurred from brainstem radionecrosis despite meeting accepted brainstem constraints.
CONCLUSIONS: PBT is deliverable in children aged ≤3 years within a national pathway. However, all local failures occurred within the high-dose target volume, high-grade late toxicity affected 14.9% over a short follow-up, and one treatment-related death occurred despite adherence to accepted constraints. These findings support biology-guided patient selection, age-adapted organ-at-risk objectives and structured long-term surveillance.

articles.title: Pediatric living-donor kidney transplantation in infants and low-weight children: what have we learned so far?
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kidney transplantation (KTx) in low-weight (LW) children is technically demanding due to the size mismatch between adult-sized kidneys and small recipients. We evaluated the impact of recipient weight on surgical morbidity, perioperative recovery, and long-term graft outcomes.
