MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 156 consecutive living-donor pediatric KTx between 2018 and 2025. Recipients were divided into three groups by body weight: Group 1 ( < 10 kg), Group 2 (10 to <15 kg), and Group 3 ( ≥ 15 kg). Primary outcomes were postoperative complications and postoperative length of stay. Graft and patient survival were analyzed among the groups.
RESULTS: Recipient weight was found to be the sole independent predictor of overall postoperative complication risk. However, in pre-specified exploratory analyses focusing on major complications, previous abdominal surgery also emerged as a significant risk factor. Recipient weight category and previous abdominal surgery were found to be independent predictors of hospital length of stay. No vascular or graft thrombosis was observed. At 1 year, death-censored graft and patient survival were 98.7% and 99.4%, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Recipients weighing <15 kg, particularly the <10 kg group, experienced higher perioperative morbidity but can achieve excellent graft and patient survival with appropriate surgical adaptations and careful perioperative care. These findings support timely KTx at experienced centers rather than delaying transplantation solely to achieve strict weight thresholds.

articles.title: Effects of Different Measures for the Treatment of Arterial Hypotension on Cerebral Oxygen Saturation During Pediatric General Anesthesia: An Observational Pilot Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intraoperative hypotension is a common complication in pediatric anesthesia. The definition of hypotension and treatment strategies are heterogeneous. The association of these treatments with cerebral regional oxygen saturation, measured by near-infrared spectroscopy, is insufficiently characterized.
AIMS: The study explores whether changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate differ after the administration of an isotonic fluid bolus, noradrenaline, adrenaline, or cafedrine/theodrenaline for perioperative hypotension in children.
METHODS: This single-center, observational pilot study included children aged 18 years or younger undergoing noncardiac surgery who developed hypotension requiring treatment. The choice of the intervention was at the discretion of the attending anesthetist and guided by an internal guideline. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate were recorded for 8 min after the first intervention and analyzed relative to the value immediately before treatment. Groups were compared using the area under the curve of these changes and linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Forty-six patients were analyzed. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation immediately before treatment did not differ from the pre-induction baseline. Cafedrine/theodrenaline was the only treatment associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, with a significantly higher area under the curve than noradrenaline (p = 0.017), adrenaline (p = 0.017), and fluid administration (p < 0.001), which was confirmed by mixed-effects models. Only cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with an increase in heart rate. Changes in heart rate were significantly correlated with changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation (Spearman's ρ = 0.376, p = 0.010), but not with changes in mean arterial pressure.
CONCLUSIONS: Cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure. Noradrenaline, adrenaline, and fluid administration were associated with unchanged or decreasing cerebral regional oxygen saturation. Randomized controlled studies are required to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Ketamine for co-occurring chronic pain and depression: A scoping review highlighting the dual-outcome evidence gap and its treatment and research implications.
articles.abstract: Chronic pain and depression frequently co-occur, share clinical features, and involve shared neurobiological substrates. Ketamine, an NMDA-receptor antagonist, has established antidepressant efficacy, whereas its analgesic efficacy for chronic pain remains uncertain. Given the overlap between chronic pain and depression, ketamine may serve as a potential dual-action treatment. We conducted a scoping review of studies in which pain and depressive outcomes were both assessed longitudinally after ketamine treatment. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus through August 2026. Experimental and observational studies reporting post-treatment pain and depression outcomes were included; acute, perioperative, perinatal, and cancer-related pain were excluded. Of 2187 records screened, 12 studies met inclusion criteria (2007-2025). Eight enrolled patients with consensus-based chronic pain (≥3 months); among these, only two used clinical diagnoses to characterize depression (one being retrospective chart review), whereas the remainder used symptom scales. Four depression-primary studies enrolled patients with major depressive disorder, treatment-resistant depression, or bipolar depression but did not rigorously establish chronic pain duration. Most studies reported concurrent improvement in pain and depressive symptoms, but heterogeneity in population definitions, ketamine administration regimens, study design, and psychiatric comorbidity precludes inference that depression modifies ketamine's analgesic effect. Prospective randomized studies using standardized chronic pain and depression measures are needed to clarify ketamine's efficacy and real-world applicability. REGISTRATION: This protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) (registration: OSF.IO/3ER5W) PERSPECTIVE: This review maps studies that assessed pain and depressive symptoms longitudinally during ketamine treatment. Concurrent improvement was commonly reported, but inconsistent depression ascertainment, pain phenotyping, dosing, and study design prevent conclusions about depression-specific analgesic effects. Prospective trials with clinically defined comorbidity are needed.

articles.title: Day-to-day migraine-related disability and mental health in children and adolescents with migraine: A longitudinal prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Migraine affects 11% of youth and causes substantial functional impairment. While youth with migraine exhibit elevated pain catastrophizing and internalizing symptoms, daily associations with migraine-related disability remain unclear due to limited longitudinal research. This study examined associations between migraine-related disability on headache days (1) state pain catastrophizing, same-day mood, and anxiety, and (2) mood and anxiety 24-48 h before and after a reported headache day. In a 30-day prospective cohort from a tertiary pediatric headache program, 53 participants (8-18 years; median age 15; 87% female; 57% chronic migraine) reported 769 headache days via electronic diaries. Measures included a daily Pediatric Migraine Disability Assessment Scale (PedMIDAS), the 3-item State Pain Catastrophizing Scale for Children (SPCS-C), and 11-point numerical rating scales for mood/anxiety. Generalized negative binomial mixed-effects models were conducted. On headache days, higher state pain catastrophizing (IRR=1.03, 95% CI=1.01-1.05) and lower mood (IRR=0.92, 95% CI=0.87-0.97) significantly associated with greater disability. Higher anxiety was associated with greater disability in primary analyses, but this association did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Mood and anxiety 24-48 h before a headache day did not predict disability, nor did disability predict mood or anxiety 24-48 h post-headache day. These findings suggest that same-day state pain catastrophizing and poor mood are associated with headache-day disability in youth, whereas short-term fluctuations in mood and anxiety surrounding a reported headache day are not. This suggests that psychological factors have an immediate, state-dependent association with functional impairment, highlighting the importance of "in-the-moment" psychological targets for clinical intervention. PERSPECTIVE: This study shows that same-day pain catastrophizing, mood, and anxiety are closely linked to migraine-related disability in youth, whereas short-term fluctuations surrounding headache days are not. Findings highlight immediate, state-dependent psychological mechanisms underlying functional impairment, suggesting targeted "in-the-moment" interventions may reduce disability and improve daily functioning in pediatric migraine.

articles.title: 'To live again': a qualitative study of patients' experiences of amputation for therapy-resistant complex regional pain syndrome.
articles.abstract: For some people with severe, therapy-resistant complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), amputation may be considered as a last resort. Evidence on outcomes after amputation remains limited and heterogeneous, while patients' experiences of this irreversible intervention remain largely unexplored. We conducted a qualitative descriptive study involving 17 individuals who had undergone amputation for CRPS at a tertiary expertise center. Semi-structured interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis combining inductive and deductive coding. Participants described how severe pain, loss of function, and an increasingly burdensome limb progressively narrowed their lives until they felt they were surviving rather than living. As hope for meaningful improvement diminished, amputation became conceivable. Pathways differed, with some amputations considered electively and others becoming medically necessary, leading to differences in agency, preparation, and expectations. After amputation, participants described varying degrees of pain relief and renewed participation, alongside persistent pain, complications, and difficulties with prosthetic use. They evaluated amputation not only through pain, but also through function, autonomy, participation, identity, and quality of life. These evaluations were often shaped by comparison with the restrictions of life before surgery. Amputation was therefore understood not merely as a surgical procedure, but as an irreversible turning point that could make life more livable. These findings should be interpreted within a carefully selected cohort from a specialized multidisciplinary setting, in which less favorable experiences may be underrepresented. Overall, the results underscore the importance of careful assessment, realistic counseling, and structured support before and after amputation. PERSPECTIVE: Among purposively selected patients with severe CRPS, amputation was understood within a longer illness trajectory rather than as an isolated procedure. Patients evaluated benefit in relation to the life they had lost and hoped to regain. These findings may inform counseling and support around this irreversible intervention.

articles.title: Cognitive load of healthcare professionals in the intensive care unit: A bibliometric analysis from 2016 to 2025.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To identify research hotspots, major contributors, and developmental trends in studies on cognitive load among ICU healthcare professionals.
METHOD: A bibliometric analysis was conducted on data retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, covering scholarly publications from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2025. CiteSpace software was used to visualize and analyze countries, institutions, cited journals, and keywords.
RESULTS: A total of 169 articles were included. The annual publication output showed a steady upward trend over the decade, rising from 7 publications in 2016 to 34 in 2025. Notably, 82 articles (48.5% of the total) were published between 2023 and 2025. The United States ranked first in contributions (63 publications, 37.28%). Capital Medical University in China was the most productive institution (6 publications, 3.55%). The most frequently cited journal was Critical Care Medicine (75 citations). Research hotspots centered on three thematic directions: workload and mental demand among ICU nursing staff, psychological outcomes and occupational well-being, and clinical assessment and patient-centered management. Emerging trends included psychological well-being promotion and risk prevention related to cognitive load.
CONCLUSIONS: Research on cognitive load in ICU healthcare professionals has grown substantially, with increasing attention to nursing workload, mental health, and patient safety.

articles.title: The Post-Sepsis Neutrophil: Lymphocyte Ratio: A Population Signal in Search of Individual Meaning.
Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge-a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics-and long-term outcomes.
DESIGN: Population-based cohort study.
SETTING: Ontario, Canada, 2010-2020.
PATIENTS: Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The exposure was the first outpatient NLR-derived from the complete blood count-measured 15-90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22-54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8-4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27-185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% (ptrend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18-1.29), 1.54 (1.48-1.62), and 2.25 (2.15-2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic.
CONCLUSIONS: Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15-90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.

articles.title: Expanding transplant access via robotics: a multi-center American experience with 671 robotic kidney transplants.
articles.abstract: The safety of robotic kidney transplantation has been shown in single-center studies, but multi-institutional outcomes in America remain understudied. This was a retrospective analysis of 671 robotic kidney transplants across three institutions, with data collected from the start of their robotic kidney transplant programs through December 2025. Outcomes were stratified by recipient body mass index, donor type, and renal artery anatomy. Median recipient age was 49 years, and 58.0% were male. Most patients had obesity (87.8%), with 47.5% having morbid obesity. Most (55.1%) received living donor grafts. Median operative and warm ischemia times were 273 and 44 min, respectively. Conversion to open surgery occurred in 0.6% of cases. Delayed graft function occurred in 16.2% of recipients, and major complications in 12.1%; neither differed by recipient body mass index. Patient survival was significantly lower for patients with BMI ≥ 40 (p < 0.001). Delayed graft function varied by donor type, ranging from 2.2% (living donor) to 48.3% (donation after circulatory death with rapid recovery). Patient survival at 1, 3, and 5 years post-transplant was 96.5%, 92.5%, and 87.3%; graft survival was 96.9%, 93.4%, and 86.8%, respectively. Robotic kidney transplantation was safe and technically reproducible with appropriate perioperative outcomes across three American transplant centers.

articles.title: Patient Perspectives on Pain During Ambulatory Gynecologic Procedures.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Pain perception during pelvic exams and gynecologic procedures varies widely and may be influenced by psychological, physiological, and clinical factors. Understanding patient experiences and desired interventions is critical to improving care and reducing unacceptable pain.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional, retrospective survey of patients seen at an ambulatory gynecology clinic within an academic medical center in Portland, Oregon. Eight hundred and twenty-four individuals completed the survey, with 690 meeting inclusion criteria. The primary outcome was acceptability of procedural pain using the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS).
RESULTS: Thirteen percent of respondents reported unacceptable PASS during prior pelvic exams or procedures. This was more common among those with dysmenorrhea (p = 0.002), chronic pelvic pain (p = 0.006), sexual trauma (p = 0.04), younger age (p < 0.001), or undergoing a first pelvic exam (p = 0.01). Moderate or severe anxiety during their most recent exam or procedure was strongly associated with unacceptable PASS (34.4% versus 23.1%, 54.4% versus 13.5%, p < 0.001), though prior diagnoses of depression/anxiety were not. Compared to the overall sample, transcervical procedure respondents were more likely to report unacceptable PASS (27.7% versus 13.0%) and moderate-to-severe pain (64.5% versus 35.7%).
CONCLUSIONS: Both patient comorbidities and modifiable clinical practices contribute to unacceptable procedural pain. Patients expressed interest in anxiolytics, moderate sedation, and topical/injectable anesthetic options. Involving patients in pain management decisions and responding to their pain was associated with more acceptable experiences. Further research is needed to evaluate effective interventions across diverse populations and procedures.

articles.title: Can Outpatient Total Knee Arthroplasty Be Performed at a Complex, Academic, Quaternary Referral Center?
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Outpatient (same-day discharge) primary total knee arthroplasties (TKAs) have been recently popularized, but results from academic medical centers remain limited. Outpatient surgery shifts perioperative responsibilities to the surgeon. Meanwhile, surgeon reimbursements continue to decrease. We retrospectively evaluated 90-day rates of emergency room (ER) visits, reoperations, revisions, and incoming/outgoing postoperative patient touches associated with outpatient TKAs at our complex, academic, quaternary referral center.
METHODS: At our institution, 1,787 outpatient primary TKAs were performed between 2019 and 2024 in 1,552 unique patients. The mean age was 65 years, 51% were women, the mean body mass index (BMI) was 33, the mean American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score was 2.4, and the mean Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was 1.5 (range, 0 to 10). Medical comorbidities, ER visits, reoperations, revisions, and postoperative touches within 90 days after TKA were collected. Univariate logistic regression analyses were completed.
RESULTS: The rates of ER visits, reoperations, and revisions within 90 days of surgery were 8.5, 3.1, and 0.7%, respectively. Knees averaged nine postoperative touches, and total touches increased from 61 in 2019 to greater than 5,800 in 2024. The most common first-time ER visit reason was a medical issue unrelated to surgery (35%), followed by evaluation for venous thromboembolism (VTE; 29%). The actual VTE incidence was 0.6%. The most common reoperation was manipulation under anesthesia (MUA; incidence 1.5%). The 90-day periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) incidence was 0.7%, and all cases required reoperation or revision. Older age and increasing ASA score were significantly associated with risk of ER visits (odds ratio [OR] 1.2; P = 0.01 and OR 1.8; P < 0.001, respectively). Increasing CCI was significantly associated with risk of ER visits (OR 1.2; P = 0.001), revisions (OR 1.5; P = 0.001), and PJI (OR 1.3; P = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS: We found a high rate of ER visits within 90 days after outpatient TKAs, with nearly 40% unattributable to surgery. Increasing age and comorbidities were associated with increased ER visit risk, and comorbidities also increased revision and PJI risk. Knees averaged nine non-clinic postoperative touches.

articles.title: Single-port robotic surgery versus laparo-endoscopic single-site surgery for the surgical staging of early-stage endometrial cancer: a sequential-period propensity-score analysis.
articles.abstract: We compared perioperative outcomes of da Vinci SP robotic surgery and laparo-endoscopic single-site surgery (LESS) for staging early-stage endometrial cancer in a sequential-period cohort. Between 2010 and 2025, 178 women with presumed and final FIGO stage I or II endometrial carcinoma underwent single-port staging with lymph node assessment; LESS was used through 2021 (n = 95), and SP surgery was introduced in 2021 (n = 83). Patients were analyzed by planned approach, including procedures requiring an additional port. The primary outcome was the hemoglobin decline from the preoperative value to the value measured on the day of surgery. The hemoglobin decline was 1.92 ± 1.14 g/dL after LESS and 0.92 ± 0.88 g/dL after SP surgery (p < .001), and estimated blood loss was 205.4 ± 192.4 and 68.5 ± 79.3 mL (p < .001). After inverse probability of treatment weighting, the between-group difference in hemoglobin decline (SP minus LESS) was - 1.06 g/dL (95% CI - 1.42 to - 0.70). This estimate was not materially changed by further adjustment for perioperative fluid volume and sampling time. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with pelvic lymphadenectomy, the difference was attenuated to - 0.72 g/dL (95% CI - 1.21 to - 0.22), and operative time was 25.5 min longer with the SP robot. Overall operative time, hospital stay, conversions, and complications did not differ significantly. SP staging was associated with a smaller hemoglobin decline. Because the 2 approaches were used in largely different calendar periods, these findings do not establish an independent effect of the platform.

articles.title: Distal Pancreatectomy in Octogenarians and the Role of Robotic Surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: A minimally invasive approach currently is the gold standard for distal pancreatectomy (DP). Robotic distal pancreatectomy (RDP) is increasingly adopted and offers technical advantages. As life expectancy rises, more octogenarians undergo pancreatic resection, and emerging evidence suggests minimally invasive approaches may benefit older adults. However, the role of RDP in this population remains underexplored.
METHODS: A multi-institutional retrospective cohort study from four high-volume North American hepato-pancreatobiliary centers was conducted. Adults undergoing elective open distal pancreatectomy (ODP) or RDP between 2007 and 2023 were stratified as < 80 versus ≥ 80 years of age. The primary outcome was 90-day mortality. The secondary outcomes included major complications and oncologic outcomes. Multivariable models were applied to adjust for relevant covariates. A subanalysis was performed on patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
RESULTS: Of 797 patients undergoing DP, 62 were aged ≥ 80 years. Despite more comorbidities and higher PDAC rates, older patients had comparable perioperative outcomes. Blood loss, conversion, complications, length of stay, readmissions, and 90-day mortality were similar between age groups. On adjusted analysis, age ≥ 80 years was not associated with major complications or 90-day mortality in the overall cohort or PDAC subgroup. Whereas RDP was independently associated with fewer major complications, longer operative time and greater blood loss increased adverse outcomes. Among PDAC patients, perioperative and oncologic outcomes, including survival, were comparable across age groups.
CONCLUSION: Octogenarians achieve perioperative and oncologic outcomes comparable with those of younger patients when treated in high-volume centers, including survival. A robotic approach proved advantageous in reducing complications. The current findings reinforce the role of resection when indicated.

articles.title: Clinical performance of i-gel and classic laryngeal mask airway in different head positions in patients aged ≥75 years: A prospective randomized study.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveSupraglottic airway devices are alternatives to endotracheal intubation under general anesthesia. However, their performance in older patients remains understudied, particularly in different head positions.MethodsThis prospective randomized controlled study included 120 patients aged ≥75 years undergoing elective urologic surgery. Patients were randomly allocated into four groups based on the device type and head position during insertion: (a) i-gel with neutral head position; (b) i-gel with right head rotation; (c) classic laryngeal mask airway with neutral head position; and (d) classic laryngeal mask airway with right head rotation. The primary outcome was the insertion time. Secondary outcomes included insertion attempts, oropharyngeal leak pressure, and perioperative variables, which were assessed in patients with successful device placement.ResultsThe overall insertion success rate was 94.2% (113/120). The i-gel was associated with a significantly shorter insertion time and higher oropharyngeal leak pressure than the classic laryngeal mask airway (both p = 0.001). Two-way factorial analysis revealed that device type significantly influenced insertion time and oropharyngeal leak pressure, whereas head position and device-by-head position interaction exerted no significant effects. No significant differences were observed in the number of insertion attempts, fiberoptic view scores, peak airway pressure, recovery times, hemodynamic variables, or perioperative and postoperative complications.ConclusionsIn patients aged ≥75 years undergoing elective surgery, the i-gel was associated with a shorter insertion time and higher oropharyngeal leak pressure than the classic laryngeal mask airway. Head position did not significantly influence insertion time, oropharyngeal leak pressure, or peak airway pressure. These findings suggest that airway device selection exerts a greater impact on supraglottic airway performance than head position, whereas the i-gel may offer practical advantages in selected clinical settings.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (https://clinicaltrials.gov), Identifier: NCT07027293, registered on 27 May 2025.

articles.title: Optimal Etomidate Induction Dosage Combined With Nerve Block Minimizes Postoperative Cognitive Dysfunction and Enhances Hemodynamic Stability in Elderly Hernia Patients.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Etomidate combined with nerve block is commonly used for elderly hernia surgery, but standardized dosing regimens remain lacking.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different induction doses of etomidate combined with nerve block on hemodynamic stability and cognitive function in elderly hernia patients, aiming to optimize the induction strategy.
METHODS: 106 elderly patients scheduled for elective hernia surgery were randomly assigned to low-dose (0.1 mg/kg, n = 35), medium-dose (0.2 mg/kg, n = 36), or high-dose (0.3 mg/kg, n = 35) etomidate groups. All received sufentanil 0.3 μg/kg and remimazolam 0.3 mg/kg with nerve block. Intraoperative vital signs, postoperative cognitive function, and adverse events were compared. Multivariate analysis identified postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) risk factors.
RESULTS: The medium-dose group showed superior hemodynamic stability with smaller fluctuations in mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and heart rate (HR), the lowest POCD rate on day 1 (8.3%) and lowest adverse events (13.9%), and shorter recovery and hospital stays. The high-dose group had the highest hypotension (28.6%) and POCD (40.0%) rates. Age ≥75 years, high-dose etomidate, and operative time >60 minutes were independent POCD risk factors.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Etomidate 0.2 mg/kg with nerve block achieves favorable hemodynamics and minimizes POCD and adverse reactions in elderly hernia surgery, supporting a moderate-dose strategy for this vulnerable population.

articles.title: The Impact of Rurality on the Standard of Care for Hip Fracture Patients: An ANZHFR Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hip fracture care requires timely, multi-disciplinary management. This study examined whether rural hospital location was associated with adherence to the Australian Hip Fracture Clinical Care Standard (HFCCS).
METHODS: Australian and New Zealand Hip Fracture Registry data from 2018 to 2023 were analysed for patients aged ≥ 50 years. Hospitals were classified using the Modified Monash Model as metropolitan (MM1-2) or rural (MM3-7). Patients transferred before surgery were excluded from the primary analysis and examined separately. Missing data were addressed using multiple imputation. Logistic regression was adjusted for age, sex and ASA classification.
RESULTS: The primary analysis included 58 757 patients (50 727 metropolitan; 8030 rural). Metropolitan hospitals had higher adherence to cognitive assessment (72.8% vs. 68.1%), nerve block administration (94.0% vs. 91.2%), delirium assessment (76.2% vs. 70.1%), surgery within 48 h (80.3% vs. 78.7%), mobilisation within 24 h (92.9% vs. 90.9%) and secondary fracture prevention (81.3% vs. 69.8%) (all p < 0.05). Rural hospitals had lower adjusted odds of adherence for these indicators (ORs 0.54-0.90). Analgesia within 30 min was more frequent in rural hospitals (80.7% vs. 77.6%; adjusted OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.13-1.28).
CONCLUSION: Rural hospital location was associated with lower adherence to several HFCCS indicators, particularly cognitive and delirium assessment, early mobilisation and secondary fracture prevention, while timely analgesia was more frequent in rural hospitals. Geographical variation in guideline-based hip fracture care persists in Australia and warrants further investigation.

articles.title: Risk Factors for Delayed Closure Following ORIF of Adult Both-Bone Forearm Fractures: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delayed wound closure after open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of diaphyseal both-bone forearm fractures is an important soft tissue consideration. This study evaluated its incidence and associated risk factors.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed at 2 level 1 trauma centers including adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent ORIF for diaphyseal both-bone forearm fractures (AO/OTA (Arbeitsgemeinschaft für Osteosynthesefragen / Orthopaedic Trauma Association) 2R2, 2U2) from 2010 to 2025. Delayed wound closure was defined as unplanned return to the operating room for definitive closure or soft-tissue coverage. Demographic, injury, and perioperative variables were analyzed. Multivariable Firth-penalized logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors.
RESULTS: Among 292 patients (mean age, 41.6 years; 56.8% male), delayed wound closure occurred in 14 (4.8%). All patients requiring delayed closure were male (100% vs 54.7%) and more frequently had Gustilo-Anderson type III open fractures (42.9% vs 3.3%), nerve injury (21.4% vs 3.7%), and vascular injury (14.3% vs 0%). Operative time was longer in patients requiring delayed closure (median, 176 vs 127 minutes). On multivariable analysis, prolonged operative time was independently associated with delayed closure (adjusted odds ratio, 7.7; 95% CI, 1.8-71.7).
CONCLUSIONS: Delayed wound closure after ORIF of both-bone forearm fractures occurred in fewer than 5% of patients and was independently associated with longer operative time, suggesting that delayed closure is associated with more complex operative courses and evolving soft-tissue considerations. Surgeons should counsel patients on the potential need for staged wound management.

articles.title: Development and validation of a Polish version of Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 (ObsQoR-10-Polish).
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 is a patient-reported outcome measure designed to evaluate early global postpartum recovery. No Polish version exists, and most prior validations excluded women with high-risk pregnancies.
METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort study at a tertiary referral center for placenta accreta spectrum, the Polish translation was administered at 24, 48 and 72 h postpartum. The primary aim was a psychometric evaluation at 24 h (structural validity, convergent validity against the EuroQol five-dimension index and visual analogue scale, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, floor and ceiling effects). The secondary aim was to explore univariable associations with obstetric and anesthetic variables.
RESULTS: Of 800 eligible women approached, 441 consented, with data from 410 analyzed. Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.90), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.85) and convergent validity (r = 0.77 and 0.69) were good, and a modified one-factor model fitted acceptably. At 24 h, 1.5% of women had a maximum score. Scores at 24 h were higher after vaginal compared with cesarean delivery (77.8 vs. 67.0; P < 0.001), higher after spinal compared with general anesthesia for cesarean delivery (68.6 vs. 51.0; P = 0.011), lower with increasing perineal injury severity (53.0 vs. 81.5; P = 0.001) and with placental pathologies (60.7 vs. 72.6; P = 0.003), and lowest in placenta accreta spectrum (42.4; n = 5).
DISCUSSION: The Polish Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 is reliable and demonstrated known-groups validity across the obstetric risk categories represented in this cohort. Associations in high-risk subgroups were unadjusted and require confirmation.

articles.title: Early Clinical Outcomes of Unilateral Biportal Endoscopic Technique for Decompression of Lumbar Foraminal Pathologies: Contralateral Sublaminar Approach Versus Contralateral Inclinatory Approach.
articles.abstract:
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective study comparing 2 types of decompressive surgery for lumbar foraminal pathologies (LFP).
OBJECTIVE: To report early surgical outcomes and compare the clinical and radiologic outcomes of the contralateral sublaminar approach (CSA) and the contralateral inclinatory approach (CIA) in unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) surgical technique for the treatment of LFP, including symptomatic foraminal stenosis or up-migrated herniated nucleus pulposus.
SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND DATA: Lumbar foraminal pathologies pose significant challenges in endoscopic spinal surgery, particularly in achieving adequate decompression of the exiting nerve root. The contralateral approach allows for sufficient foraminal decompression with less facetectomy compared with the conventional ipsilateral approach. However, no existing research has systematically described the selection of the more appropriate procedure between CSA and CIA.
METHODS: From January 2020 to September 2024, 41 patients with LFP underwent UBE decompression surgery using either CSA or CIA. Patients were classified into 2 groups: 18 in the CSA group and 23 in the CIA group. Clinical results, surgical invasion data, pain, and radiologic changes were compared between the 2 groups.
RESULTS: No significant differences were observed in the number of decompressed segments and demographic data between the 2 groups. The intracanal manipulation time and postoperative blood loss volume were significantly greater in the CSA group compared with the CIA group. Radiologic outcomes did not significantly differ between the groups. In addition, there were no significant differences in postoperative Oswestry Disability Index scores, postoperative visual analog scale scores, or perioperative complications between the 2 groups.
CONCLUSIONS: CSA-UBE and CIA-UBE yielded similar clinical outcomes for the treatment of LFP, including effective back and leg pain control and patient satisfaction. Both approaches allowed for effective preservation of the facet joint by undercutting it and saving the dorsal portion of the facet capsule. However, the CIA approach provided a more direct and shorter trajectory compared with the CSA approach, resulting in reduced postoperative blood loss volume and intracanal manipulation time.

articles.title: Intravenous Lidocaine in Liver Surgery ‒ A Randomized Double-Blind Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Managing postoperative pain is a complex challenge in liver surgery. Perioperative intravenous (IV) lidocaine can reduce postoperative pain, opioid use, bowel recovery time and the length of stay, in various types of surgery. Lidocaine is eliminated via hepatic metabolism, and IV lidocaine is rarely evaluated in liver surgery. This study aimed to evaluate the postoperative analgesic efficacy and safety of IV lidocaine administration in patients undergoing minor liver surgery.
METHODS: Patients planned for minor liver surgery were randomized 1:1 to receive either perioperative IV lidocaine, administered as a 1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 1.5 mg/kg/h until 1 hour after surgery, or placebo. All patients received postoperative opioid analgesia via a patient-controlled analgesia device. The primary outcome was postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, quality of recovery, adverse events, length of stay, and plasma lidocaine concentrations.
RESULTS: In total, 124 subjects were included. Postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery was 83 (50 - 129) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME) in the lidocaine group, and 97 (60 - 135) mg OME in the placebo group, p=0.429. Patients in the lidocaine group experienced lower pain scores at early postoperative time points, but not from postoperative day 1 onward. The Quality of recovery-40 score did not differ, and adverse events were similar between groups. In two cases, plasma concentrations of lidocaine were transiently above 5 µg/ml after bolus administration, without clinical signs of toxicity. All plasma concentrations after resection and at end of infusion were safely below toxic levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption after minor liver surgery but conferred transient early analgesic benefits and was found to be safe.

articles.title: Intraoperative Noise Isolation and Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting after Gynecological Laparoscopic Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) remain common after gynecological laparoscopic surgery despite guideline-based prophylaxis. Auditory information is still processed during clinically adequate general anesthesia, and operating rooms are persistently noisy, but whether attenuating intraoperative sound exposure alters PONV is unknown.
METHODS: In this single-center, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized trial, women aged 18 to 65 yr undergoing elective gynecological laparoscopic surgery were randomized 1:1 to wear passive noise-attenuating earmuffs from induction until the end of surgery or to usual care. All patients received dexamethasone and palonosetron. The primary outcome was PONV incidence within 48 h, defined as any episode of nausea, retching, or vomiting, assessed across three prespecified windows (post-anesthesia care unit, to 24 h, and 24 to 48 h). Secondary outcomes included PONV severity, its components, rescue antiemetic use, pain, and quality of recovery.
RESULTS: Of 364 patients assessed, 192 were randomized. PONV within 48 h occurred in 34 of 96 patients (35.4%) with noise isolation and 50 of 96 (52.1%) with control (adjusted risk difference, -0.179 [95% CI, -0.318 to -0.040]; P = 0.012). Across the three windows the overall adjusted risk difference was -0.134 (95% CI, -0.215 to -0.053; P = 0.001), with no treatment-by-window interaction (P = 0.332); window-specific values were -0.162, -0.172, and -0.068. PONV severity, retching, and three post hoc endpoints (the vomiting-or-retching composite, complete response 72.9% versus 56.2%, and total response 64.6% versus 47.9%) favored noise isolation after false discovery rate correction. Adverse events, quality of recovery, and opioid exposure (post hoc) showed no evidence of a difference.
CONCLUSIONS: Among women receiving dual antiemetic prophylaxis for gynecological laparoscopic surgery, intraoperative noise isolation was associated with a lower incidence and severity of PONV.

articles.title: Liposomal Bupivacaine versus Ropivacaine for Rhomboid Intercostal and Subserratus Plane Blocks in Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery: A Randomised Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The rhomboid intercostal and subserratus (RISS) plane block provides effective early analgesia for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), but its duration is limited by conventional local anaesthetics. To compare the analgesic efficacy of liposomal bupivacaine (LB) versus ropivacaine (RP) in RISS blocks for patients undergoing VATS.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this single-center randomized trial, 93 of the 96 enrolled VATS patients were analyzed (LB, 47; RP, 46). Patients received an ultrasound-guided RISS block with 266 mg LB or 100 mg RP. The primary endpoint was the area under the curve (AUC) of resting Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) pain scores over the first 48 postoperative hours. Secondary endpoints included rescue analgesia rate, and Quality of Recovery-40 (QoR-40) scores.
RESULTS: The resting NRS-AUC over 48 hours was lower in the LB group than in the RP group (66.5 [55.0 to 84.8] vs 112.0 [104.0 to 123.4]; P < 0.001). Similarly, the dynamic NRS-AUC over 48 hours was significantly lower in the LB group (137.0 [116.2 to 149.0] vs 191.0 [183.1 to 208.5]; P < 0.001). The 12-hour resting NRS-AUC was higher postoperatively in the LB group (22.0 [19.0 to 26.2] vs 16.5 [14.0 to 22.0]; P < 0.001), while the dynamic NRS-AUC was comparable between the groups (P = 0.846). The LB regimen also reduced the rescue analgesia rate (23.40% vs 54.35%; P = 0.004) and improved QoR-40 scores 48 hours (172.00 [169.50 to 175.00] vs 162.50 [159.25 to 164.75]; P < 0.001) postoperatively. Both groups experienced similar perioperative complications.
CONCLUSION: Compared with RP, LB for the RISS block prolonged postoperative analgesia after VATS surgery, and facilitated postoperative recovery, although its initial analgesic effect was less potent. Larger multicenter trials are needed due to the small sample size and the 72-hour follow-up period.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500107186).

articles.title: The Association Between Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Postoperative Delirium: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious complication following surgery, particularly in high-risk patients such as those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The relationship between COPD and the development of POD remains unclear, with existing studies providing inconsistent findings. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the association between COPD and postoperative delirium in surgical patients.
METHODS: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, and other grey resources. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials assessing the incidence of POD in COPD patients were included. Data were extracted on study design, participant demographics, surgical context, and POD assessment. Both fixed-effect and random-effects models were evaluated, with model selection guided by statistical heterogeneity and study characteristics. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity.
RESULTS: A total of 26 studies involving 43,051 patients were included. Both unadjusted and adjusted analyses showed a significant association between COPD and the increased risk of POD. The pooled odds ratio (OR) for the association in adjusted analyses was 2.08 (95% CI: 1.60-2.71, P < 0.001; I2 = 67.2%). In the adjusted subgroup analysis, the association remained statistically significant in non-cardiac surgery but did not reach statistical significance in cardiac surgery; however, the between-subgroup difference was not statistically significant (P for interaction = 0.139). Geographic variation was identified as a potential effect modifier, with studies conducted in Asia showing a stronger association.
CONCLUSION: The available evidence suggests an association between COPD and higher odds of POD in surgical patients, including in studies reporting multivariable-adjusted estimates. However, the predominantly observational evidence and between-study heterogeneity warrant cautious interpretation and do not establish causality. These findings highlight the potential importance of tailored perioperative management strategies for patients with COPD, although their effectiveness in reducing POD risk requires further investigation. Further well-designed prospective studies are necessary to confirm these findings and explore the underlying mechanisms. However, insufficient data on COPD severity precluded an assessment of whether this association varied across GOLD stages.
articles.journal: Int J Chron Obstruct Pulmon Dis

articles.title: Opioid-free versus opioid-sparing anaesthesia: is regional anaesthesia the variable that matters?
Opioid-Free Anesthesia: Rationale, Evidence and Current Limitations.
articles.abstract: This narrative review synthesized literature from PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library (2010-2026) to evaluate opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) as an alternative to opioid-centered perioperative care. Opioids have long been a cornerstone of modern anesthesia and analgesia due to their strong analgesic effects, helping to blunt surgical stress responses and reduce the need for other anesthetics. However, increasing concerns about the global epidemic opioid use disorder (OUD) and opioid-related side effects-such as postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), respiratory depression, ileus, and opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH)-have driven interest in opioid-sparing strategies. Therefore, opioid-free anesthesia has emerged as an alternative approach aimed at minimizing opioid use while maintaining effective analgesia. By avoiding intraoperative opioids, OFA aims to reduce opioid-related adverse effects and improve early recovery. This approach relies on multimodal pharmacology via different routes, combining intravenous infusions, regional anesthesia, and local infiltration to target multiple nociceptive pathways simultaneously. Common agents used in OFA include dexmedetomidine, ketamine, lidocaine, and magnesium. These drugs act through different mechanisms, such as α2-adrenergic agonist and NMDA receptor antagonist. Ketamine reduces central sensitization and OIH, while dexmedetomidine provides sedation, analgesia, and sympatholysis. Combined these agents may have synergistic effects on pain control and anesthetic management. Furthermore, administering these medications via different routes may enhance the analgesic effect with reduced doses of opioid or adjuvants. In the short term, the most consistent benefit of OFA is a reduction in PONV, whereas effects on pain and opioid consumption are smaller and inconsistent. Improvements in early recovery are also modest; the SOFA trial reported a statistically but not clinically significant improvement in quality of recovery-15 score at 24 hours in patients receiving OFA (mean 114.9 vs 108.7, P = 0.026). However, safety concerns persist; notably, the landmark POFA trial demonstrated increased cardiovascular adverse events linked to dexmedetomidine, highlighting the need for careful patient selection and dosing. Whether OFA reduces chronic postsurgical pain or persistent postoperative opioid use remains unproven and requires further investigation. In summary, OFA may reduce PONV within enhanced recovery after surgery protocol, but it is not free of risk and should not be regarded as a universal replacement for opioid-based anesthesia. Its optimal use requires appropriate patient and surgery selection, an individualized multimodal analgesic strategy, careful titration of non-opioid adjuncts, and vigilant monitoring for drug-specific adverse effects, particularly bradycardia, hypotension, excessive sedation, and delayed recovery. Further large-scale trials are needed to standardize regimens, identify optimal patient populations, and better define the balance between clinical benefits and potential cardiovascular and other adverse effects.

articles.title: Stress Hyperglycemia Ratio and Preoperative Acute Heart Failure in Elderly Hip Fracture Patients with Chronic Cerebrovascular Diseases.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prognostic significance of the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), calculated using admission blood glucose (ABG) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), remains unclear in the context of perioperative complications associated with hip fractures. This study evaluates the association and predictive capability of the SHR for preoperative acute heart failure in hip fracture patients with chronic cerebrovascular disease.
METHODS AND RESULTS: A total of 515 patients were analyzed, revealing a 16.8% incidence of preoperative HF. Significant intergroup differences in age (P < 0.001), ASA classification (P < 0.001), coronary heart disease (P=0.025), serum albumin level (P < 0.001), and admission SHR (P=0.033) were identified between patients with and without preoperative heart failure. Logistic regression identified SHR, CHD, ASA, neutrophils, and hypoproteinemia as independent predictors of preoperative HF, leading to the development of a nomogram that demonstrated good predictive performance (AUC 0.72). Calibration curves and decision curve analysis indicated the model's clinical utility. Machine learning algorithms, especially the XGBoost model, surpassed traditional models by achieving an AUC of 0.787, demonstrating excellent calibration and clinical applicability. SHAP analysis validated the stable contribution of SHR in risk prediction.
CONCLUSIONS: This study highlights the SHR's strong predictive ability for preoperative HF in hip fracture patients with chronic cerebrovascular disease. The XGBoost machine learning model could improve risk stratification and clinical decision-making for this at-risk group.

articles.title: Erector Spinae Plane Block Combined With Local Infiltration Analgesia for Posterior Lumbar Interbody Fusion: Prospective, Double-Blind, Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether erector spinae plane block (ESPB) combined with local infiltration analgesia (LIA) provides better postoperative analgesia than ESPB alone, LIA alone, or placebo in patients undergoing posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF).
METHODS: This prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled adults undergoing open PLIF for degenerative lumbar disease. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to placebo, LIA, ESPB, or combined ESPB with LIA. Fluoroscopy-guided ESPB or placebo injection was performed before induction of general anesthesia, while LIA or placebo infiltration was given before wound closure. All patients received standardized general anesthesia and postoperative patient-controlled intravenous analgesia. The primary outcomes were postoperative sufentanil consumption and visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores at rest and during movement at 4, 8, 12, 24, and 48 hours. Analyses were based on the modified intention-to-treat population. Longitudinal VAS trajectories were assessed using linear mixed-effects models, together with multiplicity-adjusted pairwise comparisons and factorial interaction analyses. A right-censoring sensitivity analysis of time to first patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) bolus was performed using Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, and adjusted Cox proportional hazards analyses.
RESULTS: Of the 188 randomized patients, 182 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across the 4 groups. Body-weight- and operative-time-normalized remifentanil and propofol consumption rates were lower in the ESPB-containing groups, whereas the rocuronium consumption rate did not differ significantly among groups. Linear mixed-effects models showed significant group×time interactions for both resting and movement VAS scores, indicating different postoperative pain trajectories among the groups. The combined ESPB with LIA group showed the most consistent short-term analgesic benefit, with lower pain scores at several early postoperative time points, lower postoperative sufentanil consumption, fewer analgesia pump activations, and a longer time to first PCIA bolus. After multiplicity adjustment, the postoperative rescue analgesia count was also lower in the combined group than in the control group. Factorial analyses identified a greater-than-additive effect only for time to first PCIA bolus, whereas the other analgesic outcomes showed no consistent evidence of statistical synergy. Right-censoring sensitivity analyses supported the longer time to first PCIA bolus in the combined group. Adverse-event rates were similar among the 4 groups, and no significant between-group differences were observed in VAS or Oswestry Disability Index scores at 3 months.
CONCLUSION: Fluoroscopy-guided ESPB combined with LIA improved short-term postoperative analgesia after open PLIF. The combined regimen reduced postoperative opioid requirements and analgesia pump activations and prolonged the time to first PCIA bolus without increasing adverse events. Its benefit is better interpreted as an incremental, layered multimodal analgesic effect rather than a consistently synergistic effect across outcomes. No between-group differences in pain or functional outcomes were observed at 3 months.

articles.title: Endoscopic Versus Microscopic Decompression for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: A Structured Debate and International Practice Patterns.
articles.abstract: Endoscopic spine surgery has advanced from a percutaneous niche technique to a mainstream platform for lumbar decompression. This original study examines the relationship between endoscopic and microscopic platforms across 7 contested domains, using an embedded cross-sectional single-round international survey to map patterns of expert agreement and divergence. Seven contested domains-learning curve, technical feasibility, patient selection, clinical and radiological outcomes, complications, cost-effectiveness, and reoperation-were each argued by a Pro-Microscopic and a Pro-Endoscopic advocate before reconciliation, then complemented by a structured single-round international survey of 105 spine surgeons from 5 world regions. The survey was designed to describe practice patterns and map the distribution of expert opinion, not to determine whether endoscopy can replace microscopy. Statements meeting a prespecified conjunctive threshold of at least 70% agreement overall and within each of 3 practice-profile strata were classified as meeting the consensus standard, with the 70% level adopted on the precedent of the CORE (Convergence of Opinion on Recommendations and Evidence) methodology. Seven statements met this standard: reduced approach-related trauma, lower surgical site infection, primacy of surgeon experience over platform, the training burden of endoscopy, standardized outcome reporting, comparable 1- to 2-year outcomes in selected stenosis, and health-system dependence of cost-effectiveness. Endoscopy-favoring distributions were modal in all 7 domains, reaching a majority for complications, outcomes, and patient selection; learning curve and cost-effectiveness remained areas of mixed opinion, and reoperation showed the widest divergence of views. Although 75.2% judged that endoscopy is ready to replace the microscope as the default platform, this fell to 38.5% (95% confidence interval, 13.9%-68.4%) among microscopically oriented surgeons and failed stratification. Endoscopy has demonstrated comparable outcomes for selected pathology and perioperative advantages in specific domains, but not durable long-term superiority. The evidence supports coexistence rather than replacement, with platform selection matched to pathology, patient phenotype, endoscopic platform, and surgeon expertise. The survey illustrates where expert practice patterns align with, diverge from, or run ahead of published comparative evidence.

articles.title: Endoscopic Lumbar Interbody Fusion Versus Minimally Invasive Transforaminal Lumbar Interbody Fusion: A Structured Debate and International Practice Patterns.
articles.abstract: Lumbar fusion has evolved from open transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) to minimally invasive TLIF (MIS-TLIF), the current minimally invasive benchmark. Endoscopic techniques, proven in discectomy and decompression, have been extended to fusion (uniportal endoscopic TLIF and biportal endoscopic TLIF), offering an alternative to MIS-TLIF. This structured debate-style review critically compares both techniques across 7 domains to clarify their respective roles in lumbar degenerative disease. It combined independent advocacy drafts with an international survey of 106 respondents across 35 countries, capturing procedural preferences and case-based reasoning. Using a prespecified 70% agreement threshold, domains were classified as domains with ≥70% panel agreement, whereas domains falling below this threshold were categorized as domains below the prespecified agreement threshold. This represents structured international survey agreement, not a formal Delphi process. Endoscopic fusion offers advantages in decreased blood loss, soft-tissue preservation, early postoperative back pain, and early recovery, with comparable mid-term clinical outcomes (long-term insufficiently established) to MIS-TLIF, which remains more reproducible and familiar. Complication rates are similar but technique-sensitive for endoscopic fusion. Panel responses favored endoscopic approaches for morbidity-related domains (soft-tissue preservation 89.6%, visualization 81.1%, recovery 74.5%), while fusion stability, short- to mid-term clinical outcomes, complications, and revision remained context-dependent without clear agreement. Endoscopic fusion is a credible option for selected single-level lumbar degenerative disease, offering perioperative advantages with comparable mid-term outcomes to MIS-TLIF; core endpoints, including fusion rate and revision rate, did not reach 70% panel agreement, even among endoscopy-favorable panelists. MIS-TLIF retains reproducibility advantages. The debate has shifted from feasibility to implementation, training standardization, cost-effectiveness, and long-term durability.

articles.title: Use of von Willebrand Factor in VA-ECMO‒Associated Acquired von Willebrand Syndrome: A Nationwide Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is a life-saving therapy for refractory cardiocirculatory failure but carries a high bleeding risk, partly due to acquired von Willebrand syndrome (aVWS). With limited evidence-based treatments, von Willebrand factor (VWF) is often used off-label. This study examines nationwide use of VWF in VA-ECMO patients with aVWS in Germany and compares bleeding, thromboembolic events, and survival between treated and untreated patients.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study based on reimbursement data (2019-2023).
SETTING: Multi-institutional analysis of adult VA-ECMO cases treated in German hospitals.
PARTICIPANTS: 530 adult patients supported with VA-ECMO and diagnosed with aVWS.
INTERVENTIONS: Administration of any dose of VWF during VA-ECMO support versus no VWF treatment.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Of 530 patients, 389 (73%) received VWF across 35 of 71 centers contributing patients. Intracranial hemorrhage occurred less frequently in the VWF group (8% v 15%, p = 0.0238). However, haemothorax (37% v 20%, p = 0.0028) was more common with VWF. Thromboembolic events did not differ between groups. ICU LOS was shorter in VWF-treated patients (14 v 18 days, p = 0.0168). The 90-day survival was numerically higher in the VWF group but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.188).
CONCLUSION: In this cohort of VA-ECMO patients with aVWS, VWF was frequently used and associated with lower ICH rates and shorter intensive care unit length of stay, there was no evidence of increased thromboembolic events, but higher rates of other bleeding complications. Prospective randomized trials are warranted to clarify the impact of VWF on clinical outcomes.

articles.title: The ECMO-PoCS Score: Derivation and Internal Validation of an Implantation-Time Model for In-Hospital Mortality in Postcardiotomy Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To derive and internally validate a mortality score (ECMO-PoCS) for use at venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) implantation for postcardiotomy cardiogenic shock (PCS), hypothesizing that a few implantation-time variables would discriminate in-hospital mortality better than European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II (EuroSCORE II), Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II), or pre-ECMO lactate.
DESIGN: Retrospective, single-center cohort study.
SETTING: Tertiary cardiac surgical center.
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 149 consecutive adults receiving VA-ECMO for PCS (2007-2024), excluding 7 bridged directly to transplantation.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Hospital mortality was 65.8% and 1-year survival 33.4%. A 4-variable logistic model (age, pre-ECMO lactate, peripheral artery disease [PAD], and any preoperative right ventricular [RV] dysfunction) was fitted in 133 complete cases; PAD (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 4.58; p = 0.022) and RV dysfunction (adjusted OR = 3.16; p = 0.020) were independently associated with mortality. In 130 patients with all comparators, ECMO-PoCS (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.715) discriminated better than European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II (EuroSCORE II) (0.583; DeLong p = 0.043) and lactate alone (0.601; p = 0.030) but not significantly better than APACHE II (0.610; p = 0.13); adding these variables to APACHE II increased its AUC to 0.727 (likelihood ratio p = 0.002). Bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC was 0.687 and the shrinkage factor 0.82. A 0- to 5-point score defined low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups (mortality 23.1%, 63.6%, and 86.0%, respectively; trend p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: ECMO-PoCS, based on 4 variables available at implantation, discriminated in-hospital mortality better than EuroSCORE II and lactate alone and added information to APACHE II. Internally validated only, it is intended for risk description, research stratification, and benchmarking, not for decisions to initiate or withdraw support, pending external validation.

articles.title: Analysis of the Routine Use of Factor VIIa in the Neonatal Arterial Switch Operation.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Arterial switch operation (ASO) for the correction of d-transposition of the great arteries can be associated with significant postbypass bleeding. Recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) is used off-label to improve hemostasis, yet its effects on intraoperative and postoperative outcomes remain uncertain. The primary objective was to describe the frequency and severity of thrombotic complications among infants receiving rFVIIa at contemporary, lower doses; secondary objectives were to describe present-day dosing practice and to compare perioperative characteristics and postoperative outcomes between infants who did and did not receive rFVIIa.
DESIGN: Retrospective chart review.
SETTING: Quaternary Children's Hospital from July 1, 2018, to December 31, 2025.
PARTICIPANTS: Infants undergoing ASO for d-transposition of the great arteries, including intact ventricular septum, ventricular septal defect, and aortic arch repair.
INTERVENTIONS: Not applicable.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 56 patients undergoing ASO were included in the study. Forty-four patients in the cohort were male (78%). Of these, 34 (61%) received rFVIIa during their procedure, while 22 (39%) did not receive rFVIIa. The median first dose of rFVIIa was 50 (interquartile range [IQR]: 49.7-50.1) mcg/kg; 17 (50%) patients received a second dose (median: 50.0 [IQR: 48.8-50.0] mcg/kg), and 8 (23%) patients received a third dose (median: 48.4 [IQR: 27.9-50.0] mcg/kg), corresponding to a mean of 1.7 doses per treated patient. Administration varied from 6% to 84% of cases across the 3 operating surgeons (p < 0.0001). Postoperative outcomes were comparable, including chest tube output (2 v 2 mL, p = 0.511), length of stay (13 v 13 days, p = 0.731), and time to extubation (4 v 3 days, p = 0.089). Thrombotic complications occurred in 12% of patients, with no difference between groups (9% v 14%, p = 0.670). Patients receiving rFVIIa had shorter postoperative prothrombin time and lower international normalized ratio (both p < 0.001), with no difference in partial thromboplastin time.
CONCLUSIONS: This study reveals that patients receiving higher amounts of post-bypass transfusion were more likely to recieve rFVIIa, and that receipt of rFVIIa at a median dose of 50.9 mcg/kg, was not associated with additional thrombosis risk. Given the observational design and limited number of thrombotic events, these findings provide preliminary descriptive data on safety and warrant further study in larger cohorts.

articles.title: Predictors of postoperative infections in a tertiary neurosurgical center.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative infections are common neurosurgical complications with considerable morbidity. We assessed the incidence, type and outcomes of postoperative infections in a pragmatic cohort of non-ICU neurosurgical patients.
METHOD: Demographics, medical history, operative details, perioperative interventions and hospitalization metrics were prospectively collected. Patients requiring intensive care unit hospitalization were excluded.
RESULTS: 137 postoperative infection events were recorded in 126 patients. Of 137 infections, pneumonia accounted for 70.1%, urinary tract infection for 10.2%, central-line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) for 3.6%, bacteremia of undetermined source for 5.1%, surgical site infection (SSI) for 9.5% and meningitis for 1.5%. The hospitalization was extended due to postoperative infection in 10.5% of operations, while 0.8% of the patients died. Independent factors associated with postoperative infection after multivariable analysis were age (adjusted OR 1.017, 95% CI 1.002-1.033), immobilization > 24 h (aOR 2.91, 95% CI 1.62-5.24), indwelling foley catheter > 48 h (aOR 4, 95% CI 2.01-7.99), central venous catheter (CVC) > 48 h (aOR 3.99, 95% CI 1.64-9.74), foreign material insertion (aOR 5.15, 95% CI 2.61-10.15) and spinal compared to cranial surgery (aOR 4.90, 95% CI 2.63-9.15).
CONCLUSION: Independent factors associated with postoperative infection included older age, immobilization beyond 24 h, retention of urinary and central venous catheters beyond 48 h and foreign-material insertion; prolonged operative time was associated specifically with postoperative pneumonia. Aggressive preoperative and postoperative measures utilizing ERAS-like protocols may reduce infection burden and optimize outcomes. These findings validate infection risk factors specifically within the ward-level neurosurgical population and should not be extrapolated to patients requiring ICU management.

articles.title: Post-mastectomy pain syndrome in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Breast cancer, one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide, poses a significant health burden, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Despite advances in treatment, breast cancer survivors in LMICs face unique challenges, including post-mastectomy pain syndrome (PMPS).
AIM: This systematic review synthesises evidence on PMPS prevalence, characteristics, and management in LMICs.
METHOD: We conducted a systematic review in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. We searched PubMed, CENTRAL, Embase, Web of Science, Global Index Medicus, and supplementary grey-literature sources for studies of PMPS conducted in LMICs. Eligible studies were screened in duplicate, data were extracted using a piloted form, and methodological quality was assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute critical checklists and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool for mixed-methods studies. Owing to substantial heterogeneity in study design, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Findings revealed significant variability in its prevalence. Pain was mostly mild, located in the axilla, chest wall, and ipsilateral arm, neuropathic in nature, and exacerbated by physical exertion. Key risk factors include younger age, obesity, extensive surgical procedures, and adjuvant therapies. Treatment strategies encompass simple analgesics, nerve blocks, sympathetic denervation, and advanced techniques, highlighting a multifaceted approach to managing PMPS effectively.
CONCLUSION: Post-mastectomy pain syndrome remains a complex challenge, requiring ongoing research to refine diagnostics, understand underlying mechanisms, and develop personalised treatments to improve patient outcomes.Contribution: This review synthesises evidence on the prevalence, characteristics, risk factors, and treatment options for PMPS, providing knowledge to guide evidence-based clinical interventions and improve patient outcomes.
articles.journal: Afr J Prim Health Care Fam Med

articles.title: Epidural maintenance strategies and second-stage feedback interventions during labour analgesia: a pairwise meta-analysis and narrative synthesis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Epidural maintenance strategies and second-stage feedback interventions address different aspects of labour care. We evaluated their effects on instrumental vaginal delivery, local anaesthetic consumption, labour and delivery outcomes, maternal safety, and neonatal outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception to September 7, 2026. The protocol-concordant primary comparison was programmed or automated intermittent epidural versus continuous epidural infusion after conventional epidural initiation. Combined spinal-epidural, dural-puncture epidural, and provider-administered manual-bolus regimens were examined in sensitivity analyses. Real-time visual feedback was analysed separately from prerecorded instruction. Random-effects meta-analyses used restricted maximum-likelihood estimation with modified Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman inference.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight independent randomized trials, reported in 29 publications and involving 6250 women in eligible comparisons, were included. Nine conventional-epidural trials involving 4041 women contributed to the registered primary analysis. Intermittent bolus did not clearly reduce instrumental vaginal delivery (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.61-1.04; I2 500%; conditional prediction interval 0.61-1.04). Seven trials involving 3682 women showed lower cumulative local-anaesthetic mass (RoM 0.80, 95% CI 0.74-0.86; I2 %;73.0%; conditional prediction interval 0.68-0.93). Caesarean delivery was less frequent in the pooled analysis (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.54-0.98), whereas second-stage duration was not clearly different (MD - 1.05 min, 95% CI - 2.44 to 0.34). The need for a supplemental analgesic intervention favoured intermittent bolus on average (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19-0.82), but heterogeneity was substantial (I2 .483.0%) and the conditional prediction interval crossed the null (0.06-2.63). Evidence for other maternal and neonatal safety outcomes was limited. Real-time visual feedback did not clearly reduce instrumental vaginal delivery (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.29-2.21).
CONCLUSIONS: Programmed or automated intermittent epidural did not clearly reduce instrumental vaginal delivery but was associated with lower cumulative local-anaesthetic mass. Apparent reductions in supplemental analgesic intervention and caesarean delivery require cautious interpretation because of heterogeneity, imprecision, and overall low or very-low certainty. Evidence for second-stage feedback interventions remains preliminary.

articles.title: Comparison of QLB block and TAP block in morbid obese patients: a randomized controlled study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Quadratus lumborum block (QLB) and Transverses abdominis plane block (TAP) are a fascial plane block. The study aimed to compare the efficacy of the TAP block and QLB-2 in terms of postoperative pain assessed by the VAS and morphine consumption following laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy.
METHODS: This study was conducted as a randomized controlled trial involving patients who underwent laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy in the operating room. Patients were randomly assigned to one of three groups: groups 1 (TAP block), 2 (QLB-2 block), and 3 (control). Analgesic consumption was assessed by evaluating morphine use at the postoperative 1st, 6th, 12th, and 24th hours, as well as the total morphine consumption and VAS scores. Quality of life was preoperatively evaluated, at 48 h, and 1 week using the WHOQOL-BREF scale.
RESULTS: One hundred twenty-six patients (female:103 and male:23) were included in the final analysis (44, 42, and 40) in the control, TAP and QLB-2 block groups, respectively. The block duration in the QLB-2 group was significantly longer than that in the TAP block group (p = 0.001). Total morphine consumption differed between the groups (p = 0.001). Morphine consumption in the TAP block group was lower than that in the control (p = 0.001) and QLB-2 (p = 0.001) groups. The total morphine consumption in the QLB-2 group was also significantly lower than that in the control group (p = 0.035) - 0.001) and QLB-2 (p = 0.019) groups. WHOQOL scores (48 h and 1 week postoperatively) were no statistical differences in any subgroup or timeline (p > 0.05). There was a statistically significant difference in postoperative VAS scores (1st, 6th, 12th and 24th hours) among the study groups (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: TAP and QLB-2 blocks were associated with reduced postoperative pain scores and opioid requirements in morbidly obese patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy compared to no regional block. TAP block consumed less morphine overall, had a shorter block performance time, and mobilized earlier than QLB-2 block. There were no changes in quality of life outcomes and it was no statistically significant difference in the preoperative VAS scores between the study groups.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Registration No: NCT05820620). Date of registration: 27/03/2023.

articles.title: The efficacy of suprascapular nerve radiofrequency and intra-articular steroıd injectıon in frozen shoulder treatment: randomızed controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aims to address the impacts of intra-articular steroid injection (IASI) alone versus the combination of suprascapular nerve (SSN) pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) and IASI on pain relief and improvement in shoulder range of motion (ROM) in patients with adhesive capsulitis (AC) (frozen shoulder).
METHODS: This study included 80 patients with AC. Participants were randomly assigned to two groups. A combination of suprascapular nerve pulsed radiofrequency and IASI were administered to the first group and IASI to the second. Both groups underwent a standardized physical therapy program for three weeks following the intervention. Outcome measures included active and passive ROM (AROM and PROM), Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain, and the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI), assessed at baseline and 4th week, and 12th week post-treatment.
RESULTS: 80 patients (40 patients in each group) completed this study. Both interventions were found to be effective in both groups (p < 0.05). However, intergroup comparisons revealed that patients in the SNNR group experienced significantly better improvements in pain levels (as measured by VAS and SPADI scores) and ROM (p < 0.05). No post-procedural complications were observed in either group.
CONCLUSIONS: This study revealed that the administration of PRF lesioning of the SSN utilizing a UG method combined with intra-articular steroid injection yielded better and faster pain relief, reduced disability, and better AROM and PROM in comparison to intra-articular injection alone in AC patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was retrospective registered with the U.S. Clinical Trial Registry (U.S. Clinical Trial Registry No NCT06778577, date 20241125).

articles.title: Comparison of ultrasound-guided modified thoracoabdominal nerve block through perichondrial approach (M-TAPA) and lateral transversus abdominis plane block on postoperative pain and quality of recovery after laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair: a prospective observational comparative study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The modified thoracoabdominal nerve block through perichondrial approach (M-TAPA) and the lateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block are both used within multimodal analgesia after abdominal surgery, but comparative data in laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair are limited, particularly with regard to patient-reported recovery. We compared the effects of these two blocks on postoperative pain and quality of recovery.
METHODS: This prospective observational comparative study included 63 adults (American Society of Anesthesiologists [ASA] I-III) undergoing elective unilateral laparoscopic total extraperitoneal inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia. At the end of surgery, patients were allocated to receive either an M-TAPA block (n = 32) or a lateral TAP block (n = 31) within a multimodal analgesia regimen; both blocks are used routinely for postoperative analgesia in our department, and the block given to each patient was chosen by the attending anesthesiologist as part of routine clinical care, without a predefined selection rule and independently of patient characteristics; no randomization was performed. Both blocks were performed bilaterally with 20 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine per side under ultrasound guidance. The co-primary outcomes were the resting Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) pain score at 24 h - the time point on which the sample size calculation was based - and quality of recovery assessed with the Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at baseline, 24 h, and postoperative day 15.
