Public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related care: a cross-sectional survey in Japan.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: We aimed to assess the public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related hospital care tasks in Japan and examine associated factors.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional, nationwide, quota-based web survey of adults in Japan in July 2025. Of the 1,944 respondents who initiated the survey, 1,844 completed (94.9%) it, and 1,000 responses were analyzed after quota completion (ages 20-69 yr). The outcomes were attribution (yes/no) of four anesthesia-related hospital care tasks to anesthesiologists: intraoperative anesthesia, postoperative pain management, procedural sedation/analgesia (PSA), and labour neuraxial analgesia (LNA). For each outcome, we fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, the Health Interest Scale (HIS), Communicative and Critical Health Literacy (CCHL), board-certified anesthesiologist density, information sources, and task-matched experience, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) control.
RESULTS: Attribution was highest for intraoperative anesthesia (84.7%), followed by LNA (65.2%), PSA (37.4%), and postoperative pain management (13.5%). After FDR control, university education or higher was associated with greater attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.30 to 3.32), PSA (aOR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.15 to 2.30), and LNA (aOR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.30 to 2.55). Task-matched prior experience attributed to anesthesiologists was associated with higher attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (aOR, 3.75; 95% CI, 1.76 to 8.80) and PSA (aOR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.34 to 4.43). Fictional media was the only information-source factor that remained significant after FDR control (intraoperative anesthesia: aOR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.79 to 4.25; PSA: aOR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.42 to 2.56). No factor met the FDR threshold for postoperative pain management. HIS, CCHL, and anesthesiologist density showed no consistent adjusted associations.
CONCLUSIONS: Public attribution of anesthesiologists' roles in Japan varied by task. Educational attainment, task-matched experience, and information sources were more consistently associated with attribution than general health traits or workforce context, supporting the value of role-explicit, task-specific communication strategies.

articles.title: Statewide Trends in Morbidity and Mortality in Octogenarians Undergoing Isolated Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: We sought to determine whether advanced age modifies the association between established preoperative risk factors and 30-day outcomes following isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), compare temporal trends between octogenarians and younger patients, and characterize differences in perioperative outcomes between the two groups.
METHODS: Using the Michigan Society of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeons Quality Collaborative (The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database), we identified 105,445 patients undergoing isolated CABG from 2006-2024. Outcomes and case volumes were assessed across four eras. Operative mortality was evaluated using mixed-effects logistic regression with hospital as a random effect. Secondary analyses used multiple imputation with hospital-clustered multivariable logistic regression to evaluate age-related effect modification for short-term mortality and morbidity.
RESULTS: Octogenarians comprised 8.1% of cases (8,563/105,445). Operative mortality was higher in octogenarians (4.8%; n=413) than patients <80 (1.8%; n=1,710). Operative mortality rates were stable over the study period for both patient groups. In multiple-imputation models, octogenarian status was independently associated with higher odds of operative mortality, stroke, reoperation for bleeding, and renal failure. Age-dependent effect modification was observed for select outcomes. In octogenarians, hypertension was more strongly associated with postoperative atrial fibrillation, diabetes with renal failure, and cerebrovascular disease with discharge to extended care.
CONCLUSIONS: In octogenarians, CABG remains associated with higher morbidity and mortality than in younger patients, with minimal changes in 30-day outcomes over the last 20 years. Most traditional risk factors demonstrated similar relative associations across age groups, with age-specific effects in select postoperative domains.

articles.title: Perioperative Management of Children, Adolescents and Young Adults Undergoing Surgical Treatment for Oncologic Thoracic Disease: Retrospective Single-Center Analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: No guidelines drive the perioperative management of children, adolescents, and young adults (CAYA) undergoing oncologic thoracic surgery. We analyzed our institutional procedures and perioperative results aiming to help develop standardized guidelines.
PROCEDURE: Records of CAYA patients operated on for a thoracic tumor (October 2021 to February 2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Standardized perioperative management included minimally invasive technique when feasible, early discharge to the ward, avoidance of sedation (drainage removal), systematic physiotherapy, early mobilization, and resumption of oral intake. Outcomes refer to the total number of surgeries.
RESULTS: Forty-seven CAYA (median age 15, interquartile range [IQR]: 12-18) underwent 54 operations removing localized tumor in 20 (37%), metastases in 33 (61.1%), and one (1.9%) local recurrence. In 36 cases (66.7%), surgery followed chemotherapy after 29.5 days (median; IQR: 22-47.3); in seven (13%), it was performed on a previously irradiated site. Eighteen procedures (33.3%) required resection of more than one organ; 17 (31.5%) were minimally invasive. In 10 (18.5%) cases, the first postoperative night was spent in the intensive care unit. Oral intake was resumed within postoperative day (POD) 1 in 46 (85.2%). Despite physical limitations to ambulation in 12 (22.2%) cases, in 49 (90.7%) the patient was mobilized and in 38 (70.4%) walked within POD1. Continuous intravenous opioid infusion was necessary in 23 (42.6%) cases, and sedation for drainage removal in one. There were 19 complications (35.2%), 89.5% of which were Grade I-II. Patients were discharged on POD5 (median, IQR: 4-8).
CONCLUSIONS: Standardized perioperative management in CAYA is possible and can lead to early mobilization and a low complication rate, despite complex complementary treatments (chemotherapy/radiotherapy) and limited access to intensive care resources.

articles.title: Endoscopic Hematoma Evacuation and Controlled Inner Membranectomy Using a Modified Single Burr-Hole Technique Under Local Anesthesia for Septated Chronic Subdural Hematomas in Elderly Patients: A Multicenter Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Septated chronic subdural hematoma (sCSDH) in elderly patients may contain organized components that limit conventional burr-hole drainage. This study evaluates the technical feasibility, perioperative course, and early clinical and radiological outcomes of controlled partial inner membranecotomy using modified single-port endoscopic drainage under local anesthesia in selected elderly patients with sCSDH.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed patients aged 65 and older who underwent endoscopic drainage of MRI-confirmed sCSDH under local anesthesia at two neurosurgical centers between March 2022 and July 2025. Demographic characteristics, anesthesia records, complications, radiological findings, and early clinical outcomes were evaluated.
RESULTS: Eleven of 29 patients (38%) received antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. Mean hematoma thickness was 21 ± 6 mm, preoperative midline shift was 10 ± 4 mm, and operative time was 47 ± 10 minutes. At postoperative one month, 26 patients (90%) had an mRS score of 0-1, compared with 9 (31%) preoperatively. Recurrence occurred in 3 patients (10%); 1 (3%) required reoperation, while 2 (7%) were treated conservatively. Postoperative seizures occurred in 2 patients (7%). No patient required conversion to general anesthesia, and no perioperative deaths, surgical site infections, or permanent neurological deficits were observed.
CONCLUSION: Endoscopic hematoma evacuation and controlled partial membranecotomy via a single burr hole under local anesthesia and sedation were technically feasible in selected patients and associated with acceptable short-term outcomes. Without a control group, superiority over other surgical approaches or an independent benefit of inner membranotomy cannot be demonstrated.

articles.title: Time From Operation to Discharge Correlates With Opioid Prescription Patterns After Appendectomy.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Prior studies have analyzed pediatric opioid prescription patterns following appendectomy, but data in adults remain limited. This study aims to identify factors that are associated with opioid prescription patterns following emergent appendectomy.
METHODS: A retrospective review of the 2024 American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database was performed for adult patients undergoing emergent appendectomy discharged with an opioid prescription, stratified by surgical approach. Patient factors, perioperative outcomes, and prescription characteristics were evaluated. Logistic regressions were performed to determine the odds of opioid prescription and renewal.
RESULTS: Patients undergoing open appendectomy received fewer opioids (33.9%) than those undergoing laparoscopic (61.7%) and robotic (52.1%) surgery. Postoperative hospital stay was longer after open appendectomy (5.8 d) than laparoscopic (1.3 d) and robotic (1.2 d) approaches. Time from operation to discharge decreased the odds of being prescribed opioids on discharge (odds ratio 0.78). Oxycodone was most prescribed (61.7%), followed by hydromorphone (15.4%) and tramadol (15.0%). The median quantity of pills prescribed was 10, with a median duration of 2 d. A total of 0.62% of patients had a prescription refilled. No patient factors were associated with opioid renewal.
CONCLUSIONS: We hypothesize that the lower opioid prescriptions after open appendectomy compared to minimally invasive approaches may be attributed to longer postoperative hospital stay, allowing for a narcotic weaning period. Opioid prescriptions following emergent appendectomy in adults are limited in duration and quantity, with low refill rates-0.62% nationally. Although there is adherence to opioid stewardship guidelines, postoperative opioid prescribing patterns vary greatly.

articles.title: Parental outcomes in congenital lung malformations: a transdisciplinary family-centered model.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The study aimed to evaluate a family-centered care model, the "Respiriamo, insieme" project, that supports families from prenatal diagnosis through postoperative follow-up.
METHODS: We conducted a posttest-only study comparing families of children with CLM. The intervention group received an integrated pathway combining multidisciplinary counseling, prenatal and postnatal psychological support, music therapy, minimally invasive surgery, locoregional anesthesia, and fast-track perioperative management. The standard care group included families managed at other centers where the integrated pathway was not implemented. One month after surgery, mothers and fathers separately completed validated questionnaires assessing anxiety, post-traumatic stress, and perceived quality of care.
RESULTS: Forty-one families participated (26 in the intervention group, 15 in the standard care group). Mothers in the intervention group reported significantly lower anxiety and post-traumatic stress and higher perceived quality of care; fathers showed the same direction with weaker evidence. All quality-of-care domains were significantly higher among intervention mothers; among fathers, only communication and general satisfaction differed significantly. Exploratory maternal analyses suggested lower distress with both prenatal and postnatal support.
CONCLUSION: A structured, family-centered care model reduced parental distress and improved perceived quality of care in CLM. Integrating psychosocial support into perioperative management may strengthen parental resilience and should be standard care.

articles.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort.
METHODS: In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia.
PRIMARY OUTCOMES: Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation.
SECONDARY OUTCOMES: remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events.
RESULTS: All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly.
CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

articles.title: Casting Without Reduction Versus Reduction With or Without Fixation for Mildly Displaced Pediatric Distal Radius Metaphyseal Fractures: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether immobilization without reduction is noninferior to closed reduction under general anesthesia, with or without fixation, with respect to upper-extremity function at 6 months in children with mildly displaced distal radius metaphyseal fractures.
METHODS: We conducted a randomized, open-label, noninferiority trial at a tertiary pediatric orthopaedic hospital. Children aged 5 to 10 years with unilateral mildly displaced distal radius metaphyseal fractures were assigned to immobilization without reduction or closed reduction under general anesthesia, with or without fixation. The primary outcome was the PROMIS Pediatric Upper Extremity T-score at 6 months. The prespecified noninferiority margin was -5 points for the between-group difference.
RESULTS: Sixty children were randomized: 29 to immobilization without reduction and 31 to reduction under general anesthesia. Primary outcome data were available for 59 children. The mean PROMIS scores were 45.59 (SD=9.62) in the immobilization-without-reduction group and 45.62 (SD=8.24) in the reduction-under-anesthesia group. The mean between-group difference was -0.03 points (95% CI: -4.71 to 4.65), meeting the prespecified criterion for noninferiority. No serious adverse events occurred in the immobilization-without-reduction group; 2 anesthetic-related complications occurred in the reduction-under-anesthesia group.
CONCLUSIONS: In children with mildly displaced distal radius metaphyseal fractures, immobilization without reduction was noninferior to reduction under general anesthesia with respect to upper-extremity function at 6 months. These findings suggest that routine reduction under anesthesia may not be necessary in children aged 5 to 10 years with isolated distal radius metaphyseal fractures with shortening ≤10 mm and/or angulation of 10 to 20 degrees.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I-randomized controlled trial.

articles.title: Prevalence and intensity of chronic postsurgical pain after cranial surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized studies.
Primary intraosseous anesthesia versus inferior alveolar nerve block for mandibular teeth with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Achieving profound pulpal anesthesia in mandibular teeth with symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (SIP) is challenging, and inferior alveolar nerve block (IANB) has a substantial failure rate in this setting. Primary intraosseous (IO) anesthesia delivers local anesthetic directly into cancellous bone and may provide a more targeted alternative. The objective was to compare the risk of anesthetic failure with primary IO anesthesia versus conventional IANB in patients with SIP undergoing endodontic treatment.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251180658). PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched from inception to July 2026 for randomized clinical trials comparing primary IO anesthesia with IANB in human participants with SIP. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB 2). Anesthetic failure was pooled as a risk ratio (RR) using a Mantel-Haenszel random-effect model.
RESULTS: Five randomized controlled trials involving 265 participants were included (132 IO; 133 IANB). There were 27 anesthetic failures with primary IO anesthesia and 65 with IANB. Five randomized controlled trials involving 265 participants were included (132 IO; 133 IANB). Anesthetic failure occurred in 27 participants receiving primary IO anesthesia and 65 receiving IANB. The pooled analysis demonstrated a significantly lower risk of anesthetic failure with primary IO anesthesia compared with IANB (risk ratio [RR] = 0.46; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.32-0.64;P< .001), corresponding to an approximately 54% relative reduction in the risk of anesthetic failure. Statistical heterogeneity was low (χ2= 2.82, df = 4, P = 0.59; I2= 0%). In subgroup analyses, the pooled RR was 0.42 (95% CI, 0.16-1.07; P = 0.07) for lidocaine and 0.30 (95% CI, 0.16-0.58; P = 0.0003) for articaine. No statistically significant subgroup interaction was identified.
CONCLUSIONS: Primary IO anesthesia was associated with a substantially lower risk of anesthetic failure than conventional IANB across five randomized trials. However, the small evidence base, methodological concerns, and clinical variation in anesthetic agents and delivery systems limit confidence in the magnitude of the observed effect.

articles.title: Perioperative Single-Shot Regional Blocks and Associated Rebound Pain-Related Unscheduled Utilization of Health Care After Distal Radius Surgery.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Perioperative single-shot regional blocks are commonly used for pain control in outpatient distal radius fixation surgery. While regional blocks provide initial postoperative pain control, patients often experience significant rebound pain as the block effect dissipates, which can lead to utilization of unscheduled health care (emergency department visits, phone calls, and messages sent via the electronic health record [EHR] to providers). We hypothesized that patients who received perioperative blocks are more likely to use unscheduled health care versus those who did not.
METHODS: A total of 619 patients underwent distal radius fracture fixation at a tertiary care academic center from 2013 to 2022. After excluding minors, inpatient and revision procedures, patients with insufficient records, and fixation of an impending pathologic fracture, 417 patients were included. Age, gender, mechanism, time to surgery, use of intraoperative local anesthetic, and whether a regional block was performed were collected. Returns to the emergency department, pain-related phone calls, and messages sent via the EHR system within 3 days of surgery were also collected.
RESULTS: The adjusted relative risk of using unscheduled health care for pain was 4.0 (95% CI, 1.3-12.1; P = .01) on postoperative day 1 for patients who received perioperative blocks compared with those who did not. Similarly, the adjusted relative risk within 2 days of surgery was 3.9 (95% CI, 1.4-10.5; P = .007) and within 3 days was 3.2 (95% CI, 1.4-7.5; P = .008).
CONCLUSIONS: Patients who receive perioperative regional blocks after distal radius fixation are more likely to use unscheduled health care within the first 3 days of surgery, compared with patients who did not receive blocks.

articles.title: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Intravenous Tramadol and Dexmedetomidine for the Prevention of Perioperative Shivering During Transurethral Resection of Prostate Under Spinal Anesthesia.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Perioperative shivering is a common complication during spinal anesthesia, particularly in patients undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), due to impaired thermoregulation and heat loss from irrigation fluids. "It can increase metabolic demand and cause patient discomfort, making its prevention clinically important.
AIM AND OBJECTIVES: The aim and objectives of this study were to compare the efficacy of intravenous tramadol and dexmedetomidine in preventing perioperative shivering in TURP under spinal anesthesia, and to assess associated temperature changes, sedation, need for additional interventions, and adverse events.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective, randomized, double-blind study included 100 male patients (ASA I-II, 50-80 years) undergoing TURP under spinal anesthesia. Patients were divided into two groups of 50 each. Group T received intravenous tramadol 1 mg/kg, whereas Group D received intravenous dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg, administered before spinal anesthesia. Core and surface temperatures, shivering incidence, sedation scores, and adverse events were recorded up to 90 min.
RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Group T showed significantly higher core and surface temperatures at several time points. Shivering incidence was significantly lower in Group T at 15 and 30 min." Sedation was higher in Group D. Additional interventions were required less frequently in Group T (6% vs. 26%). Bradycardia and hypotension were significantly higher in Group D.
CONCLUSION: Intravenous tramadol is more effective and safer than dexmedetomidine for preventing perioperative shivering in TURP under spinal anesthesia.

articles.title: Comparative Efficacy of Isolated Hydrodilatation and Hydrodilatation with Adjuvant Interventions for Frozen Shoulder: A Network Meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to compare hydrodilatation (HD)-based interventions for pain relief and range of motion (ROM) improvement in frozen shoulder.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched through September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Outcomes included visual analogue scale (VAS) pain scores and ROM. Effect sizes were standardized mean differences (SMDs) or mean differences (MDs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Interventions were ranked by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA).
RESULTS: Twenty RCTs (n=1,410) were included. Anterior rotator interval corticosteroid hydrodilatation (ARICHD) reduced pain (SMD=-1.30, 95% CrI -1.80 to -0.78; SUCRA=97.2%), whereas anterior shoulder joint hydrodilatation (ASJHD) increased pain (SMD=0.97, 95% CrI 0.30 to 1.60). For ROM, anterior intra-articular corticosteroid hydrodilatation combined with additional intra-articular corticosteroid injection (AIACHD + IACI) improved forward flexion (MD=23, 95% CrI 12 to 33; SUCRA=97.7%) and abduction (MD=33, 95% CrI 23 to 43; SUCRA=98.8%), while ARICHD improved external rotation (MD=21, 95% CrI 14 to 28; SUCRA=97.8%). Isolated suprascapular nerve block (SSNB) may reduce internal rotation (MD=-17, 95% CrI -34 to -0.13).
CONCLUSIONS: HD-based interventions differ in efficacy. ARICHD is associated with pain relief and improved external rotation, whereas AIACHD + IACI is associated with greater ROM improvement.

articles.title: Life course trajectories of musculoskeletal pain.
articles.abstract: A life course perspective can help identify critical periods and high-risk groups for musculoskeletal pain. However, how musculoskeletal pain develops over the adult life course and the extent to which this development varies among individuals remain largely unexplored. This Swedish population-representative survey followed a sample of 6328 individuals over 7 waves and 42 years, from ages 15 to 101 years, including about 25,000 observations. Reported musculoskeletal pain in the joints, back, or shoulders over the past year was categorized as follows: no pain (0), light pain in 1 to 3 sites (1), severe pain in one site (2), and severe pain in 2 to 3 sites (3). Age-related pain trajectories were identified through a sex-stratified latent class growth analysis. For both women and men, 2 distinct trajectories emerged. In the high-risk group, pain increased consistently throughout working age before declining postretirement. In the other group, pain levels were generally low, surpassing light pain only after retirement age. Although the trajectory patterns were similar for women and men, the high-risk group was twice as large among women (20%) as among men (9%). The general increase in pain towards the end of the life course likely reflects normal ageing processes, including disease onset and frailty, while the trajectory of the high-risk group may indicate the cumulative effect of risk factors associated with working life. Average trends across the entire sample mask the unique experience of this high-risk group and obscure the distinct effects of ageing on the development of musculoskeletal pain.

articles.title: Pain after endometriosis surgery: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Postoperative pain after endometriosis surgery has not been widely investigated, although these patients often present complex pain mechanisms. This study aimed to characterize postoperative pain and analgesic management in patients undergoing intra-abdominal endometriosis surgery at Skåne University Hospital Malmö (Sweden).
METHODS: Background, surgical, anesthetic and intra- and postoperative data were collected from records of patients who underwent intra-abdominal endometriosis surgery between 2021 and 2025. The primary endpoint was the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) for pain at admission to the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU). Secondary endpoints included NRS at PACU discharge, opioid use intraoperatively and in the PACU, and the need for pain therapy three weeks postoperatively. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used. Subgroup analyses compared pain in hysterectomy vs. other procedures and the analgesic effect of preemptive spinal analgesia in hysterectomy patients.
RESULTS: A total of 155 patient's records were examined. More than half of patients reported an NRS>3 at PACU admission, median value 5 (IQ1-IQ3: 0-7). Median opioid consumption in the PACU was 9 (0-21) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME), while median intraoperative administration was 57 (14-90) OME mg. Fifty percent of the patients still required pain therapy three weeks after surgery and 14 % sought emergency care for abdominal pain not related to surgical complication within a month from discharge. Persistent pain at three weeks was associated with preoperative pain and the need for in-hospital pain service, but not with PACU NRS or opioid use. Hysterectomy patients required more opioids and longer PACU time, and preemptive spinal analgesia was associated with less need for pain therapy at three weeks after hysterectomy.
CONCLUSIONS: Persistent postoperative pain is common after endometriosis surgery. Preoperative pain history and the involvement of a pain specialist during admission predicted persistent pain at three weeks after surgery better than PACU pain intensity alone.

articles.title: Autonomic Reactivity and EEG-defined Clusters Reveal Distinct Chronic Pain Profiles.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: This study examined whether integrating stress-related heart rate variability (HRV) with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) could characterize physiological subgroups in Chronic pain after spine surgery (CPSS).
METHODS: A total of 177 patients completed pain- and emotion-related questionnaires, a 3-minute resting-state EEG recording, and HRV assessments during baseline, mental arithmetic stress, and recovery. Participants were grouped by the direction of stress-related low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio change. Principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering were applied to 437 EEG features encompassing absolute power, cerebral asymmetry, and theta/beta ratio (TBR). After multivariate outlier detection, 168 participants underwent clustering. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA examined HRV-group and EEG-cluster effects on pain scores.
RESULTS: LF/HF -decreased group (n = 56) reported higher depressive symptom scores than the increase group (n = 121, P = 0.045), without significant pain differences. Among 437 EEG features, PC1 reflected beta activity (34.39% variance), PC2 frontal/frontotemporal asymmetry (14.52%), and PC3 TBR features (9.55%). Two EEG clusters (n = 88 and n = 80) showed no significant pain- or emotion-related differences. Factorial analysis revealed nonsignificant HRV (P = .056) and EEG main effects (P = .107), but a nominally significant interaction [P = .030, partial η² = .028 (HC3-robust P = .044)]. Within EEG Cluster 0, the LF/HF-decrease group reported higher pain scores than the LF/HF-increase group (70.9 vs. 42.3; Tukey-adjusted P = .019).
DISCUSSION: Integrating HRV-EEG profiles may help characterize CPSS heterogeneity. These exploratory findings, without study-wide multiplicity adjustment, require independent validation before clinical application.

articles.title: Under pressure: lessons from and beyond entrapment neuropathies.
articles.abstract: Entrapment neuropathies are the most prevalent focal neuropathic pain conditions globally and impose a substantial individual and socioeconomic burden. Traditionally conceptualised as purely mechanical compression syndromes, this view is increasingly challenged by converging evidence from human tissue analyses, advanced neuroimaging, and deep clinical phenotyping. Entrapment neuropathies are now recognised as biologically dynamic disorders shaped to different extents by microvascular compromise, demyelination, axonal degeneration, immune dysregulation, neuroinflammation, central nervous system adaptations, and psychosocial influences. Varying combinations and dominance of biopsychosocial processes give rise to marked clinical heterogeneity even within the same diagnostic label. This mechanistic diversity helps explain common diagnostic discordances, including extraterritorial symptom spread, normal electrodiagnostic findings despite clinical symptoms indicative of entrapment neuropathies, and imaging-clinical presentation mismatch. It also challenges one-size-fits-all treatment approaches, which have largely failed in entrapment neuropathies.Uniquely, entrapment neuropathies provide a natural human model of focal nerve injury in the context of neuropathic pain. Surgical decompression allows integration of tissue-level biology with precise clinical phenotypes and offers time-locked insights into recovery. Lessons derived from this model extend beyond entrapment neuropathies and can inform broader understanding of neuropathic and nerve-related musculoskeletal pain conditions. Here, we synthesise contemporary mechanistic insights, examine how biological heterogeneity translates into distinct clinical phenotypes, and discuss potential implications for mechanism-informed management.

articles.title: Toward precision pediatric pain care: integrating mechanistic science, real-world measurement, and patient partnership.
articles.abstract: Pediatric pain science is at an inflection point. Advances in neuroscience, behavioral science, digital health technologies, and patient engagement are rapidly expanding how chronic pain in youth can be understood, measured, and treated. Yet despite these advances, many children and adolescents continue to experience persistent pain-related disability and limited access to effective care, reflecting a gap between scientific discovery and real-world clinical practice. In this perspective, we propose the BRIDGE framework (Biobehavioral Research Integrated with Digital Monitoring and Guided Engagement) as a model for advancing pediatric pain research and care. Mechanistic science is increasingly identifying neural, behavioral, and contextual processes that contribute to pain persistence and recovery, creating opportunities to target modifiable mechanisms underlying pain-related disability. At the same time, digital health technologies including wearable sensors and ecological momentary assessment enable continuous measurement of activity, physiology, and patient-reported experiences in daily life, offering new insights into the dynamic nature of pain and the potential to develop digital biomarkers of risk, recovery, and treatment response. Central to this framework is meaningful partnership with youth and families, ensuring that innovations in measurement and intervention remain aligned with patient priorities and lived experience. Integrating these domains can support precision behavioral interventions, adaptive treatment strategies, and scalable models of care that expand access to evidence-based pediatric pain treatment.

articles.title: Molecular histochemical analysis of neuroplasticity-related gene expression in pain pathway.
articles.abstract: I am deeply honored to receive the 2026 John Bonica Prize for distinguished lifetime achievement in the basic science of pain. Reflecting on 40 years of research, this review paper will summarize my key findings to date. For the past four decades, my research has focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms of pain using animal models. By integrating morphological techniques with molecular biology, behavioral analysis, and electrophysiological recordings, I have sought to clarify how pain signals are modulated and sustained under chronic pain conditions. Since the early stages of my career, I have been particularly interested in the diverse molecular dynamics within pain pathways and their functional significance. This long-term research has been driven by the conviction that a detailed analysis of gene expression changes within pain pathways-particularly those associated with neuroplasticity-is essential to understanding the mechanisms underlying intractable pain. This review provides a comprehensive overview of our investigation into the molecular and cellular mechanisms of chronic pain, focusing on gene expression analyses related mainly to dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord plasticity, alongside historically significant contributions from the global pain research community. Finally, I will also discuss recent methodological advances and their applications, as well as the challenges and future directions facing basic pain research.

articles.title: Advancing equitable pain care worldwide requires progress in low- and middle-income settings: priorities for practice, research, and policy.
articles.abstract: Equitable, high-value pain care remains out of reach for many populations worldwide, particularly for people living in low- and middle-income countries and cultural minority groups in high-income settings. Despite carrying a disproportionate burden of chronic pain, these populations remain underrepresented in high-quality pain research, underserved by existing health systems, and constrained by social, political, environmental, and commercial determinants of health. The lack of locally generated evidence forces clinicians and policymakers to rely on externally produced research that may not translate to local cultural, linguistic, or health-system contexts. This invited viewpoint synthesizes key contributors to pain inequity-including limited prioritization of chronic pain in low- and middle-income countries, underdeveloped rehabilitation capacity, poor access to essential treatments, commercial exploitation, and misalignment between culturally shaped pain beliefs and Western-derived assessment and treatment models. I highlight opportunities to strengthen equity in clinical care through improved education of health professionals and the public, culturally and linguistically responsive assessment, and contextually adapted self-management and treatment strategies. Equitable research requires standardized collection of sociodemographic variables, deliberate inclusion of underrepresented groups, and global partnerships that avoid colonizing practices. I propose principles for fair and impactful North-South collaborations focused on co-creation of research agendas, shared leadership, sustainable capacity building, and transparent governance. Advancing equitable global pain care and research will require collective action from clinicians, researchers, institutions, policymakers, journals, funders, and communities. A coordinated shift toward culturally grounded, contextually adaptable, and ethically collaborative approaches is essential to meaningfully reduce global pain disparities and ensure all individuals benefit from scientific progress.

articles.title: The neuropathic chameleon: we are hot on the scent.
articles.abstract: A common chronic pain condition, neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease affecting the somatosensory or neural tissue and is characterized by a combination of negative (eg, numbness) and positive (eg, burning pain) sensory symptoms that significantly affect the quality of life. Common comorbidities such as depression and sleep disruption contribute to a substantial disease burden, which is further exacerbated by the apparent lack of effective therapeutic options. Current treatment options frequently achieve only partial, insufficient pain relief or may be completely ineffective in a considerable number of patients. The development of new drugs has thus far achieved moderate success, with many clinical trials failing to meet their primary endpoints; thus, a substantial unmet clinical need persists. One reason for this therapeutic deadlock is the considerable heterogeneity of neuropathic pain, driven by diverse pathophysiological mechanisms that vary between patients regardless of the underlying disease etiology. Accordingly, reclassification efforts follow a mechanism-based approach that reflects pathophysiological pain generators rather than disease etiology. Although diagnosis remains anchored in lesion- or disease-based criteria and structured clinical assessment, treatment development increasingly benefits from mechanism-informed phenotyping. A priori stratification based on individual mechanisms may help identify treatment responders, but implementation requires surrogate markers, as no biomarkers for pain mechanisms currently exist. In this article, we discuss candidate predictive markers and surrogate markers, focusing on sensory symptoms and signs assessed through patient-reported outcome measures and sensory testing, and their integration into future clinical trials.

articles.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
articles.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

articles.title: Exercise therapy for chronic pain: an updated perspective on mesocorticolimbic system function.
articles.abstract: Patients with chronic pain often experience behavioral issues linked to pain, depression, and other emotional disorders. These problems stem from dysfunction in the mesocorticolimbic system, and exercise offers a safe, accessible, and effective alternative. It not only reduces pain but also activates multiple neural pathways, helping restore normal function. First, in the periphery, exercise promotes the release of myokines, which are essential for the body-brain connection and influence neural activity. IGF-1, released from muscles during exercise, can cross the blood-brain barrier and affect the brain. IGF-1 specifically targets orexin neurons in the hypothalamus, which then stimulate dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area, triggering the reward system. Second, exercise can reshape neural circuits and restore mesocorticolimbic function, reducing chronic pain and related issues. We showed that exercise activates neurons in the basal nucleus of the amygdala that project to the nucleus accumbens, supporting patients' goal-directed behavior. Moreover, inhibiting GABAergic neurons in the central nucleus of the amygdala decreases freezing behavior. Third, chronic pain often leads to depression, mainly due to reduced activity of serotonin (5-HT) neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus, which impairs the brain's reward system. Exercise boosts activity of 5-HT neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus. Furthermore, exercise can modify gene expression through epigenetic mechanisms, leading to long-lasting improvements in brain function and behavior. Overall, exercise can restore brain function, helping individuals overcome chronic pain and lead healthier lives. These findings support exercise therapy as a key component of chronic pain management and suggest mesocorticolimbic mechanisms underlying its effects.

articles.title: Advances in research on combination therapy for the management of pain.
articles.abstract: Pharmacotherapy remains an important component of multidisciplinary, multimodal pain treatment. Based on a well-established understanding of multiple concurrent mechanisms of nociceptive transmission and modulation, the demonstrated potential for synergistic interactions of drug combinations seen in preclinical studies supports the hypothesis of superior analgesia, and possibly also, fewer side-effects as compared with monotherapy. Likely related to this hypothesis and rationale, real-world evidence shows that approximately half of all patients with chronic pain, and even more with acute pain, concurrently receive 2 or more drugs from different mechanistic classes. To date, many dozens of randomized controlled trials have evaluated various analgesic combinations for the treatment of postoperative, neuropathic, back, arthritis, fibromyalgia, pelvic, and cancer-related pain conditions. Despite this growing area of research, most analgesic drug combinations are currently administered without rigorous evidence, thus exposing patients to the added cost or risk of some combinations that are not necessarily superior to monotherapy. As such, we propose future efforts to more efficiently exploit the potential benefits of combination therapy including: (1) expansion and coordination of translational collaborations to prioritize the most beneficial and clinically relevant combinations; (2) ensuring that preclinical combination studies evaluate multiple drug dosages and multiple relevant adverse effects; (3) ensuring that clinical trials include comparisons with each and every monotherapy component of the combination; (4) conducting further real-world studies of clinically beneficial combinations to ensure safety and efficacy in broader clinical settings; and (5) the application of these principles also to the evaluation of nonpharmacological treatment combinations.

articles.title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain.
articles.abstract: Spontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber-derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective-salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry-while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints-potentially contributing to a mechanism-therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states-enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

articles.title: Prediction and prevention of pain after surgery.
articles.abstract: Postoperative pain is common and has substantial clinical consequences for patients, their families, and society. Acute pain is not the only problem: a meaningful subset of patients develops chronic postsurgical pain, which is associated with considerable functional and psychosocial burden. Because established chronic postsurgical pain is difficult to treat, prevention is a key clinical objective, but it depends on the early identification of vulnerable patients and timely mechanism-informed interventions. This review examines mechanisms of postsurgical pain, as well as the prediction and prevention of unfavorable outcomes, from a translational perspective that integrates clinical evidence with mechanistic insights from preclinical models. After briefly summarizing recent developments, we outline current challenges and argue that progress requires alignment of outcome constructs across species, rigorous selection and reporting of experimental models, and identification of shared intermediate phenotypes linking mechanisms to patient trajectories. We then summarize the perioperative risk architecture underlying the transition from acute to chronic postsurgical pain, focusing on bio-psycho-social patient-related and surgical factors. Because current risk assessment tools do not yet provide sufficiently precise, reliable, and generalizable prediction, we discuss emerging evidence, including biological signatures that may refine prediction and risk stratification. We further argue that risk emerges dynamically through interactions across pre-, intra- and postsurgical phases. Building on this multi-stage, interactive framework, we propose a strategy integrating bio-psycho-social factors into clinically relevant prognostic models. Finally, we outline how this may not only help identify patients at risk, but also support mechanism-based, personalized prevention in vulnerable patients.

articles.title: Brain sites involved in endogenous analgesia.
articles.abstract: Pain modulation is a fundamental survival mechanism that prioritises, shapes, and suppresses nociceptive inputs to optimise behaviour. Although acute pain signals potential or actual tissue damage, sustained pain can impair essential behaviours, necessitating modulatory circuits that dynamically regulate nociception according to context and motivational state. These systems are deeply conserved, embedded within primitive spinal and brainstem structures, and capable of powerful modulation independent of cortical input, although higher regions such as the prefrontal cortex can influence their function. Decades of work have sought to identify these core modulatory circuits to advance basic understanding and develop strategies for clinically meaningful hypoalgesia. More recently, dysfunction within these circuits has been implicated in chronic pain, driving efforts to characterise how their organisation and function change during persistent pain states. Although most mechanistic insights come from animal studies, human neuroimaging, particularly since the advent of functional magnetic resonance imaging, has begun to map their location and engagement during pain modulation. Early work focused on forebrain regions due to the limited spatial resolution of standard MRI, but ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging now enables mm3-scale investigation of brainstem nuclei. This review synthesises evidence from animal and human studies to outline the best-characterised modulatory pathway, consisting of projections from the midbrain periaqueductal gray to the rostral ventromedial medulla and onward to the dorsal horn/spinal trigeminal nucleus, and highlights recent work detailing its organization.

articles.title: Trustworthiness in pain research is essential. Developing and implementing the ENTRUST-PE framework.
articles.abstract: Trustworthy pain research is essential for developing a deeper understanding of the phenomena, how it is experienced, its many impacts and how it might be reduced, prevented or managed to improve the lives of those who live with pain. Recognising multiple critical challenges that undermine trust in health research, an international, interdisciplinary network was convened to create an integrated framework for enhancing the trustworthiness of research in pain. The ENTRUST-PE framework was launched in 2024 with a call to action, proposing that trustworthiness in pain research is multidimensional and underpinned by 7 Core Values: Integrity and Governance; Equity, Diversity and Inclusivity; Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement; Methodological Rigour; Openness and Transparency; Balanced Communication and Data Authenticity. The framework includes specific recommendations for a range of interest holders and resources to support those recommendations. In this paper, we summarise the framework, reflect on the response to the framework from the pain research community, consider challenges and opportunities in the evolving research landscape and suggest how we might move towards deeper implementation to enhance the trustworthiness of pain research.

articles.title: Chloride dysregulation: the next target for chronic pain therapeutics.
articles.abstract: Chronic pain affects a substantial fraction of the population, yet pharmacological management remains deeply inadequate. This failure likely reflects the focus on developing analgesics suppressing normal nociceptive signalling rather than correcting the pathological substrates distinguishing chronic from acute pain. Here we review how the identification of injury-induced downregulation of the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 in spinal dorsal horn neurons represents a landmark. It first provided a mechanistic, long-term substrate for spinal inhibitory failure. This form of disinhibition had the potential to explain several cardinal symptoms of neuropathic pain; not just hyperalgesia, through spinal hyperexcitability, and tactile allodynia, through cross-talk between sensory modalities, but also spontaneous pain, through enabling spontaneous bursts of activity in spinal nociceptive output to emerge. A second landmark is that chloride dysregulation as a substrate of disinhibition yields non-linear, non-intuitive predictions of neural circuit behaviours that shed light on several features of chronic pain and its therapeutic challenges. One is paradoxical pro-excitatory actions of tapping into normally endogenous inhibitory neurotransmission, potentially explaining failures of benzodiazepines analgesia and of conditional pain modulation. Others include degradation of sensory processing, possibly explaining diffuse pain, and leaky plasticity, predisposing to catastrophic sensitization. In turn, mechanisms regulating KCC2 itself emerge as substrates of chronification, as well as substrates of opioid-induced maladaptive paradoxical hyperalgesia. Finally, divergent yet convergent signaling cascades underlying KCC2-downregulation reveal a form of pathway degeneracy across sexes with lessons for therapeutics. All-in-all, these findings position KCC2 as a key novel target, not just for analgesia, but also for disease modification.

articles.title: An introduction to the biennial review of pain.
Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0-37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission.
METHODS: This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4-6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials' primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56-73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from - 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest (p = 0.99), and from - 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

articles.title: Cefepime Dose Individualization in Early Sepsis: A Pragmatic Feasibility Trial Protocol.
articles.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Cefepime is a core antibiotic in sepsis treatment, yet standard dosing yields 10- to 30-fold exposure variability in critical illness. In the early "golden hours" of sepsis, low cefepime levels (affecting up to 70% of cases) may lead to organ dysfunction progression, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance. Empiric dose escalation to overcome low levels can increase the risk of dose-dependent neurotoxicity. We developed and qualified a population pharmacokinetic model using patient weight and estimated glomerular filtration rate from creatinine and cystatin C that, in simulation, improved attainment of effective and safe drug levels.
OBJECTIVES: To describe the Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) 1 pragmatic feasibility trial.
DESIGN SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: This single-center, cluster-randomized, pragmatic feasibility trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07287332) was approved with a waiver of informed consent. Participants are critically ill adults (age ≥ 18 yr), hospitalized at Mayo Clinic (Rochester, MN), who are receiving cefepime for suspected or documented sepsis. A screening tool embedded in the electronic health record (EHR) identifies eligible patients newly initiated on cefepime (≤ 1 previous dose in 48 hr) who are then randomized to care groups (clusters) that use an individualized dosing algorithm (intervention) or usual-care dosing (control). Exclusions are cephalosporin allergy, acute kidney injury, kidney replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and missing inputs required for the algorithm (weight, creatinine, cystatin C). Recruitment began on January 15, 2026, and is expected to conclude by January 2027 (target enrollment, ≥ 300 patients).
INTERVENTIONS OUTCOMES AND ANALYSIS: For eligible patients, EHR-embedded clinical decision support prompts the cluster-assigned dosing approach, with final dose decisions made by the clinical team. Feasibility, fidelity, and exploratory pharmacokinetic and clinical outcomes will be assessed using mixed methods.
CONCLUSIONS: This workflow-integrated pragmatic feasibility trial will determine whether personalized cefepime dosing can be implemented in routine practice to optimize timely sepsis therapy while maintaining safety.
authors: Beta-Lactam Optimization and Outcomes Management (BLOOM) Study Group

articles.title: Individualized treatment effects of high flow nasal oxygen in immunocompromised patients.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) has become a common first-line practice for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARF). In immunocompromised patients, ARF is the leading cause of ICU admission, yet a randomized trial found no overall benefit of HFNO in this population.
OBJECTIVES: To assess whether baseline characteristics influence HFNO's effectiveness in preventing invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in immunocompromised patients with ARF.
METHODS: A causal forest machine-learning algorithm was derived in the HIGH trial (776 patients randomized to HFNO or conventional oxygen) to predict the HFNO effects on day-28 IMV incidence. Patients with a "do-not-intubate" order (n = 72) were excluded. Model performance was validated through 500 bootstrap iterations and patients were categorized into terciles based on predicted HFNO benefit. Transportability of the model was assessed in an independent observational cohort (818 patients).
MAIN RESULTS: Among the 704 participants, HFNO's average effect on day-28 IMV was not significant. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment responses was identified (predicted benefit: from 20.2% [IQR 15.5%-23.9%] absolute IMV risk reduction with HFNO to 7.4% risk reduction [2.9%-11.2%] with conventional oxygen). Patients with the highest predicted benefit were older, more frequently solid organ transplant recipients, less neutropenic, more severely hypoxemic/tachycardic, but with lower non-respiratory sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores. In this subgroup, HFNO was associated with a significant lower incidence of IMV. In the observational cohort, the benefit-ranking performance was preserved, although absolute effect estimates were less calibrated.
CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest HFNO might benefit specific immunocompromised patients with ARF. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness.
METHODS: A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting.
RESULTS: Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established.
CONCLUSION: Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

articles.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis.
METHODS: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events.
RESULTS: Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified.
CONCLUSION: Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.

articles.title: Are we there yet? No, but getting closer: CT assessment of emphysema and disease progression in COPD.

articles.title: The Modern Continuum of Care for Colorectal Liver Metastases: A Comprehensive Review.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, and the liver is its predominant site of metastatic spread; approximately half of patients with CRC develop colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Management has shifted from largely palliative intent to a multidisciplinary strategy with curative potential. Complete resection offers a chance of cure, although long-term survival varies substantially with tumor biology, disease burden, and patient selection. This review summarizes advances in prognostic stratification, molecular profiling, and the evolving definition of resectability, together with surgical innovations including parenchymal-sparing and two-stage hepatectomy, portal vein embolization, associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS), liver venous deprivation, and minimally invasive approaches. We review conversion chemotherapy informed by the TRIBE, TRIBE2, CAIRO5, and PARADIGM trials, perioperative systemic therapy, and biomarker-directed agents for RAS wild-type, BRAF V600E-mutant, KRAS G12C-mutant, and HER2-amplified tumors, alongside immune checkpoint inhibition for microsatellite instability-high disease. Locoregional therapies, including thermal ablation, stereotactic radiotherapy, and selective internal radiation therapy, are discussed in light of the COLLISION and CLOCC trials. Finally, we consider emerging roles for circulating tumor DNA in minimal residual disease assessment and for liver transplantation in highly selected patients with unresectable disease (SECA, TransMet).

articles.title: A Multicenter Prospective Study of Patient Outcomes After Three Full-Endoscopic Lumbar Decompression Techniques.
articles.abstract:
STUDY DESIGN: Multicenter prospective observational study.
OBJECTIVE: To characterize the application and outcome profiles of TELD, IELD, and UBE in routine clinical practice.
SUMMARY OF BACKGROUND DATA: Full-endoscopic lumbar surgery has been widely used in the treatment of lumbar disc herniation, yet multicenter prospective evidence on patient outcomes in real-world clinical practice remains limited.
METHODS: This multicenter prospective real-world study was conducted across 10 medical centers in four regions of China. Perioperative parameters, complications, and patient-reported outcome measures at postoperative day 1 and at 3, 6, and 12 months were recorded. Descriptive group comparisons were supplemented by adjusted repeated-measures analyses accounting for baseline outcome values, clinical covariates, operative level, and center.
RESULTS: A total of 623 patients were included: 105 in the TELD group, 109 in the IELD group, and 409 in the UBE group. Preoperative pain intensity, operative-level distribution, sensory deficit, and center distribution differed among groups. In adjusted analyses, TELD was associated with lower back-pain VAS than UBE at 3 months (mean difference, -0.73; 95% CI, -1.06 to -0.40; Holm P<0.001), 6 months (-0.51; -0.82 to -0.21; P=0.005), and 12 months (-0.77; -0.96 to -0.57; P<0.001). These differences were below the 3-point VAS MCID.
CONCLUSIONS: TELD, IELD, and UBE were associated with favorable safety and midterm outcomes in this multicenter cohort. TELD was associated with modestly lower postoperative back-pain scores than UBE after adjustment for measured differences; however, the absolute differences did not reach the prespecified MCID and do not establish causal or universal procedural superiority.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.

articles.title: Unilateral Biportal Endoscopy Versus Percutaneous Endoscopic Interlaminar Discectomy for Highly Migrated Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Retrospective Comparative Study With Quantitative MRI-Based Decompression Analysis.
articles.abstract: Study designRetrospective comparative cohort study.ObjectiveTo compare the perioperative, clinical, and radiographic outcomes of unilateral biportal endoscopy (UBE) and percutaneous endoscopic interlaminar discectomy (PEID) in the treatment of highly migrated lumbar disc herniation (HMLDH).MethodsA total of 128 patients with single-level HMLDH who underwent UBE (n = 63) or PEID (n = 65) between June 2022 and January 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. All patients completed a minimum follow-up period of 2 years. Perioperative variables, complications, and reoperation events were analyzed. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Radiographic decompression was quantitatively assessed using the postoperative dural sac cross-sectional area (DSCA) expansion rate measured on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).ResultsCompared with PEID, UBE was associated with a significantly shorter operative time, less endoscopic hemostasis time, and lower fluoroscopy time. Intraoperative blood loss was lower in the PEID group. Early postoperative back pain was significantly lower in the PEID group, whereas no significant between-group differences were observed in long-term VAS or ODI outcomes. The overall complication rate was significantly lower in the UBE group. In addition, UBE achieved a significantly greater DSCA expansion rate and a lower rate of residual disc fragments than PEID.ConclusionUBE and PEID achieved comparable long-term clinical outcomes in patients with HMLDH. UBE demonstrated advantages in perioperative efficiency, radiographic decompression, and reduced radiation exposure. Furthermore, UBE was associated with a lower overall complication rate, primarily attributable to a lower incidence of postoperative nerve root irritation.

articles.title: Increased risk of infection and reoperation following total knee arthroplasty in patients under 40.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is increasingly performed in younger patient populations. This study aimed to compare perioperative outcomes between patients under 40 and those over 65, stratified by surgical indication.
METHODS: This retrospective study used the Epic Cosmos dataset to identify primary TKA patients under 40 years old (n = 3,177) or over 65 (n = 698,662). Patients were stratified by surgical indication (primary osteoarthritis, post-traumatic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, and multiple indications) using ICD-10 codes. Outcomes included superficial wound dehiscence, infection, readmission, and ipsilateral reoperation, assessed at 90 days and 1 year postoperatively. Differences between age groups were assessed using adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) derived from multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for sex, body mass index, comorbidity burden, insurance status and smoking status with significance set at p < 0.05. A sensitivity analysis in the overall cohort tested the interaction between age group and surgical indication.
RESULTS: Surgical indications differed significantly between cohorts (standardized proportions difference 0.939, p < 0.001), with osteoarthritis accounting for 97.8% of cases in patients >65 compared to 64.6% in patients <40. Younger patients had higher rates of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (2.4% vs 0.1%) and multiple diagnoses (20.7% vs 1.6%). Among patients with osteoarthritis, those under 40 had significantly higher 90-day odds of infection (OR 3.16, 95% CI 2.29-4.35), superficial wound dehiscence (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.34-2.72) and ipsilateral reoperation (OR 3.91, 95% CI 3.34-4.58), which persisted at 1 year (infection OR 2.79, 95% CI 2.13-3.67; superficial wound dehiscence OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.41-2.59; reoperation OR 3.44, 95% CI 3.00-3.94). Patients under 40 with multiple diagnoses had elevated odds of infection at 90 days (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.15-3.69) and 1 year (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.09-2.95), and ipsilateral reoperation at 90 days (OR 3.10, 95% CI 2.25-4.25) and 1 year (OR 2.71, 95% CI 2.06-3.55). In the overall cohort, the effect of age differed significantly by surgical indication for all outcomes except superficial wound dehiscence.
CONCLUSION: Patients under 40 undergoing Total Knee Arthroplasty are at increased risk for prosthetic joint infection, superficial wound problems and ipsilateral reoperation at 90 days and 1 year when compared to those over the age of 65, independent of smoking status and comorbidity burden. Those with multiple indications for surgery are also at increased risk for infection and same-side reoperation at both time points.

articles.title: A Randomized Trial Comparing Two Balanced Crystalloids in Patients Undergoing Emergency Exploratory Laparotomy for Blunt Abdominal Trauma Under General Anesthesia.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Intravenous crystalloids are central to perioperative resuscitation of patients with blunt abdominal trauma, in whom haemorrhage and hypoperfusion produce metabolic acidosis and hyperlactatemia. Balanced crystalloids are preferred over 0.9% saline, but it is unclear whether the choice of buffer anion-lactate versus acetate-influences perioperative acid-base and electrolyte status. We compared a lactated balanced crystalloid with an acetated balanced crystalloid in this setting.
METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, double-blind study conducted at a level-1 trauma centre, sixty adults (18-50 years) undergoing exploratory laparotomy lasting more than one hour for blunt abdominal trauma were allocated to receive a lactated balanced crystalloid (Group R, n = 30) or an acetated balanced crystalloid (Group S, n = 30). Arterial blood gas, base excess, lactate and serum electrolytes were recorded at baseline (preoperative) and after surgery (postoperative). Intergroup and intragroup comparisons were performed using Student's t-test, Mann-Whitney U test, and Chi-square or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate; p < 0.05 was considered significant.
RESULTS: Demographic profiles and duration of surgery were comparable between groups. Group R showed a significant postoperative fall in pH (p = 0.041), whereas pH remained stable in Group S; the postoperative intergroup difference favoured the acetated solution (p = 0.012). Base excess improved significantly within both groups (Group R p = 0.019; Group S p = 0.031), with no significant intergroup difference. Lactate fell significantly in Group S (p = 0.027) but not in Group R, and the postoperative intergroup comparison favoured the acetated solution (p = 0.049). Bicarbonate and all measured electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺) remained stable, with no significant intra- or intergroup differences.
CONCLUSION: The acetated solution provided marginally better pH stability and avoided the exogenous lactate load associated with the lactated solution.

articles.title: Management of Hand Injuries: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Surgical and Rehabilitation Strategies.
articles.abstract: Management of traumatic hand injuries has evolved substantially with advances in anesthesia, tendon repair, biological adjuncts, fracture fixation, and rehabilitation. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence on surgical and rehabilitation strategies for improving functional recovery and reducing complications after acute hand trauma. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261320700). PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for studies published from January 2000 to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials and prospective comparative studies evaluating contemporary strategies for flexor or extensor tendon injuries and metacarpal or phalangeal fractures were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Of 3417 records identified, 354 duplicates were removed and 3063 records were screened. Following full-text assessment, 23 studies were included. Evidence supported the use of wide-awake local anesthesia no tourniquet (WALANT) as a safe alternative to general anesthesia, although functional superiority was not consistent across trials. Acellular dermal matrices, biological amnion, hydrogels, hyaluronic acid, and other adjuncts showed potential for reducing adhesions and improving tendon gliding. Early active mobilization and place-and-hold protocols produced favorable functional outcomes, while relative motion extension orthoses improved early function after extensor tendon repair. Smartphone-assisted rehabilitation improved adherence. Headless compression screws facilitated earlier functional recovery in selected metacarpal fractures, while multistrand tendon repairs provided sufficient strength for early mobilization.
