Swallowing outcomes were assessed using the Penetration-Aspiration Scale, and functional feeding outcomes were measured using the Pediatric Functional Oral Intake Scale. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise patient characteristics and feeding outcomes. Pre- and post-intervention outcomes were compared among patients with paired data.
RESULTS: Nineteen patients were included. Genetic diagnoses were present in 58% of the cohort, most commonly 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Prolonged intubation occurred in 53% of patients, and vocal fold motion impairment and necrotising enterocolitis were each observed in 42%. Among patients with paired data, median Penetration-Aspiration Scale increased from 3 pre-operatively to 6 post-operatively, and aspiration was observed in 50% post-operatively. Enteral tube use increased from 57% pre-operatively to 79% post-operatively among patients with paired data. Persistent oral aversion at six months was documented in 26% of the cohort.
CONCLUSION: Patients with major aortopulmonary collateral arteries demonstrate high rates of dysphagia and enteral feeding dependence across the perioperative period. Preliminary findings highlight the need for early, multidisciplinary feeding evaluation to optimise developmental outcomes in this high-risk population.

articles.title: Reduction in unnecessary oxytocin administration for elective first trimester suction dilation and curettage.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To reduce the rate of unnecessary oxytocin administration during scheduled first trimester uterine aspiration procedures by 50% over an eight-week intervention period.
METHODS: A quality improvement study was implemented at an urban academic ambulatory hospital. Baseline oxytocin use for first trimester uterine aspiration procedures, along with patient and provider characteristics, was recorded during an eight-week retrospective period. Iterative Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles informed the design. The first intervention removed oxytocin from a pre-populated electronic anesthesia standard care pathway, while the second was an educational presentation to anaesthesia and obstetrics providers.
RESULTS: Baseline oxytocin administration was 20% (26/130). The first and second interventions reduced oxytocin use to 10.2% (9/88) and 9.2% (6/65), respectively. Over all time periods combined, advancing gestational age was associated with oxytocin use (OR = 1.364, 95% CI 1.196, 1.556; P = 0.000), while early-career surgeons were less likely to use oxytocin (OR = 0.313, 95% CI 0.150, 0.653; P = 0.002). Adjusted odds ratios for oxytocin administration were 0.360 (95% CI 0.142, 0.838; P = 0.023) and 0.433 (95% CI 0.147, 1.118; P = 0.101), during the first and second interventions, respectively. There was no difference in the administration of antihemorrhagic agents (OR = 2.035, 95% CI 0.527, 7.857; P = 0.303) or surgical bleeding (OR = 6.486, 95% CI 0.397, 105.960; P = 0.190) between the pre and post intervention periods.
CONCLUSION: Simple interventions resulted in a 50% reduction of oxytocin administration for uterine aspiration procedures without increasing the use of antihemorrhagic agents or procedural bleeding.Résumé OBJECTIF: Réduire de 50 % le taux d'administration inutile d'ocytocine lors des aspirations utérines programmées au premier trimestre sur une période d'intervention de huit semaines. MéTHODOLOGIE: Une étude sur l'amélioration de la qualité a été menée dans un hôpital universitaire offrant des soins ambulatoires, en région urbaine. Les données de référence sur l'utilisation de l'ocytocine lors des aspirations utérines au premier trimestre et les caractéristiques des patientes et des prestataires ont été recueillies sur une période rétrospective de huit semaines. La conception de l'étude s'est appuyée sur des cycles PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) itératifs. La première intervention consistait à retirer l'ocytocine d'un parcours de soins anesthésiques standard préétabli dans le dossier médical électronique, tandis que la deuxième consistait en une présentation formative destinée aux prestataires de soins en anesthésie et en obstétrique. RéSULTATS: L'administration initiale d'ocytocine était de 20 % (26/130). Les première et deuxième interventions ont réduit son utilisation à 10,2 % (9/88) et à 9,2 % (6/65), respectivement. Sur l'ensemble des périodes étudiées, l'avancement de l'âge gestationnel était associé à l'utilisation d'ocytocine (RC = 1,364, IC à 95 % : 1,196-1,556; P = 0,000), tandis que les chirurgiens en début de carrière étaient moins susceptibles de recourir à l'ocytocine (RC = 0,313, IC à 95 % : 0,150-0,653; P = 0,002). Les rapports de cotes ajustés pour l'administration d'ocytocine étaient de 0,360 (IC à 95 % : 0,142-0,838; P = 0,023) et de 0,433 (IC à 95 % : 0,147-1,118; P = 0,101) lors des première et deuxième interventions, respectivement. Aucune différence n'a été observée entre les périodes précédant et suivant les interventions quant à l'administration d'agents antihémorragiques (RC = 2,035; IC à 95 % : 0,527-7,857; P = 0,303) ou aux saignements peropératoires (RC = 6,486; IC à 95 % : 0,397-105,960; P = 0,190).
CONCLUSION: Des interventions simples ont permis de réduire de 50 % l'administration d'ocytocine lors des aspirations utérines, sans augmenter le recours aux agents antihémorragiques ni les saignements peropératoires.

articles.title: Effectiveness of supraclavicular brachial plexus block for the cutaneous innervation of the medial elbow region: a prospective, observational study.
Layered anatomy of the greater and lesser occipital nerves with photogrammetry-based three-dimensional models: a cadaveric study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: The superficial neurovascular anatomy of the posterior occipital region is important for occipital nerve block, greater occipital nerve (GON) decompression, and posterior fossa incision planning. However, the continuous layered relationship between the medial GON-occipital artery (OA) region and the lateral lesser occipital nerve (LON) channel remains incompletely characterized.
METHODS: This cadaveric study examined 10 formalin-fixed specimens (20 sides). Layer-by-layer dissection documented nerve courses, emergence points, diameters, terminal branches, neurovascular relationships, GON-LON communications, and relationships with the OA and adjacent muscles. Photogrammetry-based three-dimensional models were constructed for visualization, not quantitative measurement.
RESULTS: The GON and LON were identified on all 20 sides. The GON had 6.0 ± 1.4 terminal branches. Its trapezius muscle/fascial emergence point was located 25.4 ± 3.2 mm horizontally from the posterior midline and 14.0 ± 2.2 mm vertically from the external occipital protuberance (EOP) level. GON-OA relationships comprised a single crossing on 3 sides, multiple crossings on 8 sides, continuous contact on 5 sides, and coiling on 4 sides. The LON traversed a trapezius muscle-related plane on 9 sides and followed a posterior sternocleidomastoid muscle-border course on 11 sides. In descriptive side-level comparisons, the trapezius muscle-related emergence point was closer to the posterior midline and EOP level but farther from the mastoid reference line than the posterior sternocleidomastoid muscle-border emergence point. GON-LON communications were observed on 17 sides.
CONCLUSION: These findings support a layered, pathway-based, and conceptual zone-based model of posterior occipital neurovascular anatomy, rather than localization based only on isolated surface landmarks.

articles.title: Pragmatic trial of a self-directed intervention for weight loss in obstructive sleep apnea (POWER).
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Self-directed lifestyle interventions may improve access to weight loss care in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but effectiveness in routine practice is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: Test whether a proactively delivered self-directed lifestyle intervention improves weight and sleep-related quality of life versus usual care.
METHODS: POWER enrolled patients with OSA and body mass index of 30-45 kg/m2, recruited from Veteran Affairs (VA) sites nationwide, and randomized participants to a self-directed intervention based on the Diabetes Prevention Program with video-based sessions, readings, and regular coaching reminders or usual care. Co-primary outcomes were change in Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ) and clinical weight in kilograms (kg) from baseline to 12 months post-randomization. Given two primary outcomes, we defined significance at p = 0.025.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: This trial randomized 696 participants. Mean age was 56.2 years (SD 12.2), with 19.7% identifying as female. Clinical weights at 12 months were available for 81.9% of intervention and 83.6% of control participants. Unadjusted weight declined 2.1 kg (SD 6.8) in intervention and 0.9 kg (SD 5.9) in control (adjusted between-group difference: -1.1 kg, 95%CI -2.0, -0.1; p = 0.037). FOSQ measures were available at 12 months for 78.2% of intervention and 90.5% of control participants. From baseline to 12 months, unadjusted FOSQ improved 1.4 (SD 2.7) points in intervention and 0.9 (SD 2.9) points in control (adjusted between-group difference: 0.6 points, 95%CI 0.2, 1.0; p = 0.001).
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: Among participants with OSA and obesity, a self-directed lifestyle intervention did not improve weight loss and led to improvements in sleep-related quality of life that are of limited clinical importance.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05104450, registered 10/19/2021.

Excessive Tidal Volume During Noninvasive Ventilation: Mechanisms of Harm Leading to Worse Clinical Outcomes.
Evaluation of De Novo Donor-Specific Antibodies After Kidney Transplantation: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study From the Debrecen Kidney Transplantation Program.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) are important biomarkers of humoral alloimmunity and are associated with antibody-mediated rejection and adverse graft outcomes. Allograft survival, the de novo development of DSAs, and subsequent rejection episodes remain the subject of extensive ongoing research. In the present study, we evaluated the impact of perioperative blood transfusion, delayed graft function (DGF), levels of HLA Class I and Class II antibodies, viral infections, prior transplantations, and demographic factors on the development of DSAs and the incidence of ABMR.
METHODS: Data from 238 kidney transplantations performed between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2023, were analyzed retrospectively. The study cohort comprised 62.6% male and 37.4% female recipients (mean age: 54.5 ± 2.3 years for males and 53.8 ± 3.0 years for females). Patients were stratified based on antibody development into a DSA-positive group and a DSA-negative control group. Statistical analyses were performed using the Chi-square test, Fisher's exact test, and logistic regression.
RESULTS: In the DSA-positive group, 17 out of 72 (23.6%) cases involved secondary transplantations (retransplantations), compared to only 8 out of 166 (4.8%) cases in the control group, representing a significant association (P = .001). Perioperative blood transfusions were administered to 42 patients in the DSA-positive group and 58 patients in the DSA-negative group (58.3% and 34.9% respectively, (P = .00099)). DGF was observed in 20 cases within the positive cohort and 21 cases in the negative cohort (27.7% and 12.6% respectively, P = .01). A significant difference was observed regarding the development of ABMR when comparing the presence of HLA Class II antibodies to HLA Class I antibodies (P = .0016). Furthermore, HLA-DR-specific DSAs with high MFI (>5000) were significantly associated with the development of ABMR (P = .031).
CONCLUSIONS: The presence of HLA Class II antibodies, particularly those directed against the DR locus, significantly increased the incidence of ABMR. The de novo formation of DSAs can be triggered by several anamnestic clinical factors, such as delayed graft function (DGF), secondary transplantation, and perioperative blood transfusion status as primary risk factors.

articles.title: Intraoperative Surgical Donor Complications in Laparoscopic Donor Nephrectomy: Single Center Experience With Video Presentations.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Laparoscopic living-donor nephrectomy improves graft function and reduces morbidity. Intraoperative complications in donor nephrectomy are rare and can be avoided by basic precautions. We aimed to investigate intraoperative surgical complications through a video presentation and to emphasize protective measures.
METHODS: This is a retrospective cohort study. We included patients who underwent donor nephrectomy between December 2015 and December 2025. All patients underwent laparoscopic transperitoneal donor nephrectomy. We obtained donors' medical data from the hospital system. We identified intraoperative complications recorded in the operation notes and obtained operation videos of complicated cases from hospital archives.
RESULTS: Our center performed 1011 living-donor nephrectomies. There were 816 laparoscopic left nephrectomies and 195 laparoscopic right nephrectomies. The mean postoperative hospitalization time for donors was 2.8 days (min-max: 2-5 days). The mean donor BMI was 28.35 (min-max: 19.33-41.73). We observed 68 (6.7%) complications. Videos of the complications are presented. One case required conversion to open surgery.
CONCLUSION: Laparoscopic donor nephrectomy is an advanced surgery with low complication risks. Experienced surgeons can manage complications laparoscopically.

articles.title: Two-Dimensional Electromagnetic Navigation-Assisted Percutaneous Transforaminal Endoscopic Discectomy for Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the clinical performance, safety, radiation exposure, and learning curve of two-dimensional (2D) electromagnetic navigation-assisted percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic discectomy (PTED) with those of three-dimensional (3D) electromagnetic navigation-assisted PTED in patients with lumbar disc herniation (LDH).
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 82 patients with LDH who underwent PTED between January 2022 and June 2024. Patients were classified into the 2D electromagnetic navigation group or the 3D electromagnetic navigation group according to the navigation workflow used during surgery. Perioperative variables, including total operative time, navigation registration time, radiation exposure, and complications, were recorded. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the visual analogue scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and modified MacNab criteria. Learning curves for both the surgeon and the radiologic technologist were evaluated using cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis.
RESULTS: Compared with the 3D group, the 2D group demonstrated a significantly shorter total operative time (66.64 ± 9.67 vs. 88.92 ± 15.98 min, p < 0.001), shorter navigation registration time (6.37 ± 0.93 vs. 12.25 ± 2.11 min, p < 0.001), and lower radiation exposure (1.77 ± 0.17 vs. 7.24 ± 0.56 mGy, p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis using linear mixed-effects models demonstrated significant time effects for VAS of back, VAS of leg, and ODI (all p < 0.001), indicating significant postoperative improvement in both groups. No significant main effect of group was observed for VAS of back, VAS of leg, or ODI. The group-by-time interaction was not significant for VAS of leg (p = 0.774), but was significant for VAS of back (p = 0.007) and ODI (p < 0.001), suggesting differences in the temporal recovery patterns between groups for these two outcomes. According to the modified MacNab criteria, favorable final outcomes were achieved in both groups, with no significant between-group difference. The learning curve was shorter in the 2D group, with proficiency reached by the 16th case for the surgeon and the 14th case for the radiologic technologist, compared with the 3D group. No significant between-group difference was observed in complication rates.
CONCLUSION: 2D electromagnetic navigation-assisted PTED is a safe and clinically effective alternative to 3D electromagnetic navigation-assisted PTED for the treatment of LDH. Relative to the 3D workflow, the 2D approach offers greater procedural efficiency, reduced radiation exposure, and a shorter learning curve. Although longitudinal analysis revealed different recovery patterns over time for low back pain and ODI between the two groups, both techniques achieved substantial postoperative improvement, favorable final clinical outcomes, and comparable safety. These findings suggest that simplified 2D electromagnetic navigation may represent a more practical and scalable option for routine clinical application.

articles.title: Subgroup deployment-readiness audit of calibration and clinical utility in perioperative infection prediction.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: We audited deployment readiness of an end-of-surgery postoperative infection model across clinically relevant subgroups and assessed mitigation of subgroup miscalibration.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed out-of-fold predictions from 10 719 procedures (2014-2022) with 504 present-on-admission (POA)-coded postoperative infection events across recorded sex, age, and a clinical physiological-reserve proxy. We assessed discrimination, calibration, threshold-specific errors, and decision-curve net benefit, treating t = 0.10 as a reference anchor. We compared no recalibration with common and group-specific cross-fitted isotonic recalibration, evaluated a refit without the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), and performed a temporal-holdout analysis.
RESULTS: Overall area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.876, with similar sex-marginal discrimination in women and men (0.878 vs 0.875). Calibration-in-the-large was -1.02 overall, -0.86 in frail, and -1.34 in prefrail patients; the 6-event nonfrail stratum was not estimable. At t = 0.10, net benefit was positive in frail and negative in prefrail patients in the source cohort, but negative prefrail utility did not persist in the ascertainable-period (2018-2022) and temporal analyses. Common recalibration moved overall calibration-in-the-large from -1.020 to -0.007. Removing SMOTE shifted overall calibration but did not reduce the reserve gradient. Temporal-holdout AUROC was 0.851 with persistent overprediction. Present-on-admission coding was effectively absent before 2018; prevalence-dependent results were therefore additionally reported for the ascertainable 2018-2022 period, and ascertainment differed by physiological reserve.
DISCUSSION: Discrimination-only or sex-marginal evaluation would have missed deployment-relevant subgroup heterogeneity, while endpoint ascertainment affected prevalence-dependent interpretation.
CONCLUSION: Joint subgroup evaluation can identify deployment-relevant limitations missed by aggregate metrics. Prospective validation with comparable outcome ascertainment remains necessary before clinical deployment.

articles.title: Urological manifestations in obesity.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: The global prevalence of obesity continues to rise, with effects ranging across urology. This review summarizes recent evidence on obesity and its impact on various urological conditions, including malignancy, infections, stone disease, functional urology and male reproductive health, chronic kidney disease, and pediatric urology, to guide comprehensive management in this population.
RECENT FINDINGS: Obesity has a paradoxical survival benefit in patients with renal cell carcinoma, while its impact drives aggressive prostate cancer. Obesity increases kidney stone risk, with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists showing divergent effects on lithogenesis and urinary tract infections. It is a modifiable risk factor for overactive bladder and stress urinary incontinence, both of which improve with weight loss/ bariatric surgery. Robotic surgery mitigates obesity-related perioperative risk. Hypogonadism secondary to obesity is a major reversible cause of male infertility. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reverse metabolic hypogonadism and helps in slowing chronic kidney progression. Maternal and childhood obesity may impair testicular descent and can also increase the risk of nocturnal enuresis.
SUMMARY: Obesity's urological effects are heterogeneous, paradoxical from pediatric to adults, mediated by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and hormonal dysregulation. Weight loss and the use of GLP-1 RA may offer a unique strategy for optimizing and treating urological conditions.

articles.title: Clinician-guided digital CBT-I improves sleep quality and apnea severity in patients with co-morbid insomnia and OSA: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract:
RATIONALE: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA.
METHODS: This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (-9.5 vs. -4.0 points; d = -1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (-4.9 vs. -1.8 points; d = -0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea-hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; -6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function.
CONCLUSION: Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457.
articles.journal: Am J Respir Crit Care Med

articles.title: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA.
RESULTS: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ.
CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Regisrty- India (CTRI) identifier [CTRI/2024/02/062201], registered [01 February 2024].

articles.title: Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy and Perioperative Complications Associated with Pulmonary Toxicity.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is widely used in multimodal cancer treatment and can improve surgical conditions and patient prognosis. However, NAC-related pulmonary toxicity may impair respiratory function and warrants attention during perioperative risk assessment.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes evidence on chemotherapy-associated pulmonary toxicity, focusing on underlying mechanisms, clinical characteristics, diagnostic strategies, and perioperative anesthetic management. Direct clinical evidence from patients receiving NAC is distinguished from findings in other treatment settings and experimental models.
RESULTS: Several chemotherapeutic agents, including bleomycin, methotrexate, taxanes, gemcitabine, and cisplatin, as well as selected targeted therapies, have been associated with drug-induced lung injury, often presenting as interstitial lung disease. Clinical and experimental evidence implicates mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, immune-mediated injury, inflammatory activation, and alveolar-capillary barrier disruption. Advanced age, pre-existing lung disease, reduced diffusing capacity, metabolic abnormalities, smoking history, and multi-agent treatment may indicate increased susceptibility, although their relevance varies by drug and treatment setting. Evidence from broader perioperative settings and experimental models suggests that mechanical ventilation, excessive oxygen exposure, and surgical stress may aggravate existing pulmonary injury.
CONCLUSION: NAC-related pulmonary toxicity merits consideration in perioperative assessment, but direct evidence linking it to perioperative outcomes remains limited. Pulmonary function testing and clinically indicated imaging can inform individualized risk assessment. Lung-protective ventilation, appropriate oxygen therapy, individualized anesthetic management, and postoperative respiratory support draw largely on evidence from other populations; their effectiveness specifically in patients with NAC-related pulmonary injury requires further evaluation.

articles.title: Propofol versus remifentanil sedation for elective gastroscopy: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Propofol and remifentanil are widely used for elective gastroscopy sedation. The aim of this randomized controlled trial was to compare their safety profiles, patient-reported recovery quality, and endoscopist satisfaction.
METHODS: This single-center randomized controlled trial enrolled 88 adults (American Society of Anesthesiologists I-III) undergoing elective gastroscopy, allocated 1:1 to propofol (Group P, n=44) or remifentanil (Group R, n=44). Sedation depth was standardized using the Bispectral Index (target 60-80) and Ramsay Sedation Scale (target 2-3). The primary outcome was the Quality of Recovery-15 score at 30 min post-procedure; secondary outcomes included complication incidence, awakening time, and endoscopist satisfaction.
RESULTS: Quality of Recovery-15 scores were comparable (median 140 vs. 140; median difference 0, 95%CI -1.0 to 1.0; p=0.95). Total complication incidence was 0% in Group P versus 61.4% in Group R (p<0.001), comprising bradycardia (27.3%), postoperative nausea and vomiting (20.5%), and desaturation (13.6%). Awakening time was shorter in Group R (3 vs. 60 s; p<0.001). Endoscopist satisfaction was significantly higher in Group P (90.9 vs. 56.8% excellent scores; p=0.003).
CONCLUSION: Despite comparable patient-reported recovery quality, propofol was associated with substantially fewer perioperative adverse events (0 vs. 61.4%) and higher endoscopist satisfaction, supporting its preferential use in routine elective gastroscopy sedation.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07336628. Registered January 2, 2026.

articles.title: Ventricular lavage (VeLa) for ventriculitis: A systematic review of techniques and meta-analysis of outcomes.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Ventriculitis is a severe complication of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion procedures associated with high morbidity and mortality despite advances in antimicrobial therapy. Ventricular lavage (VeLa) has emerged as a potential adjunctive intervention to improve infection clearance and neurological outcomes.
RESEARCH QUESTION: This study aimed to systematically review the surgical techniques of VeLa and evaluate its effectiveness in the treatment of ventriculitis compared with conventional therapy alone.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Electronic databases were searched from inception to August 2025. Studies describing VeLa for ventriculitis were included. Data on surgical techniques, perioperative variables, complications, and clinical outcomes were extracted. Quantitative synthesis was performed using a random-effects model in RevMan.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven studies were included in the qualitative synthesis and five in the meta-analysis, comprising one randomized controlled trial and four cohort studies. Common techniques involved ventricular access through Kocher's point, endoscope-assisted septostomy, high-volume irrigation until clear effluent, and antibiotic-enriched lavage solutions. Compared with conventional therapy alone, VeLa was associated with lower mortality and improved functional outcomes, including higher odds of achieving a modified Rankin Scale score <3. VeLa also significantly reduced in-hospital parameters including drain duration, hospital stay, and duration of intravenous antibiotic therapy. Reported complications were infrequent and generally manageable.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: VeLa may be associated with improved survival and functional recovery, as well as shorter hospitalization and antibiotic duration, when used as an adjunct to conventional treatment for ventriculitis. However, the limited and predominantly observational evidence, together with methodological heterogeneity, precludes definitive conclusions. These findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant validation through larger, well-designed multicenter prospective studies using standardized treatment protocols.

articles.title: Intrathecal morphine versus fascial plane blocks after caesarean delivery: An updated meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intrathecal morphine (ITM) provides prolonged analgesia after caesarean delivery but causes opioid-related adverse effects. Fascial plane blocks (FPBs) may be an alternative, although their comparative efficacy remains uncertain.
METHODS: We systematically searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus (from inception to 24 July 2026) for randomised controlled trials comparing ITM with FPBs. The primary outcome was 24-h opioid consumption in intravenous morphine milligram equivalents (IV-MME).
RESULTS: Twenty-six trials were included. Fifteen trials involving 1250 participants reported 24-h opioid consumption. ITM produced a small reduction compared with FPBs (mean difference - 3.16 mg IV-MME, 95% confidence interval - 6.30 to - 0.02; p = 0.049; I2 = 96.1%). The prediction interval crossed the null, Egger's test indicated funnel plot asymmetry, and the trim-and-fill sensitivity analysis produced a non-significant estimate in the opposite direction. These findings are difficult to interpret in the presence of substantial heterogeneity. TSA showed that the accrued information size was sufficient. Pain scores were similar, with small differences favouring ITM at isolated time points. ITM increased postoperative nausea and vomiting (risk ratio 1.87), pruritus (1.65), urinary retention (3.89), and respiratory depression (2.60). The trim-and-fill estimate for pruritus was not statistically significant, although this finding should also be interpreted cautiously. Effects differed by FPB technique but not by ITM dose. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSION: The comparative effects of ITM and FPBs varied by block technique, and the findings do not support routine replacement of ITM with FPBs. Selected FPBs may be considered when ITM is not administered, with the choice guided by technique-specific evidence, patient preferences, and the additional procedural time, expertise, and resources required.
articles.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol

articles.title: From circumferential to posterior-only fixation: evolving strategies for cervical fractures in ankylosing spinal disorders.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cervical fractures in patients with ankylosing spinal disorders are highly unstable injuries associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. While surgical stabilization is widely accepted, the optimal surgical strategy remains debated.
RESEARCH QUESTION: To evaluate surgical strategies, neurological outcomes, morbidity, and mortality following surgical treatment of cervical fractures in patients with spinal ankylosis.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 91 consecutive patients with ankylosing spinal disorders who sustained cervical spine fractures and were treated surgically between 2008 and 2025. Demographic characteristics, fracture morphology, neurological status, surgical approach, perioperative outcomes, complications, and mortality were assessed.
RESULTS: The cohort comprised 91 patients with a median age of 78 years. Low-energy trauma accounted for most injuries. Neurological deficits were present in 28.6% of patients and were significantly associated with AO type C fractures and epidural hematoma. Surgical treatment consisted predominantly of posterior fixation, with a temporal shift from combined anterior-posterior stabilization toward posterior-only navigated pedicle screw constructs. Overall complication and in-hospital mortality rates were 52.7% and 9.9%, respectively. In multivariable Firth regression, higher Charlson Comorbidity Index remained associated with in-hospital mortality, whereas age did not.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: AO type C morphology and concomitant epidural hematoma were associated with neurological compromise. Posterior long-segment fixation using navigated pedicle screws became the predominant treatment strategy, with no mechanical failures requiring revision observed in this group during the available follow-up. Additional anterior stabilization remained important when direct anterior decompression or structural anterior column reconstruction was required.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetics of isoflurane uptake and disposition in piglets.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Isoflurane is a cardioprotective inhalational anesthetic widely used in cardiac surgery, but prior studies focused primarily on uptake parameters. We examined both uptake and disposition in piglets using inspiratory, end-tidal, arterial, and mixed venous concentrations.
METHODS: Seven piglets received a fixed inspiratory concentration of 2% isoflurane during a 2-h uptake phase, followed by a 2-h disposition phase. Inspiratory and end-tidal concentrations were measured using an infrared analyzer. Femoral arterial blood and pulmonary artery mixed venous blood were sampled to determine isoflurane concentrations via gas chromatography at 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, and 120 min during both uptake and disposition phases. Hemodynamic and respiratory parameters were recorded simultaneously. Body uptake and disposition rates were calculated by multiplying the difference between arterial and pulmonary artery blood concentrations by cardiac output.
RESULTS: The rates of isoflurane body uptake increased gradually during the initial 20 min, reaching 20.7 mL min-1, before slowly declining to 10.5 mL min-1 by 120 min. Continuous decreases in washout rates were observed during the subsequent disposition phase. The concentration-time curves for end-tidal, arterial blood, and pulmonary artery blood concentrations fit well with zero-order input and first-order disposition kinetics. Arterial and pulmonary artery blood concentrations were best modeled by a two-compartment system. Only 14.5% of the isoflurane accumulated during the 2-h uptake phase was eliminated during the subsequent 2-h disposition phase.
CONCLUSION: Under a fixed inspiratory isoflurane concentration, body uptake in piglets was empirically approximated by a zero-order input process over the modeled 120-min uptake interval, whereas the subsequent 2-h disposition phase followed first-order kinetics and was best described by a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model.

articles.title: Circadian-melatonin signaling in general anesthesia: molecular mechanisms and perioperative implications.
articles.abstract: Anesthesia and surgery are delivered to a temporally organized organism whose physiology is governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peripheral molecular clocks, and pineal melatonin signaling. This review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence on how anesthetic agents, surgical stress, and the perioperative environment interact with circadian and melatonergic signaling, and on whether that interaction can be targeted therapeutically. In rodent and cellular studies, volatile and intravenous anesthetics alter clock function in an agent- and phase-dependent manner; proposed mechanisms include GABAergic and glutamatergic modulation of entrainment, transcriptional and chromatin-level repression of CLOCK-BMAL1/PER-CRY signaling, and metabolic coupling through CaMK-CREB, AMPK, SIRT1, and GSK-3β. These mechanisms have not been confirmed in humans. In patients, these effects are inseparable from surgical injury, opioids, fasting, inflammation, and disrupted light-dark exposure, all of which suppress melatonin amplitude, delay its onset, and promote internal desynchrony. Melatonin signals through MT1 and MT2 receptors to produce chronobiotic, anxiolytic, and antinociceptive effects, whereas the mitochondrial, redox, and anti-inflammatory actions, described almost exclusively in animal and cellular models, require substantially higher exposures and have not been demonstrated in surgical patients; the two arms are pharmacologically distinct and should not be pooled. Clinically, preoperative anxiolysis with melatonin in adults is the most consistently supported indication, whereas evidence for postoperative sleep, analgesia, delirium prevention, and organ protection remains heterogeneous and of low certainty. Most trials have used fixed clock-time dosing without measuring internal circadian phase or achieved plasma exposure, so null results cannot distinguish an ineffective mechanism from an inadequate intervention. The circadian-melatonin axis remains a plausible perioperative target, but clinical translation requires phase-aware, exposure-informed, and adequately powered trials.

articles.title: Nursing radiation-protection compliance and 30-day wound and pin-site adverse events after supracondylar humerus fracture fixation in children.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fluoroscopy is integral to operative fixation of supracondylar humerus fractures in children, but case-level nursing radiation-protection compliance (NRPC) has not been well characterised as a potential marker of broader perioperative process quality. We examined the association between NRPC and early wound- and pin-site-related outcomes.
METHODS: We conducted a single-centre retrospective cohort study of children aged <14 years who underwent fluoroscopy-assisted operative fixation for supracondylar humerus fractures at The Second Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, China, between 2018 and 2023. NRPC was assessed using three binary components reflecting recent formal radiation-protection training, absence of radiation-protection-related quality-control deductions, and documented implementation of radiation-protection measures during the index procedure. Components were summed to a 0-3 score and categorised as Low (0-1) or High (2-3) NRPC. The primary outcome was any wound- or pin-site-related adverse event within 30 days. The primary multivariable logistic regression model adjusted for calendar year, Gartland classification, operative duration, and emergency surgical status. Firth penalized regression, ordinal-score analyses, and separate nurse- and surgeon-clustered mixed-effects models were performed as sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Of 360 children identified, 256 children met the eligibility criteria and had ascertainable NRPC and primary-outcome data; 164 (64%) were classified as High NRPC and 92 (36%) as Low NRPC. Overall, 37/256 children (14.5%) experienced the primary outcome. The observed event rate was 11.0% (18/164) in the High NRPC group and 20.7% (19/92) in the Low NRPC group, corresponding to a crude OR of 2.11 (95% CI 1.04-4.27; p = 0.037) for Low versus High NRPC. In the primary adjusted model, the association was attenuated and imprecise (adjusted OR 1.70, 95% CI 0.80-3.57; p = 0.165). Firth penalized regression yielded OR 1.67 (95% CI 0.80-3.49; p = 0.168), while separate mixed-effects models yielded OR 1.65 (95% CI 0.76-3.58; p = 0.205) for nurse clustering and OR 1.68 (95% CI 0.77-3.66; p = 0.190) for surgeon clustering. Per 1-point increase in the NRPC score, the adjusted OR was 0.70 (95% CI 0.48-1.02; p = 0.061).
CONCLUSION: Higher NRPC was associated with lower unadjusted rates of 30-day wound- and pin-site-related adverse events, but the association was attenuated and statistically imprecise after temporal and clinical adjustment. Similar directional estimates across sensitivity analyses support NRPC as an exploratory marker of broader perioperative process quality rather than as an independently established predictor or causal determinant of wound outcomes.

articles.title: Safety and Outcomes of Prone Positioning in the Early Postoperative Period following Cardiac Surgery.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate prone positioning (PP) safety and its respiratory and hemodynamic effects in patients with moderate-to-severe respiratory failure after cardiac surgery via median sternotomy.
DESIGN: Retrospective, single-center, observational cohort study.
SETTING: Cardiovascular intensive care unit at a tertiary academic hospital.
PARTICIPANTS: Thirty-eight consecutive adult patients undergoing PP for acute respiratory failure within 30 days of median sternotomy cardiac surgery between 2004 and 2024.
INTERVENTIONS: Protocolized PP sessions under deep sedation, neuromuscular blockade, and advanced hemodynamic monitoring. Median PP duration was 24 hours (IQR 16-26); 47.4% underwent their first session within 5 postoperative days.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The primary endpoint was PP-related complications (mediastinitis/sternal dehiscence). Secondary endpoints included gas exchange, vasoactive requirements, and in-hospital mortality. Mediastinitis occurred in one patient (2.6%), comparable to non-proned populations. PP significantly improved oxygenation, with the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio increasing from 82.8 ± 26.1 mmHg at baseline to 177.5 ± 68.9 mmHg at 4 hours into the maneuver and to 175.0 ± 70.8 mmHg at PP completion (both p < 0.001). No significant hemodynamic deterioration or increased vasoactive support occurred. Overall mortality was 44.7%. Advanced age (≥75 years) and baseline hypercapnia (PaCO₂ ≥50 mmHg) were independent predictors of mortality.
CONCLUSION: PP was safe after recent median sternotomy and elicited a marked improvement in oxygenation without increasing sternal complications. These findings support considering PP for selected patients with moderate-to-severe postoperative adult respiratory distress syndrome following cardiac surgery.

articles.title: A physiology-based approach to ROTEM interpretation for bleeding management in cardiac surgery: A narrative review.
articles.abstract: Perioperative bleeding after cardiac surgery is common, multifactorial, and resource intensive. Conventional coagulation tests are often delayed and do not describe clot development in whole blood, whereas rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) provides point-of-care information about clot initiation, clot firmness, residual heparin effect, and fibrinolysis. This narrative review summarizes guideline statements, randomized trials, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant mechanistic literature on viscoelastic testing in cardiac surgery. Literature was identified through targeted searches of PubMed-indexed and major cardiothoracic anesthesia sources, prioritizing patient blood management guidelines, studies of ROTEM- or thromboelastometry-guided transfusion algorithms, and evidence relevant to FIBTEM, HEPTEM, protamine, fibrinogen replacement, platelet contribution, and antifibrinolytic therapy. The review proposes a stepwise approach that begins with clinical context, evaluates EXTEM clotting time, integrates early EXTEM and FIBTEM clot amplitude, uses INTEM and HEPTEM to distinguish residual heparin from non-heparin causes of delayed clot initiation, screens for hyperfibrinolysis, and requires repeat testing after targeted intervention. The framework is intended to complement local transfusion protocols and patient blood management programs, support interdisciplinary communication, and reduce empiric transfusion.

articles.title: Multidimensional prognostic value of preoperative Prognostic Nutritional Index for postoperative outcomes in older adults undergoing major open abdominal surgery.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the predictive value of the preoperative Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) for multidimensional postoperative outcomes in elderly patients undergoing major abdominal surgery.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 761 patients aged ≥65 years from 2015 to 2025. Patients were stratified into low-PNI (<40) and high-PNI (≥40) groups. The primary outcome was postoperative delirium within 7 days. Secondary outcomes included 90-day mortality, Clavien-Dindo classification, postoperative hospital stay, and functional recovery milestones (time to first ambulation, oral intake, and defecation). Multivariable regression models (logistic, Cox proportional hazards, and competing risk Fine-Gray models) were employed, adjusting for age, ASA grade, surgical factors, and comorbidities. PNI was further stratified into four categories (<35, 35-40, 40-45, and >45) for dose-response trend analysis.
RESULTS: Compared to the low-PNI group, the high-PNI group had a significantly lower risk of postoperative delirium (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] =0.21, 95% confidence interval [CI]:0.13-0.35, P < 0.001), 90-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] = 0.22, 95% CI: 0.10-0.48, P < 0.001), and severe complications (OR = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.12-0.27, P < 0.001). In the competing risk analysis, high PNI was independently associated with faster achievement of all functional recovery milestones (all subdistribution hazard ratios [SHR] >1, P < 0.001). The dose-response analysis confirmed a significant gradient effect: Each increment in PNI category was associated with progressively lower risks of adverse events and faster recovery.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative PNI is a robust, independent predictor of multiple postoperative outcomes in elderly abdominal surgery patients. As a simple and cost-effective tool, PNI is well suited for preoperative risk stratification and guiding personalized perioperative management.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning for prediction of postoperative complications: A systematic review focused on anesthesiology, perioperative risk stratification, and clinical applicability.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used to predict postoperative complications, but their clinical value for anesthesiologists depends on more than discrimination alone. This systematic review evaluated AI- and ML-based models for predicting postoperative complications in surgical patients, with emphasis on model performance, validation, calibration, timing of predictor availability, interpretability, and clinical applicability. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 principles. Eligible studies developed, validated, or compared AI/ML models for postoperative complication prediction and reported at least one performance metric. Risk of bias was assessed using Prediction model Risk of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST), and reporting quality was interpreted in light of Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) principles. Thirty-five studies were included. The most frequently predicted outcomes were acute kidney injury, postoperative delirium, cardiovascular complications, infectious complications, and composite postoperative morbidity. Reported best-model discrimination ranged approximately from 0.70 to 0.97. Models incorporating intraoperative variables often showed stronger performance than preoperative-only models, particularly for acute kidney injury and infectious complications, but this reduced their usefulness for early preoperative decision-making. External validation was uncommon, calibration was inconsistently reported, and the analysis domain was the most frequent source of concern in PROBAST assessment. Current AI/ML models for postoperative complication prediction are promising, but their routine use in anesthesiology requires stronger external validation, transparent calibration, workflow integration, and clinically interpretable decision-support strategies.

articles.title: Comparing perioperative complications and recovery outcomes of neuraxial versus general anesthesia in hip fracture surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To compare perioperative complications and recovery outcomes between neuraxial and general anesthesia in adult patients undergoing hip fracture surgery. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched from 2000 to April 25, 2026. Studies comparing neuraxial and general anesthesia were included. Outcomes included mortality (in-hospital, 30-day, 90-day, 1-year), intraoperative hypotension, postoperative delirium, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), pneumonia, acute kidney injury (AKI), length of hospital stay, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled effect estimates. Nineteen RCTs (n = 4,742) were included. No significant differences were observed between neuraxial and general anesthesia for mortality at any time point, postoperative delirium, ACS, pneumonia, or PONV. Neuraxial anesthesia was associated with a lower risk of intraoperative hypotension (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.40-0.77) and AKI (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38-0.84), and shorter length of hospital stay (MD - 0.58 days, 95% CI - 1.08 to - 0.07). Heterogeneity was substantial for some outcomes. Neuraxial anesthesia decreases the risk of intraoperative hypertension and acute kidney injury in comparison to general anesthesia in patients undergoing hip fracture repair.

articles.title: Quantitative electromyographic train-of-four monitoring to determine rocuronium infusion requirements during major surgery in pediatric patients.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are commonly used during anesthetic care to facilitate endotracheal intubation, prevent intraoperative movement, and provide muscle relaxation during surgical procedures. Options for dosing include both intermittent bolus administration and continuous infusion.
METHODS: This prospective study investigated rocuronium infusion requirements during intraoperative care in a cohort of pediatric patients, using an electromyography (EMG)-based train-of-four monitor. Neuromuscular block (NMB) was provided by an initial intravenous bolus of rocuronium (0.5-0.6 mg/kg), followed by a continuous rocuronium infusion at 0.6 mg/kg/h, and titrated to maintain a train-of-four count (TOFC) of 1/4.
RESULTS: The final study cohort included 48 pediatric patients, ranging in age from 3 months to 18 years (median age 13 years) and in weight from 5.2 to 132 kg (median weight 55.9 kg). The total rocuronium infusion time across all patients was 11,735 min. The median initial bolus dose of rocuronium was 0.8 mg/kg (interquartile range [IQR]: 0.7, 1.1 mg/kg). The infusion dose ranged from 0.1 to 0.72 mg/kg/h (median dose 0.48 mg/kg/h). Twenty-six patients (54%) received at least one rescue bolus to maintain one twitch in the TOFC. Among these patients, the majority (n = 15, 58%) received only one rescue bolus during the procedure. The median rescue bolus dose administered was 0.2 mg/kg (IQR: 0.2, 0.3). There were no cases of residual NMB, no need for additional rescue reversal after the initial dose of sugammadex, or other adverse effects related to anesthetic care.
CONCLUSION: Rocuronium infusion requirements can be accurately titrated using an EMG-based TOF monitor during prolonged surgical procedures. This study accurately provides a dosing scheme for the intraoperative use of rocuronium infusions during these procedures, demonstrating that the median infusion requirement is 0.48 mg/kg/h.

articles.title: A comparative study between hyperbaric prilocaine 2% versus hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% for intrathecal anesthesia in cesarean section.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bupivacaine has a variable block duration, while prilocaine provides a shorter, more predictable block but is less used in obstetrics. The goal is to compare the onset and duration of block induced by hyperbaric prilocaine 2% and hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% in intrathecal anesthesia for women undergoing elective cesarean sections (CS).
METHODS: A prospective randomized and double-blind clinical trial included 144 individuals with uncomplicated pregnancies belonging to the American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status I or II. Patients were divided into two equal groups randomly: prilocaine group (Group A): received 60 mg hyperbaric prilocaine 2% (3 ml) intrathecally, and bupivacaine group (Group B): received 12.5 mg hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% (2.5 ml) intrathecally and 0.5 ml of normal saline. As 60 mg hyperbaric prilocaine 2% is equipotent to 12.5 mg of hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5%. Onset time and duration of sensory and motor block recorded.
RESULTS: Mean arterial blood pressure was higher in Group A than in Group B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min (P < 0.001), with no differences at baseline or 25-45 min. Intraoperative heart rate was substantially higher in Group B at 5, 10, 15, and 20 min, with comparable values at other time points. Visual analog scale (VAS) scores were higher in Group A at 1 h (P < 0.001) but substantially lower at 2 and 3 h (P < 0.001); VAS scores at 4 h were similar between groups.
CONCLUSION: Hyperbaric prilocaine 2% provides faster onset, shorter sensory and motor block duration, more stable hemodynamics and less maternal hypotension than hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% in CS, with similar neonatal outcomes and side effects.

articles.title: Monitoring neuromuscular block in infants and children.
articles.abstract: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) have become a key component of anesthetic care as a means of facilitating endotracheal intubation, providing surgical relaxation of the skeletal musculature, and ensuring an immobile patient during surgical procedures. Although generally safe and effective, dosing of NMBAs and their reversal with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (such as neostigmine) or encapsulating agents (such as sugammadex) require monitoring, including a means to quantify the degree of neuromuscular (NM) block and residual NM function. Although clinical evaluations (head lift, hip flexion, and grip strength) or respiratory parameters (tidal volume and vital capacity) have historically be used to assess return of muscle strength, these parameters have been shown to be insensitive means of detecting residual NM block and weakness. Furthermore, these subjective evaluations are not feasible during intraoperative anesthetic care and therefore cannot be used to guide initial and ongoing dosing of NMBAs, nor the adequacy of reversal. Assessing NM function using a peripheral nerve stimulator (PNS) and visual observation of the train-of-four (TOF) response was previously accepted as the standard monitor when administering NMBAs. However, subjective visual or tactile assessment is an indirect and insensitive measure of NM function, and measurement of the TOF ratio (T4/T1) is not feasible. It is generally accepted that a quantitatively determined TOF ratio ≥0.90 is the optimal method to document return of baseline NM function, avoid residual paralysis, and confirm the safe timing of tracheal extubation. The following educational review discusses the normal function of the NM junction, outlines clinical concerns of inadequate reversal of NM block, and reviews quantitative TOF monitoring with an emphasis on its use in the pediatric patient.

articles.title: Defining plasma concentration ranges for central nervous system and cardiovascular toxicity of local anesthetics: A systematic review.
articles.abstract: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), although rare, can lead to severe central nervous system (CNS) and cardiovascular system (CVS) complications, including seizures and cardiac arrest. Reliable human plasma concentration thresholds associated with CNS and CVS toxicity remain poorly defined, limiting clinicians' ability to contextualize measured concentrations. This systematic review aimed to evaluate human data to define plasma concentration ranges associated with moderate and severe CNS and CVS toxicity following the administration of commonly used local anesthetics in adult and pediatric patients. This systematic review was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251274220). MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception through December 27, 2025, with no language restrictions. Eligible studies included human participants who developed CNS or CVS toxicity after exposure to bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine, or ropivacaine, with reported arterial or venous plasma concentrations measured within 5 min of symptom onset. Due to substantial heterogeneity, evidence was synthesized narratively without a formal meta-analysis. Forty-eight studies were included, predominantly case reports and case series, with a smaller number of pharmacokinetic studies. CNS toxicity generally occurred at lower plasma concentrations than severe CVS toxicity across all agents. Moderate CNS symptoms occurred at lower concentrations than seizures or coma, whereas severe CNS toxicity often overlapped with concentrations associated with moderate CVS toxicity. This review provides clinically relevant plasma concentration ranges associated with CNS and CVS toxicity for commonly used local anesthetics in humans. These values should not be interpreted as absolute toxicity thresholds but may aid clinicians in interpreting plasma concentrations during suspected LAST events. Clinical Trial Number: CRD420251274220.

articles.title: The opioid-sparing efficacy of ultrasound-guided quadro-iliac plane block versus transversus abdominis plane block after cesarean delivery: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-cesarean pain comprises somatic and visceral components, yet the transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block addresses only somatic afferents. The quadro-iliac plane block (QIPB) is a novel posterior fascial plane technique theorized to provide broader coverage of both nociceptive pathways. Comparative evidence between these techniques in the obstetric population is lacking.
METHODS: This prospective, randomized, single-blind, controlled trial enrolled 36 ASA I-II parturients undergoing elective cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia at Mansoura University Hospital (IRB: R.25.04.3145; PACTR202505592518309). Patients were randomized 1:1 to bilateral ultrasound-guided TAP block (n = 18) or bilateral QIPB (n = 18). The primary outcome was total nalbuphine consumption within 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included time to first rescue analgesic request, postoperative Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain scores, hemodynamic parameters, and adverse effects.
RESULTS: Twenty-four-hour nalbuphine consumption was significantly lower in the QIPB group (5.28 ± 0.96 mg vs. 9.56 ± 2.04 mg; P < 0.001), representing a 45% reduction. The time to first rescue analgesia was significantly prolonged with QIPB (9.78 ± 1.22 vs. 7.0 ± 1.32 hours; P < 0.001). VAS scores were significantly lower at 6 and 12 hours postoperatively (P < 0.001 and P = 0.007, respectively). No clinically relevant hemodynamic differences were observed between groups, and adverse event rates were comparable.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with the TAP block, the QIPB provides superior and more prolonged postoperative analgesia following elective cesarean delivery, with a favorable safety profile. These findings support further evaluation of the QIPB within multimodal Enhanced Recovery After Cesarean protocols, particularly where intrathecal opioid is not employed, and inform the design of future multicenter trials.

articles.title: Mapping the scientific landscape of regional analgesia for total knee arthroplasty: A bibliometric study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is associated with significant postoperative pain, and regional anesthesia (RA)-based analgesic strategies have evolved substantially over the past three decades. Understanding the intellectual structure, influential publications, and thematic evolution of analgesic techniques for TKA is essential to contextualize current practice and guide future research.
METHODS: A bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Scopus database. Publications related to analgesic strategies and RA for TKA published between 1998 and 2026 were retrieved and analyzed. Data were exported in BibTeX and comma-separated values (CSV) formats and analyzed using the Bibliometrix package (R-Studio: Posit PBC, Massachusetts, United States) and visualization of similarity (VOS) viewer. Bibliometric indicators included annual publication trends, citation analysis, prolific authors, institutions, countries, journals, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, and co-citation networks to identify highly cited and landmark publications.
RESULTS: A total of 288 publications were included. Annual scientific output demonstrated a steady increase, with a marked surge after 2013. Early highly cited literature focused predominantly on neuraxial techniques and femoral nerve block-based analgesia. From 2013 onward, a distinct shift toward motor-sparing strategies was observed, coinciding with landmark publications on the adductor canal block. More recent research emphasized multimodal and anatomy-driven approaches, including adductor canal block-based bundles, posterior knee pain management strategies, and periarticular infiltration (PAI) techniques. Citation and co-citation analyses identified a small number of highly influential publications that shaped successive phases of analgesic strategy evolution in TKA.
CONCLUSIONS: This bibliometric analysis demonstrates a clear temporal evolution of analgesic strategies for TKA, progressing from neuraxial and femoral nerve-dominant paradigms toward motor-sparing and multimodal RA techniques. A limited number of landmark publications have disproportionately influenced this transition. These findings provide a macroscopic overview of research trends, highlight foundational evidence underpinning current practice, and identify areas for future investigation in TKA analgesia.

articles.title: Blocking the pericapsular nerve group against the lumbar erector spinae plane for pain management following total hip replacement: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Both the pericapsular nerve group block (PENG) and the lumbar erector spinae plane block (L-ESPB) are emerging regional anesthetic techniques, yet comparative data remain limited.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This randomized, controlled study included 60 patients undergoing THA, assigned to receive either a PENG block (n = 30) or an L-ESPB (n = 30). The primary outcome was the time to the first analgesic request. Secondary outcomes included total analgesic consumption, pain scores measured by the numeric rating scale (NRS) at rest and during movement, assessment of quadriceps motor strength, and any block-related complications. All participants were administered a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol.
FINDINGS: The PENG group demonstrated a significantly longer time to the first analgesic request compared to the L-ESPB group (12.88 ± 4.56 hour vs. 8.45 ± 3.49 hours; P < 0.001) and lower total analgesic consumption (25.84 mg ± 5.59 mg vs. 40.18 mg ± 7.89 mg; P < 0.001). Resting NRS scores were comparable early postoperatively but were significantly lower in the PENG group at 24 hours. Dynamic pain scores were consistently lower in the PENG group across all time points. Quadriceps motor weakness was more frequent in the PENG group at 6 hours (P = 0.04), but resolved completely by 12 hours. No major complications were observed in either group.
CONCLUSION: For postoperative analgesia following THA, the PENG block is superior to L-ESPB, offering prolonged analgesia and reduced opioid requirements. Although transient quadriceps weakness may occur, it resolves early without clinical sequelae.

articles.title: Efficacy of intravenous lipid emulsion in enhancing the recovery of spinal anesthesia: An exploratory double-blinded, randomized controlled study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Prolonged motor recovery associated with spinal anesthesia (SA) limits its utility in day-case surgery. We evaluated the efficacy of intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) in accelerating recovery from sensory-motor blockade in patients undergoing day-case surgery under SA.
METHODS: In a double-blinded randomized study, 60 adult patients who underwent short surgical procedures under SA were randomly allocated to receive either ILE (1.5 mL/kg bolus, followed by 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion) over 30 minutes (test group) or normal saline (control group) in the immediate postoperative period. The primary objective was the time to recovery of sensory and motor blockade. The study was registered in the clinical trial registry of India CTRI/2021/11/038080 dated 11/6/2021 (www.ctri.nic.in).
RESULTS: Demographic characteristics (age, gender, American Society of Anaesthesiologists physical status grading, height, and weight) were comparable between the two groups. The recovery of sensory (200.6 ± 19.8 min versus 237.1 ± 17.9 min, P ≤ 0.001, absolute standard difference: --1.9 (95% confidence interval [CI]: --2.5 to --1.3) and motor block (157.8 ± 13.1 min versus 193.6 ± 23.0 min, P ≤ 0.001, absolute standard difference: --1.9 (95% CI: --2.5 to --1.3) were significantly faster in the test group compared to the control group.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates that 20% ILE accelerates recovery from SA (both sensory and motor blocks), highlighting its potential utility in day-case surgery. Further trials on a larger sample size are required to validate the same.Trial Registration: CTRI/2021/11/038080 dated 11/6/2021.

articles.title: Comparative effectiveness of liposomal bupivacaine versus standard bupivacaine alone for brachial plexus block in upper limb surgery: A meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Single-injection brachial plexus block is widely used for postoperative analgesia in upper limb surgery, particularly shoulder arthroplasty, rotator cuff repair, and distal radius fixation. However, the finite duration of standard bupivacaine may be followed by rebound pain and opioid rescue requirements. Liposomal bupivacaine is an extended-release formulation designed to prolong local anesthetic exposure, but randomized trials comparing liposomal bupivacaine added to standard bupivacaine with standard bupivacaine alone have reported inconsistent results. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and trial registries were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) enrolling adults undergoing upper limb surgery with interscalene or supraclavicular brachial plexus block were eligible if they compared perineural liposomal bupivacaine, generally combined with standard bupivacaine, with standard bupivacaine alone. The primary outcome was postoperative opioid consumption expressed as morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Secondary outcomes included early postoperative pain scores, quality of recovery, satisfaction, sensory or motor outcomes, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs) using random-effects models. The search identified 51 records, of which eight RCTs published between 2017 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria (n = 684 analyzed patients). Six studies contributed to the opioid-consumption meta-analysis. Liposomal bupivacaine was associated with a statistically significant but modest reduction in postoperative opioid consumption (MD = -11.86 MME, 95% CI: -20.17 to -3.56; P = 0.005; I2 = 46.0%). Six studies contributed to the early pain meta-analysis that showed lower pain scores with liposomal bupivacaine by approximately one point on a 0-10 scale (MD = -1.03, 95% CI: -1.34 to -0.72; P < 0.001; I2 = 19.1%). Recovery and satisfaction outcomes favored liposomal bupivacaine in selected trials, whereas longer-term function and overall adverse-event profiles were generally similar between groups. For adult upper limb surgery performed with brachial plexus block, liposomal bupivacaine added to standard bupivacaine provides a small early analgesic and opioid-sparing advantage compared with standard bupivacaine alone. The average effect is statistically significant but modest, and routine use for all patients may not be justified. Selective use in patients at higher risk of rebound pain or opioid-related harm appears more appropriate pending larger pragmatic trials and cost-effectiveness analyses. Categories: Anesthesiology, Regional Anesthesia, Orthopedic Surgery.

articles.title: Ultrasound with nerve stimulation versus ultrasound alone for obturator nerve block in transurethral resection of bladder tumor: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The obturator nerve block (ONB) is commonly used during transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) to prevent adductor spasm. Both ultrasound (US)-guided and nerve stimulation (NS) techniques are available, but whether adding NS to US improves block outcomes remains debated.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science up to 6 April 2026. The rate of adductor spasm prevention, block performance time, onset time, number of needle passes, patient and surgeon satisfaction, and complications were evaluated. Pooled odds ratios (OR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated.
RESULTS: Five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comprising 451 patients were analyzed. The US + NS group significantly improved block rate of adductor spasm prevention compared to US alone (OR = 3.20, 95% CI: 1.72-5.93, P < 0.001; I² =0%), but required longer performance time (MD = 1.99 min, 95% CI: 1.51-2.47, P < 0.001; I² =91%). No differences were found in needle passes or onset time. Complications were rare and comparable.
CONCLUSIONS: Combining nerve stimulation with US guidance for ONB significantly improves rate of adductor spasm prevention and patient/surgeon satisfaction compared to US guidance alone, although with a longer block performance time. The two techniques are similar in onset time and needle passes. US + NS is recommended for ONB during TURBT.

articles.title: Target-level epidural catheter placement in lower thoracic spine using preprocedural ultrasound marking: A prospective observational study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Accurate insertion of catheters into the target intervertebral level is essential for effective epidural anesthesia. However, conventional palpation-based methods are often unreliable, resulting in unintended motor weakness of the lower limbs when insertion is performed at the lower thoracic level. In this study, we evaluated the accuracy of placing an epidural catheter at the target intervertebral level in the lower thoracic spine using preprocedural ultrasound marking.
METHODS: In this prospective observational study, we enrolled 40 adults undergoing elective surgery with planned lower thoracic epidural anesthesia. After identifying the spinal level using ultrasound and marking the spinous and transverse processes as landmarks, the epidural catheter was placed at the target level. Postoperative radiographs were used to confirm the actual placement level. Accuracy was assessed based on whether the level at which the epidural catheter was actually placed matched the target intervertebral level.
RESULTS: Of the 40 patients, data of 37 were included in the final analysis. The accuracy rate relative to the target intervertebral level was 89.2% (33/37; 95% confidence interval: 74.6-97.0%). No major misplacements (≧2 interspaces) were observed.
CONCLUSION: In the lower thoracic spine, the use of preprocedural ultrasound marking enabled highly accurate placement of epidural catheters at the target intervertebral level.

articles.title: Rectus sheath block for postoperative analgesia in abdominal surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: The rectus sheath block is a potentially effective regional anesthetic technique for postoperative analgesia. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness across different surgical approaches and comparator techniques has remained inconsistent. We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate the postoperative analgesic effectiveness of the rectus sheath block in abdominal surgery. Our study adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. In October 2025, we searched four databases (PUBMED, OVID Medline, SCOPUS, and Web of Science) for randomized controlled trials assessing the analgesic efficacy of the rectus sheath block following abdominal surgery. The primary outcomes were pain scores at rest measured at 0-2, 10-12, and 12-24 hours postoperatively. The secondary outcome was postoperative 24-hour intravenous morphine-equivalent consumption. Thirty-one randomized controlled trials involving 1076 participants who received the rectus sheath block and 1,065 who received alternative analgesic care were included. The rectus sheath block significantly reduced postoperative pain at 0-2 hours (mean difference [MD], -1.46, 95% CI, [ -2.26 to -0.66]; P < 0.001), 10-12 hours (MD, -0.94, 95% CI, [ -1.40 to -0.48]; P < 0.001), and 12-24 hours (MD, -0.65, 95% CI, [ -1.07 to -0.23]; P = 0.002). Twenty four-hour intravenous morphine-equivalent consumption was significantly lower with the rectus sheath block (MD, -7.40, 95% CI, [ -11.86 to -2.94]; P = 0.001). Rectus sheath block was associated with reduced postoperative pain scores and reduced opioid use in the first 24 hours after abdominal surgery. Clinical trial registration: CRD420251208643 (PROSPERO).

articles.title: Comparative evaluation of sciatic obturator femoral nerve block technique versus central neuraxial blockade for anesthesia and post-operative analgesia for below knee orthopedic trauma surgeries.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Trauma and Surgery lead to various hemodynamic and metabolic changes occurring in our body affecting the hemostasis is unpredictable manner. We conducted this study considering the blunting of compensatory responses which could be blunted because of the sympathetic block due to spinal anesthesia. In this study we have compared a single puncture technique of major lower limb nerve block [Sciatic, Obturator, Femoral nerve block (S.O.F.T.)] with central neuraxial block.
METHOD: It was a prospective randomized study. Group T (n = 35)- Central neuraxial block; Group S (n = 35)- S.O.F.T. using single prick technique. The primary objective of the study was to assess and compare sensory and motor characteristic and total analgesic consumption post operatively in 24 hours between the two groups.
RESULTS: Group S led to significant decrease of mean arterial pressure at 2 min (Group T: 110.2 + 6.9, Group S: 127.9 + 8.1; P < 0.01), 4 min (Group T: 102.5 + 9.7, Group S: 129.5 + 7.7; P < 0.01), and 6 min (Group T: 101.8 + 9.3, Group S: 127.6 + 7.8; P < 0.01). The time of performance was more in Group S (Group T: 2.5 + 0.57, Group S: 12.76 + 0.76; P < 0.005). The onset and duration of S.U.V. sensory block was significantly increased in Group S. The time to first rescue analgesia was greater in Group S.
CONCLUSION: The One Prick technique to block Femoral, Sciatic and Obturator Nerve is a feasible and effective technique of anesthesia for successful conduction of below knee surgeries with no hemodynamic fluctuations.

articles.title: Procedural sedation and analgesia outside the operating room: Drug selection, safety, and emerging trends.
articles.abstract: Procedures performed outside the operating room now account for a substantial proportion of all anesthetic activity, with nonoperating room anesthesia projected to represent up to 50% of anesthetic interventions within the next decade. Workforce constraints in anesthesiology have accelerated the need for structured frameworks enabling nonanesthesiologists to provide procedural sedation and analgesia (PSA) safely.
