articles.title: The Future of AI in Critical Care: An Exploration in Ten Parables.
articles.abstract: We cannot know how artificial intelligence (AI) will ultimately change critical care, only that it is driving substantial change quickly. Through ten parables, we describe plausible benefits, harms, and trade-offs involving prognosis, monitoring, liability, research, clinical work, data governance, education, and triage. These parables are not predictions. They are intended to help clinicians, institutions, and regulators envision a range of potential scenarios and think broadly about which applications to pursue, which risks to consider, and which rules to establish before AI systems become entrenched. Each parable reveals how the outlook for AI in critical care is characterized by uncertainty. This includes uncertainty about what a single prediction means for the patient in front of us, how an application built and tested in one setting performs in another, accountability frameworks, professional practice and learning, patient privacy and autonomy, and more. Within each parable we try to keep visible what current evidence already supports and what remains speculative. We close with a set of questions designed to focus that speculation among the interested parties who will shape the future of AI in critical care.

articles.title: Beyond 28-Day Mortality: The Unfinished Story of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Survivorship.

Variation in Pediatric Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Development and Validation of a Survival Model for Risk-Standardized Survival Rates: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To develop and internally validate a multivariable prediction model for survival to hospital discharge after pediatric extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), and to use this model to derive risk-standardized survival rates (RSSRs) and quantify between-hospital variation in outcomes.
DESIGN: Retrospective multicenter cohort study.
SETTING: Hospitals contributing to the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry between 2020 and 2023.
PATIENTS: Children (< 18 yr) treated with ECPR for IHCA.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Eligible patients were identified from the ELSO Registry and split into derivation (N = 1060) and validation (N = 317) cohorts using a hospital-stratified split to preserve within-hospital clustering. Survival prediction models were derived using penalized logistic regression with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. A full-event model incorporating 14 routinely available clinical variables demonstrated fair discrimination (area under the curve, 0.728 in the derivation cohort and 0.678 in the validation cohort) and good calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, 0.995; Brier score, 0.222 in the validation cohort). This model was embedded in a multilevel logistic regression model to generate hospital-level RSSRs for centers reporting five or more ECPR cases. Between-hospital variation was quantified using the median odds ratio, which was 1.30 (95% CI, 1.11-1.93), indicating significant differences in survival likelihood between centers after adjusting for patient-level risk.
CONCLUSIONS: In a large, international cohort of pediatric ECPR patients, we developed and internally validated a clinically interpretable model for survival to hospital discharge. The model performance as a discriminator likely limits its use as a standalone tool for clinical decision-making. However, strong internal calibration allowed for determination of hospital-level RSSRs, which revealed significant inter-hospital variability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of developing a risk-adjustment model capable of estimating hospital-level RSSRs. Additional external validation and evaluation of residual case-mix differences are needed before such models can be used for benchmarking across pediatric ECPR centers.

articles.title: Candida Septic Shock: If Every Hour Matters, Who Requires Empiric Therapy?
Implementation of a same-session outpatient diode laser ablation pathway for suspected recurrent low-grade NMIBC: feasibility, safety, and early outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate feasibility, safety, tolerability, and early outcomes of a same-session "see-and-treat" pathway involving cold-cup biopsy followed by diode laser ablation during surveillance cystoscopy for suspected recurrent low-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed a prospectively maintained single-centre database of patients undergoing outpatient transurethral laser ablation (TULA) during surveillance cystoscopy. Eligible patients had one or two suspected low-grade papillary recurrences ≤ 1 cm. Procedures were performed without prior scheduling or intravesical anaesthesia, using intraurethral lidocaine gel. Biopsy was obtained whenever feasible.
RESULTS: Fifty-three patients underwent same-session ablation, completed in all without rescheduling, conversion to transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), or hospital admission; 50/53 (94.3%) underwent biopsy. Median pain score was 1 [IQR 1-2], and all patients preferred TULA over TURBT. One patient (1.9%) experienced immediate gross haematuria (Clavien-Dindo grade I). Among 52 patients with 30-day follow-up, 2 (3.8%) experienced gross haematuria (Clavien-Dindo grade I) and 2 (3.8%) developed urinary tract infections requiring antibiotics (Clavien-Dindo grade II); no Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ III events occurred. Biopsy identified pTa low-grade carcinoma in 18 (34.0%), pT0 in 27 (50.9%), carcinoma in situ (CIS) in 4 (7.5%), and intestinal-origin adenocarcinoma in 1 (1.9%). At 3 months, 46/49 (93.9%) had negative cystoscopy; only one had histologically confirmed urothelial recurrence (2.0%).
CONCLUSION: Same-session biopsy and diode laser ablation were feasible, safe, and well tolerated in selected patients. Biopsy provided clinically relevant information, including detection of unexpected CIS. Longer follow-up and comparative studies are required.

articles.title: A Feasibility Trial Examining Acupressure Wristbands in Ambulatory Surgery Patients at Risk for Post-Discharge Nausea and Vomiting.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (NV) can lead to complications like pain and bleeding. In ambulatory surgery patients, post-discharge NV impacts 40% to 80% of patients undergoing laparoscopically assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH). Pericardium 6 (PC6) acupressure may prevent postoperative NV in hospital, but little is known regarding its effect on post-discharge NV. The purpose of this study was to examine the feasibility of a trial to test the effects of bilateral PC6 acupressure wristbands plus usual care versus placebo plus usual care on post-discharge NV.
DESIGN: A parallel-arm feasibility randomized controlled trial was employed.
METHODS: Primary outcomes included rates of consent, randomization, intervention/placebo delivery, continuous wristband wear, and retention. Twenty participants undergoing ambulatory LAVH were randomized to either a) usual post-discharge NV care plus bilateral PC6 acupressure wristbands, or b) usual care with bilateral placebo wristbands. Wristbands were placed on arrival to the recovery room and worn until 24 hours after discharge. Follow-up calls were made to gather outcome data.
FINDINGS: Three a priori criteria for feasibility success were met: rates of randomization, continuous wear, and retention.
CONCLUSIONS: It was feasible to conduct a trial where a registered nurse delivered acupressure wristbands versus placebo wristbands to patients in the recovery room following LAVH under general anesthesia. Post-discharge symptom management is an important component of nursing practice. If acupressure wristbands are found to be effective at preventing post-discharge NV in larger trials, registered nurses are well-positioned to educate patients about a cost-effective intervention with minimal risk of side effects.

articles.title: Single-incision mini-sling (SIMS) under local anesthesia for stress urinary incontinence: A single-center prospective cohort study-12 months of follow-up.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a prevalent and costly condition, with an estimated lifetime risk of surgery reaching 20% by the age of 80 years. Single-incision mini-slings (SIMS) represent the latest advancement in midurethral sling technology, offering a minimally invasive alternative to traditional retropubic and transobturator tapes (TOT). Studies indicate comparable subjective and objective cure rates between SIMS and TOT, with potential advantages in postmenopausal women owing to earlier mobilization and reduced morbidity. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of SIMS under local anesthesia in the management of SUI.
METHODS: A prospective cohort study was conducted in a tertiary academic urogynecology unit from December 2019 to December 2024. Consecutive patients meeting the inclusion criteria were enrolled following a standardized diagnostic and treatment protocol. Informed consent was obtained, and ethical approval was granted by the institutional review board. All patients underwent SIMS placement (Altis©, Coloplast) performed by two experienced urogynecologists under local anesthesia. Sling tensioning was performed via a standardized cough stress test at bladder volumes equal to normal voiding volume, as per pre-operative urodynamics. Patients were followed for 3 weeks and 12 months post-surgery. Data analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel. Descriptive statistics were applied, and paired t-tests compared pre- and post-operative results. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.
RESULTS: A total of 124 women underwent SIMS for SUI, with a mean age of 63.8 ± 11.1 years and a body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters) of 29.0 ± 4.3. Among them, 21.8% had severe and 78.2% had moderate SUI, while 30.6% presented with mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Pre-operatively, mean International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire (ICIQ) Urinary Incontinence Short Form (ICIQ-UI-SF) and Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (ICIQ-FLUTS) scores were 14.3 ± 2.4 and 19.0 ± 6.0, respectively. All surgeries were performed in an ambulatory setting, with 95.2% discharged the same day. The mean surgical time was 31.5 ± 8.0 min, and peri-operative pain was 2.8 ± 1.8/10. At discharge, all but one patient had a negative stress test, and 99.2% would recommend the procedure. At 12 months, the composite outcome was successful for 103 (83.1%) patients, with an objective cure rate of 94.3% and a subjective cure rate of 83.1%. A clinically important difference in ICIQ-FLUTS was observed in 92.7% of cases. Patient Global Impression of Improvement (PGI-I, scores 1 or 2) was reported by 93.5%, and Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S, score 1) was reported by 83.9%. There were no cases of bladder perforation, major bleeding, mesh erosion, or reoperation.
CONCLUSION: The present study evaluates SIMS under local anesthesia as a minimally invasive and effective treatment for SUI, highlighting its potential benefits in post-operative recovery and resource optimization. The findings contribute to the ongoing advancements in SUI management, particularly in addressing modern healthcare challenges.

articles.title: When toxicity limits cure: Repositioning radiation in esophageal and rectal cancers by proton therapy.
articles.abstract: For locally advanced esophageal and rectal cancers, radiotherapy (RT) provides essential local control but is frequently limited by acute and late toxicities that erode survival and quality of life (QoL). Over the last decade, evidence has implicated radiation dose to the heart, lungs, bowel, and pelvic bone marrow in increased postoperative morbidity, cardiopulmonary deaths, and hematologic toxicity, compromising chemotherapy delivery and long-term outcomes. The physical properties of proton beam therapy (PBT), which eliminate exit dose and reduce integral dose, offer a fundamental advantage. Systematic evidence confirms PBT consistently lowers low- to intermediate-dose exposure to organs at risk (OARs). For esophageal cancer, robust dosimetric data show reductions of approximately 50-65% in mean heart dose and 40-50% in lung V5, translating to reduced total toxicity burden (TTB) and perioperative complications in randomized and real-world studies. In rectal cancer, PBT reduces pelvic bone marrow V10 by 40-55% and small bowel V15-V30 by 30-50%, a prerequisite for improving the tolerability of intensive regimens. While definitive Phase III survival data are awaited, current evidence supports the selective use of PBT to improve the therapeutic index of radiotherapy, allowing its benefits to be realized with less collateral damage.

articles.title: Disease Severity and Frailty Capture Complementary Dimensions of Surgical Risk in Octogenarians with Acute Cholecystitis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Age alone poorly characterizes perioperative risk in octogenarians with acute cholecystitis. Disease-specific severity, graded by the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18), and patient-level frailty, measured by the 5-item modified Frailty Index (mFI-5), may reflect different risk dimensions. We assessed their associations with severe morbidity and operative difficulty, whether they are complementary, and the incremental value of C-reactive protein (CRP).
METHODS: Retrospective single-center cohort of patients ≥80 undergoing cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis within 7 days (2010-2025). The primary endpoint was severe postoperative morbidity (Clavien-Dindo ≥IIIa); the secondary endpoint was difficult cholecystectomy (conversion, bile duct injury, blood loss ≥500mL, or operative time ≥120min). Multivariable logistic regression modeled TG18, mFI-5 (per point), and CRP (per 5mg/dL); complementary information was assessed by nested likelihood-ratio (LR) tests.
RESULTS: Among 336 patients, severe morbidity occurred in 22.0% and in-hospital mortality in 6.3%. Both scores were independently associated with severe morbidity (mFI-5 OR 1.41, 95% CI 1.06-1.86; TG18 Grade III vs I OR 2.66, 1.25-5.62), and adding TG18 to mFI-5 improved model fit (LR p=0.033). Difficult cholecystectomy (34.8%) was associated with TG18 Grade II (OR 2.28, 1.36-3.81) but not with mFI-5 (LR p=0.970). CRP added no information (both LR p>0.20). Discrimination was poor across all models (AUC ≤0.64).
CONCLUSIONS: In octogenarians, TG18 and mFI-5 capture complementary but non-equivalent dimensions of perioperative risk, TG18 relating to both morbidity and operative difficulty, frailty predominantly to postoperative vulnerability, whereas CRP adds little. Poor discrimination argues against using either as a standalone rule. Both should inform a multidimensional preoperative assessment.

articles.title: Cervical cancer in older women - A narrative review of age-specific management issues from the French cervical cancer guidelines group.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To summarize the available evidence on the management of cervical cancer in older women across early and advanced disease stages, with particular attention to treatment selection, feasibility, tolerance, and specific clinical situations, including cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Studies addressing surgery, radiotherapy, concurrent chemoradiotherapy, brachytherapy, para-aortic lymphadenectomy, cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse, and pre-treatment geriatric assessment were considered. The evidence was synthesized qualitatively according to six predefined clinical questions.
RESULTS: In early-stage disease, radical hysterectomy is feasible in selected fit elderly patients but is associated with increased perioperative morbidity, with advancing age. The available evidence does not establish whether surgery or definitive radiotherapy provides superior oncological outcomes in this population. In locally advanced cervical cancer, concurrent chemoradiotherapy appears to improve survival compared with radiotherapy alone in selected older patients, but with increased toxicity. Brachytherapy is associated with improved local control and survival, yet its use decreased with advancing age. No age-specific evidence demonstrated a survival benefit form pretreatment para-aortic lymphadenectomy. Data on cervical cancer associated with pelvic organ prolapse are limited to heterogeneous case reports and small retrospective studies. Pretreatment geriatric assessment influences treatment decisions in mixed cancer populations, but cervical cancer-specific outcome data are lacking.
CONCLUSION: Age-specific evidence remains limited and largely retrospective, and chronological age alone should not determine access to standard treatment. Treatment selection requires integration of tumor characteristics, frailty, comorbidities, functional status, expected treatment tolerance, quality of life, and patient preferences.
authors: members from the FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP

articles.title: Obesity Medications in Older Adults: A Geriatrics 5Ms Framework for Safe and Patient-Centered Prescribing.
articles.abstract: Obesity medications that act through gut-derived hormonal pathways include glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1), dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1/GIP), and emerging triple glucagon-like peptide-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon receptor agonists. These therapies are increasingly prescribed for weight management and glycemic control, as well as for their cardiometabolic and renal benefits. While these medications offer substantial benefits to patients across multiple health conditions, their use in older adults warrants heightened scrutiny. Older adults face increased risks of sarcopenia and frailty, and evidence from major clinical trials suggests that a substantial proportion of medication-associated weight loss agents may result in loss of lean mass, potentially posing risks for this population. Other adverse effects that may be more consequential in older adults include dehydration, malnutrition, perioperative aspiration, and fat-predominant weight regain after discontinuation. This paper provides a clinically oriented framework to guide prescribing decisions for older adults. Drawing on patient scenarios from common geriatric contexts, including frailty, cognitive impairment, glucocorticoid use, and surgical planning, we propose prescribing approaches that optimize therapeutic benefits while mitigating potential harms. We integrate these recommendations within the Geriatrics 5Ms Framework (Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most) to contextualize treatment within geriatrics practice. Lifestyle co-interventions, particularly resistance training, adequate protein intake, and ongoing functional monitoring, emerge as essential components for older adults receiving these therapies. We also discuss identifying priority areas for future research, including age-stratified clinical trials and the routine inclusion of body composition and physical function outcomes.

articles.title: The Influence of Anesthetic and Surgical Factors on Spinal Late Motor Responses: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Late motor responses, including F-waves and H-reflexes, are commonly recorded during electrophysiological diagnostic evaluation in awake patients. Although these responses could offer added value during intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, their use has not yet been widely adopted. This systematic review aims to assess current knowledge on how anesthetic and surgical factors influence the recording and monitoring of spinal late responses during surgery. The authors searched PubMed and EMBASE for relevant articles on studies of late response recording. Studies were considered eligible if the influence of one or more of the following parameters on late responses were assessed: (1) ventilation and metabolic parameters, (2) volatile agents, (3) intravenous agents, (4) neuromuscular blocking agents, (5) epidural or intrathecal agents, or (6) surgical factors. The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability. Sixty-two studies were included. Respiratory conditions like hypercapnia reduced H-reflex amplitude, whereas hyperoxia and intermittent hypoxia had limited impact. Volatile agents, including isoflurane, sevoflurane, and nitrous oxide decreased late response amplitudes, with dose-dependent effects. Most intravenous anesthetics, particularly propofol, reduced H-reflex amplitude and F-wave persistence in a dose-dependent manner. Conversely, ketamine was found to increase H-reflex amplitude. During spinal and vascular surgeries, H-reflex monitoring proved feasible and provided valuable supplementary data to the conventional motor evoked potential (MEP) and somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) modalities. This systematic review demonstrates that H-reflexes and F-waves are significantly influenced by anesthetic factors. The reviewed studies indicate that intravenous and volatile anesthetics significantly affect late responses, by reducing H-reflex and F-wave amplitudes, whereas latencies appear unaffected. The methodological quality varied significantly across the included studies and affects the interpretation of their conclusions. These findings support the potential integration of late response monitoring into intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) protocols, provided that anesthetic management and surgical context are carefully considered.

articles.title: Effect of intraoral glossopharyngeal nerve block on hemodynamic response to mouth retractor placement in transoral robotic surgery: a randomized clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Placement of rigid oral retractors during transoral robotic surgery (TORS) elicits a sympathetic hemodynamic response that may be harmful in high-risk patients. The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the oropharyngeal structures stimulated during retractor placement, yet no previous trial has evaluated glossopharyngeal nerve block (GPN block) for attenuating this response. In this prospective, single-center, randomized clinical trial, 42 patients (ASA I-II, aged 18-65 years) undergoing TORS were allocated 1:1 to the block group, which received bilateral intraoral GPN block with 2 mL of 2% lignocaine per side or the Control group, which received no block. The outcome assessor was blinded; no sham procedure was performed, and the anaesthesiologist performing the block was not blinded. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with a > 20% increase in mean arterial pressure (MAP) from the pre-retractor baseline within 10 minutes of Feyh-Kastenbauer retractor insertion. Bayesian logistic regression with a Normal (0, 5) prior on the group coefficient was used; the pre-specified decision criterion was a posterior probability of directional benefit P (ARD < 0) exceeding 0.95. The trial was registered in the Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI/2022/03/041013, dated 11 March 2022) https://ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/searchbyctri.php , with a date of first patient enrolment of 21/03/2022. The increase in MAP > 20% occurred in 8 of 21 patients (38.1%) in the control group versus 3 of 21 (14.3%) in the block group. The posterior mean absolute risk difference was - 23.9% (95% credible interval [CrI]: - 49.4% to 2.2%), with P (ARD < 0) = 0.964, exceeding the pre-specified threshold. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the direction of effect under neutral, sceptical, and optimistic priors (P(ARD < 0) range: 0.934-0.967), although the posterior probability under the sceptical prior did not exceed the prespecified 0.95 threshold; evidence was equivocal under the pessimistic prior (P(ARD < 0) = 0.57). Maximum MAP and heart rate were lower in the block group (P (difference < 0) = 0.998 and 0.995, respectively). Bispectral index values were comparable between groups throughout the procedure. The GPN block is associated with a high posterior probability of attenuating the hemodynamic response to mouth retractor placement in TORS. The credible intervals were wide, reflecting uncertainty about effect magnitude. A larger confirmatory trial assessing clinical endpoints is warranted.

articles.title: Medicarpin Alleviates Isoflurane-Induced Cognitive Dysfunction in Mice by Regulating the BDNF/TrkB Pathway.
articles.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) seriously threatens elderly surgical patients and has garnered substantial attention in recent years. Anesthesia and/or surgery-induced POCD remains a major issue. This study aimed to evaluate the potential protective effect of medicarpin, a bioactive pterocarpan, against isoflurane-induced cognitive dysfunction. The isoflurane exposure-induced cognitive dysfunction model was established using aged mice. We found that medicarpin reduced isoflurane exposure-induced neuroapoptosis, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial damage in hippocampal tissues and isoflurane-exposed HT22 cells. We also found that medicarpin prevented the inactivation of BDNF/TrkB pathway in cognitive dysfunction mice and isoflurane-exposed HT22 cells, implying that the neuroprotective effect of medicarpin might be mediated by the BDNF/TrkB signaling. Inhibition of TrkB signaling by K252a attenuated the beneficial effects of medicarpin against isoflurane‑induced neuronal damage in HT22 cells. These findings suggest that medicarpin improves cognitive dysfunction by suppressing neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction via activation of the BDNF/TrkB pathway. The results of this study provide important evidence for developing medicarpin into a potential therapeutic agent for POCD in elderly surgical patients.

articles.title: Comparison of sterile silicone studs and scalp infiltration with lignocaine for the attenuation of the hemodynamic and stress response to skull pin insertion during craniotomy in pediatric neurosurgical patients: a randomized controlled trial : Sterile silicone studs versus lignocaine infiltration for skull pin insertion.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Skull pin application during pediatric neurosurgery elicits a pronounced nociceptive and sympathetic response, adversely affecting cerebral hemodynamics. We compared the efficacy of sterile silicone studs (SSS) with pin site lignocaine infiltration in attenuating the response to skull pin insertion in pediatric neurosurgical patients.
METHODS: Sixty-four pediatric patients (≤ 12 years, ASA I-II) were randomized to receive either SSS (Group SS, n = 32) or 2 ml of 2% plain lignocaine infiltration (Group LO, n = 32) at each skull pin insertion site. We assessed the requirement of rescue analgesia (fentanyl). The hemodynamics (Heart rate, mean arterial pressure) were also recorded at baseline, at pin insertion and at 1, 3, 5, and 10 min post pin insertion. Perioperative complications related to skull pin insertion and surgeon satisfaction were also assessed.
RESULTS: Rescue fentanyl consumption was significantly lower in Group SS than Group LO (10.3 ± 7.5 µg vs. 18.5 ± 8.6 µg; Cohen's d = 1.02; 95% CI, 0.51-1.53; P < 0.001). Fewer patients required rescue analgesia in Group SS (65.6% vs. 90.6%; Relative Risk, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.05-1.81; P < 0.03). Group LO showed significantly higher HR and MAP at pin insertion and up to 10 min thereafter (P < 0.05). Minor pin-site bleeding was more frequent in Group LO, while surgeon satisfaction was higher in Group SS.
CONCLUSION: SSS effectively attenuated the hemodynamic response to skull pin insertion and reduced the need for rescue opioids. They offer a safe, non-pharmacological, opioid-sparing alternative to lignocaine infiltration. Larger multicenter trials are warranted to conclusively establish the safety of SSS.

articles.title: Hemorrhagic Vocal Fold Inflammation Following Endotracheal Intubation in a Patient Undergoing Endovascular Neurosurgery Under Dual Antiplatelet Therapy: A Case Report.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic vocal fold inflammation is an uncommon complication of endotracheal intubation. Its clinical course in patients receiving perioperative antithrombotic therapy remains unclear.
CASE PRESENTATION: A woman in her 60 s receiving dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) underwent endovascular neurosurgery with flow-diverter stent deployment and coil embolization. Endotracheal intubation was uneventful, and cuff pressure was appropriately maintained. Hoarseness developed on postoperative day 1, and laryngoscopy on day 2 revealed hemorrhagic vocal fold inflammation. Intraoperative fluoroscopic images suggested proximal migration of the endotracheal tube, with possible changes in tube and cuff position that may have contributed to minor vocal fold mucosal injury. The symptoms improved with conservative management, and complete recovery was confirmed at 1 month.
DISCUSSION: Hemorrhagic vocal fold inflammation occurred following apparently uneventful endotracheal intubation in a patient receiving perioperative antithrombotic therapy. Although the underlying mechanism remains uncertain, changes in endotracheal tube and cuff position during the procedure represent one possible contributing factor.

articles.title: Preoperative Predictors of Prolonged Hospital Stay after Appendectomy in Children: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To identify preoperative predictive factors of prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy in children.
METHODS: A prospective cohort study was carried out in a tertiary pediatric surgical referral center in Tunisia between January 2022 and December 2025. All consecutive children younger than 14 y who underwent appendectomy during the study period were eligible for inclusion.
RESULTS: During the study period, 653 pediatric patients underwent appendectomy, including 132 patients (20.2%) with prolonged hospital stay. The mean age was 9.5 ± 2.7 y, and 436 patients (66.8%) were male. Six variables emerged as independent predictive factors of prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy. These included age less than 6 y, duration of symptoms greater than 48 h, pre-hospital antibiotic use, Sun's Pediatric Comorbidity Index ≥3, Alvarado score ≥7, and CRP >90 mg/L. Among these predictors, elevated CRP demonstrated the strongest association with prolonged hospital stay.
CONCLUSIONS: Several simple and readily available preoperative factors were independently associated with prolonged hospital stay following appendectomy in children. Early recognition of these factors may support improved perioperative planning, optimized resource allocation, and more accurate communication with caregivers.

articles.title: Reporting of commercial involvement and the direction of stated conclusions in the neuromodulation-for-pain literature: a meta-research study of 896 publications.
Robotic Ileocecal Resection for Crohn's Disease Using Hugo RAS System.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Robotic-assisted ileocecal resection using the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) system represents a novel alternative to conventional laparoscopic surgery for the management of Crohn's disease (CD). This study aimed to assess its feasibility, safety, and perioperative outcomes.
METHODS: A retrospective case series including 7 consecutive patients with CD who underwent fully robotic-assisted ileocecal resection using the Hugo RAS system was conducted after multidisciplinary team discussion. Demographic, clinical, and perioperative data were collected, including operative time, estimated blood loss, conversion rates, intraoperative and postoperative complications, length of hospital stay, and short-term postoperative outcomes. A narrative review of the literature on robotic-assisted ileocecal resection for CD was also performed.
RESULTS: Between December 2024 and January 2026, 7 consecutive patients with CD (mean age 45 years) and no previous intestinal resections underwent fully robotic-assisted ileocecal resection using the Hugo RAS system. Disease was limited to the terminal ileum in all cases, with a fistulizing phenotype in 2 patients. The median operative time was 235 minutes. No conversions to laparoscopic or open surgery, intraoperative complications, or blood transfusions were observed. Two postoperative complications occurred, with no hospital readmissions or mortality. After a mean follow-up of 11 months, endoscopic recurrence occurred in two patients (28.6%), whereas no clinical recurrence was observed.
CONCLUSIONS: Fully robotic ileocecal resection using the Hugo RAS system appears feasible and is associated with favorable short-term perioperative outcomes in this initial series. Further studies with larger cohorts and longer follow-up are needed to validate these findings and determine its long-term role.

articles.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder is associated with higher rates of healthcare utilization but similar clinical outcomes after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is increasingly recognized as a factor that may impact surgical recovery. Currently, its effect on outcomes following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) remains unclear. This study investigates whether a preoperative diagnosis of PTSD is associated with increased postoperative healthcare utilization.
METHODS: A retrospective, multi-institutional cohort study was performed using a large electronic medical record database. Patients undergoing primary, single-level ACDF were identified and stratified by the presence of PTSD diagnosis before surgery. Propensity score matching was performed in a 1:1 ratio using over 300 demographic and clinical variables. Outcomes were assessed at 30 days, 90 days, and two years postoperatively.
RESULTS: A total of 3774 patients were included after matching, with equal distribution between cohorts. Patients with PTSD had increased opioid utilization at both 30 days (OR: 1.4, 95% CI: 1.2-1.7; P<0.001) and 90 days (OR: 1.5, 95% CI: 1.2-1.8; P < 0.001), as well as higher rates of emergency department visits at 90 days (OR: 1.2, 95% CI: 1.0-1.5; P = 0.020). No significant differences were observed in long-term complications, including adjacent segment disease or reoperation rates at two years.
CONCLUSION: Preoperative PTSD diagnosis is associated with increased short-term healthcare utilization following ACDF but does not seem to impact long-term surgical outcomes. These findings support the need for targeted perioperative management strategies in this patient population.

articles.title: First Experience With a New Active Bone Conduction Device in Pediatric Patients.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this retrospective analysis was to evaluate the feasibility, surgical safety, and early audiological benefit of the new active transcutaneous bone conduction implant Sentio in pediatric patients.
DESIGN: Retrospective case series.
STUDY SAMPLE: Seven children (8 ears), aged 3.6 to 9.7 years, underwent implantation of a Sentio system between December 2024 and March 2025 for congenital aural atresia (6 ears) or single-sided deafness due to cochlear nerve aplasia (2 ears).
RESULTS: All surgeries were completed successfully using the Sentio Ti Implant. Limited exposure of the dura, sigmoid sinus, and/or mastoid air cells occurred during bone-bed preparation, but there was no laceration, bleeding, cerebrospinal fluid leak, compression, or clinical sequela. No perioperative or postoperative adverse events occurred through initial fitting. Bone conduction thresholds remained stable postoperatively, confirming preservation of cochlear reserve. Mean Sentio-aided free-field thresholds were 22.5, 20.0, 18.6, and 18.6 dB HL at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz, respectively. Word recognition scores at initial fitting averaged 96.3% in all patients (range: 85-100%) at a conversational level of 65 dB SPL. The relatively flat transducer and flexible band fixation facilitated safe implantation in young children with thin cranial bone.
CONCLUSION: Sentio Ti implantation was technically feasible in this selected cohort, with no clinical adverse events through initial fitting and favorable early aided outcomes. Larger prospective studies with standardized testing and longer follow-up are required to assess long-term safety, skull growth, implant stability, MRI-related limitations, and sustained benefit.

articles.title: Perioperative Management of Coexisting Mast Cell Activation Syndrome and Malignant Hyperthermia Susceptibility: A Case Report and Novel Approach to Local Analgesia.
articles.abstract: The coexistence of mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) and malignant hyperthermia (MH) presents a significant perioperative challenge due to combined risks of anaphylaxis and anaesthesia-related hypermetabolic crisis. We describe the successful anaesthetic management of a man in his 60 s with confirmed MCAS and a strong family history of MH who underwent excision of multiple malignant cutaneous lesions. A structured perioperative strategy incorporating immunological optimisation with omalizumab, strict trigger avoidance, dexmedetomidine and remifentanil procedural sedation, prophylactic corticosteroids and a controlled low-dose adrenaline infusion enabled safe completion of surgery without complication. In the absence of tolerated local anaesthetic agents, dilute adrenaline infiltration was used as an adjunct to improve procedural tolerability. This case highlights the importance of multidisciplinary planning and individualised perioperative strategy in patients with high-risk perioperative profiles.

articles.title: Anticoagulant Prophylaxis with Edoxaban for Asymptomatic Isolated Distal Deep Vein Thrombosis in Perioperative Hip Fracture Patients.
articles.abstract: Most distal deep vein thrombosis (DVT) presents a low risk of central progression and pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE), and uniform anticoagulation is not recommended. However, the perioperative period of hip fracture (HF) is associated with a high risk of DVT progression, but a therapeutic dose of anticoagulation raises concern about bleeding risk. There is no clear recommendation for anticoagulation for asymptomatic distal DVT during the perioperative period of HF. We retrospectively evaluated the appropriateness of general anticoagulant prophylaxis with edoxaban. From April 2017 to September 2022, among patients who underwent HF surgery at our hospital, 74 consecutive cases who were diagnosed with asymptomatic distal DVT were examined. Of the 52 cases receiving anticoagulant prophylaxis with edoxaban, 23 received the prophylactic standard dose (30 mg), and 29 received the prophylactic lower dose (15 mg). The duration of anticoagulation ranged from 5 to 28 days, with a median of 14 days. There were no recurrences of symptomatic venous thromboembolism (VTE) within 3 months after starting anticoagulation. This study suggests that a general perioperative prophylactic dose, rather than a therapeutic dose, can effectively suppress symptomatic VTE and enhance safety in patients with asymptomatic distal DVT developed during the perioperative period of HF. (This is a translation of Jpn J Phlebol 2025; 36: 33-38.).

articles.title: Clinical Impact of Prognostic Immune and Nutritional Index on Short- and Long-term Outcomes of Older Patients with Colorectal Cancer.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Although the prognostic immune and nutritional index (PINI) has attracted increasing attention as a prognostic marker for various cancers, its clinical significance in older patients has not been fully clarified. This retrospective single-center study aimed to investigate the association among PINI, long-term prognosis, and postoperative complications in older patients with colorectal cancer (CRC).
METHODS: We analyzed 181 patients aged ≥75 years with pathological stage I-III CRC who underwent curative surgery at our institution between 2015 and 2023.
RESULTS: Overall survival (OS) (p < 0.001) and cancer-specific survival (CSS) (p < 0.001) rates in patients with low PINI were significantly worse than those in their counterparts. Low PINI was an independent prognostic factor for OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 5.22, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.45-11.1, p < 0.001) and CSS (HR = 2.94, 95% CI: 1.03-8.36, p = 0.042). Moreover, low PINI was an independent risk factor for postoperative complications (odds ratio = 2.90, 95% CI: 1.10-7.82, p = 0.030). Additionally, patients with low PINI had a significantly higher recurrence rate for locoregional metastasis than those with high PINI (2.79% vs. 22.6%, p < 0.001); no significant differences were observed in the recurrence rates for other patterns.
CONCLUSIONS: Low PINI was an independent risk factor for postoperative complications and poor prognosis in older patients with CRC. Preoperative inflammatory and immunonutritional assessments using the PINI may contribute to comprehensive risk stratification and individualized perioperative management in this vulnerable population.

articles.title: Quadratus Lumborum versus Transversus Abdominis Plane Block with Oxycodone or Sufentanil for Recovery Quality After Laparoscopic Gastrointestinal Cancer Surgery: A Factorial Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Quadratus lumborum block (QLB) theoretically provides broader visceral analgesia than transversus abdominis plane block (TAPB), while oxycodone, a dual μ- and κ-opioid receptor agonist, may offer superior visceral pain control compared with sufentanil. We evaluated these two regional techniques and two opioid regimens simultaneously in a factorial design to determine their effects on recovery after laparoscopic gastrointestinal cancer surgery.
METHODS: In this single-center, randomized, 2×2 factorial trial, 120 adults were randomly assigned to bilateral QLB or TAPB (0.375% ropivacaine 20 mL per side) and oxycodone or sufentanil patient-controlled analgesia. All patients received intraoperative dexmedetomidine and flurbiprofen axetil. The primary outcome was 24-h recovery quality (15-item quality of recovery scale; minimal clinically important difference 6 points). Secondary outcomes included recovery quality at 48 and 72 h, visceral and incisional pain, opioid consumption, rescue analgesia, and adverse events.
RESULTS: For 24-h recovery quality, no significant interaction was found between block and opioid (P = 0.283); QLB vs TAPB (mean [SD] 102.1 [7.9] vs 102.6 [7.6]; mean difference -0.5, 95% CI -3.3 to 2.4; P = 0.740) and oxycodone vs sufentanil (103.7 [6.9] vs 100.9 [8.3]; mean difference 2.8, 95% CI 0.1 to 5.6; P = 0.045) did not reach the Bonferroni-corrected threshold (P < 0.025) or the 6-point difference. Oxycodone was associated with lower visceral pain scores at 1, 6, 24 and 48 h, lower incisional pain scores at 1 and 6 h, and decreased rescue analgesia use (13.3% vs 29.3%). Other outcomes were comparable.
CONCLUSION: Within comprehensive multimodal analgesia, neither QLB nor oxycodone demonstrated superior recovery compared with TAPB or sufentanil. Exploratory findings of lower postoperative pain and less rescue analgesia with oxycodone should be considered hypothesis-generating.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2400080766).

articles.title: Opioid-Free versus Opioid-Based Anesthesia for Quality of Recovery After Knee Arthroscopy: A Randomized Non-Inferiority Trial.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: We determined whether dexmedetomidine- and esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) was non-inferior to opioid-based anesthesia (OA) for 24-hour Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) after elective knee arthroscopy with femoral nerve block.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: In this patient- and assessor-blinded randomized trial, 70 adults undergoing knee arthroscopy with femoral nerve block were allocated to OFA or OA. The primary outcome was 24-hour QoR-15 (non-inferiority margin, -6 points). Secondary outcomes included pain, rescue analgesia, and adverse events. The primary modified intention-to-treat (mITT) analysis included 66 randomized participants with an assessable 24-hour QoR-15 score (33 per group).
RESULTS: Mean 24-hour QoR-15 scores were 126.7 ± 6.4 with OFA and 125.3 ± 6.1 with OA (mean difference 1.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.60 to 4.51), establishing non-inferiority but not superiority. OFA increased rescue opioid requirements (Hodges-Lehmann estimate 10 mg oral morphine equivalents, 95% CI 0 to 10; p=0.037), shortened time to rescue analgesia (hazard ratio 2.11, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.92; p=0.018), and increased early pain. OFA reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting (21.2% vs 48.5%; relative risk 0.44, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.92; p=0.038). Two postoperative bradycardia events occurred with OFA.
CONCLUSION: In adults undergoing elective knee arthroscopy with femoral nerve block, dexmedetomidine- and esketamine-based OFA was non-inferior to OA for 24-hour QoR-15. OFA was associated with lower postoperative nausea and vomiting, but higher early pain and an earlier need for rescue analgesia.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2400084207; registered 13 May 2024, before enrollment. URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=230255.

articles.title: Post-cardiopulmonary bypass colloid osmotic pressure and creatinine-defined acute kidney injury in infants undergoing cardiac surgery: an age-modified association.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is common after infant cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Colloid osmotic pressure (COP) changes during CPB in response to hemodilution, albumin administration, ultrafiltration, and hemoconcentration, but its association with postoperative AKI in infants remains incompletely defined. Because renal physiology matures rapidly during the first year of life, the clinical meaning of COP may also vary across infancy.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 230 infants aged ≤12 months and weighing ≤10 kg who underwent cardiac surgery with CPB between May 2020 and September 2022. The primary exposure was COP measured immediately after CPB, and the primary outcome was creatinine-defined postoperative AKI based on KDIGO thresholds within a prespecified 48-hour postoperative window. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the covariate-adjusted association between post-CPB COP and AKI. Restricted cubic splines assessed dose-response form, and a generalized additive model (GAM) with a tensor-product smooth of COP and age was used to explore age-related heterogeneity. Time-specific analyses additionally evaluated pre-CPB, intra-CPB, and post-CPB COP.
RESULTS: AKI occurred in 57 infants (24.8%). After adjustment for covariates, for every 1 mmHg increase in post-CPB COP, the risk of AKI increased by 16% (OR = 1.16; 95% CI: 1.04-1.28; P = 0.004). The dose-response relationship was broadly linear. The GAM curve combining age and COP suggested age-related heterogeneity (P = 0.022); in an exploratory age-stratified analysis, the estimated odds ratio was highest in the group of infants aged 10-12 months (OR per 1 mmHg increase: 1.79; 95% CI: 1.09-3.64; P = 0.048); however, due to the small number of events in this subgroup, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory. There was no significant association between pre-CPB or during-CPB COP and AKI, whereas post-CPB COP exhibited the strongest time-specific signal. Incorporating COP into the clinical model resulted in only a slight, non-statistically significant improvement in discrimination performance (AUC: 0.701 vs. 0.723; P = 0.324); no significant improvement was observed in NRI, and the overall net benefit was minimal.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher post-CPB COP was associated with creatinine-defined AKI after infant cardiac surgery, with the clearest risk information observed at the end of CPB. COP is better interpreted as a peri-CPB physiologic risk marker that should be considered alongside age and perfusion context, rather than as an independent prediction tool or a fixed therapeutic target.

articles.title: Animation-assisted psychological intervention in pediatric care: mechanisms, clinical applications, and emerging evidence.
articles.abstract: Children frequently experience fear, anxiety, and pain during medical encounters, and this distress can lead to poor cooperation, longer procedures, and lasting avoidance of care. Animation, delivered as cartoons, preparation films, applications, serious games, and virtual reality (VR) scenes, has become one of the most widely deployed non-pharmacological adjuncts in pediatric settings because it is inexpensive, non-invasive, and easily standardized. Drawing on a structured search of six databases through July 2026, this mini-review synthesizes randomized and meta-analytic evidence across perioperative anxiety, procedural pain, pediatric dentistry, chronic-disease self-management, and mental health promotion. It organizes the evidence around five psychological pathways: attentional competition, observational learning, exposure and inhibitory learning, narrative-affective processing, and self-efficacy. Additionally, it examines a sixth, non-psychological use in which animation is used to provide therapeutic visual stimulation. Evidence supports moderate short-term benefits for anticipatory anxiety and for needle- and dentistry-related distress, with weaker and less consistent effects for high-intensity procedures and physiological outcomes. We argue that the field's core issue is conceptual rather than empirical: animation refers to a delivery medium, not a treatment, and trials have compared media rather than mechanisms. This obscures three unresolved problems: discordance between self-reported and autonomic outcomes; an untheorized moderating role of the developmental stage; and a theoretical tension between distraction, which withdraws attention from the feared stimulus, and exposure, which requires engagement with it. Mechanism-matched comparators, core outcome sets, developmentally stratified designs, transparent intervention reporting, and follow-up across repeated procedures are prerequisites for cumulative progress.

articles.title: Totally single-incision laparoscopic choledochal cyst excision with intracorporeal hand-sewn Roux-en-Y reconstruction in children: clinical outcomes and learning curve.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility, perioperative outcomes, and learning curve of totally single-incision laparoscopic choledochal cyst excision with intracorporeal hand-sewn Roux-en-Y reconstruction in children.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed children who underwent laparoscopic choledochal cyst excision between January 2018 and December 2024. Thirty-five children underwent totally single-incision laparoscopic intracorporeal hand-sewn reconstruction (TSILC), and 40 underwent conventional single-incision laparoscopic-assisted reconstruction (SILC). Baseline characteristics, operative outcomes, recovery, complications, and follow-up were compared. Multivariable linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors was used to adjust continuous outcomes for baseline differences. The TSILC learning curve was assessed using cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis of jejunojejunostomy time.
RESULTS: TSILC patients were older (29.86 ± 12.99 vs. 19.60 ± 13.62 months, P = 0.001), heavier (14.90 ± 5.07 vs. 9.22 ± 4.40 kg, P < 0.001), and had a different sex distribution (P = 0.030). After adjustment, total operative time did not differ significantly (adjusted β=8.75 min, 95% CI -12.10 to 29.60; P = 0.411), whereas jejunojejunostomy time remained longer with TSILC (adjusted β=12.02 min, 95% CI 3.02 to 21.02; P = 0.009). TSILC was associated with less blood loss, a shorter incision, and earlier first flatus and defecation (all adjusted P < 0.001); oral intake time did not differ significantly after adjustment (P = 0.568). Early complications occurred in 3/35 TSILC and 5/40 SILC patients. Thirty-three TSILC procedures were completed without an additional port or open conversion; one required an additional port and one required open conversion. Median follow-up was 40.0 months (IQR 21.5-59.5) for TSILC and 46.5 months (IQR 27.2-66.2) for SILC. The CUSUM curve peaked at case 17, suggesting relative stabilization after case 18.
CONCLUSION: TSILC with intracorporeal hand-sewn Roux-en-Y reconstruction was technically feasible in selected children and showed a measurable learning curve. The findings suggest that TSILC may offer perioperative advantages in appropriately selected older and larger children.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine-containing patient-controlled intravenous analgesia after elective caesarean delivery: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dexmedetomidine is used as an adjunct in multimodal postoperative analgesia, but evidence from routine clinical care after caesarean delivery remains limited. We evaluated whether dexmedetomidine-containing patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) was associated with postoperative analgesic and early recovery outcomes.
METHODS: This single-centre retrospective cohort study included women aged 18-45 years undergoing elective term caesarean delivery between January and September 2025. Women were classified according to the initial postoperative PCIA regimen as receiving dexmedetomidine-containing or conventional PCIA. The primary outcome was movement pain on a 0-10 numerical rating scale at 24 h. Secondary outcomes included pain through 48 h, sufentanil delivery, patient-controlled analgesia demands, rescue analgesia, treatment-related events, and early recovery milestones. Propensity-score overlap weighting was used for the primary analysis. Propensity-score matching, conventional multivariable adjustment, complete-case and restricted-cohort analyses, and an expanded propensity-score model incorporating attending anaesthesiologist and calendar month were used to assess robustness.
RESULTS: Among 304 eligible women, 132 received dexmedetomidine-containing PCIA and 172 received conventional PCIA. Mean movement pain at 24 h was 3.1 (SD 1.2) versus 3.7 (SD 1.3), corresponding to an overlap-weighted mean difference of -0.51 points (95% CI -0.80 to -0.22; P < 0.001). The primary estimate was similar across sensitivity analyses, including the expanded propensity-score model incorporating attending anaesthesiologist and calendar month. Among 290 women with complete 48-h pump records, median cumulative sufentanil delivery was 84 μg (IQR 78-91) versus 90 μg (82-98; median difference -5.2 μg, 95% CI -7.8 to -2.6; P < 0.001). Rescue analgesia was required in 24 of 132 women (18.2%) versus 46 of 172 (26.7%; risk ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-0.99; P = 0.044). First mobilisation occurred at 16.9 versus 19.3 h (time ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.84-0.95; P < 0.001), and first passage of flatus at 25.8 versus 28.9 h (time ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.98; P = 0.012). Estimates for uncommon adverse events were imprecise.
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, dexmedetomidine-containing PCIA was associated with modestly lower early movement pain and lower analgesic requirements, with shorter observed times to selected early recovery milestones. Estimates for uncommon adverse events did not establish safety equivalence. These observational findings should not be interpreted as establishing a causal treatment effect.

articles.title: A European algorithm and strategy for management of chronic postoperative inguinal pain (EurA-CPIP).
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic postoperative inguinal pain (CPIP) is a disabling complication affecting 8%-17% of all patients after inguinal hernia repair. It is a complex pain condition with several pathophysiological mechanisms involved, including neuropathic pain, inflammation, and mechanical effects (e.g., mesh or scar tissue). Management remains inconsistent, probably due to limited high-quality evidence, heterogeneous approach, and insufficient standardisation of outcomes. This study aimed to develop EurA-CPIP, a multidisciplinary treatment algorithm and prospective data-collection platform designed to support consistent phenotyping, step-up management, and standardised outcomes across centres, creating an iterative platform for future hypothesis-driven research and multicentre trials.
METHODS: An international multidisciplinary working group from European tertiary referral centres developed the European Algorithm and Strategy for Management of Chronic Postoperative Inguinal Pain (EurA-CPIP). Development was informed by the evidence synthesis underpinning the updated international HerniaSurge guidelines and a critical appraisal of previously published CPIP algorithms. A pragmatic step-up algorithm was designed, integrating pharmacological, interventional, surgical and supportive treatments, with prospective outcome registration and planned data-driven revision on a regular basis.
RESULTS: EurA-CPIP provides a multidisciplinary algorithm with entry at multiple levels depending on prior treatment attempts. The concept is to begin and, if needed, advance from conservative measures such as systemic medication and topical therapy, to more invasive treatments such as trigger point injections, and ultrasound-guided nerve blocks; predefined investigational add-ons (radiofrequency, cryoneurolysis, botulinum toxin A) are embedded after documented block response. Multidisciplinary team review precedes escalation to more invasive interventions such as surgery. A supportive and rehabilitative coping trajectory is integrated early on. Standardised outcomes include patient-reported pain outcomes, functional impairment, psychological factors, analgesic use, and patient global impression of improvement.
CONCLUSION: EurA-CPIP is a pragmatic consensus-based strategy intended to harmonise and improve specialised CPIP care while utilising existing and developing emerging therapies. Future research should investigate pathophysiology and intervention effects within this step-up algorithm.

articles.title: The impact of perioperative adverse events on kidney transplant surgeons: a mixed-methods study.
articles.abstract:
AIM: Adverse events (AEs) are an inevitable part of every surgeon's career. There is currently no evidence regarding the impact of perioperative AEs on transplant surgeons. This study aims to evaluate the impact of perioperative AEs on kidney transplant surgeons, exploring the emotional, professional and personal consequences when they occur.
METHOD: A mixed-methods exploratory sequential design was used. Purposive sampling was completed to recruit 15 consultant kidney transplant surgeons to be interviewed about an AE that they had experienced. Individual, semi-structured qualitative interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed. Alongside this, participants completed two personality questionnaires: the Big Five Inventory and the DOSPERT attitude to risk questionnaire. Integration of the two data sets occurred during the analysis stage.
RESULTS: Four main themes with relevant subthemes were identified: (1) AEs have a psychological impact; (2) the surgical environment influences response; (3) changes in practice following an AE; (4) the influence of personality on response. Triangulation of findings displayed how external factors such as personality, severity of the AE, seniority and the family's reaction can all influence how AEs are processed.
CONCLUSION: This study highlights the psychological and professional impact of perioperative AEs on kidney transplant surgeons. Findings suggest team dynamics, coping strategies and identity shape responses. Further research is needed to inform future support services that are currently not routinely relied upon by transplant surgeons.

articles.title: Function-preserving plasma kinetic enucleation of the prostate with bladder neck and 12 o'clock urethral mucosal preservation for large-volume benign prostatic hyperplasia: a single-center retrospective case series.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Large-volume benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) poses a significant surgical challenge, as conventional transurethral resection yields suboptimal tissue removal efficiency and high rates of ejaculatory dysfunction. While endoscopic enucleation techniques (e.g., HoLEP and PKEP) offer improved efficacy, the systematic preservation of functional anatomical structures - particularly the bladder neck and anterior urethral mucosa - remains inadequately addressed in current practice.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, efficacy, and functional outcomes of function-preserving plasma kinetic enucleation of the prostate (FP-PKEP) - a modified technique incorporating systematic preservation of the bladder neck circular fibers and the 12 o'clock urethral mucosal strip - in patients with large-volume BPH.
METHODS: This single-center, retrospective case series included 52 consecutive patients with large-volume BPH (prostate volume >80 mL, International Prostate Symptom Score [IPSS] > 20, maximum urinary flow rate [Qmax] < 10 mL/s) who underwent FP-PKEP between January 2025 and December 2025. The primary outcome was the change in IPSS at 3 months postoperatively; secondary outcomes included Qmax, post-void residual urine volume (PVR), quality of life (QoL) score, perioperative safety parameters, and functional preservation outcomes (urinary continence and ejaculatory function at 6 months).
RESULTS: All 52 patients (mean age 67.8 ± 7.2 years; mean prostate volume 93.7 ± 15.2 mL) successfully underwent FP-PKEP without conversion. Mean operative time was 72.5 ± 15.8 min; postoperative hemoglobin decrease was 9.8 ± 4.2 g/L; catheterization duration was 2.8 ± 0.9 days; and hospital stay was 4.2 ± 1.3 days. At 3 months, IPSS decreased from 26.1 ± 3.0 to 6.8 ± 2.6 (P < 0.001), and Qmax increased from 7.2 ± 1.6 to 21.2 ± 4.5 mL/s (P < 0.001). Transient stress urinary incontinence occurred in 4 patients (7.7%), all requiring no more than one pad per day and resolving within 1 month without surgical intervention. Among the 16 patients who were sexually active before surgery, antegrade ejaculation was preserved in 14 (87.5%) and suspected retrograde ejaculation was recorded in 2 (12.5%). No clinically apparent cases of permanent urinary incontinence, bladder neck contracture, or urethral stricture were observed during the 6-month follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: In this uncontrolled case series, FP-PKEP showed a favorable safety profile and achieved significant relief of bladder outlet obstruction, with promising early urinary continence and ejaculatory outcomes. The systematic preservation of the bladder neck and 12 o'clock urethral mucosa warrants further evaluation in prospective randomized controlled trials, as these preliminary findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Outcomes following elderly femoral shaft fractures: A GOLD-FEM (geriatric outcomes and long-term data on FEMoral fractures) multicenter study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Elderly femoral shaft fractures present unique challenges due to physiologic vulnerability and medical comorbidity, yet the perioperative outcomes associated with these injuries remain poorly defined.
METHODS: A multicenter retrospective study of patients 60-90 years with an isolated, operatively managed femoral shaft fracture was completed. Pathologic, intra-articular, and peri-implant fractures were excluded. Perioperative outcomes, medical and surgical complications, and mortality were analyzed.
RESULTS: 432 patients averaging 73.7 years old met inclusion criteria. 74% were female and 85% had a low-energy mechanism. Fixation consisted of intramedullary nail (91%), plate (3%), or combined nail-plate constructs (6%). Two-thirds of the cohort experienced at least one complication, and the reoperation rate was 23.2%. At final follow-up (mean 24 weeks), the mortality rate was 18.2%, and 16% had not achieved radiographic union.
CONCLUSION: Geriatric femoral shaft fractures, even in isolation, carry high morbidity and mortality. Patient counseling and perioperative management should acknowledge these risks.
authors: Investigation performed by the GOLD-FEM team

articles.title: Fluoroscopy-Free Esophageal Temperature Probe Positioning During Hybrid Atrial Fibrillation Ablation.
Safety of Methadone in Older Adults Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Remimazolam Versus Propofol for Anesthesia Induction and Maintenance in Adult Cardiac Surgical Patients: A PRISMA-Compliant Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare remimazolam-based with propofol-based anesthesia for induction and maintenance in adult cardiac surgery.
DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
SETTING: Cardiovascular centers.
PARTICIPANTS: Adults undergoing cardiac surgery.
INTERVENTIONS: Remimazolam-based versus propofol-based general anesthesia for induction and maintenance.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Fourteen reports describing randomized trials, including three theses, contributed 1,773 reported participants to the primary synthesis. All were conducted in China, and no key pooled result was supported exclusively by results at low risk of bias. One terminated European registry-results trial (23 treated patients) was included as supplementary sensitivity evidence. Data on major postoperative morbidity and mortality were too sparse to pool. Remimazolam was associated with fewer trial-defined intraoperative hypotension events (odds ratio [OR], 0.31; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.20-0.47; p < 0.001; I² = 0%) and fewer bradycardia events (OR, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.12-0.34; p < 0.001; I² = 0%). It was also associated with shorter mechanical ventilation duration (mean difference [MD], -1.84 hours; 95% CI, -2.34 to -1.35 hours; p < 0.001; I² = 71%). Hospital length of stay crossed the line of no effect (MD, -0.48 days; 95% CI, -0.99 to 0.02 days; p = 0.06; I² = 37%). Certainty of evidence was very low for the hemodynamic and mechanical ventilation findings.
CONCLUSIONS: Across the cardiac surgical populations represented in the included trials, remimazolam was associated with fewer trial-defined intraoperative hypotension and bradycardia events and shorter mechanical ventilation duration. The certainty of evidence for these associations was very low. The evidence does not establish improved major morbidity or mortality. Future multicenter confirmation is required.

articles.title: Pulmonary Artery to Aorta Ratio Adds Predictive Value to Index for Mortality Prediction After Cardiac Transplantation (IMPACT) Score for Prolonged Inotropic Support After Heart Transplantation.
Immediate Post-Bypass Thromboelastography and Concordance With Transfusion Practice in Cardiac Surgery: A Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the concordance between immediate post-cardiopulmonary bypass thromboelastography (TEG) findings and intraoperative transfusion practice in adult cardiac surgery.
DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational study.
SETTING: Tertiary academic hospital.
PARTICIPANTS: Adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass who had immediate post-bypass TEG performed in the operating theater.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Manufacturer-derived TEG thresholds for fresh frozen plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, and procoagulant therapy were compared with observed intraoperative transfusion practice. Among 207 patients, thresholds were met in 56% for fresh frozen plasma, 20% for platelets, 17% for cryoprecipitate, and 16% for procoagulants. Intraoperative transfusion rates were higher for platelets, cryoprecipitate, and procoagulants, particularly in complex surgery, whereas fresh frozen plasma transfusion was lower than the threshold-based proportion. Among patients meeting thresholds but not receiving transfusions intraoperatively, fewer than 15% required the corresponding product within 24 hours. Postoperative chest tube output was broadly similar across TEG-transfusion patterns, with no clear association between TEG concordance and early postoperative bleeding.
CONCLUSIONS: Substantial discordance existed between manufacturer-derived post-bypass TEG thresholds and intraoperative transfusion practice. Transfusion appeared to reflect surgical complexity more closely than measured coagulation abnormalities.

articles.title: Serum Beta-Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (β-hCG) Trends and Their Association With Abdominal Wound Healing After Cesarean Section: An Observational Study.
articles.abstract: Background and objective Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) is an established biomarker in pregnancy assessment and in the management of trophoblastic and germ cell disorders. Beyond its classical endocrine role, β-hCG has biological relevance to inflammation, angiogenesis, endothelial function, immune regulation, and tissue remodeling, all of which are central to wound repair. The relationship between postoperative β-hCG decline and abdominal wound healing after cesarean section remains insufficiently characterized. The objective of this study was to evaluate the association between serial postoperative serum β-hCG trends and abdominal wound healing following cesarean section. Methods This hospital-based observational analytical study included 436 women undergoing elective or emergency lower-segment cesarean section. Baseline demographic, obstetric, and perioperative variables were recorded. Serum β-hCG levels were measured preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, and on postoperative days (PODs) 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 14, and 21. Post-cesarean abdominal wound outcomes were clinically assessed and categorized as healthy or unhealthy. Comparative analysis and receiver operating characteristic curve analysis were performed. Results Mean β-hCG declined from 15,881.99 IU/L preoperatively to 143.13 IU/L on POD 21. Preoperative and immediate postoperative β-hCG levels did not differ significantly between wound groups. From POD 2 onward, women with unhealthy wounds had significantly higher β-hCG levels than those with healthy wounds (p < 0.001). POD 7 β-hCG showed excellent discrimination, with an area under the curve of 0.901. A cutoff of 1884 IU/L yielded 82.6% sensitivity and 81.2% specificity. Conclusions Slower postoperative β-hCG decline was associated with impaired abdominal wound healing after cesarean section. POD 7 β-hCG may serve as an adjunctive biomarker for early risk stratification.

articles.title: Comparing General Anaesthesia With Spinal Anaesthesia for Holmium Laser Enucleation of Prostate: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) is an established surgical treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Although it is conventionally performed under general anaesthesia (GA), spinal anaesthesia (SA) may represent an important alternative for patients with significant medical comorbidity. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing peri-operative outcomes of HoLEP performed under GA versus SA. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A comprehensive search of electronic databases was performed (MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE and Google Scholar) for comparative studies evaluating GA versus SA for HoLEP. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed using mean difference (MD) or odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A search of electronic databases found four studies, enrolling a total of 2323 patients. SA was associated with a significantly shorter operative time than GA (P=0.03), although this finding was not robust on leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. There were no significant differences in resected tissue weight (P=0.73), Hb drop (P=0.07), post-operative catheter reinsertion (P=0.34), Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications (P=0.14), change in IPSS (P=0.91), change in QMax (P=0.60), or change in PVR (P=1.00). Moderate to high heterogeneity was observed for several outcomes, and the available evidence was limited to retrospective and propensity-matched studies. Current evidence suggests that spinal anaesthesia could be a safe and effective alternative to general anaesthesia for HoLEP, with comparable intra- and post-operative outcomes. SA may expand access to HoLEP for patients at increased risk from GA. However, the available evidence remains limited, and high-quality prospective randomised studies are required to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Characteristics and Outcomes After General Anaesthesia in Elderly Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elderly patients are more frail and have a higher burden of comorbidity, which could influence the risk of complications after anaesthesia. The aim of this study was to describe the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark.
METHODS: This was a national registry-based observational cohort study of adult patients (≥ 18 years) undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark in 2020 and 2021, with a primary focus on patients 80 years and above. Patient and procedure characteristics of interest were age, sex, BMI, ASA classification, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, comorbidities, type of procedure, and class of priority. The primary outcome of interest was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury within 7 days, length of hospital stay, and number of days in the ICU.
RESULTS: A total of 453,133 cases of general anaesthesia in 328,951 unique patients in Denmark during 2020 and 2021 were included in this study. Of these, 25,955 (8%) patients were 80 years of age and above. Elderly patients undergoing general anaesthesia were of higher ASA classification, suffered from a higher degree of comorbidity measured by Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, had a lower proportion of elective procedures and a higher proportion of expedited and urgent procedures. Mortality for all patients at 30 days was 1.5% (n = 4814). While mortality was low for cases aged between 18 and 65 years, 30-day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates. Mortality was especially high for patients with high Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, high ASA classification, and for non-elective procedures.
CONCLUSION: In this nationwide registry-based cohort study, we described the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark. We found that 30-day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates.
EDITORIAL COMMENT: This large cohort study from Denmark assesses perioperative case factors including age, comorbidity and more, then describing different risk levels for 30 day mortality, particularly with advanced age.

articles.title: The Effect of Using Heated IV Fluids With Underbody Warmers on Maternal and Neonatal Well-Being in Cesarean Delivery Operations: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of underbody warming and heated IV fluids on maternal and neonatal outcomes during cesarean delivery. In a university hospital, 105 pregnant patients were randomized into three groups that dictated heating methods applied during their cesarean delivery: underbody warmer only, underbody warmer plus heated IV fluids, or passive heating with blankets. Primary outcomes were maternal and neonatal body temperatures. Secondary maternal outcomes included intraoperative blood loss, analgesic use, and time to first gas and urination. Secondary neonatal outcomes included cord blood cortisol levels, glucose levels, and Apgar scores. Neonatal temperature, Apgar scores, and maternal intraoperative temperature were significantly higher in the intervention groups. Active warming was associated with lower cortisol levels, reduced analgesic use, and faster recovery. In total, active warming improved maternal recovery and neonatal adaptation, and its routine use as a simple, safe, and effective strategy to enhance perioperative outcomes may be warranted.

articles.title: Reply: Serratus Anterior Plane Block with Methylene Blue and Ropivacaine for Analgesia in Prosthetic Breast Augmentation: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

Clinical Outcomes of Fascia Iliaca Compartment Block Combined With Two Different Patient-Controlled Analgesia Regimens for Hip Arthroplasty: A Propensity Score-Matched Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The objective of our study was to retrospectively evaluate the analgesic efficacy, safety, and postoperative recovery of fascia iliaca compartment block combined with patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (FICB + PCIA) versus patient-controlled continuous nerve block analgesia (FICB + PCNB) in patients undergoing hip arthroplasty.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective observational study was based on routinely collected clinical data. A total of 136 patients (68 per group) were selected via stratified random sampling from 1,500 eligible patients who underwent unilateral hip arthroplasty. A 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (PSM) was performed with multiple clinical covariates to balance baseline characteristics. Standardized mean difference (SMD) was used to evaluate baseline balance after matching, with an SMD less than 0.1 defined as good balance. The primary end point was postoperative resting visual analog scale (VAS) scores at six, 12, 24, 48, and 72 hours. The secondary end points included 72-hour adverse events, analgesic consumption, lengths of hospital stay, and postoperative complications.
RESULTS: All SMDs of baseline covariates were below 0.1 after matching, with no intergroup differences. The VAS scores decreased significantly over time in both groups (Ftime = 22.846, P < 0.001). The FICB + PCNB group had lower overall resting VAS scores (Fgroup = 4.974, P = 0.026), with no significant time-group interaction (Finteraction = 1.728, P = 0.142). The total 72-hour adverse reaction rate was 10.29% in both groups. Opioid consumption was significantly lower in the FICB + PCNB group (P < 0.001). The duration of analgesic pump use, length of hospital stay, and complication rates were comparable between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: The FICB + PCNB provides superior postoperative analgesia and reduces opioid consumption without increasing risks of adverse reactions or complications. It aligns with enhanced recovery after surgery principles and has favorable clinical application value.

articles.title: Minimally invasive versus open liver resection for hepatocellular carcinoma in older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUNDS/AIMS: As the population ages, an increasing number of older adults are diagnosed with resectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Although minimally invasive liver resection (MILR) has shown perioperative advantages, its safety and efficacy in older patients are not fully established.
